<P>49. <B>other side A'th City</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The people had At this time retired
to the Mons Sacer, which was About three miles from the city Along the Via
Nomentana. The other side of the city would, therefore, be the part beyond the
Tiber. But in All probability Shakespeare had in his mind the topography of
London And not of Rome, And the Tower was to him the Capitol. [Is it not pass-
ing strange that Apparently Wright has inadvertently failed to recall his own
stage-direction At the beginning of this scene&mdash;&lquo;Rome: A Street&rquo;&mdash;and has changed
its locality to the Mons Sacer?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>50. <B>To th'Capitoll</B>] <SC>Bayfield</SC> (p. 184): The versification of this play, which
is not surpassed by Any other in delicacy And variety, has suffered perhaps more
than Any As it passed through the hands of those responsible for its present con-
dition. The misdivisions Are extraordinarily numerous. [Bayfield then gives
&lquo;eight out of 100 examples of <I>th'</I> before A consonant, practically All of which Are
unpronounceable without introducing the vowel which it is sought to elide. Before
a vowel we get <I>th'</I> 27 times, And before the Aspirate, which must be dropped, 7
times.&rquo; On the subject of these elisions in his <I>Introduction,</I> p. vii, he says: &lquo;Mod-
ern editors habitually Alter <I>th'</I> to <I>the, th' Art to thou'rt,</I> And (naturally not daring
to leave it) <I>y'are</I> to <I>you're,</I> retaining the rest; but this is An Arbitrary And partial
method of procedure which does not solve the problem or even touch it, And is
not justified by Any sound principle of criticism. At the same time the retention
of All the Abbreviations except <I>th'</I> indicates An imperfect recognition of what was
Shakespeare's ideal of dramatic verse&mdash;the ideal At which he was Aiming Almost
from the first, And to which in the end he Absolutely Attained in the incomparable
versification of <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> Yet Attention has Actually been drawn to &ldquo;the irreg-
ular verse of the later plays.&rdquo; The result is that the most perfect of All dramatic
verse has been systematically travestied; its native freedom is hampered As by
fetters. As left by their Author, the measures moved with the lightness And ease
and rhythmic grace of A beautiful And elaborate dance, And they made music
to the ear. Read As we must read them, they stump About As it were in clogs;
their grace is gone And the music is &ldquo;beastly dumb'd.&rdquo; Consequently, the enjoy-
ment of A play At home is marred by An irritation which grows in proportion to
the beauty of the verse that is distorted, And in the theatre the Actors Are com-
pelled to vex our ears And their own with halting measures that have no balance,
and to deliver much of the finest of All drama in A jargon that is unworthy both
of the Author And themselves. This cobbled patch work is given to us for Shake-
speare's verse As he was satisfied to leave it, And while it is proclaimed with simple
truth that he is the world's greatest poet, it has been found necessary to beg us to
make Allowances&mdash;yes, to <I>make Allowances</I> for the numerous imperfections of his
versification!&rquo;

<P>53. <B>Menenius Agrippa</B>] <SC>S. Lee</SC> (<I>Caxton Sh. Introd.,</I> p. xxxii.): Shakespeare
follows Plutarch in Assigning to Menenius &lquo;many good persuasions And gentle
requests made to the people on the behalf of the senate,&rquo; And puts in his mouth
the &lquo;notable tale&rquo; of the belly's rebellion Against the members of the human body
[<I>sic.</I> &lquo;Aliquando dormitat,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]. But Menenius disappears from Plutarch's
page As soon As he has drawn his moral from this Apologue. He retires As soon As
he has proved in parable that the senate is to the body politic what the belly is
to the human frame. Shakespeare prolongs Menenius' history to the end of the
piece. Throughout the tragedy he is A level-headed observer of events. He
criticizes their progress with ironical detachment After the manner of A chorus in
classical tragedy. His place in the dramatic scheme resembles that of Enobarbus
in <I>Antony &amp; Cleopatra,</I> And the turn of events involves him in Almost As melan-
choly A fate. He is no bitter partisan, And Although Associated with the patricians
has the reputation of loving the people. He jests As complacently At what he
conceives to be his own failings As At those which he detects in others. His iron-
ical wit sharpens the zest of his sagacious comments until the cruel catastrophe of
Coriolanus's repudiation. Then his spirit breaks And despair overwhelms him.
There is no more pathetic episode in the tragedy than Coriolanus' dismissal of
him, practically unheard, from the Volscian camp. Not the newly crowned Prince
Hal's rejection of his old Associate Falstaff inflicts A deeper wound on the reader's,
or the spectator's, heart. [For various estimates of the character of Menenius
Agrippa, see <I>Dram. Person.,</I> s. v. <I>ante.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>57-59. <B>What work's . . . I pray you</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): Notice the in-
troduction of blank verse to mark the dignity of the Patrician.

<P>given to <I>1 Cit.</I> &lquo;The second,&rquo; he adds, &lquo;is rather friendly to Coriolanus.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>:
We adhere to the original copy for the precise reason which Malone gives for

<P>60. <B>Our busines . . . to th'Senat</B>] <SC>MacCallum</SC> (524): Hardly a line in [Plu-
tarch's] description of this movement which the plebeians conducted so moderately
and sagaciously to a successful end has passed into the picture of Shakespeare.
He ignores the reasonableness of their cause, the reasonableness of their means,
and fails to perceive the essential efficiency and steadiness of their character,
though all these things are expressed or implied in Plutarch's narrative. This
episode in which the younger contemporary of Nero favours the people, the elder
contemporary of Pym summarily dismisses, and substitutes for it another far less
important, in which they appear in no very creditable light, but which had nothing
to do with the institution of the Tribunate, and occurred in consequence of the
dearth only after the capture of Corioli. &lquo;Now those busie pratlers . . . spread
abroad false tales and rumours against the Nobilitie, that they in revenge of the
people had practised and procured the extreme dearthe among them.&rquo; This
circumstance, combined with the still later demand for a distribution of corn,
Shakespeare transposes, and makes the surely rather inappropriate cause of the
appointment of the Tribunes. Inappropriate, that is, to what the logic of the
situation requires, and to what the sagacity of the traditional plebs would solicit.
They ask for bread and they get a magistrate. But not inappropriate to the
unreasoning demands of a frenzied proletariat. Many parallels might be cited from
the French revolutions. But this is just an instance of Shakespeare's inability
to conceive a popular rising in other terms than the outbreak of a mob.

<P>62, 63. <B>poore Suters . . . strong breaths</B>] A diligent search through Ray's
<I>English Proverbs;</I> Bohn's <I>Polyglot of Foreign Proverbs;</I> Lean's <I>Collectanea of Proverbs
and Folklore;</I> Heywood's <I>800 Epigrams on 800 Proverbs;</I> Florio's <I>First Frutes;</I> Florio's
<I>Second Frutes;</I> the Indices to the twelve series of <I>Notes &amp; Queries</I> has failed to
trace even a parallel to this saying put in the mouth of the <I>2 Citizen.</I> I am there-
fore reluctantly come to the conclusion that it is original with Shakespeare; I
say reluctantly, since were another example forthcoming we might be led to an
interpretation of its exact meaning better than that thus far offered.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Lex.</I>), under the meaning of &lquo;strong,&rquo; of evil odor, quotes the present line, as does
also <SC>Bradley</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>).&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>) likewise so explains this phrase, saying
that the word is here used in a double sense. Now, in spite of this formidable
array, I cannot but think that &lquo;strong&rquo; is here used only in direct opposition to
&lquo;poor.&rquo; A suitor with an evil-smelling breath would hardly be likely to com-
mend either himself or his suit; but one who realises that he has a poor, or weak
gift of oratory, would have need to have a strong, or a large amount of, breath to
carry out his argument. Schmidt cites <I>All's Well,</I> V, ii, 5: &lquo;I am now, sir, muddied
in fortune's mood, and smell somewhat strong of her strong displeasure&rquo;; but this
is merely an example of &lquo;strong&rquo; in the sense of <I>evil-smelling,</I> and is in no way par-
allel with the present line. Case quotes other passages both in this play and
<I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> wherein reference is made to the malodorous breaths of the multitude.
An ounce of civet, good apothecary!&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>74. <B>your impediment</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, the impediment you make. For

<P>82. <B>famish, and</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 95): &lquo;And&rquo; (in old Swedish <I>aen</I> is used for &lquo;and,&rquo;
&lquo;if,&rquo; and &lquo;even&rquo;) emphatically used for &lquo;also,&rquo; &lquo;even,&rquo; &lquo;and that too.&rquo; We still
use &lquo;and that&rquo; to give emphasis and call attention to an additional circumstance,
<I>e. g.,</I> &lquo;He was condemned <I>and that</I> unheard.&rquo; This construction is most common
in participial phrases. The &lquo;that&rquo; is logically unnecessary and is omitted by
Shakespeare.

<P>83-86. <B>Make Edicts . . . the poore</B>] <SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 529): Shakespeare not
only completely suppresses the remarkable secession to the Mons Sacer, but barely
mentions the social grievances that led to it. The Citizen says, indeed, of the
Patricians [ll. 83-86]; but this is a mere passing remark, and no stress is laid on
these the real causes of the discontent, in comparison with the dearth, which for
the rest seems to end with the Coriolun campaign, when there is, as Cominius
promises, a &lquo;common distribution&rquo; of the spoils. Now the dearth is represented
as a mere disastrous accident for which no one is responsible, and for which there
is no remedy save prayer&mdash;or such a foray as presently took place. Menenius
expressly says so [ll. 74-76]. It is alleged, no doubt, by the mutineers that the
&lquo;store houses are crammed with grain,&rquo; but there is no confirmation of this in the
play, and the way in which &lquo;honest&rquo; Menenius reports the rumour, and Marcius,
who is never less than honest, receives it, implies that it is mere tittle tattle and
gossip of the chimney corner.
<P>83. <B>Edicts for Vsurie</B>] Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): The grievance, accord-
ing to Plutarch, of the first insurrection, the one that took place before the siege
of Corioli, was that &lquo;the Senate did favour the rich against the people, who did
complain of the sore oppression of usurers, of whom they borrowed money. For
those that had little, were yet spoiled of that little they had by their creditors,
for lack of ability to pay the usury.&rquo; This is the basis for Shakespeare's <I>Edicts
for Usurie.</I>
<P>85. <B>piercing Statutes</B>] <SC>Rolfe</SC>: Schmidt is in doubt, whether this is = morti-
fying, revolting to the feelings, or = sweeping; entering and affecting all the
interests of the people.&rquo; It may be simply = sharp, severe.&mdash;<SC>E. J. White</SC> (p.
405): A statute is generally defined as a law enacted by the legislative power, or
a written expression of the legislative will, in the form necessary to make it the law
of the state or country where it is to obtain. The Poet many times speaks of
&lquo;biting statutes&rquo; and &lquo;piercing statutes,&rquo; showing that he had the lawyers&rquo; regard
for such strict legislative provisions as made it hard upon the individual citizen,
when enforced, with the Poet's sympathy for the individual in any hardship that
he suffered, even though it resulted from the enforcement of the law. Speaking
of the repeal of such statutes as were enacted for the benefit of the poor, the idea
is that such acts were rendered migratory by inconsistent provisions, by which
an implied repeal of a previous statute may be effected. The legal observations in
these lines are made in strict accord with the struggle then going on, between the
plebeians and the patricians, for supremacy, and show an accurate knowledge not
only of the legal requirements of legislative enactments but also of the historical
facts existing at this period of the world's history.

<P>92. <B>A pretty Tale</B>] In the earliest known version of the <I>Fables of Bidpai, The
Morall Philosopie of Doni,</I> translated by Sir Thomas North, 1570 (ed. Jacobs,
p. 64), this fable of the belly and members is related, and it is prefaced with these
words: &lquo;That noble Romaine that fought and laboured to bring the people and
communaltie to loue their Magistrates and superiours, tolde them a pretie tale
(to write it happilye in this Booke for him that knoweth it not) howe the handes
were angrie with the bodie.&rquo; It is, however, not necessary to transcribe the rest
of the fable as there given; it is in no way like to that in other collections. The
writer thus concludes: &lquo;With this pretie tale he made the people sensibly to
vnderstand what became them, and how they should behave themselves to their
superiours.&rquo; We have no possible means of knowing whether Shakespeare either
knew of or had ever seen this particular version of the story, but that it should
be therein twice referred to as &lquo;a pretty tale&rquo; and that same phrase be used by
Shakespeare are points which would seem to indicate at least a recollection of this
translation by North.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>94. <B>To scale't</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: Thus all the editions, but without any manner of
sense that I can find out. The Poet must have wrote as I have corrected the
text [see <I>Text. Notes</I>], and then the meaning will be plainly this: &lquo;Perhaps you
may have heard my tale already, but for all that, I'll venture to make it more
<I>stale</I> and familiar to you by telling it over again.&rquo; And nothing is more common
than the verb in this sense with our three capital dramatic Poets. To begin with
our own Author: &lquo;Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale Her infinite variety,&rquo;
<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> II, ii, 240; &lquo;Were I a common laugher, or did use To stale with ordi-
nary oaths my love,&rquo; <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> I, ii, 72; &lquo;imitations Which out of use, and staled
by other men Begin his fashion,&rquo; <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> IV, i, 38. [To these examples from
Shakespeare of &lquo;stale&rquo; used in this sense Theobald adds four others, one of these
from Jonson's <I>Cynthia's Revels,</I> and three from Beaumont and Fletcher, <I>Beggar's
Bush, Queen of Corinth,</I> and <I>Wit at Several Weapons.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Warburton</SC>: Mr
Theobald alters it to <I>stale't.</I> And for a good reason, <I>because he can find no sense,</I>
he says, <I>in the common reading.</I> For as good a reason I, who can, have restored
the old one to its place, &lquo;To scale't,&rquo; signifying <I>to weigh, examine,</I> and <I>apply it.</I>
The author uses it again, in the same sense, in this very play: &lquo;Scaling his
present bearing with his past,&rquo; [II, iii, 261]. And so Fletcher, <I>The Maid in the Mill:</I>
&lquo;What, scale my invention beforehand?&rquo; [ed. Dyce, ix, 259, where &lquo;<I>scale</I>&rquo; is printed
<I>stale</I> and whereon the editor has the following note: &lquo;So Sympson.&mdash;Both the
folios &ldquo;scale&rdquo;; and so the editors of 1778. The same misprint occurs in the old
copies of Shakespeare's <I>Coriolanus,</I> I, i, and has been carefully retained in the three
latest editions of the great dramatist, though Theobald had long ago corrected the
passage, and though Gifford in a most decisive note had proved that the true
reading is <I>stale.</I>&rquo; (See Note by <SC>Steevens</SC> and Gifford's comment thereon, <I>supra.</I>)

<P>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: Neither of Dr Warburton's examples afford a sense congruous

critics, I think Theobald has the advantage.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 81) charac-

&lquo;&ldquo;scale't,&rdquo; <I>i. e.,</I> weigh or examine it, is neither pertinent to the matter in hand nor
suitable to the speaker.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: To &lquo;scale&rquo; is to <I>disperse.</I> The word is used
in the North. If emendation was at all necessary, Theobald's is as good a one
as could be proposed. The sense of the old reading is: Though some of you have
heard the story, I will spread it yet wider, and impart it to the rest. A measure
of wine spilt is called &lquo;a scal'd pottle of wine&rquo; in Dekker's comedy, <I>The Honest
Whore,</I> 1635. So in <I>The Hystorie of Clyomen,</I> a play published in 1599: &lquo;[Ah
sirrah, now] the hugy heapes of cares that lodged in my minde Are scaled from

Holinshed and from the Glossary to Douglas's <I>Translation of Virgil;</I> and in later
editions he added several more. Gifford, who seldom let slip an opportunity to
gird at Steevens, says, in a note on the line, &lquo;I'll not stale the jest By my relation&rquo;
(Massinger, <I>The Unnatural Combat,</I> IV, ii, p. 203). &lquo;This is one of a thousand
instances which might be brought to prove that the true reading in <I>Coriolanus</I> is:
&ldquo;To stale't a little more.&rdquo; . . . Steevens prefers <I>scale,</I> which he proves from a variety
of learned authorities to mean <I>scatter, disperse, spread;</I> to make any of them,
however, suit his purpose, he is obliged to give an unfaithful version of the text:
&ldquo;Though <I>some of you</I> have heard the story, I will <I>spread</I> it yet wider, and diffuse
it among <I>the rest!</I>&rdquo; There is nothing of this in Shakespeare; and, indeed, I cannot
avoid looking on his long note as a feeble attempt to justify a palpable error of the
press, at the cost of taste and sense.&rquo; Gifford, in his edition of Jonson published
ten years later, in a note on the line in <I>Every Man in His Humour,</I> &lquo;To stale

&lquo;So the word is used by Shakespeare, and, indeed, by every writer of his age.
By a very common oversight it is printed <I>scale</I> in <I>Coriolanus,</I> which has happily
furnished occasion for much perverse ingenuity to justify the poet's adoption of
a word which he would steadily have rejected.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc.,

<C>[94. <B>To scale't</B>]</C>
<P>latter reason only is entitled to a hearing; after giving a list of the various sig-
nifications of the word &lquo;scale&rquo; in English and other languages Tooke declares that
all of these have but one meaning in common: viz., &lquo;<I>Divided, Separated.</I> The
tale of Menenius was &ldquo;scaled a little more&rdquo; by being divided into particulars and
degrees, told more circumstantially and at length. That, I take, to be Shake-
speare's meaning by the expression, and not the <I>staling</I> or <I>diffusing</I> of the tale,
which, if they had heard it before, could not have been done by his repetition.
For Menenius does not say that <I>some</I> of them had heard it before; that word
<I>some</I> is introduced by Mr Steevens in his note merely to give a colour to his
explanation of &ldquo;<I>diffusing</I> it among the rest.&rdquo; Clyomen's cares were <I>scaled</I> (i. e.,
<I>separated</I>) from their nestling-place&rquo; (ed. 1857, p. 482).&mdash;<SC>Nares</SC> (<I>Glossary,</I> s. v.
<I>Scale</I>): To weigh as in scales, to estimate aright. I am convinced that this sense,
which was given by Warburton, conveys the true meaning of the following passages:
&lquo;By this is your brother saved, the poor Mariana advantaged, and the correct
[<I>corrupt</I>] deputy scaled.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Meas. for Meas.,</I> III, i, 266. [Here follows the present
line.] In the following passage it is manifest: &lquo;Scaling his present bearing with
his past,&rquo; II, iii, 261, and this has the more force, as occurring soon after in the
same play. That it does also mean to separate and fly off, as <I>scales</I> fly from heated
metal, is proved by the passages which Mr Steevens cites for that purpose. The
other passages adduced are hardly relevant, and the Scottish dialect will not often
authorise English words.&mdash;<SC>Brockett</SC> (s. v. <I>Scale</I>): To spread abroad, to separate,
to divide. [The present line quoted.] Nearly all the commentators have mistaken
the meaning of &lquo;to scale't.&rquo; I am quite satisfied that it was the author's intention
to have the tale <I>spread</I> a little more minutely; or, as Horne Tooke better expresses
it, to have it divided into more particulars and degrees, told more circumstantially
and at length. If Archdeacon Nares, to borrow his own language, will &lquo;weigh as in
scales, to estimate aright,&rquo; Mr Lambe's observations on this passage, and on the
means of acquiring a competent knowledge of the old English tongue (<I>Notes on the
Battle of Flodden</I>), I entertain a hope that the learned author of the elaborate
and valuable Glossary may not be indisposed to alter in more respects than one
the article, <I>To Scale,</I> in a future edition.&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: It is necessary to see how
Shakspere has used this verb [to scale] in other passages. In the second act
Sicinius tells the citizens: &lquo;Scaling his present bearing with his past, That he's
your fixed enemy.&rquo; Dr Johnson explains this: &lquo;<I>Weighing</I> his past and present
behaviour.&rquo; This interpretation seems obvious and natural; and none of the

<SC>B. Nicholson</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Q.,</I> May 4, 1878, p. 342): Theobald's change is a very

understood by modern readers than the one that is somewhat antiquated. The
rule, however, is beginning to be better understood (except by some emending
critics) that a change which the emender believes to be an improvement is not to
be adopted if the old reading gives a sufficient sense. Here, I believe, it gives not
only a sufficient, but a better sense. To &lquo;scale a fish&rquo; is to disfurnish, or clear, or
clean it from its scales that it may be used by man. To &lquo;scale a piece of old and
rusty metal&rquo; is to clear off its rusty scaling, and so furbish it up anew for use or
ornament. To &lquo;scale a bone,&rquo; as practised by the old surgeons, was to scrape off
the diseased surface, and so clear or clean it. The ordinary supposition (founded
on the reading <I>stale't</I>) is that Menenius only intends to say that &lquo;he will tell the
tale again.&rquo; But he does not merely do this nor intend to do it. What he intends
to do, and afterwards does do, is intimated in the words &lquo;but since it serves
my purpose.&rquo; In accordance therewith he not only tells the tale but also takes

<P>for supposing it the invention of &AElig;sop as there is for making him the parent of
many others. The first person who has introduced Menenius as reciting this
fable is Dionysius of Halicarnassus [25 B. C.], book vi. Then follow Livy, lib.
ii.; Plutarch, in the life of Coriolanus; Florus, lib. i, cap. xxiii; each of whom gives
it in his own manner. During the middle ages there appeared a collection of
Latin fables in hexameter verse that has agitated the opinions of the learned to
little purpose in their endeavors to ascertain the real name of the compiler or
versifier. He has been called Romulus, Accius, and Salo. Nor is the time when
he lived at all known. These fables are sometimes called <I>anonymous,</I> and have
been published in various forms. An excellent edition by Nilant appeared in
1709, 12mo. Many of them were translated into French verse in the eleventh
century by a French lady who calls herself <I>Marie de France,</I> in which form they
have been happily preserved with many others extremely curious composed by
the same ingenious person. . . . William Herman of Gouda, in Holland, reduced
them into Latin prose about the year 1500, omitting some and adding others.
The works of Romulus and Herman of Gouda have been published in a great
variety of forms and languages, and constitute the set of &AElig;sopian fables which
commences with that of the cock and the precious stone; in all which the apologue
of the belly and the members is to be found, and sometimes with considerable
variation. . . . Nor was this fable unknown in the Eastern world. Syntipas, a
Persian fabulist, has placed it in his work, published for the first time from a MS.
at Moscow, by Matth&aelig;us, Lips. 1781, 8vo. Lafontaine has related it in his own
inimitable manner; and, lastly, the editor of Baskerville and Dodsley's <I>&AElig;sop</I>
has given it in a style not inferior perhaps to that of any of his predecessors. [See,
also, note by <SC>Douce,</SC> l. 144 <I>supra.</I>]&mdash;<SC>Jacobs</SC> (<I>Fables of &AElig;sop,</I> i, 82): There is a
reference in the <I>Mahabharata</I> (xiv, 688) to a fable similar to <I>The Belly and Mem-
bers</I> which deserves closer attention, as it is, in many ways, the most remarkable
fable in existence. A variant of it, or something very like it, was discovered six
years ago by M. Maspero in a fragmentary papyrus, which he dates about the
twentieth dynasty (c. 1250 B. C.). It is, consequently, the oldest fable in exist-
ence. . . . The fable, if fable it can be called, takes the form of a mock-trial,
corresponding, as M. Gaston Paris has pointed out, to the <I>d&eacute;bat</I> which is so familiar
in medi&aelig;val French literature. From this point of view the <I>d&eacute;bat</I> of <I>Belly and
Head</I> affords us the earliest example of legal procedure extant. We again meet
with the fable in the <I>Upanishads,</I> whence it doubtless got into the <I>Mahabharata,</I>
and perhaps too into the <I>Zend Yacna: Dispute of the Senses and the Soul</I>. . . . A
similar apologue existed among the Buddhists as we know from the fact that it
exists in the Chinese Buddhistic work <I>Avadanas</I> (No. 105); it occurs also in the
<I>Pantschatantra: The Bird with Two Heads.</I> I have also found a Jewish variant,
though with a somewhat different moral: <I>The Tongue and the Members.</I> But
there is a still more striking use of the fable by a Jew. There can be little doubt
that St. Paul had a similar fable in his mind in the characteristic passage (<I>1 Cor.,</I>
xii, 12-26). The passage combines the Indian idea of the contest of the members
with the Roman notion of the body politic. As this passage is the foundation
of the doctrine of the Visible Church, and indirectly of the conception of the
Body Politic (of which Hobbes made such quaint use), we cannot well overrate
the importance of the fable on which it is founded. We have thus seen this fable
of the Body and its Members with its Belgian motto, <I>L'union fait la force,</I> forming

<P>part of the sacred literature of Egyptians and Chinese, of Brahmins, Buddhists and
Magians, of Jews, and Christians. The reader must not, however, assume that
these are all necessarily derived from one source. . . . The various versions [afford]
an instructive example of how different nations may hit upon the very same apo-
logue to illustrate the same idea. Carefully examined, the various versions may
be reduced to four independent ones. The Egyptian <I>d&eacute;bat</I> stands by itself, the
Brahmin <I>Contest of Senses and Soul,</I> occurring in the <I>Upanishads,</I> recurs in the
Indian epic, in the Persian scripture, and possibly through the latter, in Jewish
commentaries, and may thence have influenced St. Paul. The lost Buddhist
apologue of <I>The Bird with Two Heads</I> found its way to China, and was received
into the Bidpai literature. The Roman fable is remarkable as being the only fable
of its kind in Latin literature which can claim to be current among the Romans.
It occurs late, and may have been interpolated by Livy, like so much of his work.
But, on the whole, I am inclined to regard it as a genuine Roman folk-fable and
another instance of the sporadic use of the fable . . . by nations who have not other-
wise shown a turn towards that form of the apologue. The whole enquiry ought
to make us careful in the future how we admit borrowing without sure evidence
either of identity of the fables or of contact between the nations using them. [See
<I>Appendix: Fable of the Belly and the Members.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Bucknill</SC> (<I>Medical Knowledge,</I>
etc., p. 203): Rabelais uses this same fable of &AElig;sop to illustrate the social miseries
which would result if the world should be filled with a rascally rabble of people
that would not lend; his hero, in the witty classification of men into those who
borrow and those who lend, decidedly belonging to the former category, and being
as decidedly inimical to all who did not belong to the latter.&mdash;<SC>Wordsworth</SC> (<I>Sh's
Knowledge and Use of Bible,</I> p. 340): The well-known apologue of Menenius
Agrippa is not to be traced to St Paul's <I>First Epistle to the Corinthians,</I> ch. xii,
but rather to the common source in Roman history, from which they both, we
may suppose, adopted it; except that St Paul probably read it in Livy, and
Shakespeare in North's translation of Plutarch.

<P>of distinction even now, since we use <I>un</I>grateful, <I>in</I>gratitude; <I>un</I>equal, <I>in</I>equality.
<I>Un-</I> seems to have been preferred by Shakespeare before <I>p</I> and <I>r,</I> which do not
allow <I>in-</I> to precede except in the form <I>im. In-</I> also seems to have been in many
cases retained from the Latin, as in the case of &ldquo;<I>in</I>gratus,&rdquo; &ldquo;<I>in</I>fortunium,&rdquo; &amp;c.
As a general rule, we now use <I>in-</I> where we desire to make the negative a part of
the word, and <I>un-</I> where the separation is maintained&mdash;&ldquo;<I>un</I>true,&rdquo; &ldquo;<I>in</I>firm.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): The only instance of this word (there is none of its modern
equivalent <I>inactive</I>) in Shakespeare. Compare Milton, <I>Paradise Regained,</I> &lquo;his life,
Private, unactive, calm, contemplative,&rquo; II, 80, 81.

belly &lquo;laughed at their folly&rquo; in North, so that Menenius&rquo; jest is really a bit of
literary criticism on Shakespeare's part.

scarcely necessary. Only thus does this story by Menenius with its pauses and

<P>119. <B>Kingly crown'd</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, having a kingly crown. This is
an example of the words, participial in form, which are derived from nouns. Of
the ten <I>sephiroth</I> or intelligences, which appear in the philosophy of the Kabbalah,
the first, which is called the &lquo;crown,&rquo; is placed in the head.
<P>120. <B>Counsailor Heart</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The heart was anciently esteemed the seat
of prudence. <I>Homo cordatus</I> is a <I>prudent man.</I>&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The heart was con-
sidered by Shakespeare as the seat of the <I>understanding.</I> [See note by Malone on
l. 144 <I>supra.</I>&mdash;<SC>Wright</SC> notes that in the Kabbalah the Heart is called the seat of
the understanding.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>122. <B>Muniments</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, <I>supports, defences;</I> like the Latin
<I>munimenta.</I>&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): The <I>N. E. D.</I> quotes this passage under the sense,
&lquo;Things with which a person or place is provided, furnishings,&rquo; and also cites
among other references Spenser, <I>The Faerie Queene,</I> IV, viii, 6, &lquo;By chance he
certain muniments forthdrew, Which yet with him as relickes did abide.&rquo;
<P>123. <B>that</B>] For other examples of &lquo;that&rquo; as a conjunctional affix see <SC>Abbott</SC>,
&sect; 287.
<P>124. <B>Foreme</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: A petty oath, probably substituted for the more
common &lquo;'Fore God,&rquo; to avoid the penalties imposed by the Act of Parliament,
3 James I, ch. 21, to restrain the abuse of players. See <I>Mer. of Ven.,</I> I, ii, 99.
It occurs again in <I>All's Well,</I> II, iii, 31: &lquo;Why, your dolphin is not lustier: 'fore me,
I speak in respect.&rquo; In <I>2 Henry IV:</I> III, ii, 186, where the quartos read &lquo;'Fore
God,&rquo; the Folio's have &lquo;Trust me&rquo;; and in two other passages of the same play
where the objectionable expression occurs it is omitted in the Folios. Compare
also <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> III, iv, 34: &lquo;Afore me! it is so very late.&rquo; And <I>Othello,</I> IV, i,
149, &lquo;Before me! look where she comes.&rquo;

<P>136. <B>deliberate</B>] Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Menenius is taking the part

<P>141. <B>Store-house, and the Shop</B>] <SC>R. G. White</SC>: According to modern British
usage Shakespeare is here somewhat pleonastic, but according to the best English
usage, which is still preserved in New England and her off-shoots, he is not at
all so. &lquo;Shop&rquo; means properly a place where fabrics are made or work is done;
and such is the sense in which it is always used with us, but in Great Britain it is
rarely so applied, and is almost universally misused to mean a store or collection
of articles kept or stored for sale&mdash;a confusion avoided in Elizabethan usage and
of that in the present day in this country. Thus, for instance, we say a watch-
maker's shop, a milliner's shop, . . . but a book store, a grocery store, . . . a shoe-
maker's shop, but a shoe store. . . . The transatlantic use of the word and its
active verbal sense are clearly traceable to the custom of having the booth or the
sales-room in front of the shop, such a vivid picture of which is presented in the
opening chapter of <I>The Fortunes of Nigel.</I>&mdash;In the passage before us the stomach
is represented as both the store house of the body&mdash;&lquo;still cupboarding the viand&rquo;&mdash;
and its shop&mdash;&lquo;sending it through the rivers of the blood.&rquo;
<P>143. <B>I send it . . . of your blood</B>] <SC>A. H. G. Doran</SC> (Article, <I>Medicine,</I> ch. xiv,
<I>Sh's England,</I> i, 421): Shakespeare's plays show that he had heard much about
the teaching of practical anatomy and understood certain theories about the move-
ment of the blood. He described the belly as sending &lquo;the general food . . . through
the rivers of your blood.&rquo; Such language, however, is perhaps merely figurative,
and the poet died before Harvey's views were made public, and doubtless held the
old notion that the blood flowed in the veins, and that the arteries held, besides
blood, the vital spirits.

<P>expression. I believe we should read, with the omission of a particle, &lquo;to the
seat, the brain.&rquo; He uses &lquo;seat&rquo; for <I>throne,</I> the <I>royal seat,</I> which the first editors
not apprehending, corrupted the passage. It is thus used in <I>Rich. II:</I> &lquo;Yea,
distaff-women manage rusty bills Against thy seat,&rquo; III, ii, 118. It should be
observed, too, that one of the Citizens had just before characterized these prin-
cipal parts of the human fabric by similar metaphors: &lquo;The kingly crowned
head.&rquo; . . . &lquo;The counsellor heart.&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>Rann</SC> is Trywhitt's only follower in thus
reading.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I have too great respect for even the conjectures of my
respectable and very judicious friend to suppress his note, though it appears to me
erroneous. In the present instance I have not the smallest doubt, being clearly of
opinion that the text is right. &lquo;Brain&rquo; is here used for <I>reason</I> or <I>understanding.</I>
Shakespeare seems to have had Camden as well as Plutarch before him; the former
of whom has told a similar story in his <I>Remaines,</I> 1605, and has, like our poet,
made the <I>heart</I> the <I>seat</I> of the <I>brain,</I> or <I>understanding:</I> &lquo;Hereupon they all agreed
to pine away their lasie and publike enemy. One day passed over, the second
followed very tedious, but the third day was so grievous to them that they called
a common counsel. The eyes waxed dimme, the feete could not support the body,
the armes waxed lazie, the tongue faltered and could not lay open the matter.
Therefore they all with one accord desired the <I>advice</I> of the <I>heart.</I> There <SC>Reason</SC>
laid open before them,&rquo; &amp;c., p. 109. [See <I>Appendix: Date of Composition,</I> Malone.]
I agree, however, entirely with Tyrwhitt, in thinking that &lquo;seat&rquo; means here the
<I>royal seat,</I> the throne. &lquo;The seat of the brain&rquo; is put in opposition with the heart,
and is descriptive of it: &lquo;I send it (says the belly) through the blood, even to
the <I>royal residence,</I> the heart, in which the kingly crowned understanding is en-
throned.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Douce</SC> (ii, 77): What Camden has given is from John of Salisbury,
who wrote in the reign of Henry II, and professes to have received it from Pope
Hadrian IV. See his <I>Polycraticon, sive de nugis curialium,</I> hb. vi, ch. 24. Camden
has omitted the latter part; and the learned reader will do well to consult the
original, where he will find some verses by Q. Serenus Sammonicus, a physician in
the reign of Caracalla, that allude to the fable. John of Salisbury has himself
composed two hundred Latin lines De membris conspirantibus, which are in the
<I>first edition</I> of his <I>Polycraticon</I> printed at Brussels, without date, about 1470.
These were reprinted by Andreas Rivinus at Leipsic, 1655, 8vo; and likewise at
the end of the fourth volume of Fabricius's <I>Bibliotheca medi&aelig; et infim&aelig; &aelig;tatis,</I>
Hamburg, 1735. They are, most probably, the lines which are called in Sinner's
catalogue of the MSS at Berne, &lquo;Carmen <I>Ovidii</I> de altercatione ventris et artuum,
vol. iii, p. 116. [See also note by <SC>Douce</SC>, l. 99 <I>ante.</I>]&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. i.) maintains
that the interpretation given to this line by Malone in the last paragraph of his
note is &lquo;evidently wrong; the right sense being, apparently, &ldquo;I send the general
food through the rivers of your blood to the heart, which is the court; I send it
to the seat of the brain,&rdquo; that is, the head; for the belly may as justly claim the
honour of sending nourishment to the head as to the heart.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>):
The confusion between two different bodily organs, and awkwardness of under-
standing one literally and the other figuratively, disposes one to reject Malone's
view, but it certainly receives some support from the use of the two words <I>court</I>
and <I>seat,</I> both equivalent to &lquo;royal residence.&rquo;

<P>etc., p. 347): It is evident that this line is not measure; and we are instructed
[by the MS. Corrector] to read it and the next in a way that not only cures this
defect, but much improves the sense, by following up the figure of &lquo;the court,
the heart,&rquo; and completing the resemblance of the human body to the various parts
of a commonwealth: &lquo;Even to the Court, the heart, the <I>Senate,</I> brain; And through

senate was easy; and the change (which never occurred to any commentator) is
supported both by what precedes and by what follows it, going through the
various degrees in a state&mdash;the court, the senate, persons of different ranks, the
holders of offices, &amp;c.&mdash;<SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Blackwood's Maga.,</I> Sep., 1853, p. 320): The senate

This, indeed, is the very <I>point</I> of the fable. Surely nothing except the most
extreme degree of dotage can account for such a manifest perversion as that; yet
Mr Collier says that &lquo;it much improves the sense.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> p.
208), referring to the MS. Corrector's two new readings, says: &lquo;Perhaps there was

or understanding; and there is no doubt that <I>seat</I> means the <I>royal seat,</I> the throne.

&ldquo;cranks&rdquo; are sinuosities . . . and &ldquo;offices&rdquo; the functionary parts, as Shakespeare

their due functions.&rdquo; The Corrector's <I>instructions to read it</I> otherwise will there-

alteration <I>ranks and offices,</I> if <I>senate</I> be right, only furnishes a description of the
great machine of state, since &lquo;through the veins&rquo; has preceded it, thus it is more
pertinent here to understand &lquo;cranks.&rquo;

<P>155. <B>What say you too't</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): Menenius gives his apologue

he has got the mob into better humour, and so, before the First Citizen has time
to discover the <I>non sequitur,</I> takes up the safer weapon of ridicule [l. 164].

<P>&lquo;For examine&rquo; is introduced merely to diversify the discourse and to fix the atten-
tion of the listeners; it might be wholly omitted without injury to the sense, but
in the passage, as it now stands, &lquo;examine&rquo; is made an effective verb, having for
its objects the counsels and the cares of the senators, while &lquo;digest&rquo; is made auxiliary
to and synonymous with &lquo;examine,&rquo; and, like it, is in the imperative mood, as
though addressed to the people, instead of being, as it ought to be, in the indicative,
with &lquo;counsels&rquo; and &lquo;cares&rquo; for its agents. It is a curious instance of how com-
pletely the true sense of a passage may be distorted by the misapplication of a
few commas. &lquo;Digest,&rquo; therefore, in this passage, as elsewhere, is in direct allusion
to the animal function. The very essence and pith of the parable of &lquo;the belly
and the members&rquo; is to place in opposition the <I>digestive</I> function of the belly with
the more active offices of the members; and the application of the parable is
that &lquo;<I>the senators</I> are this good belly,&rquo; <I>their</I> counsels and <I>their</I> cares <I>digest</I> for the
general good, and distribute the resulting benefits throughout the whole com-
munity. This is the true reading; and no person who duly considers it, or who
has compared it with the original in Plutarch, but must be satisfied that it is so.
[See also note by A. E. Brae on III, i, 158.]
<P>161-163. <B>No publique . . . your selues</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): The Citizens
might have retorted that they earned these &lquo;public benefits&rquo; (if any) by public
services, such as fighting for the State; also that, as a matter of fact, they were
starving, while the &lquo;members&rquo; of the body, on Menenius's own showing, received
from the belly their &lquo;natural competency&rquo; in return for <I>their</I> services.&mdash;[Verity's
point is, I think, well taken; but then Menenius knew well the intelligence of his
audience, and that they would not be likely to detect the flaws in his argument
either here or at l. 155, as shown by Beeching. Had it not been so, the Citizen
might easily have turned the whole of Menenius's fable against him by showing
that, in the present situation, although actually in rebellion, the Citizens were
more like to the Belly, in the fable, and the Senate to the limbs, than as repre-
sented by Menenius. By starving and depriving them of their rights the Senate's
power would be weakened.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>163. <B>What do you thinke?</B>] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): Menenius has
learnt one of the arts of the public speaker, to single out the most prominent
of his interrupters and disconcert him by making him ridiculous. But, on the
whole, his speech has not been a success. In North his persuasions &lquo;pacified the
people&rquo;; in Shakespeare they have no effect. The whole episode only serves to
bring out the complete divergence between the noble and the plebeian points of
view. And one feels that the Citizen, who has shown a good deal of shrewd
common sense, and has escaped all the pitfalls of Menenius' dialectic, has really
had the best of it. Menenius' argument, when analysed, is only the ordinary
sophistry by which the middlemen and the unproductive classes generally justify
to themselves their own appropriation of nine-tenths of the profits of industry.

<P>It is very plausible, but not calculated to convince a starving proletariate.&mdash;
[The observation by Chambers that the persuasions of Menenius have no effect
is one that must be apparent to any reader or auditor, and if to us, how much
more so must it have been to Shakespeare with his abundant knowledge of dra-
matic construction. That he realised how difficult was the task before him is
shown at the beginning of the colloquy where the Citizen says that Menenius
must not think &lquo;to fob off their disgraces with a tale.&rquo; Menenius does attempt
it, but does not succeed in making the mob put down their weapons and quietly
disperse, a course of action, on so slight a cause, which Shakespeare rightly realised
would be perfectly inconsistent with a crowd in such an ugly mood, bent on
destruction. All that Menenius accomplishes is to delay their precipitate action.
It can hardly be said, therefore, that this fable is here without any dramatic
effect.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>164. <B>the great Toe</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (ed. p. 35): Menenius so calls him, following out
the fable of the Belly and the Members.
<P>168. <B>Thou . . . to run</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> (<I>Supplemental Observations,</I> i, 218) in reference
to the pointing of this line as in the <I>Variorum</I> of '78 (see <I>Text. Notes</I>) suggests that
a comma be placed after &lquo;run&rquo; instead of after &lquo;blood.&rquo; 'Tis true, 'tis pity, and
pity 'tis, 'tis true that Malone has, in this case, neglected to glance at the Folio
text wherein is the punctuation that he proposes as a change.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>:
Menenius is supposed to mean: &lquo;thou, meagre wretch, least in heart and resolu-
tion, art prompt enough to lead when profit points the way.&rquo; Yet if nothing
better can be extracted from these words in their metaphorical sense, we would
rather understand them literally, and believe &lquo;worst&rquo; to be a misprint, as it might
easily be, for <I>last.</I> The passage then becomes perfectly intelligible and in character
with the speaker: &lquo;Thou rascal, that art last in blood (that is, <I>into blood shed</I>) to
run, Lead'st first to win some vantage.&rquo;

<P>being English. Nor can it, I think, be doubted that the English <I>raskaille</I> stands
for an Old French <I>rascaille,</I> which is clearly the same word as modern French
<I>racaille,</I> &ldquo;the rascality or base and rascall sort, the scumme, dregs, offals, outcasts
of any company,&rdquo; Cotgrave.' This last bears out Malone's remark as to the
equivocal use of the word in the present passage.&mdash;<SC>Madden</SC> (p. 60, foot-note)
says: &lquo;In the sense in which [rascal] is now used as a term of reproach, it was in
the first instance spoken by the &ldquo;figure <I>Metaphore . . .</I> as one should in reproch
say to a poore man, thou raskall knaue where <I>raskall</I> is properly the hunters terme
giuen to young deere, leane and out of season, and not to people.&rquo;&mdash;Puttenham:
<I>Arte of English Poesie,</I> 1589 (ed. Arber, p. 191).&mdash;<SC>Hon. J. W. Fortescue</SC> (<I>Shake-
speare's England,</I> vol. ii, ch. xxvii, &sect; 1, <I>Hunting,</I> p. 339, foot-note): Shakespeare's
use of the word [rascal] is peculiar: &lquo;Horns? Even so. Poor men alone? No,
no; the noblest deer hath them as huge as the rascal.&rquo;&mdash;<I>As You Like It,</I> III, iii,
58. [The present line here quoted.] Reading these quotations together with the
speech of John Talbot [<I>1 Henry VI:</I> IV, ii, 48] it is plain that Shakespeare con-
ceived of &lquo;rascal&rquo; as a deer with a great head and a small body, who would neither
fight nor run. Such deer though not unknown are very uncommon, though it is
by no means unusual for a deer past his prime to carry an inferior head on a very
large body. Shakespeare's rascal would be at a great disadvantage, for deer fight
by shoving before they come to goring; and here the light weight of his body would
place him at the mercy of a stag of heavier frame. Moreover, the enormous mass
of bone upon his head, . . . with no sufficient strength of body to carry it, would
make such a deer weak and helpless. Hence the legitimate conclusion that he
could neither run far nor fight well, for he would be overweighted and over-
balanced by his head. He might very likely be in the foremost place in a herd,
for, when a herd is moved the hinds and young male deer always move in front,
and the big stags bring up the rear; but he could never bully anything bigger than
a four year old. . . . It may be questioned if Shakespeare was correct in using the
word &lquo;rascal&rquo; only in this restricted sense; and if the term be extended to its
legitimate limits, so as to cover all young male deer, then Shakespeare's similes are
false; for a young stag (as the sportsmen of the day well knew) can and will run
better than any other and can fight savagely enough if he husbands some strength
for the bay; which, however, as a rule he does not. [It is to be feared that Fortescue
has taken the words of Touchstone too literally as an indication of Shakespeare's
knowledge of venery. The context, of which this line is but a small part, shows
that there is here intended but another allusion to a jest which was never stale to
Shakespeare and his fellows, unsavory as it may be to us. &lquo;Rascal,&rquo; as Touchstone
uses it here, is simply following out the idea expressed in &lquo;poor men&rquo; in contrast to
the &lquo;noblest.&rquo; That is, Both noble and poor are alike subject to the same mis-
fortune.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<C>[168. <B>that art worst in blood to run</B>]</C>
<P>that art the meanest by birth, art the foremost to lead thy fellows <I>to ruin,</I> in hope
of some advantage. The meaning, however, is perhaps only this: &lquo;Thou that
art a hound of the lowest breed, lead'st the pack, when anything is to be gotten.&rquo;
&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Worst in blood&rquo; may be the true reading. In <I>1 Henry VI:</I> &lquo;If
we be English deer, be then in blood; Not rascal-like to fall down with a pinch,&rquo; IV,
ii, 48.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The phrase &lquo;in blood&rquo; was a phrase of the forest. Our author
seldom was careful that his comparisons should answer on both sides. He seems to
mean here &lquo;thou worthless scoundrel, though like a deer not in blood, thou art in
the worst condition for running of all the herd of plebeians, takest the lead in this
tumult, in order to obtain some private advantage to yourself.&rquo; What advantage
the foremost of a herd of deer could obtain is not easy to point out, nor did Shake-
speare, I believe, consider. Perhaps, indeed, he only uses &lquo;rascal&rquo; in its ordinary
sense. So afterwards, &lquo;From rascals worse than they,&rquo; [I, vi, 56]. Dr John-
son's interpretation appears to me inadmissible; as the term, though it is applic-
able both in its original and metaphorical sense to a man, cannot, I think, be
applied to a dog; nor have I found any instance of the term &lquo;in blood&rquo; being applied
to the canine species. [Malone refers to a note of his on &lquo;The deer was, as you
know, sanguis, in blood,&rquo; <I>Love's Labour's Lost,</I> IV, ii, 3, but as he there merely
discusses a question as to a textual change in regard to the word &lquo;sanguis,&rquo; his
remarks are of no assistance in the present passage. As to Malone's remark that
&lquo;in blood&rquo; is a &lquo;phrase of the forest&rquo; I can but say that so it may be, but a careful
search of the Duke of York's volume, <I>The Master of Game, circa</I> 1400; of Turber-
ville's <I>Noble Arte of Venerie,</I> 1576, and of N. Coxe's <I>Gentleman's Recreation,</I> 1674,
has not yielded any example of such a phrase either in the lists of terms used in
the chase or in the various descriptions of the Hart, the Buck, the Roebuck, or the
Deer; with these writers the usual term applied to a Hart in his prime condition
is either &lquo;pride&rquo; or &lquo;prime of grease.&rquo; The <I>N. E. D.,</I> s. v. Blood, under the cap-
tion <I>Hunting phrase,</I> quotes the passages from <I>1 Henry VI.</I> and <I>Love's Labour's
Lost,</I> given above, and but one other as follows: &lquo;When hounds are out of blood,
there is a kind of evil genius attending all that they do, while a pack of fox hounds
well in blood, like troops flushed with conquest, are not easily withstood.&rquo;&mdash;P.
Beckford (1781), <I>Hunting,</I> p. 308. It would, I think, be unfair to Malone to
say that he did not know of this when he remarked that he had not &lquo;found any
instance of the term applied to the canine species&rquo;; all that he means apparently
is that in writings contemporary with Shakespeare the phrase, as far as he knows,
does not appear; the comparatively modern date of the quotation from Beckford
seems to justify such a conclusion. I speak with great diffidence, but possibly

<P>172. <B>baile</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: It must be the vanquisht side, sure, that could want it;
and who were likely to be their <I>Bail?</I> But it is endless to question with negligence
and stupidity. The Poet undoubtedly wrote as I have restor'd: <I>Bale,</I> i. e.,
<I>Sorrow, Misfortune,</I> must have the worst of it. I have restor'd this word in some
other passages of our Author; and we meet with it in a play attributed to him,
call'd <I>Locrine,</I> &lquo;Yea, with these eyes thou hast seen her, and therefore pull them
out, for they will work thy Bale,&rquo; [ed. Brooke, I, ii, 21. Theobald furnishes
several other examples from other sources of <I>bale</I> used in this sense; but according
to <SC>W. A. Wright</SC> this is the only passage wherein Shakespeare uses the noun.
Theobald's statement that he had corrected the spelling in some other passages
is, therefore, a slight exaggeration. Wright gives its derivation as from A. S.
<I>bealu,</I> injury, mischief, and quotes, as a use by Shakespeare of an adjectival form
of the word, &lquo;With baleful weeds, and precious juiced flowers,&rquo; <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I>
II, iii, 8, a passage which Mason had earlier quoted to illustrate the fact that
Shakespeare uses both <I>bale</I> and <I>bane</I> to signify <I>poison.</I> <SC>Malone</SC> remarks that
&lquo;This word was antiquated in Shakespeare's time, being marked as obsolete by

<P>176. <B>the poore Itch . . . Opinion</B>] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): That the
rabble should have an opinion at all is to Coriolanus a sign of an unhealthy con-
dition in the state. Unless they leave it alone they will only make themselves
the more uncomfortable for it. The choice of metaphor is characteristic. The
mob are always, physically as well as spiritually, offensive to Coriolanus. The
grammar may either be &lquo;make for yourselves scabs&rquo; or &lquo;make yourselves into
scabs.&rquo; &lquo;Scab&rquo; was a common term of abuse; compare: &lquo;<I>Con.</I> Here, man, I am
at thy elbow. <I>Bor.</I> Mass, and my elbow itch'd; I thought there would a scab
follow.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Much Ado,</I> III, iii, 105.

not possibly have written &lquo;thee&rquo; here is manifest. [<SC>R. G. White</SC> agrees with
Dyce that &lquo;thee&rquo; is clearly a misprint, but I am not wholly persuaded that the
Folio reading is not more dramatic than Dyce's proposal. The words of Marcius

<P>181, 182. <B>That like nor . . . you proud</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That they did not like

not like peace (and the reason of that too is assigned) will be very hard to con-

and power, for those are what make a people proud; but then those are what
they like but too well, and so must needs <I>like peace,</I> the parent of them. This
being contrary to what the text says, we may be assured it is corrupt, and that
Shakespeare wrote: &lquo;That <I>likes not</I> peace, nor war?&rquo;&mdash;<I>i. e.,</I> Whom neither peace
nor war fits or agrees with, as making them either proud or cowardly. By this

<P>reading &lquo;peace&rquo; and &lquo;war,&rquo; from being the accusatives to <I>likes,</I> become the nom-

a verb singular, to &lquo;Curs,&rquo; a noun plural, which they supposed the nominative to
it, would, in order to show their skill in grammar, alter it to &lquo;like&rquo;; but <I>likes</I> for
<I>pleases</I> was common with the writers of this time.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: That <I>to like</I> is <I>to
please</I> every one knows, but in that sense it is as hard to say why peace should
not <I>like</I> the people as, in the other sense, why the people should not <I>like</I> peace.
The truth is, that Coriolanus does not use the two sentences consequentially, but
first reproaches them with unsteadiness, then with their other occasional vices.
&mdash;<SC>Theobald</SC>, writing to Warburton, 12<SUP>th</SUP> February, 1729, says: &lquo;You would
make nominatives of <I>peace</I> and <I>war.</I> I had always reconciled it to myself thus,
that neither like <I>war,</I> nor can be content <I>with</I> peace. War frights you, and peace
and plenty make you so <I>insolent</I> and <I>exacting</I> that you do not know what you would
have yourselves, and thereby seem not to <I>like</I> tranquillity&rquo; (Nichols: <I>Illus-
trations,</I> etc., ii, 479).&mdash;<SC>Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc., p. 246): If it were not for the com-
ments that have been made on this passage, I should have passed it over as one
that required no manner of explanation. &lquo;That like nor peace nor war&rquo; means,
that are not contented with either peace or war; the one affrighted them, and
they therefore disliked it; the other made them proud, and pride is the parent
of discontent. I don't understand the force of Warburton's amendment, as I
think the case is pretty much the same, whether we say &lquo;that they like not peace&rquo;
or &lquo;that peace does not please them.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (409): The excessive affectation of
subtilty misled Mr Warburton into this violent construction [&lquo;that likes not,&rquo; etc.].
The common reading to a common understanding is plain enough and would meet
with no difficulty. The meaning is: Neither peace nor war can satisfy you, or
content you. In war you are always afraid of the consequences; and in peace
your pride won't let you be quiet, or think any treatment of you, however kind
and favourable, equal to your deservings. But Mr Warburton by a long train of
profound reasonings, hath discovered that the mob must necessarily love peace
because it brings with it an increase of wealth and power, whereas the very
contrary of this was the constant experience of the Roman republic. In peace
the Plebeians were always most oppressed because the Patricians had then most
need of their assistance; whereas in time of war they were obliged to pay court
to them for their own preservation. [It is, I think, quite beside the point here
to enter into any discussion as to the relative value of the statements of either
Warburton or Heath regarding the attitude of the Plebeians to the states of war
and peace in the days of the Roman republic. Coriolanus says they are satisfied
with neither state. That is all there is to it; we must, moreover, bear in mind that
this is the petulant retort of a very testy and irritable man to a set of persons
whom he despises. The Englishman's attitude of mind, in the time of Shakespeare
at least, is, perhaps, reflected in the colloquy between the <I>Servingmen</I> in Act IV,
sc. v, lines 217-230, and from that we learn that the preference was on the side of
the stirring times of war, and not for the lethargic days of peace.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

so ready to break and disturb it.

<P>185. <B>coale of fire vpon the Ice</B>] <SC>Hales</SC> (<I>Academy,</I> July 20, 1878; reprinted in
<I>Notes and Essays,</I> p. 292): [There may be here] a reference to the famous frost
of 1607-8. It must be allowed that this is a somewhat out-of-the-way image.
Coals on ice are not usually a common spectacle; but it would seem they were
so in the winter of 1607-8, and at that time the image would be by no means far-
fetched or unfamiliar; it would, in fact, be obviously suggested. Of course one
would lay no great stress on it if there was nothing else to connect the play with
that time; but there being other things that so connect it, the allusion may per-
haps be taken as confirmatory. &lquo;Above Westminster,&rquo; writes Chamberlain to
Carleton, January 8, 1607-8, &lquo;the Thames is quite frozen over, and the Archbishop
came from Lambeth on Twelfth Day over the ice to Court. Many fantastical
experiments are daily put in practice, as certain youths burnt a gallon of wine
upon the ice, and made all the passengers partakers.&rquo; An account of this frost,
written during its prevalence, is given in a tract called &lquo;The Great Frost: Cold
doings in London, a Dialogue,&rquo; reprinted by Arber in <I>An English Garner,</I> vol. i,
p. 79. The Citizen in this dialogue tells&mdash;to quote a side-note&mdash;of beer, ale, wine,
victuals, and fires on the Thames. &lquo;Are you cold with going over?&rquo; runs the text,
&lquo;You shall ere you come to the middle of the river spy some ready with pans of
coals to warm your fingers.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, no more lasting, having no
more endurance; disappearing as rapidly at the approach of danger as a hot coal
melts its way through ice, or a hailstone melts in the sun. Compare: &lquo;Rogues,
hence, avaunt! vanish like hailstones, go.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Merry Wives,</I> I, iii, 90.
<P>186-188. <B>Your Vertue . . . did it</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, Your virtue is to speak
well of him whom his own offences have subjected to justice; and to rail at those
laws by which he whom you praise was punished.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): The thought
is similar in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> I, ii, 192-194, &lquo;our slippery people, Whose love is never
link'd to the deserver Till his deserts are past&rquo;; and again (<I>Ibid.,</I> I, iv, 43), &lquo;the
ebb'd man, ne'er loved till ne'er worth love.&rquo;

1790, the explanation of the word &lquo;seeking&rquo; alone being retained in subsequent
editions, it would seem that, having freed his soul by admission of the heinous

<P>206. <B>Who thriues . . . giue out</B>] <SC>Badham</SC> (p. 9) gives this line as an example

<P>206. <B>Side factions</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, take part in factions. The verb
is used intransitively in IV, ii, 5. Similarly, Webster in <I>The White Devil</I> (p. 14,
ed. Dyce, 1857) has &lquo;Do you bandy factions 'gainst me?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC> (p. 286): Why
say that &lquo;side factions&rquo; means &lquo;<I>take part in factions</I>&rquo; unless <I>that</I> be the only tol-
erable, or decidedly the best, meaning that the words can bear? As a matter of
fact, it is neither the only possible nor, in my opinion, the most probable one.
These fire-side gossips affected to know the state of the political just as they
affected to know the state of the social world; they patched up imaginary parties,
making this man belong to this side, and that man to that, just as they gave out
conjectural marriages; faction-makers and match-makers were they, albeit their
factions and their matches had no existence save in their idle imaginations and
brainless babble.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): That is, take the side of. But in view of
the whole passage, and especially the making of imaginary matches and the arbi-
trary estimation of parties, there is excuse for those who prefer to take &lquo;side fac-
tions&rquo; in some such sense as&mdash;invent factions and the composition of these opposite
&lquo;sides.&rquo;
<P>207. <B>Coniecturall Marriages</B>] <SC>Wordsworth</SC> (<I>Historical Plays,</I> i, 116): I find
no explanation of this, but the matter of intermarriage between upper and lower
social classes was made a political and party question in the early days of the
Roman Republic.

<P>210-213. <B>Would the Nobility . . . my Lance</B>] <SC>Minto</SC> (p. 304): Let us see what
can be said for and against the extravagant ramps of some of Shakespeare's heroes.
There are passages in <I>Julius C&aelig;sar</I> and <I>Coriolanus</I> almost as bombastic as any-
thing to be found in Shakespeare's dramatic predecessors. C&aelig;sar's bearing in the
interview with the conspirators, when they beg the repeal of Cimber's banish-
ment, is not less lo$ty than Tamburlaine's inflation, though more calm and dig-
nified&mdash;&lquo;Know C&aelig;sar doth not wrong, nor without cause Will he be satisfied.&rquo;
And the speech beginning &lquo;I could be well moved, if I were as you,&rquo; may not
be an offence against the modesty of nature, but, taken by itself, is an offence
against the modesty of art. The boasts and brags of Coriolanus out-Herod the
Herod of the Mysteries. For example [the present lines here quoted], and:
<BQ>
&lquo;Let me twine<LB REND=RIGHT>
Mine arms about that body, where against<LB>
My grained Ash an hundred times hath broke<LB>
And scarr'd the moon with splinters.&rquo;&mdash;IV, v, 109-112.<LB>
</BQ>
<P>[This last is, however, in the speech of Aufidius to Coriolanus.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] It is
a noticeable circumstance that these inflated speeches&mdash;as well as one or two in
<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I>&mdash;are put in the mouths of Roman heroes. I am not quite sure that
this is not one explanation and justification of them: they may have been Shake-
speare's ideal of what appertained to the Roman character. But apart from
their being true to the Roman manner, they may be justified also on the prin-
ciple of variety. It must have been a relief to Shakespeare's mind, ever hungry
for fresh types of character, to expatiate in the well-marked high astounding
ideal; and it is equally a relief to the student or spectator who may have followed
his career and dwelt with appeciative insight on his varied representation of
humanity. This is the broadest justification: if we consider more curiously,
other justifications make themselves palpable. The inflation of Coriolanus and
C&aelig;sar is not like Tamburlaine's, presented to us as a thing unquestioned and ad-
mired by those around them, as being, for aught said upon the stage to the con-
trary, the becoming language of heroic manhood. The violent language of Corio-
lanus is deprecated by his friends and raises a furious antagonism in his enemies.
Side by side with C&aelig;sar's high conception of himself we have the humorous
expression of his greatness by blunt Casca and the sneering of cynical Cassius.
In the case of C&aelig;sar, too, there is a profound contrast between his lofty declara-
tion of immovable constancy and the immediate dethronement of the god to life-
less clay. We must not take the rant of C&aelig;sar, Coriolanus, or Antony by itself
simply as rant, and wish with Ben Jonson that it had been blotted out. We
must consider whether it does not become the Roman character; we must remem-
ber that a varied artist like Shakespeare may be allowed an occasional rant as a
stretch to powers weary of the ordinary level; and, above all, we must observe

<P>210. <B>ruth</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, pity, compassion; from A. S. <I>hre&oacute;w,</I> grief,
sorrow. The word occurs in Early English in the forms <I>reowthe</I> or <I>reouthe;</I> later
<I>reuthe</I> or <I>rewthe</I> and <I>ruthe;</I> but, although we find in Icelandic the corresponding
word <I>hryggth,</I> it does not appear that the form with <I>th</I> occurs in Anglo-Saxon.
&lquo;Ruth&rquo; has survived in the adjective <I>ruthless,</I> but is only used by itself as an
archaic word. Compare <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> V, iii, 48: &lquo;Spur them to ruthful work,
rein them from ruth.&rquo;
<P>211. <B>Quarrie</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Why a quarry? I suppose not because he would
pile them square, but because he would give them for carrion to the birds of prey.
[This complete misunderstanding of the word &lquo;quarry&rquo; called forth from both
Monck Mason and Steevens an array of quotations wherein this word is used for
either slaughtered animals or men. Malone closed the controversy by remarking,
somewhat contemptuously, &lquo;Bullokar, in his <I>English Expositor,</I> 1616, says that
&ldquo;a quarry among hunters signifieth the reward given to hounds after they have
hunted, or the venison which is taken by hunting.&rdquo;&rquo; This sufficiently explains the
word of Coriolanus.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>212. <B>quarter'd</B>] Rev. <SC>John Hunter</SC>: That is, war-shunning; home-sheltered.
In North's <I>Plutarch</I> they are called &lquo;home-tarriers and house-doves.&rquo; [Hunter
was perhaps led to this roundabout interpretation by the line above, &lquo;They'll
sit by the fire and presume to know,&rquo; etc., but &lquo;quarter'd&rquo; here, I think, bears its
more usual meaning, cut in quarters, as in the sentence pronounced against trait-
ors. There is, thus, a certain propriety in Coriolanus using the judicial term in
connection with the rebellious citizens.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>214. <B>almost</B>] <SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>New Readings,</I> etc., <I>Blackwood's Maga.,</I> Sep., 1853, p.

<P>215. <B>lacke discretion</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, discretion, which is the better
part of valour, lacking which they might be supposed to have courage.
<P>218. <B>dissolu'd</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.,</I> s. v. 16): Of an assembly or collective body:
To break up into its individual constituents; to disperse, to lose its aggregate or
corporate character, 1513. More in Grafton <I>Chron.</I> (1568), II, 795: &lquo;The com-
pany dissolved and departed.&rquo;
<P>218. <B>Hang em</B>] <SC>Bayfield</SC> (p. 186): Altogether '<I>em</I> occurs 11 times [in <I>Coriol.</I>],
sometimes at the end of the line, sometimes in the middle. If the cases were
genuine, it would be quite clear that Shakespeare never knew what he might
write next, for <I>them</I> occurs in an unstressed position at least 32 times, and often
at the end of the line, as for instance: &lquo;May they perceive '<I>s</I> intent: he will re-
quire <I>them.</I>&rquo;&mdash;II, ii, 174. &lquo;You must not speak <I>of</I> that, you must desire <I>them</I>
To thinke upon you.&mdash;Thinke upon me? Hang '<I>em.</I>&rquo;&mdash;II, iii, 56. &lquo;Ere yet the
fight be done, packe up: downe with them!&rquo;&mdash;I, v, 11. If Shakespeare ever wrote
'<I>em,</I> surely he would have done so here.
<P>219. <B>an hungry</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Coriolanus imitates the rustic language of the
plebeians and uses what, in all probability, was a provincialism in Shakespeare's
time. In the <I>Merry Wives,</I> I, i, 280, Master Slender excuses himself with &lquo;I am
not a-hungry, I thank you forsooth&rquo;; and in <I>Twelfth Night,</I> II, iii, 136, Sir Andrew
Aguecheek says, &lquo;'Twere as good a deed as to drink when a man's a-hungry.&rquo;
<P>219. <B>sigh'd forth Prouerbes</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: &lquo;In a fastidious age, indeed,&rquo; re-
marks Archbishop Trench (<I>Proverbs and their Lessons,</I> pp. 2, 3), &lquo;and one of false
refinement, they may go nearly, or quite out of use among the so-called upper classes.
No gentleman, says Lord Chesterfield, or &ldquo;no man of fashion,&rdquo; as I think is his
exact phrase, &ldquo;ever uses a proverb.&rdquo; And with how fine a touch of nature Shake-
speare makes Coriolanus, the man who, with all his greatness, is entirely devoid
of all sympathy for the people, to utter his scorn of them in scorn of their prov-
erbs, and of their frequent employment of these.&rquo; [In a note on <I>King John,</I> I, i,
169, Wright calls attention to the use of proverbial sayings by Faulconbridge as
characteristic of the rusticity of his breeding.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>225. <B>breake . . . generosity</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, to give the final blow to the
nobles. &lquo;Generosity&rquo; is <I>high birth.</I>&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: So in <I>Meas. for Meas.,</I> &lquo;The
generous and gravest citizens.&rquo;&mdash;IV, vi, 13. [<SC>Wright</SC> also quotes in illustration:
&lquo;The generous islanders, By you invited, do attend your presence.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Othello,</I> III, iii,
280.]&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>) gives quite a different interpretation of
this: &lquo;Make it useless for generosity to have any heart, or yield any favors, since
by this measure feebleness was given strength enough to make <I>bold power</I> show
alarm. Martius, distrusting the people thoroughly, regards concessions as ex-
tremely dangerous. These vigorous speeches, pelting with direct hard words
those standing before him, are Shakespeare's freely dramatic creations. Yet he
has infused the spirit of Martius's advice to the Senate about the people into this
mould of his own. According to Plutarch, in the first disturbance, Martius held
that &ldquo;leuity . . . was a beginning of disobedience&rdquo; that would &ldquo;bring all to con-
fusion&rdquo;; also, in the second, that the people did not equal the nobles &ldquo;in true
nobility and valiantness.&rdquo; When Plutarch's words directly fit his situation, the
Poet finds them good enough to borrow with adaptations; when he needs some-
thing more direct and biting, as here, he himself fashions it, but not without
foundation.&rquo;
<P>227. <B>hang them . . . a'th Moone</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: So in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> &lquo;Let me
lodge Lichas on the horns o'the moon,&rquo; IV, xii, 45.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: So also
Heywood, <I>The Silver Age,</I> &lquo;Blowne And hang'd vpon the high hornes of the moone&rquo;
(<I>Works,</I> iii, 153).

<P>according to him, &lquo;they threw their caps so high as a suitable demonstration of
their aspiring thoughts&rquo;; though Coriolanus himself had said but a few lines
before that their thoughts aspired no higher than barely to get bread in order
to preserve themselves and their families from starvation. [Johnson in his <I>Preface</I>
says in reference to Heath's attacks on Warburton that the assailant &lquo;bites like
a viper, and would be glad to leave inflammations and gangrene behind him.&rquo;
In the present instance the malignant serpent might have added to the rancor
of his bite had he but remarked, in conclusion, that Rowe, in his 2<SUP>nd</SUP> ed., had,
long before, anticipated Warburton.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC> interprets these words in
accordance with the paraphrase given above by Heath.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Emulation&rquo;
in the present instance, I believe, signifies <I>faction.</I> &lquo;Shouting their emulation&rquo;
may mean &lquo;expressing the triumph of their faction by shouts.&rquo; Thus in <I>1 Henry
VI:</I> &lquo;the trust of England's honour keep off aloof with worthless emulation,&rquo; [IV,
iv, 21]. Again in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.:</I> &lquo;Whilst emulation in the army crept,&rquo; [II, ii,
212], i. e., <I>faction.</I>&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC> corroborates Steevens in this interpretation
of &lquo;emulation&rquo; and quotes, also, in illustration: &lquo;My heart laments that virtue
cannot live Out of the teeth of emulation,&rquo; <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> II, iii, 14. Wright calls
attention to the fact that in I, ix, 63 &lquo;<I>shout</I>&rquo; is spelt &lquo;shoot&rquo; in the first three Folios.
&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emendations,</I> etc., p. 347): &lquo;Shooting their emulation&rquo; is
altered [by the MS. Corrector] to &lquo;shouting their exultation.&rquo; Modern editors
have adopted <I>shouting;</I> and &lquo;emulation,&rquo; in the sense in which Shakespeare uses it,
does not seem to require change; <I>exultation,</I> however, better expresses what is in-
tended, and &lquo;shooting&rquo; for <I>shouting</I> shows that the compositor was careless.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC>
(ed. ii, p. 241): The MS. Corrector reads &lquo;Shouting their exultation.&rquo; But the text
is certainly right, and seems to be rightly explained by Malone.&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC> (ed., p.
119): The sense of the last word [&lquo;emulation&rquo;] is not very clear in this place (if
it does not mean &lquo;They shout at the success of their emulation&rquo;); perhaps we
ought to read instead of &lquo;their emulation&rquo; <I>the innovation.</I> &lquo;They shout at the
innovation, with which they have succeeded.&rquo; [This somewhat unfortunate
emendation Leo repeats in his collected edition of <I>Notes,</I> published in 1885,
twenty-one years later.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Herwegh</SC> (ap. <SC>Ulrici</SC>, p. 159): It is not very
evident that there is here a misprint. If there were, Leo's suggestion might
solve the difficulty. . . . If we retain &lquo;emulation&rquo; then, according to my opinion,
it must be understood that they exult over their rivalry with the nobles for the
dominance, or rather over the happy success of that rivalry.

<P>235. <B>Win vpon power</B>] <SC>Rann</SC>: That is, Gain ground from such concessions,
which will be improved into fresh occasions of insurrection.&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC>: Should
we not read &lquo;Win open power&rquo;? The rhythm and the sense of the passage leave
me hardly a doubt that we should.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, get the advantage
over authority. So in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> II, iv, 9, &lquo;You'll win two days upon me&rquo;; that
is, you will get the advantage of me by two days. Compare &lquo;got on the Antiates,&rquo;
III, iii, 5.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC> explains this as &lquo;gradually make an inroad upon the power
wielded by the nobles&rquo;; and objects to White's suggestion, &lquo;open,&rquo; since &lquo;the text
seems better to indicate the <I>gradual</I> process.&rquo; [It is somewhat difficult, I think,
to get the force of Deighton's objection; the preceding words &lquo;will in time&rquo;
convey the idea of gradual progress quite as well in one case as the other. As to
the other words in this line Deighton adds: &lquo;It seems tempting to read &ldquo;<I>throe</I> forth,&rdquo;
as in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> III, vii, 81, &ldquo;With news the time's in labour, and throes forth,
Each minute, some.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): That is, encroach on the
aristocracy (&lquo;the powerful class&rquo;).&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): That is, take
advantage of the power won to win more.
<P>236. <B>For Insurrections arguing</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: That is, for insurgents to debate upon.

is foreshadowed early. His prophecy, in fact, is a piece of dramatic irony.
