<P>been well nigh quelled not by the methods of Menenius or Coriolanus, but by the
grant of tribunes. The outbreak of war completes the business. And now the
finer side of Coriolanus, to which our attention is to be directed in this act, comes
into play. At the first whisper of danger he becomes the champion of Rome.
His high-bred courtesy towards his fellow captains contrasts markedly with his
former manner towards the Plebeians.
<P>243, 244. <B>I am glad on't . . . superfluity</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): The spirit
which prompts these words is surely that which ultimately leads to his great wrong
done against his country. [In the remaining part of this sentence] there is an echo
of a sentence in North's <I>Plutarch.</I> Velitr&aelig;, a Latin town, being depopulated by
a plague, prayed the Romans to send them &lquo;new inhabitants to replenish&rquo; their
town. The Senate thought this would be a good way of getting rid of many
&lquo;mutinous and seditious persons, being the superfluous ill humours that grievously
fed this disease&rquo; of civil turmoil at Rome.
<P>243. <B>vent</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, to dispose of, get rid of. See l. 217 above,
and III, i, 310.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC> also takes &lquo;vent&rquo; as here meaning to get rid of, but
further explains it as &lquo;to sell, and the idea is that of getting rid to foreigners of
goods not fit for home consumption, here, of course, by getting them killed off.&rquo;
As corroboration of this use of &lquo;vent&rquo; Deighton quotes Skeat (<I>Dict.,</I> s. v. Vent.
3.), who gives as an example: &lquo;The Merchant adventurers likewise . . . did hold
out bravely; taking off the commodities, . . . though they lay dead upon their
hands for want of vent,&rquo; Bacon, <I>Life of Henry VII,</I> ed. Lumby, p. 146, l. 6.

<P>249-253. <B>They haue a Leader . . . onely he</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): This

<P>254. <B>together?</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The folios print this as a question, and there

in this question of punctuation, Beeching is on the side of the majority of editors.

<P>255-257. <B>Were halfe . . . with him</B>] <SC>Gervinus</SC> (p. 753): In this declaration
how delicately is a very characteristic stain cast on the valour of Coriolanus!
He betrays by these words that his personal renown is of more value to him than
his party, his cause, his country; he would fight as a hireling against Aufidius,
no matter on which side!&mdash;<SC>Boas</SC> (<I>Sh. &amp; His Predecessors,</I> p. 489): Like Hotspur,
Coriolanus cares far more for personal glory than for the triumph of a common
cause, as is shown by his declaration about the Volscian general, Tullus Aufidius.
. . . This is to treat war merely as a gigantic duel between rival champions, and
to ignore those patriotic aspects of it which alone give it moral justification. It
is the same exaggerated passion for solely personal distinction that makes Corio-
lanus reject all material rewards for his services. He feels that the glory of
achievements such as his is tarnished by the acceptance of spoils, however splendid,
and similarly he refuses to listen to any laudation of his deeds not from humility,
but because he deems them above the reach of due recognition by the voices of
his fellow-men.&mdash;<SC>Prolss</SC> (p. 93): Here there is made evident a new virtue in
Marcius&mdash;he is without hate and envy. He recognises without reservation the

<P>279, 280. <B>Exeunt . . . Manet Sicin. &amp; Brutus</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): Ac-
cording to the modern method of dramatic construction&mdash;the method, that
is, of making the curtain fall at the climax of the scene&mdash;this scene would close,
I should think, at the exit of Coriolanus. Shakespeare, however, allows char-
acters to remain behind, as the Tribunes remain here, and wind up the scene
with further comments or some <I>slight extension</I> of the action. Thus in <I>Richard
II,</I> I, iii, when the stirring scene at the lists at Coventry has culminated in the
King's passing sentence on the rivals and then sweeping from the field with all
his train, Gaunt and Bolingbroke stay behind for an interview which a modern
playwright would throw into a scene. Cf. again <I>Mid. N. Dream,</I> I, i, 127, where
strictly it is an artificial device to let Hermia and Lysander remain behind to-
gether, while her father, Egeus, who is angry with Lysander for stealing her affec-
tions, leaves the stage with all the others. Another illustration is the conversa-
tion between Goneril and Regan at the end of the first scene in <I>Lear.</I> In such
continuations of the scene there is some risk of an anti-climax. I think that
this peculiar feature of the structure of Shakespeare's plays is attributable to the
scenic poverty of the Elizabethan stage, on which Shakespeare himself dwells

<P>so strongly in the first and fourth Prologues of <I>Henry V.</I> In the Elizabethan
theatre there was no curtain to fall, and practically no scenery to mark a change of
scene. Hence the tendency was to extend a scene instead of starting a fresh
one in a fresh locality, as if the playwright thought that certain of his <I>person&aelig;</I>
might as well stay behind as go off and return to the same spot.
<P>280. <B>Sicin. &amp; Brutus</B>] <SC>S. Lee</SC> (<I>Caxton Sh., Introd.,</I> p. xxxiv.): These repre-
sentatives of the popular faction, with whom Coriolanus has no bond of sym-
pathy, are the primary instruments of his ruin, and the contrast between their
natures and the character of the hero is drawn in high relief. The demagogues
are corrupt and cowardly bullies, and the rabble whom they dupe, although it
has some brighter aspects, is mainly characterised by fickleness and gullible
ignorance.
<P>286. <B>gird the Gods</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, to taunt them, use sarcasm
against them. Falstaff (<I>2 Henry IV:</I> I, ii, 7) says of himself, &lquo;Men of all sorts
take a pride to gird at me.&rquo; And in Earle's <I>Microcosmographie,</I> 6, we find the same
construction as here: &lquo;His life is a perpetuale Satyre, and hee is still girding the
ages vanity&rquo; (ed. Arber, p. 28). To &lquo;gird&rquo; (or &lquo;gyrd&rquo;) originally signified to smite
or strike, and hence in its figurative sense a &lquo;gird&rquo; or jest is analogous to <I>bob,</I>
which originally meant a blow or rap . . . That the original meaning of the word
was <I>blow</I> is evident from <I>Tam. of Shrew,</I> V, ii, 58: &lquo;<I>Bap.</I> O ho, Petruchio! Tranio
hits you now. <I>Luc.</I> I thank thee for that gird, good Tranio.&rquo;

&lquo;He that is proud eats up himself. Pride is his own glass, his own trumpet, his

<C>[288, 289. <B>The present Warres . . . so valiant</B>]</C>
<P>then we must conclude that when Shakespeare had a mind to say <I>A man was
eaten up with pride,</I> he was so great a blunderer in expression as to say <I>He was
eaten up with war.</I> But our poet wrote at a different rate, and the blunder is his
critic's. &lquo;The present wars devour him&rquo; is an imprecation and should be so
pointed. As much as to say, <I>May he fall in those wars!</I> The reason of the curse
is subjoined, for (says the speaker), having so much pride with so much valour,
his life, with increase of honours, is dangerous to the republic.&mdash;[The arrogant and
contemptuous tone of the foregoing doubtless caused&mdash;as the writer intended&mdash;
both consternation and pain, coming as it did from one who but a few short
years before had subscribed himself in many letters, &lquo;<I>ever, my dearest friend, yours
affectionately,</I> <SC>W. Warburton</SC>.&rquo; The head and front of Theobald's offence was
that he had not, as Warburton thought, been sufficiently recognisant of the deep
obligation he was under for the various notes and emendations which Warburton
had contributed for Theobald's own edition. Warburton made no mention of the
fact that Hanmer, his preceding editor, prints this line as an imprecation with
an exclamation point instead of the Folio's comma after &lquo;him&rquo;; and Hanmer does
not refer to Warburton as the source of this pointing. Hanmer should, therefore,
I think, be given credit for this reading in spite of Warburton's elucidation.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 82): Pointed [as an imprecation] in the two latter
moderns [Han. and Warb.], and properly, but what the first of them has put in

is, indeed, the sense which the Poet intended in &lquo;to be so valiant,&rquo; though a more
refin'd one is pitch'd upon for it by the last of those gentlemen.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I am
by no means convinced that Dr Warburton's punctuation or explanation is right.
The sense may be that &lquo;the present wars annihilate his gentler qualities.&rquo; To <I>eat

[the crown] most fine, most honour'd, most renown'd, Hast eat thy bearer up,&rquo; IV,
v, 165. To be &lquo;eat up with pride&rquo; is still a phrase in common and vulgar use.
&lquo;He is grown too proud to be so valiant&rquo; may signify &lquo;his pride is such as not to
deserve the accompanying of so much valour.&rquo; [&lquo;But it is difficult to see,&rquo; com-
ments W. A. Wright on the foregoing, &lquo;how &ldquo;the present wars,&rdquo; in which Corio-

his past achievements.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I concur with Mr Steevens. &lquo;The
present wars&rquo; Shakespeare uses to express the pride of Coriolanus grounded on

<P>Hanmer's pointing.&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 356): <I>To</I> was originally used not with the infinitive,
but with the gerund in <I>-e,</I> and, like the Latin &lquo;<I>ad</I>&rquo; with the gerund, denoted a
purpose. Thus &lquo;<I>to</I> love&rquo; was originally &lquo;<I>to</I> lovene,&rquo; <I>i e.,</I> &lquo;<I>to</I> (or <I>toward</I>) loving&rquo;
(ad amandum). Gradually, as <I>to</I> superseded the proper infinitival inflection, <I>to</I>
was used in other and more indefinite senses, &lquo;for,&rquo; &lquo;about,&rquo; &lquo;in,&rquo; &lquo;as regards,&rquo;
and, in a word, for any form of the gerund as well as for the infinitive. [Among
other examples of the infinitive thus indefinitely used Abbott quotes and para-
phrases l. 289: &lquo;Too proud to be (of being) so valiant.&rquo; Also: &lquo;&ldquo;To fright you
thus methinks I am too savage.&rdquo;&mdash;<I>Macbeth,</I> IV, ii, 70. Not &ldquo;too savage to fright
you,&rdquo; but &ldquo;<I>in</I> or <I>for</I> frighting you.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.) discards the Folio
pointing and, without comment, adopts Hanmer's.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. i.) follows the
Folio pointing, explaining the line, &lquo;his pride on account of his valour and success
in &ldquo;the present wars&rdquo; devours him.&rquo; Hudson likewise gives the line from <I>Tro. &amp;
Cress.,</I> &lquo;He that is proud eats up himself,&rquo; which both Theobald and Malone had
already quoted in support of this; and Hudson concludes his note with Malone's
interpretation of the latter part of the sentence. In his ed. ii. Hudson, influenced,
as ever, by Dyce, makes a complete recantation, and without reference to his
former opinion says: &lquo;The first part of this speech is imprecative: &ldquo;May the
present war devour him!&rdquo; that is, <I>make an end</I> of him.&rquo; In conclusion he retains
his agreement with Malone.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC>, both in his <I>Expositor</I> and in his text,
adopts Hanmer's punctuation; he likewise explains &lquo;to be,&rquo; l. 289, as the gerundial
infinitive with Malone and Hudson.&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>):
This is elliptically expressed, but we think the sense is obviously, &lquo;The wars absorb
him wholly: he is grown too proud of being so valiant.&rquo; In the speech of Gower,
as Chorus, in <I>Pericles,</I> IV, iv, we find: &lquo;And Pericles in sorrow all devoured,&rquo; [l.
25;] and to be &lquo;devoured by grief&rquo; or &lquo;eaten up by pride&rquo; are idioms still in use.
We think, therefore, that the idea of &lquo;pride in his own valour, strengthened by
the occasion for its display afforded by these wars, devours him entirely&rquo; is
presented by this sentence.&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): That is, May he perish in the
present wars! The consciousness of his being so valiant has made him too proud.
[The complete suppression of the fact that such an interpretation of l. 288 is based
upon a modern text and not upon the Folio reading may seem somewhat singular.
In fairness to Leo it may, however, be stated that such an omission is, I think, an
example of an avowed purpose in his Edition of <I>Coriolanus.</I> In his <I>Preface,</I>
p. vi, where, among other features which should constitute an <I>ideal</I> edition of
Shakespeare, he says: &lquo;Every passage that has succeeded in establishing its title
to respect, either by the agreement of the old editions or of later emendators,
should be adopted in the text, without the slightest mention of all arguments for
and against, which hitherto have been bandied about respecting it. The mention
of them is not of the least advantage to the public, and does not at all advance
the purification of the text. There are emendations which have stood the ordeal
of time, and the errors they are intended to remove, the errors of copyists,
printers, and early editors, errors which the rust of centuries has consecrated in
the eyes of fanatics, might at length be consigned to a lasting repose.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;Rev.
<SC>John Hunter</SC>: &lquo;Devour him,&rquo; that is, Take up all his thoughts; engage his whole
soul; actuate his whole conduct. We similarly say of a very proud person that
he is <I>eaten up</I> with pride. &lquo;The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up,&rquo; <I>Psalm</I>
lxix, 9, and <I>John,</I> ii, 17, [where this verse from the <I>Psalm</I> is quoted.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>].&mdash;<SC>Rolfe</SC>:

<P>We take this to be the expression of a wish, as Hanmer makes it.&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC> (p.
286): The punctuation of the Folio, though not always to be depended upon, may
[here] be accepted with confidence; it certainly is not an advantageous exchange to
put a note of exclamation after &lquo;The present wars devour him&rquo;; the Tribunes are
telling each other what they think of Coriolanus; how proud he was; how he had
scorned and taunted them when they were appointed tribunes; they aggravate his
offence by the remark, while perhaps they comfort themselves by the reflection,
that even the gods themselves&mdash;those most high sacrosanct irresponsible arbiters
&mdash;even the moon, the very ideal of modesty, he would not scruple to &lquo;gird&rquo;&mdash;to
mock at; what wonder, then, if <I>their</I> tribunitian majesty, <I>their</I> tribunitian modesty
he despised, he insulted! And now what further? Do they, as some would have
it, invoke a curse on Coriolanus, and wish him perdition by the wars? No such
thing. &lquo;This man,&rquo; they continue, &lquo;who has no regard for god or tribune, what
does he care for?&rquo; &lquo;<I>The wars</I>&rquo;&mdash;for the poet here, with a license which is common
to him . . . uses <I>the plural form as an exact equivalent of the singular,</I> an example
of which we have in <I>Cymb.,</I> IV, iii, 43, where &lquo;These present <I>wars</I>&rquo; is said of a <I>war
then instant</I>&mdash;&lquo;the <I>wars</I>&rquo; then, or, as we may express it, the <I>war,</I> such as at that
very moment was brewing with the Volsci&mdash;&lquo;this is his devouring passion; he is
carried away, he is swallowed up, he is wholly absorbed by the <I>war;</I> and this is how
he has grown&mdash;grown far &ldquo;too proud&rdquo;; and the reason he is so proud is because he
is so valiant.&rquo; Such I conceive to be a fair gloss on a much misconceived passage,
though I am not quite sure that I have correctly expounded just the fag end of it.
&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Henry Irving Sh.</I>) follows Hanmer without either note or comment;
in the <I>Falcon Ed.,</I> some five years later, he accepts the Folio reading, placing an
exclamation point after &lquo;grown,&rquo; but this is doubtless a misprint. In the latter
edition Beeching, in reference to l. 288, says: &lquo;Is this a statement or an impreca-
tion? The Folio has a comma; reading which the sense will be, &ldquo;These warlike
times spoil him by making him proud; the pride of valour devours him.&rdquo; Cf.
<I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> II, iii, 164, &ldquo;He that's proud eats up himself.&rdquo; This sense seems to
suit best with the speech of Sicinius which follows. If it be construed as an
imprecation, <I>the present wars</I> will mean &ldquo;the war now set on foot.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Wordsworth</SC>
(<I>Historical Plays,</I> i, 116), in explanation for his omission of these lines, says: &lquo;The
former clause, though probably imprecative, is doubtful; the latter, though capable
of explanation, is unbearably harsh.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Page</SC> [follows Hanmer's reading, but adds:]
The Folio reading may be right, in the sense of &lquo;His military pride, elated at the
thought of acquiring additional glory in the impending war, takes complete
possession of him.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>) follows the Folio, but remarks
that &lquo;&ldquo;devour him&rdquo; is rather an optative than an indicative. Brutus goes on,
&ldquo;Such valour, coupled with such pride, is dangerous.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>),
following Hanmer, remarks that &lquo;the passage is commonly interpreted thus&rquo; as
an imprecation, and after quoting Perring's interpretation of the Folio reading,
says in conclusion, &lquo;But the allusion to <I>particular</I> wars (&ldquo;the present wars&rdquo;) surely
does not suit a <I>general</I> description of Coriolanus's character. One would have
expected &ldquo;War&rdquo; personified, with some epithet descriptive of its general attributes,
or &ldquo;the wars&rdquo; (without &ldquo;present&rdquo;).&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Stanley Wood</SC> (<I>Oxford &amp; Cambridge Sh.</I>):
That is, he is consumed with pride, the result of his triumphs in war.&mdash;<SC>H. D.
Weiser</SC>, following Hanmer, says: &lquo;Not to be regarded as an assertion, in view of
the fears expressed in the remainder of Brutus's words.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Shakespeare</I>):

<P>Mr Craig evidently intended to retain this, practically the Folio punctuation, [<I>i. e.,</I>
a semicolon instead of a comma], though he had not set down his reasons. The
sentence stretches with difficulty to a meaning which is perhaps expressed as
well as anywhere else by Perring [see <I>ante</I>]. . . . The objection to the interpretation
that the <I>present</I> wars would not be given as the cause of a permanent character-
istic of Coriolanus does not seem altogether valid if we consider that it is not the
<I>existence</I> of the quality of pride in him, but its excessive manifestation <I>at the time</I>
that has given rise to the dialogue. After all, most readers will prefer the usual
punctuation (Hanmer's) and sense: May he fall in these wars!&mdash;[In all cases where
the Folio text or punctuation yields an intelligible meaning it should, I think, be
retained; that it does so in the present instance is manifest by the several para-
phrases given in the foregoing notes. On the other hand, while Hanmer's and
Warburton's change is more forcible than the original, it is actually a refinement
of expression and is, therefore, <I>meo judicio,</I> unnecessary. I have placed in the
<I>Text. Notes</I> the names of those editors only who have followed Hanmer's pointing
without comment, since, in general, a reading given in the commentary is not
repeated in the <I>Text. Notes.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>290. <B>good successe</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: In Shakespeare's time &lquo;success&rquo; was fre-
quently a colourless word, which required a qualifying adjective &lquo;good&rquo; or &lquo;ill.&rquo;
Compare <I>Joshua,</I> i, 8: &lquo;Then thou shalt have good success.&rquo; The modern usage is,
however, also common in Shakespeare. See I, ix, 90. [See also <I>Macbeth,</I> I, vii,
3, 4, &lquo;and catch With his surcease success,&rquo; where &lquo;success&rquo; means simply <I>termi-
nation.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>291. <B>the shadow</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): A man's imaginary conduct to his
shadow is used by Shakespeare several times as an illustration of character.
Gratiano will fence with his shadow (<I>Mer. of Ven.,</I> I, ii, 66); Malvolio practises
behaviour to his (<I>Twelfth Night,</I> II, v, 21); a drunkard is one who discourses
fustian with his (<I>Othello,</I> II, iii, 282); a madman curses his for a traitor (<I>Lear,</I>
III, iv, 58); &lquo;Coriolanus's solitariness&rquo; (as Plutarch called it) or &lquo;singularity&rquo;
(l. 311) could not be better expressed.

<P>300. <B>cry out of Martius</B>] That is, cry out <I>concerning</I> or <I>about</I> Marcius. <SC>Abbott</SC>
(&sect; 174) will furnish many examples of this meaning. This were hardly worth
the noting were it not that <SC>Schmidt</SC> takes exception to the silence of other editors
on this point, which reticence he thinks takes it too easily for granted that &lquo;of&rquo;
here means <I>about</I> or <I>concerning.</I> &lquo;But this,&rquo; he says, &lquo;after &ldquo;cry out&rdquo; is impos-
sible&rquo;; and therefore declares that it is &lquo;more likely that &ldquo;of&rdquo; here stands for
<I>on,</I> as exactly similar in &ldquo;he cried out of sack,&rdquo; [<I>Henry V:</I> II, iii, 297], &lquo;he called
out <I>for</I> sack.&rquo;&mdash;In this last passage &lquo;of&rquo; means, as in the present line, <I>about,</I> and
not as Schmidt takes it. Is it necessary to instance as examples the titles to each
of Bacon's <I>Essays?</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>303, 304. <B>Opinion that . . . Cominius</B>] <SC>Roderick</SC> (ap. <SC>Edwards</SC>, <I>Canons,</I>
etc., p. 275): This passage, as it stands here, presents us with a strange kind of
mock-reasoning. Brutus and Sicinius are reasoning together about Martius's
contenting himself with the <I>second</I> place in the army, leaving the <I>first</I> to Cominius.
&lquo;Herein (says Brutus) he acts prudently; for, Fame being his motive, and he
having already an established character, he by this means less risks the losing
of it. For, in case of any miscarriage, the fault will be thrown on Cominius, the
General; and giddy censurers will be apt enough to cry: It would have been
otherwise if Martius had had the management!&rquo; To this observation Sicinius
might very pertinently add the following: &lquo;That, moreover, if things should go
well the opinion of the people was so firmly to Martius that he would certainly carry
off some part of the praise due to Cominius.&rquo; And this sense will be obtained:

beyond his usual peculiarity of character, he enters upon the war,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> whether

tricity.&rquo; . . . Malvolio is advised in the letter (II, v, 164): &lquo;Be opposite with a
kinsman, surly with servants, . . . put thyself into the trick of <I>singularity,</I>&rquo; on which
he comments: &lquo;I will be <I>proud, . . .</I> I will wash off gross acquaintance.&rquo; There,
as here, the essential notion seems to me to be &lquo;unlike to other people, apart from
others,&rquo; and the nearest rendering is &lquo;peculiarity.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: That is, over and
above his natural singularity (which, Sicinius implies, may be taken for granted in
anything he may do).

if needful, <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 30.
<P>1. <B>Tullus Auffidius</B>] <SC>Prolss</SC> (p. 94): After we have thus been made acquainted
with one despised opponent, at whom Marcius has railed, the Roman people
and its Tribunes, Shakespeare, in this second scene of the drama, presents to us
</CC>
<PB N=80>
<HE>80 <I>THE TRAGEDIE OF</I> [<SC>act i, sc.</SC> ii.</HE>
<BO>
That they of Rome are entred in our Coun$ailes,<LB N=3>

<CC>
<P>in person another opponent, one both sought for and highly regarded by Marcius,
Tullus Aufidius. He is perhaps quite as blood-thirsty and brave as Marcius; in
any case he possesses quite as strong a feeling of self-confidence, which draws
him towards Marcius in no less degree than that which attracts the latter. Yet he
has no word of praise for Marcius, but rather he cherishes the wish to conquer him
either now or later, in honourable battle, because the fame of Marcius allows
him no rest. This scene as well as the following is designed to foreshadow and
prepare for the battle scenes. The sudden uprising of the Romans has com-
pletely thwarted the designs of the Volscians to fall upon them unprepared. They
are themselves on the point of attack. Corioli, which must bear the first brunt,
must protect itself, and, while Aufidius with the army awaits the enemy in the
field, must, if needful, bring reinforcements.
<P>1. <B>Coriolus</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC>, whose stage-direction here reads, &lquo;<I>Corioles. The Senate-
house,</I>&rquo; says: &lquo;This is the standing form of the name of the Volscian town not
only in Shakespeare but also in North's translation.&rquo; Schmidt has evidently
overlooked the present line, and likewise two other passages, I, iv, 3 (stage-
direction) and I, iv, 23, where there is still another variation in the spelling, viz.:
&lquo;Corialus&rquo;; in the six other passages wherein the name occurs it is spelt &lquo;Corioles&rquo;
as Schmidt gives it; this last, as he says, is the only form in which the name
appears in North's translation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>S. Lee</SC> (<I>Caxton Sh., Introd.,</I> p. xxxiii.): The
character of Aufidius is developed by Shakespeare on lines which Plutarch sug-
gested, and the mingling in him of meanness and liberality lacks completeness
in either author. At the opening of the play he figures as a brave soldier, &lquo;a
lion&rquo; whom Coriolanus is &lquo;proud to hunt,&rquo; but the rivalry between the two
warriors has generated a personal hatred which evokes a characteristic divergence
of expression. It is Coriolanus's highest ambition to meet and kill his hated
adversary in a fair personal encounter. Aufidius confesses that he cares not by
what device he overcome his enemy, provided only he get the better of him.
&mdash;<SC>Bradley</SC> (<I>Coriolanus,</I> p. 16): The drawing of the character of Aufidius seems
to me by far the weakest spot in the drama. At one place, where he moralizes
on the banishment of the hero, Shakespeare, it appears to some critics, is himself
delivering a speech which tells the audience nothing essential and ends in desper-
ate obscurity, [IV, vii, 30-59]. Two other speeches have been criticized. In the
first, Aufidius, after his defeat in the field, declares that, since he cannot overcome
his rival in fair fight, he will do it in any way open to him, however dishonour-
able. The other is his lyrical cry of rapture when Coriolanus discloses himself
in the house at Antium. The intention in both cases is clear. Aufidius is con-
trasted with the hero as a man of much slighter and less noble nature, whose
lively impulses, good and bad, quickly give way before a new influence, and
whose action is in the end determined by the permanent pressure of ambition
and rivalry. But he is a man of straw. He was wanted merely for the plot,
and in reading some passages in his talk we seem to see Shakespeare yawning as
he wrote.

<P>3. <B>entred in</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, initiated into, admitted to; and so, ac-
quainted with. Compare &lquo;<I>man-enter'd</I>&rquo; in II, ii, 107. The term is perhaps bor-
rowed from the Universities, where it still survives, and this is rendered more
probable by the recurrence of the word &lquo;proceed,&rquo; which has also a technical
academic sense. An undergraduate enters the University and &lquo;proceeds&rquo; to a
degree, and the taking a degree in any faculty, such as arts, law, physic or divinity,
is called &lquo;proceeding&rquo; in that faculty. Bacon says of travellers (<I>Essay xviii.</I>):
&lquo;He that travelleth into a country, before he hath some entrance into the language,
goeth to schoole, and not to travaile,&rquo; where entrance = initiation, preliminary
instruction.
<P>6. <B>What euer . . . thought one</B>] <SC>Boswell</SC>: Ellpitically, whatever <I>things.</I>&mdash;
<SC>Delius</SC>: &lquo;Have&rquo; is here the subjunctive, that is, <I>may have;</I> hardly as Boswell
explains it.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC>: In order to retain the interrogative form of this sentence
as in the Folios it is not possible to take &lquo;have&rquo; as an ellipsis, as does Boswell;
still less as a subjunctive, as does Delius, since both are ungrammatical; but after
the word &lquo;what&rquo; we must supply the foregoing word &lquo;counsels,&rquo; a use of the pronoun
which would not be unusual, but, on the other hand, is quite customary.&mdash;<SC>W. A.
Wright</SC>: If the reading of the Folio be correct we must understand &lquo;what&rquo; to
mean <I>what things.</I> Delius regards &lquo;have&rquo; as the subjunctive, but this cannot be.
In <I>Henry V:</I> II, ii, 75 the first Folio reads: &lquo;Why what reade you there, That
haue so cowarded and chac'd your blood Out of apparance.&rquo;

<P>usual, and &lquo;impress'd&rquo; only the legal word now.&mdash;<SC>Skeat</SC> (<I>Dict.,</I> s. v. (2).): To
hire men for service, to engage men by earnest-money for the public service, to
carry men off forcibly to become sailors or soldiers. The Dictionaries do not
explain this word at all well; the only adequate explanation is in Wedgwood. It
is quite certain, as he shews, that <I>press</I> is here a corruption of the old word <I>prest,</I>
ready, because it was customary to give earnest-money to a soldier on entering
service, just as to this day a recruit receives a shilling. This earnest-money
was called <I>prest-money,</I> i. e., ready-money advanced, and to give a man such money
was to <I>imprest</I> him, now corruptly written <I>impress.</I> &lquo;At a later period the practise
of taking for the public service by <I>compulsion</I> made the word to be understood as
if it signified to force men into the service, and the original reference to earnest-
money was lost sight of,&rquo; Wedgwood.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> adopts Malone's explanation of
<I>press'd</I> as meaning <I>constrained.</I>&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC> (<I>Glossary</I>): That is, impressed.
Nothing to do with <I>prest,</I> &lquo;ready&rquo; (Latin <I>pr&aelig;sto,</I> Fr. pret.), which could not be used
as an active participle.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): That is, levied an army. Shake-
speare uses <I>press</I> and <I>impress</I> several times with the idea of compulsory military
service. Cf. <I>Richard II:</I> III, ii, 58, &lquo;For every man that Bolingbroke hath press'd
To lift shrewd steel against our golden crown,&rquo; etc. See also <I>1 Henry IV:</I> I, i, 21;
<I>Hamlet,</I> I, i, 75 (&lquo;such impress of shipwrights&rquo;).

<P>28. <B>ere (almost) Rome</B>] <SC>P. Simpson</SC> (<I>Shakespearian Punctuation,</I> p. 89) quotes
the present line in illustration of parentheses used to mark &lquo;a qualifying expression
or an afterthought,&rquo; and further quotes &lquo;That (almost) might'st haue coyn'd
me into Golde,&rquo; <I>Henry V:</I> II, ii, 98. The use of parentheses as a guide to the man-
ner in which the word or words enclosed are to be spoken is again treated by
Simpson in his article, <I>The Bibliographical Study of Shakespeare</I> (<I>Proceedings of
Oxford Bibliographical Society,</I> 1922-23, p. 33); he there quotes from Richard Mul-
caster's <I>Elementarie</I> (1582, pp. 148-153): &lquo;<I>Of Distinction,</I>&rquo; as follows: &lquo;<I>Paren-
thesis</I> is expressed by two half circles . . . and in reading warneth vs, that the words
inclosed by them, ar to be pronounced with a lower and quikker voice, then the
words before or after them.&rquo; &lquo;Modern punctuation,&rquo; says Simpson, &lquo;aims at
making a sentence clear by marking off the clauses; it is logical, at least in inten-
tion. Elizabethan stopping, on the other hand, aimed at guiding the reader.
It was elocutionary and rhetorical in principle.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 29) gives other
instances wherein &lquo;almost&rquo; follows the word it qualifies.

<P>33. <B>for the remoue</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: The first part of this sentence is without
meaning. The General had told the Senators that the <I>Romans</I> had <I>prest a power,</I>
which was on foot. To which the words in question are the answer of a Senator.
And to make them pertinent we should read them thus: &lquo;<I>fore they</I> remove Bring
up your army,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> Before that power, already on foot, be in motion, bring up
your army; then he corrects himself and says, but I believe you will find your
intelligence groundless, the Romans are not yet prepared for us.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I do
not see the nonsense or the impropriety of the old reading. Says the senator to
Aufidius, <I>Go to your troops, we will garrison</I> Corioli. If the Romans besiege us,
bring up your army <I>to remove them.</I> If any change should be made, I would read:
for <I>their</I> remove.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 411): Mr Warburton, in explaining his conjecture,
hath made a very pleasant blunder, which the vulgar would be apt to call a bull.
[Heath here gives Warburton's interpretation.] It will perhaps puzzle Mr War-
burton's philosophy to explain, how the Roman power could set down, and lay
siege to Corioli, before they were in motion. But the common reading, &lquo;for the
remove&rquo; was perfectly right, if he had but endeavored to understand it. The
sense is, In order to oblige them to raise the siege, bring up your army; in the
mean time we are fully sufficient to guard the city.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;The remove&rquo; and
&lquo;<I>their</I> remove&rquo; are so near in sound that the transcriber's ear might easily have
deceived him. But it is always dangerous to let conjecture loose where there is
no difficulty.

<P><B>Scene III.</B>] <SC>Miss C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): This scene was set in the rear-
stage, whose compartment-like semi-separation from the fore-stage could simulate,
without interruption for stage-setting, an interior somewhat removed from the
outdoor turmoil of the preceding part of the action. There could conveniently be
placed the two <I>lowe stooles</I> where Volumnia and Virgilia <I>set them downe</I> and sewed.
Possibly when Volumnia and Valeria made their exeunt &lquo;over the threshold,&rquo;
which Virgilia declared she would not pass, nor turn her <I>solemnesse out a doore</I>
as Valeria begged her to do, the effect for the audience was that she was still at
home in Rome, as the curtains, with which the rear-stage seems to have been fur-
nished in Shakespeare's plays, closed her from view, after the other ladies were
seen to pass through the central door in the rear-stage into the &lquo;tyring-room.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Rhodes</SC> (<I>The Stagery of Sh.,</I> p. 40): The setting of properties upon the after-stage

<P>in no way precluded, but usually demanded the action&mdash;at least in part&mdash;taking
place upon the fore-stage. Indeed, in very few scenes was the action confined
to the after-stage. . . . Again, because &lquo;moveables&rquo; were used in a scene, it does
not always follow that they were discovered on the after-stage. (<I>Note,</I> p. 98:
In <I>The Taming of the Shrew,</I> as revived for continuous performance in full text by
Sir John Martin Harvey, in 1913, the stage properties, such as chairs, tables, and
so on, were placed in position, in full view of the audience, by the servants dressed
&lquo;in the period.&rquo; This method was perhaps due to his adviser, Mr William Poel,
who has always been enamoured with it; but there is no reason to suppose that
on the stage of Shakespeare it was the general practice or anything but an ex-
pediency. Moreover, where the men appeared, to move properties, it is usually
clear that they appeared in the dramatic character of household servants. Some-
times, however, it was otherwise. As Mr Puff said to the scenemen in <I>The Critic</I>
(1779): &lquo;It is always awkward, in a tragedy, to have you fellows coming on in
your playhouse liveries to remove things. I wish it could be managed better.&rquo;)
In <I>Coriolanus,</I> Act I, sc. iii, whose initial direction is: &lquo;They set them downe on
two lowe stooles and sowe,&rquo; was played on the fore-stage, since the after-stage
could not be used &lquo;with set movables&rquo; in two successive scenes, and it was needed
for the next scene, which is before the Gates of Corioli. This is the only direction
in Shakespeare which points to the early origin of &lquo;Two chairs to the front. It's
a custom in our profession,&rquo; as it is styled in Robertson's <I>David Garrick</I> (1864).
[Who shall decide when two such critics disagree? Miss Porter's descriptive ar-
rangement&mdash;be it said nowise in disparagement&mdash;is evidently based on a theoretic
knowledge of the Elizabethan stage, while that of Rhodes is, just as evidently,
based on the pragmatic. His illustrations of the actual working out of other
scenes inclines me to favour his view of the present case.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>1. <B>Enter Volumnia and Virgilia</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): The main purpose of
this scene is to show up the character of Volumnia, the typical Roman matron,
to whom Virgilia is obviously meant as a foil. Volumnia is important not only
<I>per se</I> in that she has so much to do with the actual working of the plot but also
in relation to Coriolanus, who is what he is largely through her and her training.
As a scene of domestic interest set in a framework of natural stress this scene
may be compared with the scene between Lady Macduff and Ross in <I>Macbeth,</I>
IV, ii. The resemblance is heightened by the introduction of the little boy.
There are not very many portraits of children in Shakespeare's plays, and (as has
been well said) about almost all of them clings a certain pathos. Witness, above
all, Prince Arthur in <I>King John.</I> Perhaps, indeed, this lies not in the presentment
of the individual child, but in the ever-felt contrast between simple childhood
and great surroundings.
<P>3. <B>Volum. I pray you, etc.</B>] <SC>Delius</SC> (<I>Jahrbuch,</I> vol. v, p. 268): The intimate
conversation of the mother and wife of the hero, to whom later their friend Valeria
comes, is carried on in trustful terms bespeaking domestic relations in homely
prose. Only as Volumnia, in the ecstasy of her maternal pride, describes her son
in the middle of the turmoil of battle, does she rise to expressing herself in blank
verse. [In this long article Delius attempts to show by examples the various
reasons for Shakespeare's use of prose and blank verse. On the blank half-page
at the beginning the late Editor of this edition&mdash;whose lightest word ever gave

in Spenser, <I>Faerie Queene,</I> VII, vii, 56: &lquo;<I>troph&eacute;e,</I> a trophee, a sign or mark of vic-

Shakespeare, viz.: <I>All's Well,</I> II, iii, 146, &lquo;&mdash;on every grave A lying trophy&rquo;;
<I>Henry V:</I> V, <I>Prol.</I> 21: &lquo;Giving full trophy, signal and ostent&rquo;; <I>Ibid.,</I> V, i, 75:
&lquo;worn as a memorable trophy of predeceased valour&rquo;; <I>Hamlet,</I> IV, v, 214: &lquo;No
trophy, sword, nor hatchment o'er his bones.&rquo; In all these passages the word is
spelt <I>trophee</I> in the Folio. Its spelling in the present line, &lquo;trophe,&rquo; is, therefore,
merely an error of the compositor. It is, perhaps, interesting to observe that
by the time of the second Folio, 1632, the word had assumed its present form,
<I>trophy.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

them.&rquo; Although the witless notes of E. H. Seymour, published in 1805, have
long since been banished from the pages of this edition, it is but fair to say that
this reading (&lquo;At Grecian swords, contemning&rquo;) was first proposed by him, thus
anticipating Collier's conjecture and the punctuation of the Cambridge Edd.,
neither of whom, however, mention Seymour as the originator.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Verplanck</SC>:
&lquo;Contenning,&rquo; I think, is clearly an error for <I>contemning.</I> With that correction
the sense is clear, giving the strong but natural image of the hero's forehead
spitting forth its blood; not as from the injury of the enemies&rquo; sword, but as in
contempt of them. This reading differs little whether we take the <I>sword</I> of F<SUB>1</SUB> or
the &lquo;swords&rquo; of F<SUB>2</SUB>. [Verplanck objects to Capell's reading on the ground that thus
taking &lquo;contending&rquo; substantively yields &lquo;a very harsh and obscure sense&rquo; and loses
&lquo;the bold figure of the warrior's forehead thus bleeding as in contempt of his adver-
sary.&rquo;&mdash;It will be noticed that Verplanck does not credit the reading <I>contemning</I>
to his predecessor, Collier.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> p. 209): The self-
evident correction, which I long since adopted, of &lquo;At Grecian swords contemning,&rquo;
should have been also adopted by Mr Collier when he suggested that <I>contemning</I>
seemed &lquo;possibly the word which was written by Shakespeare,&rquo; and yet contented
himself with the very inferior reading &lquo;contending.&rquo; [Collier might have replied
to Singer &lquo;Tu quoque&rquo;&mdash;as Singer in his first ed., 1826, had also contented himself
with the very inferior reading; in his second ed., 1856, three years later than the
foregoing note in <I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> he prints &lquo;contemning,&rquo; without any mention
either of Collier's conjecture or the MS. correction, remarking merely that he adopts
this reading because he considers that &lquo;it improves the passage,&rquo; certainly a lapse
in editorial courtesy to which Collier in his second ed. resentfully calls his attention.
Singer's remark that he had &lquo;long since adopted&rquo; the reading, <I>contemning,</I> is difficult

<C>[46. <B>At Grecian sword. Contenning</B>]</C>
<P>reading of these lines: &lquo;At Grecian swords contending.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. i.): Collier's
MS. Corrector reads: &lquo;At Grecian swords contemning.&rquo; . . . But qy. is &lquo;<I>contemning</I>
<SC>at</SC>&rquo; legitimate phraseology? (Since this note was written W. N. Lettsom has
proposed to me, &lquo;As Grecian swords contemning.&rquo;)&mdash;[In his ed. ii. Dyce adopted
Collier's MS. Corrector's reading, but placed a comma after the word &lquo;swords.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC> (ed., p. 120): Dyce is right in asking whether &lquo;contemning at&rquo; is legiti-
mate phraseology. But Volumnia does not speak about &lquo;contemning at&rquo;; she says
<I>spit at,</I> and the construction of the phrase must be: when contemning it spit forth
blood at Grecian sword.&mdash;<SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 48): Why <I>contending,</I> which is a reciprocal
process, involving both Grecian and Trojan swords? Something more definite,
something peculiar to the enemy, seems required, as <I>e. g.,</I> &lquo;at the stroke of Grecian
swords.&rquo; My suggestion, in accordance with this view, is the alteration of merely
a single letter: &lquo;At Grecian swords' <I>contunding,</I>&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> the forehead spits forth blood
at the bruising inflicted by Grecian swords. The objection against this, that
<I>contund</I> is a verb not employed by our author, although he has <I>contusion,</I> and
rarely by anybody else, is certainly formidable, and I can set against it only the
pleas that the emendation requires the smallest of changes in the text, that it yields
the exact sense wanted, and that Shakespeare was in the constant habit of using
what we should now consider uncouth and pedantic terms derived from the Latin,
yet seldom without a precise and even forcible meaning. The last clause of this
remark is, in fact, exemplified by the proposed emendation. The Latin <I>contundo</I>
signifies to batter, bang, bruise; and since the old Grecian warriors wore helmets
that completely hid the forehead, the only way of drawing blood from that part
with the sword was by <I>contunding</I> the casque. Had our author written <I>piercing</I> or
<I>pricking,</I> the language would have been less appropriate.&mdash;[On philological grounds
alone Bailey's extravagant proposal is quite inadmissible. The earliest example
of the verb <I>contund,</I> in the sense <I>to bruise</I> or hurt the human body, is given in the
<I>N. E. D.</I> as 1654. Prior to that date the verb is used only in its technical sense
to break or macerate in pieces for medicinal purposes.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. i.):
There can be little doubt that <I>contemning</I> is the right word, and certainly it makes
a most apt and striking figure. [In his ed. ii. Hudson prints from Dyce's ed. ii,
&lquo;swords, contemning.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC>: I will not say that I am certain that
the compositor was in error [when he printed &lquo;Contenning&rquo; as the name of the
gentle-woman.] The reading of F<SUB>2</SUB> is given in the text because it has been generally
received and I have no better one to substitute, rather than from any confidence
on my part that it is what Shakespeare wrote. The word &lquo;contending&rquo; is at least
superfluous. [White records the reading of Collier's MS. Corrector without com-
ment.]&mdash;<SC>Cambridge Edd.</SC> (<I>Note</I> II.): Perhaps we might read, &lquo;At Grecian, con-
temning't.&rquo; It has also been suggested to us that &lquo;<I>Contenning</I>&rquo; is the remnant of
a stage-direction [<I>containing herself</I>]. But we know of no similar instance in any
old edition.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): The reading we have adopted in the text,
&lquo;at Grecian sword-contending&rquo; (as if it spit forth blood at Grecian sword-contest),
makes no higher claim for acceptance than the conjectures already proposed. The
hyphen between &lquo;sword&rquo; and &lquo;contending&rquo; would account for the period of the
Folio; likewise a carelessly written <I>d</I> could easily be mistaken for a <I>u,</I> and thus
<I>contending</I> was made &lquo;contenuing.&rquo; But perhaps there actually remains in &lquo;<I>con-
tending</I>&rquo; a name, and the whole line is not as corrupt as it appears. [It will be
noticed that Schmidt throughout his note gives the Folio reading as <I>contenuing.</I>

<SC>Perring</SC> (p. 289) rejects the participle &lquo;contemning&rquo; as it &lquo;does not add much

as &lquo;spit forth blood&rquo;; likewise the reading of F<SUB>2</SUB>, while it must claim attention,
Perring casts aside; then, since the word in F<SUB>1</SUB> is in Italics and is followed by a full

one of the stage-directions which Perring has &lquo;taken at random&rquo; from <I>Timon</I>
appears in the Folio text; they are all additions by later editors. Further com-
ment is, therefore, needless. Perring ends his remarks with the valuable infor-
mation &lquo;that stage-directions were usually printed in italics.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Rolfe</SC>:
&lquo;<I>Contemning</I>&rquo; is, on the whole, the best emendation that has been proposed.

Virgilia, or &lquo;content thee&rquo;? Such a phrase is constant in Shakespeare to bespeak
acquiescence, as, <I>e. g., Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> III, ii, 135: &lquo;Pray you, content you,&rquo; as it is
found, too, in Scripture, <I>2 Kings,</I> v, 23: &lquo;Be content, take two talents.&rquo; Here it
expresses Volumnia's desire that Virgilia will allow of Valeria's visit, and turning
to the Gentleman (<I>sic</I>) she bids her to be admitted.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> in both the <I>Henry
Irving Sh.</I> and the <I>Falcon Sh.</I> reads: &lquo;At Grecian swords, contemning,&rquo; with the note
that this is Collier's reading; as will be noticed, by reference to the <I>Text. Notes,</I>
it is a combination of Collier's reading and the punctuation of the Cambridge
Edd. and was originally given by Seymour.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio
Sh.</I>): &lquo;<I>Contenning</I>&rquo; after all is likelier to be some slightly misprinted name (names
being commonly put in Italic) than a verb referring to &lquo;swordes.&rquo; It is common
for Shakespeare to introduce a servant's name thus casually. He does so in IV,
v, 5, in the case of a servant of Auffidius, whom he names <I>Cotus.</I>&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: Per-
haps &lquo;<I>Contenning</I>&rquo; is a name corrupted. If it is not, then Collier's <I>contemning</I> is
excellent and may be right.&mdash;[<SC>Verity, Deighton, Chambers, Page</SC>, and <SC>Gordon</SC>
follow Collier's and Seymour's reading, merely recording the textual emendations
proposed.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>51. <B>Enter Valeria</B>] <SC>C. C. Clarke</SC> (<I>Sh. Characters,</I> p. 485): There is but one sub-
ordinate character among the females in this play, and that is Valeria, the friend
of Volumnia and Virgilia. The part is necessarily a very slight one; yet, being a
patrician lady, and an intimate of the principals, the poet takes occasion to exalt
her qualities with the reader through a third party. Coriolanus describes her as
<BQ>
&lquo;The noble sister of Publicola,<LB REND=RIGHT>
The moon of Rome; chaste as the icicle<LB>
That's curded by the frost from purest snow,<LB>
And hangs on Dian's temple.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>A passage which, for the beauty of the poetry, and as a lustrous image of wom-
an's perfection, I should suppose has never been surpassed. In Act I, sc. iii,
where Valeria comes to pay a morning visit to the two ladies, we again have an
example&mdash;even upon so minim an occasion&mdash;of Shakespeare's perception of all
the characteristic points to be produced, and with advantage. One would sup-
pose, from this effective little scene, that he had put himself upon &lquo;a course&rquo;
of etiquette, and had taken honours and degrees in the science of making &lquo;morning
calls.&rquo; . . . After reading this very unimportant part of Valeria, and which consists
of but a half-dozen short sentences, no one, I should think, would be so hardy as to
maintain (which nevertheless has been asserted in the fantastical spirit of criticism)
that Shakespeare slovened his insignificant characters in order to throw his prin-
cipals into high relief.

229: &lquo;You know my father left me some prescriptions Of rare and proved effects,
such as his reading And manifest experience had collected.&rquo;

<P>61-69. <B>A my word . . . mammockt it</B>] <SC>J. C. Collins</SC> (<I>Studies in Sh.,</I> p. 202):
Longinus has observed of a celebrated sentence in Demosthenes that so abso-
lutely perfect is the construction that if a synonym be substituted, if the slightest
alteration be made in the order of the words, the whole is ruined&mdash;the music is a
discord (<I>De Sublimitate,</I> xxxix.). What is true of the sentence in Demosthenes
is true also of the paragraph we have just quoted [from <I>Coriol.</I>] and of many
other prose paragraphs in Shakespeare. Alter or omit a single word, invert a
sentence, strike out a clause, change in the smallest particular a particle, and you
would jar the ear of a sensitive critic, as a false note would jar the ear of a mu-
sician. Now we do not believe that, with the exception of Cranmer and the
translators of the Bible, any other sixteenth-century prose writer had so fine a
perception of the native harmony of our tongue, as distinguished from a harmony
borrowed from Rome.

<P>63. <B>confirm'd</B>] <SC>C. C. Clarke</SC> (<I>Sh. Characters,</I> p. 486): In that comprehensive
term of one word Shakespeare has conveyed the perfect ideal of a self-willed char-
acter. It has been frequently remarked that we cannot alter a phrase or an epithet
of his without injuring it. Let any one try to select a word more apt to the pur-
pose, in this instance, of conveying the idea of a sturdy child, and his success will
be fortunate&mdash;not to say, singular.
<P>64. <B>I saw him . . . a gilded Butterfly</B>] <SC>Tetzlaff</SC> (p. 58): This portrayal is so
characteristic of the boy that from this alone we can judge his whole nature. Here
pre-eminently has the poet achieved his purpose of presenting the boy as the
veritable portrait of his father. Just as the proud, lordly nature of the father
regards the plebs as unconditionally subject to him, so likewise the son looks upon
the butterfly. As the father at once tramples under foot and destroys any actual
or imagined opposition of the people whatsoever, in the same manner the son
tears to pieces the butterfly when it seeks to escape him. [Tetzlaff's <I>Essay</I> on
the Child-characters of Shakespeare and Chamber's edition appeared in the same
year.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Courtenay</SC> (ii, 224): The visit of Valeria is from Plutarch, who tells
us that Virgilia was found with her children in her lap; and the language of the
ladies is unquestionably characteristic; but the proof afforded of young Marcius
inheriting the spirit of his father, in his cruelty to a butterfly, is not. I venture
to suggest, a pleasing or graceful addition by the poet. [In answer to the charge
of &lquo;cruelty&rquo; in the foregoing note <SC>Wordsworth</SC> (<I>Historical Plays,</I> i, 119) says: &lquo;If
so, the boyishness of the poet Wordsworth, as recorded by himself, must fall under
the same condemnation. See his &ldquo;Lines to a Butterfly.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>64. <B>a gilded Butterfly</B>] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): Does Shakespeare
mean the pale Sulphur, or the orange and white Orange-tip, or one of the Clouded
Yellows, of various shades, or one of the orange-brown Fritillaries? &lquo;Gilded&rquo;
is not a very happy epithet for any one of them, but, on the other hand, it hints
at the superficial gloriousness of Coriolanus's ideal.

nearest flieth away, and lighteth a little before, and then the child after it again,
and so <I>ad infinitum,</I> I am weary of it.&rquo;

<P>71. <B>Indeed la</B>] <SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): &lquo;La&rquo; is here an expletive
giving additional force to the word &lquo;Indeed,&rquo; as the French occasionally use their
word <I>l&agrave;,</I> and we sometimes use our word <I>there,</I> to give an emphatic and final effect
to such a sentence as this: &lquo;I won't do it, and so I tell you; there!&rquo; &lquo;La&rquo; is thus
used by Shakespeare elsewhere. See, for instance, <I>Merry Wives,</I> I, i, 322, Master
Slender's flabbily emphatic protest that he will not take precedence of Mistress
Anne Page: &lquo;Truly, I will not go first; truly, la, I will not do you that wrong.&rquo;
And again, &lquo;You do yourself wrong, indeed, la,&rquo; [l. 326].

<P>89. <B>full of Mothes</B>] <SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): There is here a

the swarm of persecuting idlers attracted round the light of Penelope's beauty.
[This can hardly be said to be a play on the word, since the destructive insect,
<I>Tinea,</I> and the nocturnal lepidoptera were not differentiated until long after the
time of Shakespeare. Bacon in the <I>Sylva Sylvarum,</I> 1626, says: &lquo;The Moath
breedeth upon Cloth; . . . It delighteth to be about the flame of a Candle&rquo;
(&sect; 696).&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Herford</SC> (<I>Eversley Sh.</I>): The word was pronounced <I>motts.</I> There
is thence, apparently, a play upon the cant meaning <I>lovers,</I> a sense still current
in Ireland. The <I>Slang Dict.</I> gives <I>mot,</I> a girl of indifferent character. [This is, I
think, quite impossible. The earliest quotation in Henley &amp; Farmer's <I>Slang
Dictionary,</I> s. v. <I>Mot,</I> is 1785, and the only definition is that of <I>a wench</I> or <I>light
woman;</I> it could not therefore refer in any way to the suitors of Penelope.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): The suitors who ate up Ithaca during their
long visit appear under this whimsical image of the moths attracted by Penelope's
yarn. This humorous way of alluding to Penelope's devotion to Ulysses during
his long wanderings while she kept off these troublesome suitors till the funeral
vesture was spun, which each night she ravelled out, is one of Shakespeare's deft-
est light touches. By this scene and the praise Coriolanus later gives her (V, iii,
71-74) the influential, clever unmarried woman of Rome's best days is memorably
sketched.&mdash;<SC>Sherman</SC> (<I>Tudor Sh.</I>): An example of similar levity toward classical
story may be found in the <I>Tempest,</I> II, i, 76, &lquo;Not since widow Dido's time,&rquo; etc.
In both cases the effect is a touch of realistic characterization.

<P>112, 113. <B>Fare you well . . . Prythee</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 235): In almost all cases
where <I>thou</I> and <I>you</I> appear at first sight indiscriminately used, further considera-
tions show some change of thought, or some influence of euphony sufficient to
account for the change of pronoun. [In the present passage the formal &lquo;you&rquo;
is, I think, intended to suggest a slight irritation on the part of Valeria at the
obstinacy of Virgilia; the familiar &lquo;thee&rquo; indicates a relenting and return to play-
ful cajolory.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>116. <B>At a word</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: In one word, in short; a strong expression of
emphasis. Compare <I>Much Ado,</I> II, i, 118: &lquo;I know you well enough; you are
Signor Antonio. At a word, I am not.&rquo;
<P><B>Scene IV.</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): This and the remaining scenes of this Act
in which he appears show us Coriolanus at his greatest, <I>i. e.,</I> as a great soldier.
The picture is necessary to the peculiar pity and pitifulness of his end. And we
must know him fully in the field before we can grasp the causes of his failure in
the Forum. He is as detached from the average citizen in the one place as in
the other. In the very virtues which make him so splendid &lquo;Before Corioli,&rquo;
but so unlike others, lie the tragic possibilities that work his downfall.

<P>on the fore-stage outside the rear-stage, and talk of the horses, from which the
audience are to be quick to assume they have just dismounted as from a journey.
The scene then is no longer to be imagined as Rome. And their talk is long
enough to permit that arrangement of the rear-stage which all the siege-scenes in
the plays indicate, namely, bare walls, denuded of curtains, presenting the appear-
ance of gates on a level with the audience and high city walls. On the top of these,
that is, on the upper-stage, <I>the two Senators</I> of the besieged city <I>with others on the
Walles of Corialus</I> appear, according to the Folio stage-directions, when, after their
brief dialogue, Martius and his force turn to the rear-stage, <I>as before the City
Corialus,</I> and blow their <I>blast,</I> sounding <I>a Parley.</I> The First Senator refers to
the rear-stage folding-doors below them when he says &lquo;our Gates Which yet
seeme shut.&rquo; The call of Lartius for &lquo;Ladders hoa&rquo; adds to this effect. As in
<I>Henry V.</I> and other plays depicting a siege scaling ladders to set against the walls
and climb upon added to the effectiveness of the stage action. In this case much
play with these ladders was not indulged in, for, as Martius rejoins, the Volscians
did not &lquo;feare&rquo; them. They issued forth through the gates, which, as the Senator
promised, opened &lquo;of themselves,&rquo; beating the Romans forward on to the fore-
stage, until Marcius alone, not having been beaten forward with the rest, enters
as from these gates, charging his men to come on, and then, following the returning
Volscians, is with them <I>shut in,</I> while the Roman soldiers near him turn back at
l. 66, <I>Enter the Gati</I> [<I>Gates</I>]. After the stage-direction at l. 91, <I>all enter the City,</I>
that is, the rear-stage, many of them, of course, making their <I>exeunt</I> under this
cover. But at what is now marked scene v. three of the soldiers re-enter, appearing
with booty they evidently lug from behind the scenes into the rear-stage.&mdash;[<SC>Prolss</SC>
(pp. 9-13) discusses at length the probable arrangement and acting of this and
the following scenes on the Elizabethan stage. His description calls for dividing
curtains and the use of the fore- and middle-stages, but the whole account is so
involved that it soon becomes quite incomprehensible, and could only be clearly
visualised by the aid of a detailed diagram numbered and lettered, which, unfor-
tunately, Prolss does not provide. Miss Porter's foregoing remarks on this point
are, I think, all sufficient.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Oechelha&uuml;ser</SC> (<I>Einf&uuml;hrungen,</I> etc., i, 301)
compresses the remaining scenes of this Act into one long scene, beginning, how-
ever, with the Folio's second scene, between Aufidius and his lieutenant; for this
he advises a very deep stage and gives the following description of the scenic
arrangement: &lquo;In the background the walls and fortifications of Corioli; diagonally
left, the gate of the stronghold. The border-space remains quite open for the
entrance of troops and the conference of the commanders. The middle-stage
rises gradually towards Corioli; from the level of the border-space the road winds
up to the gate of Corioli. This middle space is cut off by set pieces (Rocks, mounds,
etc.), back of which the actions, skirmishes, and fights take place, partly concealed
to the audience. Corioli is raised to such a height that the figures of Coriolanus
and the soldiers may be easily seen as they struggle before the gates.&rquo;

<P>25. <B>a man . . . lesse then he</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The sense requires it to be read, &lquo;nor
a man that fears you <I>more</I> than he&rquo;; or, more probably, &lquo;nor a man but fears you
less than he.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The text, I am confident, is right, our author almost
always entangling himself when he uses <I>less</I> and <I>more.</I> &lquo;Lesser&rquo; in the next line
shows that &lquo;less&rquo; in that preceding was the author's word, and it is extremely
improbable that he should have written &lquo;<I>but</I> fears you less,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I,
pt i, p. 83): This &lquo;less than he&rquo; must be an error; <I>more</I> is the word requir'd by
the sense and which the poet intended, but was betray'd into a use of the other
for the sake of contrasting it with &lquo;lesser,&rquo; which occurs in the next sentence.
&mdash;<SC>Douce</SC> (ap. <SC>Steevens</SC>, 1793): Dr Johnson's note appears to me unnecessary,
nor do I think with Mr Malone that Shakespeare has here <I>entangled</I> himself, but,
on the contrary, that he could not have expressed himself better. The sense is:
&lquo;however little Tullus Aufidius fears, there is not a man within the walls that fears
you <I>less.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>: &lquo;He is not within our walls, and of all men living <I>he</I> fears

<P>you least.&rquo; [Dr Johnson's alteration] is better sense, and perhaps &lquo;less&rquo; is due
to a confusion not unlike that in <I>Lear,</I> II, iv, 142: &lquo;You less know how to value
her desert Than she to scant her duty.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>):
The sentence, we think, means: &lquo;No, he is not within the walls, nor is there there
a man that fears you less than he, who fears you less than next to nothing.&rquo; No
man can fear less than one who fears less than a little; and this is one of those
simple verities which Shakespeare often gives under the form of an apparent an-
tithesis.&mdash;<SC>T. Page</SC>: We are inclined to accept Clarke's interpretation here. Prob-
ably, however, &lquo;That's lesser than a little&rquo; is equivalent to &lquo;which is indeed <I>nothing
at all.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>) objects to Whitelaw's interpretation on the ground
that even were it grammatically possible it would furnish not a commendation
of the absent Aufidius, but an arrogant boast on the part of his advocate. &lquo;It
is much better,&rquo; Schmidt adds, &lquo;to consider this one of those instances, quite
frequent in Shakespeare, where by the use of negatives the negation is doubled,
apparently illogically, but not contrary to the character of vivid speech. Thus
in <I>Richard III,</I> &lquo;You may deny that you were not the cause.&rquo; In <I>Winter's
Tale,</I> &lquo;wanted less impudence&rquo; = had less impudence. If any alteration is permis-
sible we might write, &lquo;nor a man that fears you&mdash;less than he,&rquo; etc., and thus
interpret: &lquo;Nor a man that fears you&mdash;even less than he (are we frightened); with a
natural ellipse for which parallels may easily be found.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: &lquo;That
fears you less than he&rquo; is probably what Shakespeare wrote, though, as Johnson
pointed out, he ought to have said &lquo;<I>more</I> than he.&rquo; But there is a similar mistake
in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> I, i, 28: &lquo;Patience herself, what goddess e'er she be, Doth lesser
blench at sufferance than I do.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): A confusion of &lquo;nor a
man that fears you more than he&rquo; with &lquo;and no man fears you less than he.&rquo;
Confusion in the use of the comparatives is not uncommon in the best writers.
See, <I>e. g., Paradise Lost,</I> i, 257, &lquo;And what I should be, all but less than he&rquo; (a
confusion of <I>less</I> with <I>all but equal</I>).&mdash;<SC>Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): Johnson would
read &lquo;<I>more</I> than he&rquo;; but it is Aufidius's contempt for Coriolanus on which stress
is being laid, not that of the other Volsces.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): Two ideas
struggle for expression because the speaker is thinking simultaneously but differ-
ently of the citizens inside Corioli and of Aufidius&mdash;thus: (1) There is no man in
the city who fears you more than Aufidius does, <I>i. e.,</I> the besieged are not afraid
of you at all; (2) &lquo;Aufidius is not here, and (if he were) there is no man who fears
you <I>less</I> than he does.&rquo; Neither <I>less</I> (the Folio's reading) nor the suggested
alteration <I>more</I> can cover both ideas. &lquo;Less&rquo; is undoubtedly right; cf. <I>lesser</I> in
the next line. Moreover, &lquo;less&rquo; agrees with that tendency to intensify a negative
idea which we get so often in Shakespeare; compare the frequent use of the double
negative. The tendency to repeat a negative is a general principle of language and
may be illustrated not from Shakespeare alone.

<P>supposed to be within Corioli rousing the Volscians, and they beat during the
Roman attack. The whole back-stage represented Corioli. The balcony was
&lquo;the walls&rquo; upon which the Volscians came to parley with the Romans. A side-
door represented &lquo;the gates.&rquo; Through it the Volscians made a sortie and drove
back the Romans. Through it again Marcius drives them back and is shut in
with them.
<P>28. <B>Wee'l breake our Walles</B>] <SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): There is a possible but not
very probable alternative to the ordinary sense here. &lquo;Break&rquo; may be used in
the sense of break cover, escape from, issue out of, which, perhaps, also occurs in
<I>Timon,</I> IV, iii, 354: &lquo;How has the ass broke the wall, that thou art out of the city?&rquo;
The <I>N. E. D.</I> gives an instance of &lquo;break&rquo; in the sense of to break cover, from
<I>The Returne from Pernassus,</I> II, 5, &lquo;the Buck broke gallantly.&rquo; See also the ex-
amples of to break prison or jail, <I>e. g.,</I> 1674, J. [Brian], <I>Harv. Home,</I> viii, 52: &lquo;Who
is himself; and breaks the jayl must die.&rquo;
<P>36. <B>Their . . . our instruction</B>] <SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Schmidt (<I>Lex.</I>) explains
&lquo;instruction&rquo; here as <I>information,</I> citing <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> V, i, 54, but Lartius's words
signify, Let the sound of their activity teach us to play our own part without
delay. Nor is the usual sense of instruction necessarily absent from the passage
adduced from <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> &lquo;The queen . . . Of thy intents desires <I>instruction,</I>
That she preparedly may frame herself To the way she's forced to.&rquo;
<P>38. <B>forth their Citie</B>] For other examples of &lquo;forth&rquo; thus used as a preposition =
<I>from,</I> see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 156.

<P>49. <B>You Shames . . . you Heard of</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Shakespeare Restored,</I> p. 151),
referring especially to Pope's strange pointing of this line, &lquo;You shames of Rome;
you herds; of boils and plagues,&rquo; etc., says: &lquo;Here the old copies are defective in
the pointing, by which the sense is so maim'd that this too must be a passage which
either was not revised by Mr Pope, or in which he would not indulge his private
sense to make it intelligible. Mr Dennis, who has alter'd this Play, was obliged,
by a different disposition of the Fable, to leave out this passage, otherwise, I am
persuaded, there would have been no room for my making a correction upon it.
The meanest judges of English must be aware that no member of any sentence
can begin with a genitive case, and a preceding nominative be wanting to govern
that and the verb. Where, therefore, is the nominative to <I>of boils and plagues
plaster you o'er?</I> Or what sense or syntax is there in the passage as it now stands?
Restore it without the least doubt, &lquo;You shames of Rome, you! Herds of boils
and plagues,&rquo; etc. It is not infrequent with Shakespeare to redouble his pro-
nouns, as in this place. So, &lquo;I am no baby, I; that with base pray'rs I should
repent the evil I have done,&rquo; <I>Titus And.,</I> [V, iii, 185]. So, <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> &lquo;I will not
budge for no man's pleasure, I,&rquo; [III, i, 58].&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: This passage, like almost
every other abrupt sentence in these plays, was rendered unintelligible in the old
copy by inaccurate punctuation. &lquo;You herd of <I>cowards!</I>&rquo; Marcius would say, but
his rage prevents him. In a former passage he is equally impetuous and abrupt:

<C>[49. <B>You Shames . . . you Heard of</B>]</C>
<P><I>per se</I> as a probable misprint, but bad in this place as a substitute for the sus-
pected words. The reason is this: Passion takes concrete forms and avoids
generalities. Martius would, in the hands of a master, have been made to de-
nounce a specific malady on the Romans rather than have weakened the force
of his substantives by the prefix &lquo;unheard-of.&rquo; But there is yet another reason.
We cannot part with &lquo;heard&rquo; in the sense of <I>Armentum.</I> Twice in this play the
people are so designated, and once in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.;</I> in all with the same contemptuous
usage as in the passage under consideration. We adduce this passage not be-
cause the difficulty admits of removal, but because it does not. It is just one of
those which we must be content to take and leave as we find it. A score of sup-
positions may be made to account for the presence of the preposition &lquo;of.&rquo; We
might treat that preposition as governing &lquo;boils and plagues,&rquo; with the sense of
<I>with;</I> or as governed by &lquo;you herd,&rquo; followed by an aposeopesis; or we might treat
&lquo;of&rquo; as an adverb, equivalent to &lquo;off!&rquo; and so forth; all these expedients being equally
unsatisfactory, and there are still other possibilities to consider. But in such a
case it is not decision that is required, but faith. We must stand by the text
and wait. The passage resembles one in <I>Timon:</I> &lquo;Of man and beast the infinite
malady Crust you quite o'er.&rquo;&mdash;III, vi, 108.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>) is unwilling to
accept unreservedly the regulation of this line as printed by Johnson, since it would
be more in character for Coriolanus to apply to the retreating soldiers the worst
epithet he could utter. Schmidt therefore gives the line as in the Folio, placing
an exclamation point after &lquo;Plagues&rquo; and taking the verb &lquo;plaster&rquo; as reflexive.
&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC> in reference to this interpretation says: &lquo;Although Shakespeare's
vocabulary of terms of abuse was most copious, I do not think he would employ
so violent a figure as to designate by the names of diseases those who were the
subjects of them. It is true that in I, i, 171 &lquo;scab&rquo; is a term of contempt, but this
is rather the result of disease than the disease itself. And similarly, when Stephano
says in <I>The Temp.,</I> V, i, 286, &ldquo;O touch me not; I am not Stephano, but a cramp,&rdquo;
he uses the word of the contortions and soreness which are the result of cramp.
Hence I cannot regard &ldquo;boils and plagues&rdquo; in the present passage as descriptive of
the cowardly soldiers, and therefore connected with the preceding &ldquo;herd of,&rdquo; but
rather as the subject of &ldquo;plaster&rdquo; and the beginning of Coriolanus's curse. &ldquo;Byle&rdquo;
or &ldquo;Bile&rdquo; is the old spelling of <I>boil</I> in the early copies of Shakespeare as well as
in the Authorised Version, and represents the pronunciation of the word.&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>F. A.
Leo</SC> (<I>Jahrbuch,</I> xv, p. 48) in a review of Schmidt's edition objects to the editor's
elucidation and his regulation of this passage on grounds almost similar to those
set forth by Wright, but at greater length. It is, I think, sufficient to record this
without entering more fully into Leo's arguments, which are comments on Schmidt
rather than on Shakespeare's <I>Coriolanus.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>R. M. Spence</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Q.,</I> Dec. 1,
1877, p. 423): I cannot believe that Coriolanus would have stopped short at &lquo;You
herd of&mdash;.&rquo; He would have had no difficulty in completing the invective with
&lquo;hinds&rquo; or some such word. Like the grand old lady, his mother, from whom he
had inherited at once the nobility of his nature and the impetuosity of his temper,
he was never at a loss for words, and least of all when his passion was roused. I
venture to suggest a reading which involves the change only of a single letter in
the passage as it stands in the Folio, where &lquo;herd&rquo; is found in its old form &lquo;Heard.&rquo;
&lquo;You shames of Rome, you! Hoard of boils and plagues,&rquo; etc. The contemptuous
repetition of &lquo;you&rquo; is quite in Shakespeare's manner. The play upon words in

make Martius in his wrath and Shakespeare in his Elizabethan freedom entirely
bookish and coherent after the manner of the eighteenth century still remains
evident in the change of punctuation here. A characteristic reflexive use of the
verb, as pointed out by Schmidt, is thus effaced. The sense is, <I>You heard of
Byles and Plagues</I> (may Byles and Plagues) <I>Plaister you o're,</I> etc. The same
economy of diction, swiftly re-applying, without repetition, the words just used, as
subject, also, for what follows, appears later in the same battle-speech (l. 64),
which in sense runs thus: <I>'Tis for the followers</I> (of) <I>Fortune</I> (that Fortune) <I>widens
them.</I>

<P>60. <B>As they . . . Trenches followes</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): The Folio has &lquo;follows,&rquo;
a typographical error, perhaps, for <I>Follow us!</I> The ordinary reading is in the past
tense, but it should most likely be in the present&mdash;an invitation from the hero to
his soldiers.&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.,</I> iii, 207): The structure of the verse shows that some-
thing is wrong, the lines must have run somewhat on this wise, &lquo;&mdash;we'll beat them
to their wives, as they Us to our trenches follow'd.&rquo; As to the rest of the arrange-
ment, <I>non liquet.</I> [<SC>Lettsom</SC>, Walker's editor, in a foot-note on this, remarks:
&lquo;I cannot agree with Walker here. The received reading (<I>followed</I>) is a sophis-
tication by the editor of the Second Folio. The first gives &ldquo;followes,&rdquo; which I
suspect to be a mere misprint for <I>follow me.</I> I would, therefore, read and
point, &ldquo;As they us to our trenches: follow me.&rdquo; For the accentuation com-
pare <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> IV, iii, 23: &ldquo;No, n&oacute;! th&iacute;s shall forb&iacute;d it.&rdquo; The old stage-
direction [ll. 61, 62] probably caused the error. The four words, &ldquo;<I>and is shut
in,</I>&rdquo; belong to the next direction, l. 66, <I>Enter the Gati.</I> What a cluster of blunders
in the <I>authentic</I> edition! Since writing the above I have found that Collier pro-
poses, &ldquo;Follows <I>us,</I>&rdquo; but the singular is requisite; see the context.&rquo;]&mdash;<SC>W. A.
Wright</SC>: The word &lquo;followes&rquo; is superfluous and has probably crept into the text
from the stage-direction, &lquo;<I>Martius followes them to the gates.</I>&rquo; I have therefore
omitted it.&mdash;<SC>Anon</SC>. (<I>Times Literary Supplement,</I> 27 July, 1922, p. 482): It is
important to note that this stage-direction [ll. 61, 62] is altered in the modern
editions [see <I>Text. Notes,</I> Malone]. Whether the new direction is better is of no
moment; the point is that it is different. The real question at issue is whether
Shakespeare wrote &lquo;As they us to our trenches followes.&rquo; The rhythm is appalling
in itself, and doubly appalling as a desperate appeal in battle. Nor is it improved,
save in a purely mechanical sense, by reading &lquo;follow&egrave;d.&rquo; The dramatic force is
frittered away by the rhythmical debility. The same incident is referred to a
little further on by a Messenger (&lquo;I saw our party to their trenches <I>driven</I>&rquo;) and
by Cominius (&lquo;Where is that slave which told me they had <I>beat</I> you to your
trenches?&rquo;). Nothing so weak as &lquo;followes&rquo; there. Is it conceivable that the
prime actor in the heat of the battle should have used the flabby word? At all
events, no one will deny that &lquo;We'll beat them to their wives, As they us to our
trenches&rquo; is better poetry, better Shakespeare, and better drama. Have we the
right to improve the Folio? If we take the Folio stage-direction, we find the
suspect word in it. If we count spaces as letters the distance from &lquo;As&rquo; to &lquo;fol-
lowes&rquo; in the text is twenty-seven letters; while the distance from &lquo;Another&rquo; to
&lquo;followes&rquo; in the stage-direction is also twenty-seven letters. Surely the conclu-
sion is that in the copy from which the play was set up &lquo;followes&rquo; came immedi-
ately after &lquo;trenches,&rquo; but in the line below. The change of the stage-direction

at greater length. In reviewing the changes proposed in l. 60 it is, however, to be
regretted that Rhodes has not made better use of the <I>Text. Notes</I> in the Cambridge

after a skirmish, he &ldquo;enters the gate.&rdquo; A reviser making a text clear for readers

&ldquo;Enter the Gate&rdquo; and &ldquo;Followe&rdquo; may easily have been written in the player's part,
which conjecture justifies the assertion that <I>Coriolanus</I> was an assembled text.

text into a prompt-book, and not merely revising it for printing, &ldquo;Alarum&rdquo;
