<P>70. <B>To th'pot I warrant him</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes and Emend.,</I> etc., p. 349): This
is an expression that nobody has attempted to elucidate; it is explained at once
by the MS. Corrector: &lquo;<I>Sold.</I> See, they have shut him in. <I>All.</I> To the <I>port,</I> I war-
rant him.&rquo; They finish the sentence the soldier has begun. The enemy had
shut Marcius into the <I>port</I> or gate; and very shortly Lartius directs: &lquo;Let the
<I>ports</I> be guarded.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (ed. ii.): As doubts have been thrown upon this reading
of the old copy, it may be as well to observe that the phrase is put into the mouth
of characters of a much higher grade by Shakespeare's contemporaries; Whetstone
in his poem to the memory of Sir Nicholas Bacon, does not disdain to use it:
&lquo;When death doth come all pleasures goe to pot.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ibid.</SC> (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> p. 210):
What possible meaning &lquo;to the <I>port</I>&rquo; could have I am at a loss to imagine, not-
withstanding Mr Collier's attempt to reconcile it to sense as the continuation of
an interrupted sentence. I therefore hold this to be another perfectly unnecessary
interference with the text.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;To the pot,&rquo; as Mr Collier better than
anyone else ought to know, was one of the most familiar expressions in our early
dramatists. Take the following examples from plays which that gentleman must
be familiar with: &lquo;Thou mightest sweare, if I could, I would bring them to the
pot,&rquo; <I>New Custome,</I> II, iii; &lquo;For goes this wretch, this traitor, to the pot,&rquo; Peele,
<I>Edward I.,</I> ed. Dyce, i, 115; &lquo;They go to the pot for't,&rquo; Webster, <I>White Devil,</I> ed.
Dyce, i, 117.&mdash;<SC>Mommsen</SC> (<I>Der Perkins-Shakespeare,</I> p. 246): If reference be not
made to the fact that the common phrase <I>to go to pot</I> is used without the verb
and with the article we must accept the excellent reading <I>to the port.</I> Since the
soldiers who have seen it speak to the others running past: &lquo;Inside the gate,
only think of that!&rquo; pointing to the gate. That is very life-like and natural.&mdash;
<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Strictures,</I> etc., p. 155): It is lamentable that Mr Collier should cover
himself with ridicule by thus labouring to defend the worst vagaries of the MS. Cor-

(in <I>Dodsley's Old Plays,</I> vol. xi.) is alone sufficient to show the atrocity of the
alteration, &lquo;To the port.&rquo; [Dyce then quotes the line from Peele's <I>Edward I.</I>
which Staunton has already given in illustration <I>ante;</I> Dyce acknowledges, in
parentheses, that since writing the foregoing he has read Staunton's note <I>ad loc.,</I>
wherein not only this line from <I>Edward I.</I> is given, but other passages in illus-

<P>tration.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>, after quoting Staunton's illustrative passages from
Peele and Webster, adds, &lquo;The phrase is taken from the melting-pot.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Skeat</SC> (<I>Notes
on English Etym.,</I> s. v. <I>Pot,</I> p. 226): I have (hitherto) adopted Wright's note to
<I>Coriolanus,</I> I, iv, to the effect that &lquo;the figure is taken from the melting-pot.&rquo; I
now believe that the figure was taken from the much more common <I>cooking-pot.</I>
Whoever looks at the word <I>pot</I> in Littr&eacute; will see how many French phrases refer
to the cooking-pot, and Dr Schmidt, in his <I>Shakespeare-Lexicon,</I> seems to take the
same view, for he quotes the German parallel phrase which Fl&uuml;gel gives as &lquo;<I>in
die Pfanne hauen,</I> to put to the sword,&rquo; lit. to hew into the pan. The reference
is here to the shredding of vegetables before they are thrown into the pot to be
cooked. I venture to think this expression is far more graphic when we thus refer it
in the natural way to the ordinary cooking-pot. Without arguing the point further
I add an unmistakable example from King's <I>Art of Cookery,</I> first printed in 1708:
<BQ>
&lquo;In days of old, our father's went to war,<LB>
Expecting sundry blows, and hardy fare;<LB>
Their beef they often in their murrions stew'd,<LB>
And in their basket-hilts their beverage brew'd.<LB>
Some officer perhaps might give consent<LB>
To a large cover'd pipkin in his tent,<LB>
Where everything that every soldier got,<LB>
Fowl, bacon, cabbage, mutton, and what not,<LB>
Was all thrown into bank, and <I>went to pot.</I>&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>With this graphic and simple explanation I can rest satisfied. Hence, when the
soldiers remark that Coriolanus has gone &lquo;to the pot,&rquo; they mean that he will be
cut in pieces. &lquo;The weaker goeth to the pot&rquo; occurs in Heywood's <I>Proverbs</I>
(1562). And still more clearly, in Udall's translation of the <I>Apophthegmes of
Erasmus</I> (1564), bk i, Diogenes, &sect; 108: &lquo;by the said tyranne <I>Dionisius,</I> the ryche
and welthy of his subiectes <I>went</I> daily <I>to the potte</I> and were chopped vp.&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>Case</SC>
(<I>Arden Sh.</I>) gives several other examples of the use of this phrase, all tending,
as he says, to confirm Skeat's deduction that reference is to the cooking pot. The
<I>N. E. D.</I> follows Wright's interpretation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>lanus has the feeling of pain like other men, he is more hardy in daring exploits

<SC>Steevens</SC>: The thought seems to have been adopted from Sidney's <I>Arcadia:</I>
&lquo;Their very armour by piece-meale fell away from them: and yet their flesh abode
the wounds constantly, as though it were less sensible of smart than the senselesse
armour,&rquo; &amp;c., ed. 1633, p. 293; [ed. 1593, p. 317.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 411): I think
the common reading, &lquo;out-dares,&rquo; that is, feels less fear, has less apprehension
of danger, though it be an hyperbolical expression, hath greater propriety than
Dr Thirlby's emendation [see <I>Text. Notes</I>]. It is the sense, and not the deed,
which is the point of the present comparison. For where would be the wonder,
that a sensible agent should do more than a senseless instrument, which is incapable
of doing anything, further than it is employed by that, or some other, agent?
&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Johnson unnecessarily changed this [adverb to the adjective].
But this use of the adverb is of frequent occurrence in Shakespeare. Compare,
for instance, <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> III, iii, 2, where modern editors substitute the adjective:
&lquo;And things unluckily charge my fantasy.&rquo; Similarly <I>Temp.,</I> III, iii, 2; <I>As You Like
It,</I> I, ii, 162; and <I>Sonnet</I> xi, 3: &lquo;And that fresh blood which youngly thou bestowest,&rquo;

<P>79. <B>Thou art left Martius</B>] <SC>Collier</SC>: Possibly we ought to read <I>lost</I> for &lquo;left,&rquo;
a very easy misprint, when in MS. both the <I>s</I> and the <I>f</I> were carried below the line.
&lquo;Thou art <I>left,</I>&rquo; however, affords a very clear sense.&mdash;[Singer in his ed. ii. adopted
Collier's conjecture in his text, with a short note to the effect that <I>s</I> and <I>f</I> were
easily confounded, but without any acknowledgement as to the source of this new
reading. Collier had been more than human had he let this pass without remark.
Accordingly in his ed. ii. he likewise adopts his former conjecture, commending
Singer for so doing, and adding that he might at least have mentioned whence
this reading was derived, since &lquo;it would not have materially lengthened his note;
and his unwillingness to give credit to others may do him some wrong by leading
to the supposition that he has a much smaller claim to credit for himself than he
really possesses.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC> also adopts Collier's reading, but, equally as
blameworthy as Singer, does not give Collier the credit, merely remarking that

has not a sense suited to the context.&rquo; <SC>Hudson</SC> and <SC>Dyce</SC> (in his ed. ii.) accept

<P>82. <B>Euen to Calues wish</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: T. Lartius is here summing up his friend's
character, as a warrior that was terrible in his strokes, in the tone of his voice,
and the grimness of his countenance. But who was this <I>Calvus,</I> that wish'd these
three characteristics in a soldier? I'm afraid Greek and Roman History will be
at a loss to account for such a man and such circumstances join'd to signalize
him. I formerly amended the passage and prov'd that the poet must have wrote,
&lquo;Even to Cato's wish.&rquo; The error probably arose from the similitude in the manu-
script of <I>to</I> to <I>lv,</I> and so this unknown wight, Calvus, sprung up. I come now to
the authorities for my emendation. Plutarch in the <I>Life of Coriolanus,</I> speaking
of this hero, says: &lquo;He was a man (that which Cato requir'd in a warrior) not only
dreadful to meet with in the field, by reason of his hand and stroke, but insup-
portable to an enemy, for the very tone and accent of his voice, and the sole terror
of his aspect.&rquo; This again is confirm'd by the Historian in the <I>Life of Marcus
Cato, the Censor:</I> &lquo;In engagements&rquo; (says he) &lquo;he would use to strike lustily,
with a fierce countenance stare upon his enemies, and with a harsh threatening
voice accost them. Nor was he out in his opinion whilst he taught that such
rugged kind of behaviour sometimes does strike the enemy more than the sword
itself.&rquo; Mr Pope owns I have clearly prov'd this point, but he seems inclin'd
to think the blunder should rather have continued than I should have discover'd
the Author guilty of such a terrible anachronism. But is Mr Pope conscious of
no other anachronism committed by our Poet in this play? Menenius in one
passage talks of Alexander the Great, tho that Prince was not born till 130 years
after Coriolanus's death; nay, in another he mentions Galen, whose birth was
above 420 years later than that of Alexander.&mdash;[In the foregoing note there are
two statements which it may be interesting to elucidate. The first is where

<P>Theobald says that he had &lquo;formerly amended&rquo; the passage as it stands in
his text; this refers, not to his <I>Shakespeare Restored</I> which appeared in 1726,
but to a letter written by him to Mr Matthew Concanen that was subsequently
communicated to <I>Mist's Journal,</I> March 16, 1727, and there printed without
Theobald's permission. The second point is Theobald's reference to Pope.
Pope's ed. ii. appeared in 1728, and in vol. viii. he added as an Appendix an
article entitled: <I>Various Readings or Conjectures on Passages of Shakespeare.</I>
This is, in reality, a venomous attack on Theobald's <I>Shakespeare Restored.</I> Pope,
nettled by this demonstration of the many faults in his first edition, belittles and
discounts the value of certain corrections. The reading <I>Cato's</I> for &lquo;Calvus&rquo; is,
however, the only one from the present play to which Pope refers, and in almost
the very words Theobald quotes; Pope evidently is referring to the communication
in <I>Mist's Journal</I> of the preceding year, which corresponds almost word for word
with the note as it later appears in Theobald's own edition. (See Nichol's <I>Illus-
trations,</I> etc., vol. ii, p. 200.) It is to this passage in the Appendix of Pope's vol-
ume that Theobald refers when he says that Pope accepts his emendation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc., p. 247): Theobald's alteration has been adopted
by all the subsequent editors, who silently admit the charge preferred by Theobald
against our author, of great chronological impropriety, in quoting a saying of
Cato's in the days of Coriolanus; but the impropriety is to be imputed to the edi-
tors themselves and not to Shakespeare, who though he may have been guilty,
upon other occasions, of crimes as great as that which he is now accused of, is
certainly innocent of this, and has with some degree of art avoided the impro-
priety with which he is charged. He liked this saying of Cato's, and wished to
apply it to Coriolanus, but in order to avoid the anachronism in question, he
puts it into the mouth of a certain Calvus, who might have lived at any time.
This is, I believe, the first time that an editor ever amended an author merely to
make him commit a blunder.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>, in answer to the foregoing remark of
Mason, says: &lquo;Had Shakespeare known that Cato was not born till the year of
Rome 519, that is, 253 years after the death of Coriolanus (for there is nothing in
the foregoing passage to make him even <I>suspect</I> that was the case), and in conse-
quence made this alteration, he would have attended in this particular instance to
a point of which almost every page of his works shows that he was totally negli-
gent; a supposition which is so improbable that I have no doubt the correction
that has been adopted by the modern editors is right. In the first Act of this play
we have <I>Lucius</I> and <I>Marcius</I> printed instead of Lartius in the original copy.&rquo;
Malone concludes his note with an explanation of the misprint &lquo;Calves&rquo; for <I>Catoes</I>
which, as it is substantially identical with that by Theobald (to whom he does
not refer), need not be repeated. He mentions that usually the possessive case of
nouns ending in a vowel was formed by adding <I>es.</I> It is, however, somewhat
curious that in the three other passages wherein the name &lquo;Cato&rquo; appears in the
possessive in the Folio it is uniformly spelt <I>Cato's.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.&mdash;Knight</SC>: We quite agree
with Malone that the manuscript was <I>Catoes;</I> easily mistaken and rendered by
the printer &lquo;Calves.&rquo; But we do not agree with him that Shakspere committed
the anachronism in ignorance. Shakspere puts nearly the same words [as in North's
<I>Plutarch</I>] in the mouth of Lartius; feeling that Lartius, in thus conveying the
sentiment of Plutarch, was to the audience as a sort of chorus. He had no vision
of a critic before him, book in hand, calling out that Cato was not born until two

<P>hundred and fifty years after the death of Coriolanus. Now Malone, with his

(<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Since Niebuhr and other modern historians question the histor-
icalness of Coriolanus himself, whose story is based only on Plutarch, who died
<I>circa</I> A. D. 120, and Livy, who was born only fifty-eight years before Christ, neither
historian being regarded, by modern scrutiny, as unimpugnable authority for
what occurred in the third century after the founding of Rome, the modern
reader may be justified in caring even less than the Poet that Cato, the Censor,
followed Martius Coriolanus and his associates by a mere century and a half.
&mdash;<SC>Gervinus</SC> (p. 768): Shakespeare must have known the time when Cato lived
from Plutarch's <I>C&aelig;sar.</I> But it is possible that as he found several republican
Brutuses, so he must have concluded there were several severe Catos. It is cer-
tain that he was not so early schooled in Eutropius as we are, nor had he any
chronological dictionary to refer to in order to set himself right in his dates. Never-
theless we ought to consider how valuable to the poet was the brevity and suggest-
iveness of such an intimation as he puts in the mouth of Titus Lartius; it is doubt-
ful whether, if the mistake had been pointed out to him, he would have corrected
it, seeing it was so serviceable; nay, it is doubtful whether it was a mistake at all,
and not rather a license like Goethe's when he made Faust mention Luther. There
is a passage in <I>Lear</I> which ought to make us cautious&mdash;a passage where the <I>ob-
servance</I> of chronology constitutes a much greater license than the neglect of it&mdash;
a passage which looks like a capital stroke of satire addressed to all self-opinionated
and pedantic censors (a set of people not lacking even at the poet's time); the
passage where the poet says: &lquo;This prophecy Merlin shall make; <I>for I live before
his time,</I>&rquo; [III, ii, 95].&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The readers of <I>Westward Ho</I> will remember

<P>order to assist him. It seems to me that, according to Shakespeare's intention,
Coriolanus, assaulted by the Volscians, in order to defend his back, fights his way

<P>4. <B>Murrain</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Murrain, which is properly a cattle plague (see
<I>Mid. N. Dream,</I> II, i, 97), is used in such execrations like &lquo;plague&rquo; itself. See <I>Temp.,</I>
III, ii, 88: &lquo;A murrain on your monster!&rquo; and <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> II, i, 20: &lquo;A red
murrain o' thy jade's tricks!&rquo; The word was also used of human diseases. In
Stow's <I>Summarie</I> (1565), fol. 28<I>a,</I> under the date 1094, is a marginal note, &lquo;Great
morein of men.&rquo; [According to <SC>Skeat</SC> (<I>Dict.,</I> s. v.) the word is closely allied to Old
French <I>morine,</I> a dead carcass.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>7. <B>mouers</B>] <SC>Whitelaw</SC>: These clamourers for their rights, these disturbers
of the State.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>), for this use of &lquo;mover&rquo; in the sense of <I>a
living, moving</I> creature, compares: &lquo;O fairest mover in this mortal round.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Ven.
&amp; Ad.,</I> l. 368.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, these active stirring fellows; contemptu-
ously used of the loiterers for plunder. Others take it as equivalent to &lquo;these
agitators.&rquo; Shakespeare elsewhere uses &lquo;mover&rquo; as he does &lquo;liver&rquo; in the sense of
<I>living creature,</I> a human being simply. See <I>Ven. &amp; Ad.,</I> l. 368. There is probably
a play upon all these senses in the present instance.

<P>8. <B>Drachme</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 486) and <SC>Browne</SC> (p. 16) mark <I>drachm,</I> as in modern
texts, as a dissyllable. <SC>Smith</SC> (<I>Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities</I>) gives
the value of the drachma as about 9d 3 farthings.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>9. <B>of a Doit</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, of a doit in value, worth but a doit. A
doit was the smallest piece of money (German <I>deut,</I> Dutch <I>duit</I>), and was worth
half a farthing. For &lquo;of&rquo; with the price of anything compare <I>Meas. for Meas.,</I>
II, i, 95: &lquo;A dish of some three pence.&rquo; See IV, iv, 23.
<P>9, 10. <B>Dublets . . . that wore them</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Instead of taking them as their
lawful perquisite.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Shakespeare dressed his ancient Romans like
the English of his own day. (See <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> I, ii, 264.) In the same way he makes
the English custom of giving to executioners the clothes of their victims as a
perquisite prevail in Rome.&mdash;[&lquo;And of universal custom, also, it may be,&rquo; adds
Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC>, &lquo;the Roman custom, being indicated when the soldiers of Rome,
who executed Christ, cast lots for his vesture.&rquo;]
<P>14. <B>Then Valiant</B>] <SC>Wordsworth</SC> (<I>Historical Plays,</I> i, 118): Shakespeare uses
&lquo;valiant&rquo; as either dissyllable or trisyllable. Here, if it is to stand at all, the
metre seems to require the omission of the preceding &lquo;then,&rquo; which perhaps is
otherwise desirable, to mark the abruptness with which Marcius would here
naturally address Titus. Accordingly, I have left it out.
<P>18. <B>thou bleed'st</B>] In dialogue as sharp and forceful as is here intended it is, I
think, needless to require absolute consistency in the use of &lquo;thou&rquo; and &lquo;you.&rquo;

<P>20. <B>a second course</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: As though fighting were as a feast to him,
with an allusion to the second or principal course of viands at a dinner; compare
<I>Macbeth,</I> II, ii, 39: &lquo;Sleep that knits up the ravell'd sleave of care . . . great nature's
second course, Chief nourisher in life's feast&rquo;; and below, I, ix, 14: &lquo;Yet cam'st
thou to a morsel of this feast Having fully dined before.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>), in
reference to the foregoing note by Deighton, says: &lquo;It more probably means bout,
encounter of fight; see <I>Tragedy of Hoffman,</I> 1631, Act II. <I>ad init.,</I> &ldquo;Well Ile trie one
course with thee at the halfe pike,&rdquo; etc. The <I>N. E. D.</I> gives <I>Course,</I> The rush
together of two combatants in battle or tournament; charge, onset; a passage at
arms, bout, encounter. In <I>King Lear,</I> III, vii, 54, Gloucester says: &ldquo;I am tied to
the stake, and I must stand the course,&rdquo; <I>i. e.,</I> I must endure a second relay of dogs
set upon me.&rquo;

judge of what I can do. In the passage in <I>Twelfth Night</I> Olivia says: &lquo;I will
give out divers schedules of my beauty: . . . Were you sent hither to praise me?&rquo;
[It seems hardly necessary to find any meaning for &lquo;praise&rquo; here other than its
usual one. Marcius deprecates any commendation yet, as he is but at the begin-
ning of what he intends doing.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>30. <B>those</B>] <SC>Orger</SC> (p. 58): There are many passages in Shakespeare which seem
to indicate that he used &lquo;those&rquo; for a genitive plural, as <I>their</I> or <I>theirs,</I> which use in
these places might be marked by an apostrophe, <I>those'</I>. This has not been observed
by Dr Abbott in his account of his pronouns, but deserves, I think, consideration
as affording an easy solution of constructions otherwise exceedingly irregular,
<I>e. g.,</I> II, ii, 25, &lquo;his ascent is not by such easy degrees as those, who,&rquo; etc., <I>i. e.,</I>
as <I>theirs who.</I> Again, <I>Rich. III:</I> I, iii, 217: &lquo;If heaven have any grievous plagues
in store Exceeding those that I can wish on thee,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> exceeding &lquo;theirs,&rquo; the plagues,
viz., which she had been imprecating on the others, which might seem to have
exhausted her power of cursing, and the line should be read: &lquo;Exceeding <I>those'</I>
that I can wish on thee.&rquo; [Does not &lquo;those&rquo; there refer directly to the &lquo;plagues,&rquo;
and not to any previous imprecations of Anne?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] Again, in <I>Mer. of Ven.,</I>
I, i, 97: &lquo;&mdash;would almost damn those ears Which hearing them would call their
brothers fools.&rquo; And in <I>Henry VIII:</I> II, i, 152: &lquo;To stop the rumour and allay
those tongues That durst disperse it.&rquo; &lquo;Those ears&rquo; and &lquo;those tongues&rquo; may
mean <I>those hearers</I> and <I>those speakers,</I> as in French they call a person a <I>mauvaise
langue</I> who speaks evil of others. But it will be scarcely possible to understand
on the same principle <I>Pericles,</I> I, iv, 39, &lquo;Those palates, <I>who,</I>&rquo; and I, iv, 34, &lquo;These
mouths, <I>whom.</I>&rquo;
<P>32. <B>Go sound</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The comma after &lquo;Go,&rquo; which has been inserted
in most modern editions, has no right to be there. Compare <I>Temp.,</I> I, ii, 301, &lquo;Go
make thyself like a nymph o' the sea&rquo;; and in the same play, II, i, 190, &lquo;Go sleep,
and hear us.&rquo;
<P>34. <B>Away</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.,</I> p. 273) arranges this line ending with the word
&lquo;minde,&rquo; and places the single word &lquo;Away&rquo; in a line by itself, for the reason that
&lquo;lines of eight or nine syllables, as they are at variance with the general rhythm
of Shakespeare's poetry, so they scarcely ever occur in his plays&mdash;it were hardly
too much to say, not at all.&rquo; Besides the present line, among other examples,
Walker gives from <I>Cymb.,</I> IV, iii, near the end: &lquo;We grieve at chances here. Away,&rquo;
which he treats as here, placing &lquo;Away&rquo; in a line by itself.

C&aelig;s.,</I> V, iii, 99: &lquo;The last of all the Romans, fare thee well!&rquo; In <I>1 Henry IV:</I> I,
ii, 177, the old copies read: &lquo;Farewell, the latter spring,&rquo; and in <I>3 Henry VI:</I> V, v,
38, the Folios have: &lquo;Take that, the likeness of this railer here.&rquo; Again in <I>Pericles,</I>
III, i, 1, the early copies read: &lquo;The god of this great vast, rebuke these surges.&rquo;
It may be said that all these instances are misprints, but the number of them is
against such an explanation.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Henry Irving Sh.</I>): For the definite article,
where we should rather use the pronoun <I>ye,</I> compare IV, i, 44. The awkwardness
in the present passage is that there is nothing until the pronoun &lquo;you&rquo; in l. 10 to
decide whether &lquo;the Roman gods&rquo; is the second or third person; where there is
no ambiguity, as in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> V, iii, 99, &lquo;The last of all the Romans, fare thee
well!&rquo; the difference from modern usage hardly attracts attention.
<P>16. <B>speakest</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: So printed in the Folios, which have &lquo;speak'st&rquo;
in the next line. There is nothing in the metre to necessitate the abbreviation to
&lquo;speak'st&rquo; in the first instance, for in these broken lines it is not uncommon to
have a redundant syllable.
<P>19. <B>briefely</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 35): That is, a short time <I>ago,</I> instead of (as with us)
<I>in</I> a short space of time. Similarly we use the Saxon equivalent <I>shortly</I> to signify
futurity.
<P>20. <B>confound</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Confound&rquo; is here used not in its common acceptation,
but in the sense of <I>to expend.</I> Conterere tempus.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: So, in <I>1 Henry IV:</I>
I, iii, 100, &lquo;He did confound the best part of an hour In changing hardiment with
great Glendower.&rquo;

<P>&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Although the speech is impatient, reckless
of formal words as the speaker is of details, we think Martius is less apt to be
disjointed than to be at once swift and compact. For this reason it seems to us
more in keeping with the whole to heed the sharp pelt of the reply closed with
the colon after &lquo;truth.&rquo; He exonerates the Messenger at once, whom Cominius
has just called &lquo;that Slave&rquo; and was going to reprimand for bringing false news.
Then Martius goes on naturally in thought to the action that did in truth turn the
tide from retreat to victory. Instead of telling this, however, which would
amount to praising himself as one equal to the desperate situation, he blames with
scorn and irony those who were not, namely, the would-be <I>Gentlemen,</I> who, in his
sense of what nobility exacts, showed they were unworthy to be trusted. As
for this gentry, they ran like the mouse from the cat.
<P>54. <B>a plague-Tribunes for them</B>] Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Rowe's
arrangement is objectionable because it makes a halting instead of a swift paren-
theses [see <I>Text. Notes</I>]. Martius, in character and speech alike, is a flame. This
side flare of imprecation suffers, also, in the modernised text from being taken out of
the parentheses. His thought recurs to the battle-charge, when he stemmed the flight
of the &lquo;common file,&rquo; cursing them as &lquo;you heard of Byles and Plagues.&rquo; So here,
between breaths, as it were, he wishes these unworthy clamorers for the privileges
of the worthy <I>Tribunes</I> bringing down <I>a</I> plague. He says it in the quickest
way possible&mdash;&lquo;(a plague-Tribunes for them).&rquo; The play shows, of course, that
the &lquo;Tribunes for them&rquo; did, indeed, bring down &lquo;a plague&rquo; in a peculiar sense
when they caused the people to banish Valor in his person later. Surely the
formalisms of the eighteenth century have not so deadened the minds of this
century that they cannot see how feeble in comparison is the modernised text:
&lquo;a plague! Tribunes for them!&rquo; Martius, as his poet makes him talk, hated the
small words carrying no weight in the sentence as he hated the mob of weak men
making up the &lquo;common file&rquo; in number, not in valor.
<P>55. <B>budge</B>] That is, give way, flee. Compare &lquo;Here pitch our battle; hence
we will not budge,&rquo; <I>3 Henry VI:</I> V, iv, 66; also <I>Mer. of Ven.,</I> II, ii, 20.&mdash;<SC>W. A.
Wright</SC>: Coriolanus puts all his contempt for the mob into this colloquial word.

<P><I>Folio Sh.</I>): This is an example of his swift, compressed, but not disjointed diction.
He does not break off. . . . The words he has already used serve to complete his
sentence, which if fully expanded will run thus: Will the time serve to tell, I do
not think the time will serve to tell, what Cominius asks&mdash;how they prevail'd.
So he turns to the next business.
<P>63-66. <B>Know you . . . the Antients</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: So, in the old translation of
Plutarch: &lquo;Martius asked him howe the order of the enemies battell was, and on
which side they had placed their best fighting men. The consul made him aunswer
that he thought the bandes which were in the vaward of their battell, were those
of the Antiates,&rquo; etc. The old copy reads &lquo;Antients,&rquo; which might mean <I>veterans;</I>
but a following line, [l. 74], as well as this quotation, seems to prove <I>Antiates</I> to be
the proper reading. Our Author employs <I>Antiates</I> as a trisyllable, as if it had been
written <I>Antiats.</I>
<P>66. <B>Vaward</B>] That is, the <I>advance guard,</I> the <I>Vanguard.</I>&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> compares
<I>Henry V:</I> IV, iii, 130: &lquo;My lord, most humbly on my knee I beg The leading of
the vaward.&rquo;
<P>68. <B>heart of Hope</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: The same expression is found in Marlowe's
<I>Lust's Dominion:</I> &lquo;Your desperate arm Hath almost thrust quite through the
heart of hope.&rquo; [<SC>Wright</SC>, who furnishes the missing reference for this line, IV,
ii, and <SC>Case</SC>, who gives its further location as in Hazlitt's <I>Dodsley,</I> xiv, p. 151,
both call attention to Malone's wrong assignment of the play to Marlowe; but
Malone was doubtless influenced by the fact that the earliest printed copy of the
play, 1657, bore Marlowe's name upon the title-page. It has been shown, how-
ever, that the play is first mentioned several years subsequent to Marlowe's death.

<C>[95. <B>Oh me alone, make you a sword of me</B>]</C>
<P>[Through inadvertence, possibly, Singer's text reads &lquo;Come! along!&rquo; and not as
he asserts it should read in his note.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shake-

seeing them <I>all</I> wave their swords in reply and then take himself up in their arms,
which leaves him solely waving his sword, he rapturously exclaims, &lquo;Oh take me
alone for weapon among you all! make yourselves a sword of me!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>
(p. 23): The reading of the Folios has been explained: (1) Let me alone. Set
me down. (2) Oh me! that I should have said &lquo;alone!&rquo; Both explanations seem
inadmissible. Two emendations deserve notice: (1) that proposed by Collier &lquo;of me
alone?&rquo;&mdash;adopting which it would be better to punctuate &lquo;O' me alone make you a
sword? O' me?&rquo; (When everyone of you is as good as four Volscians, why am I
your only sword? What so great need have you of me?); that of Singer, &lquo;O come
along&rquo; (more Shakespearian would be &lquo;<I>Go we along</I>&rquo;). The sense is then&mdash;con-
necting &lquo;Make you a sword of me&rquo; with what follows&mdash;&lquo;Use me for your sword,
as now you use me&rquo; (in a literal sense they had taken him in their arms), &lquo;and
every man of you (such men with such a leader) will be worth four Volscians.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus,</I> p. 71): Both Collier's emendation (&lquo;Of me alone&rquo;) and
Singer's (&lquo;O come along&rquo;) are of slight probability, since according to the former
we do not understand why Coriolanus finds so strange what has happened to him
when it should occur to any other; according to the latter the order &lquo;go we along&rquo;
has no agreement with the rest of the sentence. Perhaps the verse runs thus:
&lquo;Oh me! all one; make you a sword of me,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> &lquo;What are you doing?&rquo; (since <I>oh
me</I> is always an exclamation of painful or at least unpleasant surprise). &lquo;Yet it
is all one to me; make a sword of me and wave me as I order you to wave your
swords.&rquo; <I>Make</I> is thus the imperative, and the pointing of the Folio correct.&mdash;
<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: I do not think any of the proposed emendations is less obscure
than the original reading. Coriolanus is taken by surprise at the eagerness with
which the soldiers rush forward in answer to his appeal. Instead of waving their
swords in the air as he had directed, they make a sword of him. Instead of vol-
unteers coming forward singly the whole mass would follow Coriolanus only; none
would stay behind. When he saw this he exclaimed, &lquo;Oh, me alone!&rquo; and then
when they raised him aloft, &lquo;make you a sword of me? brandish me as if I were a
sword?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Rolfe</SC>: Of the various conjectures, that of Collier seems most probable,
especially if we put it &lquo;O' me alone!&rquo; but possibly we might get the same meaning
out of the original reading: &lquo;What, me alone! do you make me your sword?&rquo;
Any interpretation of the first clause which makes it independent of the second
seems to us inadmissible.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): [The reading suggested by Whitelaw]
gives about the same meaning as Singer's, and is, I think, more in the Poet's
manner. That meaning is, of course, &lquo;Let us proceed to the work; use me as your
sword&rquo;; and, as they already have the speaker in their arms, the language is not
strained. We have repeated instances of <I>me</I> and <I>we</I> confounded, and also of <I>along</I>
misprinted <I>alone.</I>&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC> (p. 293): I take these words to be partly a sort of gentle
protest against the hero-worship which they were paying him, partly a preface
to the remarks which immediately after he addresses to them. Who were these
men who were now so eager for the fray? They were the very men who under
Cominius had failed to beat the enemy; yet now that Coriolanus was to captain
them, they made sure that they had a very engine of war, a talisman of victory&mdash;
<I>they made a sword of him</I>&mdash;they regarded <I>him</I> as their sword, <I>him</I> as their confidence

<P>&mdash;him and him alone. Coriolanus says not a word to damp this newly kindled

outwardly, no need to set their hopes on him, and him alone; they themselves

<P>always remember that Shakespeare's plays were written to be acted.&mdash;Miss <SC>C.
Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): This line has had a hard fate in tame minds. Martius is
enraptured when he finds picked men willing to be served by their leader instead of
needing to be goaded by him. Finding men with mettle like his own, he offers him-
self as their sole weapon to use&mdash;himself bodily to make a sword out of. As the rest
of the excited speech goes, hurried with business, too, as to the selection out of these
picked men of a smaller guard to go with him, he imagines them as forming a
shield, as he himself will be a sword against Auffidius. This almost poetic battle-
ecstasy in a man whose eminence in daring has made him know loneliness is
excited by a feeling, for once, of peership in the fellows who are his companions
at arms. The speech is completely Shakespearian, owing nothing to Plutarch.
The text [of the Folio] best expresses it without any change, even of punctuation.
&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: The meaning is, What are you for me alone? is it me alone that you
will follow? And do you drop your swords to make me your sword instead, that
you lift me thus in the air?&mdash;<SC>Sherman</SC> (<I>Tudor Sh.</I>): Many editors have considered
this line obscure and in need of emendation. It makes, however, excellent and
spirited sense as it stands in the Folio: Oh me alone, make you a sword of me;
with a sense of exaltation excited by the instant response of the soldiers to his
personal appeal, Coriolanus thinks of himself, borne on the shoulders of the
troops, as an animated blade, singly invincible against the enemy. &lquo;Take me
alone,&rquo; the line means as printed in the Folio, &lquo;and use me like a sword.&rquo; The
introduction of the interrogation mark, proposed by Capell, slightly alters the
mood, but not the meaning.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: I have followed Singer in reading <I>Of</I> for
&lquo;Oh,&rquo; though to give a stronger emphasis I have put a note of interrogation after
&lquo;sword&rquo; and repeated it after &lquo;me.&rquo; The meaning seems to be: Do you by thus
raising me in your arms, brandish me as it were your sword, the only sword you
would use?&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): If we accept Capell's note of interrogation at the
end of this line it would appear that the soldiers' answer to &lquo;Wave thus&rquo; was to
uplift Marcius, leading him to say: &lquo;What, you wave <I>me</I> only? You make <I>me</I> your
sword?&rquo; There is one objection, perhaps, in the fact that the stage-direction is
old and shows that the stage-practice was to wave swords as well as to shout and
take up the leader.

be under it, most dispos'd to go with me; and &lquo;four&rquo; in that line is made to stand
for four men, four of my officers, by a license that is not commendable, and which
might have been avoided by putting <I>I</I> in its stead.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 412): What sense
the word &lquo;four&rquo; can have here is difficult to guess. Perhaps the poet wrote, &lquo;And
<I>so I</I> shall quickly draw out,&rquo; etc. That is, As the troops march by I shall readily

offered themselves to followe him, he went out of the cittie.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC> (<I>Com-

an expression of more than &ldquo;envy&rdquo;&mdash;fierce hatred.&rquo; [It will be noticed that this

acknowledgement, in his editions.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: There is probably some cor-
ruption in this line, which would better read, &lquo;More than thy fame <I>I hate</I> and
envy.&rquo; So, in Plutarch, &lquo;Martius knew very well that Tullus did more malice and
envy him than he did all the Romans besides.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.): Collier is probably
right in observing that &lquo;the compositor mistook <I>I</I> for the contraction for &ldquo;and.&rdquo;&rquo;
Whether Malone's or Steevens's explanation of the Folio reading be the most ridic-
ulous is doubtful. Staunton's suggestion would make the line over-measure. Here
&lquo;envy&rquo; means <I>hate, bear ill will to.</I>&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: The construction commonly put upon
the passage is: &lquo;Not Afric owns a serpent that I more abhor and envy than I do
thy fame, &lquo;envy&rquo; being interpreted in the old sense of <I>hate.</I> But why should
Aufidius profess to abhor and hate the fame of Marcius? when the plain truth is
that he <I>desires</I> or <I>covets</I> his fame, and therefore <I>envies</I> him the possession of it. We
adopt, with little hesitation, a correction from Collier's second folio.&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M.
Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): It appears to us that the sentence means &lquo;Not
Africa owns a serpent I abhor more than thy fame and hatred of me&rquo;&mdash;that hatred
which Marcius has just professed.&mdash;Rev. <SC>John Hunter</SC>: Thy renown in connection
with thy malice towards me.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus,</I> p. 73) asks what could have
forced the poet to adopt any such construction as that suggested by Steevens in
his alternative explanation, and therefore considers that the proper view of the
case is that &lquo;fame and envy&rquo; here mean <I>odious fame.</I>&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Steevens
rightly explains this as an instance of the grammatical figure, hendiadys, in
which one idea is expressed by two different words. His second thoughts are
not best. The First Folio prints &lquo;fame&rquo; and &lquo;envy&rquo; with initial capitals to show
that they were both regarded as substantives.&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>):
That is, thy fame and envy of mine. Each being fixed by the consciousness that
the other was the most valiant leader on his side must hate both this eminence
and its discount of his own supremacy. Hence the double expression.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC>
(<I>Henry Irving Sh.</I>) quotes Steevens's explanation, but adds that &lquo;more probably
&ldquo;envy&rdquo; is a verb parallel to &ldquo;abhor.&rdquo;&rquo; Beeching does not repeat this alternative
explanation in his later edition (<I>The Falcon Sh.</I>).&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC> follows Collier's
MS. correction, <I>I envy,</I> since &lquo;Marcius says of Aufidius, &ldquo;I sin in envying his
nobility,&rdquo; I, i, 245; and it is not so much his hatred as his jealousy that he here
expresses.&rquo;
<P>7, 8. <B>Let the first . . . doome him after</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: So, in <I>Macbeth,</I> &lquo;And
damn'd be him who first cries, Hold, Enough!&rquo;&mdash;V, viii, 34.

<P>15, 16. <B>Wer't thou the Hector . . . bragg'd Progeny</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The Romans

Greeks, which cannot be but by a very unusual construction, or the author must
have forgotten the original of the Romans; unless &lquo;whip&rquo; has some meaning which
includes <I>advantage</I> or <I>superiority,</I> as we say &lquo;he has the <I>whip hand</I>&rquo; for &lquo;he has the
<I>advantage.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: Dr Johnson considers this as a very unusual construction,
but it appears to me only such as every page of these plays furnishes; and the
foregoing interpretation is undoubtedly the true one. An anonymous correspondent
justly observes that the words mean, &lquo;the whip that your bragg'd progeny <I>was
possessed of.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Whip&rquo; might anciently be used, as <I>crack</I> is now, to
denote anything peculiarly boasted of, as the <I>crack</I> house in the county, the <I>crack</I>
boy of a school, &amp;c. Modern phraseology, perhaps, has only passed from the
<I>whip</I> to the <I>crack</I> of it. [The foregoing is, I think, an instance of Steevens's love

ing terms, but I believe the owner of the best horse of his year is said to hold
the whip, and has actually a whip consigned to his keeping. [It is somewhat
unusual for Mason to display such a complete lack of sagacity as in the foregoing.
The use of &lquo;whip&rquo; in any such sense as he suggests is utterly unknown before the
end of the eighteenth century.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 361): Here
&lquo;bragg'd&rquo; is bragged of, that you brag of; &lquo;progeny,&rquo; progenitors; and &lquo;whip,&rquo; the

<P>14. <B>a Morsell of this Feast</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): This cannot here mean a
morsel of this feast, but rather, thou hadst in this feast only a morsel, this feast
was to thee but a morsel. The use of &lquo;of&rquo; is therefore similar to other Shake-
spearian expressions: &lquo;We lost a jewel of her,&rquo; [<I>All's Well,</I> V, iii, 1], we lost a jewel
in her; &lquo;You shall find of the king a husband,&rquo; [<I>All's Well,</I> I, i, 7].&mdash;<SC>W. A.
Wright</SC>: Cominius appears to mean that the previous reputation of Marcius was
so little increased by his present achievement that he was like one who took but
a morsel of a feast, having fully dined before.

<P>20. <B>Pray now, no more</B>] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): The humility of
Coriolanus only covers a subtler pride. He will not be praised for his valour, for
that praise implies that he has done something exceptional and surprising; and he
does not wish brave deeds to be thought exceptional and surprising in him.
<P>21. <B>a Charter to extoll</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: A privilege to praise her own son.
<P>24. <B>Countrey</B>] Here, <I>metri gratia,</I> pronounced as a trisyllable. For other
examples of this lengthening of a syllable after the letter <I>r,</I> see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 477.
<P>25, 26. <B>He that . . . mine Act</B>] <SC>Prolss</SC> (p. 69): If this and other remarks, as
Cominius has it [l. 66], be likewise modesty, it is yet indeed a proud modesty. It
may annoy a great and noble nature to be openly and fulsomely praised. It may,
however, be asked whether the deprecation of such praise does not afford a greater
satisfaction to the self-consciousness. It may well be that what Marcius here
says is truly meant&mdash;and assuredly he is not one to seek praise, or is in the least
as the Tribune Brutus and, later, Aufidius call him, a braggart&mdash;but he would
perhaps have felt wounded in his self-love had his deeds and deserts remained
quite unnoticed. At all events his behaviour on this occasion throws a very clear
light on his bearing later in the Senate and on his candidature for the Consulate.
Here once again he allows to the soldiers of the people a certain recognition and
reference to their own feelings, which is contrary to Plutarch, who makes no refer-
ence to this at all.

<P>34, 35. <B>not to reward What you haue done</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: So, in <I>Macbeth,</I>
&lquo;Only to herald thee into his sight, Not pay thee,&rquo; [I, iii, 102. With all deference
to Steevens I must say that the parallelism between these two passages is of the
slightest, and the idea conveyed is totally different; here Cominius remonstrates
with Marcius for his modesty, and asks that he be allowed to tell the army the
real state of affairs before Marcius rewards, or praises, what he himself has done.
For &lquo;reward&rquo; we might, perhaps, read <I>re-word,</I> that is, <I>repeat,</I> as in <I>Hamlet,</I> III,

meaning, Cominius begs Marcius not to repeat his detractions as his deeds, but to

<P>39. <B>'gainst Ingratitude</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, when exposed to ingratitude.
Compare <I>Numbers,</I> xxv, 4: &lquo;Take all the heads of the people, and hang them up
before the Lord against the sun.&rquo; And see <I>King John,</I> V, iv, 25: &lquo;Which bleeds
away, even as a form of wax Resolveth from his figure 'gainst the fire.&rquo; Com-
bined with this sense of &lquo;against&rquo; there is also the other idea of the wounds closing
themselves against external aid and becoming their own deadly surgeons.
<P>40. <B>tent themselues with death</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: A &lquo;tent&rquo; is a roll of lint which
was used by surgeons for probing wounds and introducing into them the means
of healing. Hence &lquo;to tent&rquo; is first <I>to probe,</I> and in a secondary sense <I>to cure.</I>
See III, i, 286. The wounds having closed themselves against external influences
are filled with deadly festering matter instead of the health-giving surgeon's tent.
For the substantive &lquo;tent,&rquo; see <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> II, ii, 16, &lquo;doubt is call'd The
beacon of the wise, the tent that searches To the bottom of the worst.&rquo; [In <I>Notes
&amp; Queries,</I> Ap. 30, 1881, p. 344, J. D. quotes the present passage, and defines
&lquo;tent&rquo; as here used in the sense of a <I>liniment</I> or <I>embrocation,</I> quoting in support
of this from Migne's <I>Ducange,</I> s. v. <I>tenta:</I> &lquo;linamentum quod vulneribus apponitur;
compresse, bande de lin, olim tente.&rquo; But here &lquo;linamentum&rquo; is merely the Latin
word for <I>lint,</I> as may be seen by the French paraphrase.&mdash;<SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>) does
not include the meaning <I>liniment</I> or <I>emollient</I> among the various meanings of &lquo;<I>tent.</I>&rquo;

<P>54-59. <B>May these same Instruments . . . for th'Warres</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: Many
of the verses in this really fine passage are dismounted, unnumerous and imperfect.
For this reason I have ventured to transpose them to their measure; and the sense,
'tis plain, has been no less maimed than the numbers. To remedy this part I
have had the assistance of my ingenious friend Mr Warburton; and with the
benefit of his happy conjectures, which I have inserted in the text, the whole, I
hope, is restored to that purity which was quite lost in the corruptions. I shall
now subjoin his comment in proof of the emendations: &lquo;The meaning that sense
requires in the antithesis evidently designed here is this: If one change its usual
nature to a thing most opposite, then let the other do so too. But Courts and Cities,
being made all of smooth-fac'd soothing, remain in their proper nature. In the
second part of the sentence the antithesis between steel and the parasite's silk
does not indeed labour with this absurdity, but it labours with another equally
bad, and that is, Nonsense in the expression. The Poet's whole thought seems to
be this: If drums and trumpets <I>change their nature preposterously, let</I> Camps <I>do
so too.</I> And in the latter part of the sentence the emendation seems to give a
particular beauty to the expression. He had said before, If drums and trumpets
prove flatterers; now here, alluding to the same thought, he says, <I>Then let</I> Hymns,
<I>soft music</I> destined to the praises of gods and heroes, be an overture for the wars;
where the overture is used with great technical propriety. I should observe one
thing, that the members of these two antitheses are confounded one with another,
which is a practice common with the best authors; and it is a figure Rhetoricians
have found a name for.&rquo; [In his own edition, fourteen years later, Warburton
has apparently completely re-written the note on this passage. The main drift
</CC>

<C>[54-59. <B>May these same Instruments . . . for th'Warres</B>]</C>
<P>is similar, but it is much less verbose. His revision may be read in the <I>Variorum</I>
of 1821, ad loc., p. 50.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Upton</SC> (ed. ii, p. 170): Marcius Coriolanus says
this after a flourish of drums and trumpets, and the acclamations of the people.
The whole difficulty of the passage (if any) consists in the line, &lquo;<I>Let</I> <SC>Him</SC>, &amp;c.,&rquo;
which he speaks striking his hand upon his heart&mdash;<G>dei/ktikws</G>, as the Grammarians
term it. The editors, not seeing this, have strangely altered the whole.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC>

in the folios and the two elder moderns [Rowe and Pope], but have nothing else
that is wrong in them except the word &lquo;him,&rquo; rightly altered to <I>hymns</I> in the other
moderns, the word <I>overture</I> plainly demanding it. The censure that is contain'd
in a part of them has two distinct aspects, the tendency of which may be seen in
the following paraphrase: When flattery shall creep into camps, let it be no shame
for cities and courts to use it; let the practice be general there, be they &lquo;all made
of false-fac'd soothing&rquo;; and when this happens, that soldiers shall have the soft-
ness of parasites, let them be consistent and do other soft things; forgo the drum
and the trumpet and march to battle to the sound of soft musics, let the overture
to fight be a hymn.&mdash;<SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>: The first part of the passage has been altered,
in my opinion, unnecessarily by Dr Warburton; and the latter not so happily, I
think, as he often conjectures. In the latter part, which only I mean to consider,
instead of &lquo;him&rquo; (an evident corruption) he substitutes <I>hymns;</I> which perhaps may
palliate, but certainly has not cured, the wounds of the sentence. I would propose
an alteration of two words: &lquo;When steel grows Soft as the parasite's silk, let
<I>this</I> (i. e., silk) be made A <I>coverture</I> for the wars!&rquo; The sense will then be apt and
complete. When <I>steel</I> grows soft as <I>silk,</I> let armour be made of silk instead of <I>steel.</I>
&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: It should be remembered that the personal pronoun &lquo;him&rquo; is not
unfrequently used by our author and other writers of his age instead of <I>it,</I> the
neuter; and that overture, in its musical sense, is not so ancient as the age of
Shakespeare. What Martial has said of Mucius Sc&aelig;vola may, however, be
applied to Dr Warburton's proposed emendation: &lquo;Si non errasset, fecerat ille
minus,&rquo; [Bk I, <I>Epigram,</I> xxi.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: Bullokar, in his <I>English Expositor,</I>
1616, interprets the word &lquo;overture&rquo; thus: &lquo;An overturning; a sudden change.&rquo;
The latter sense suits the present passage sufficiently well, understanding the word
&lquo;him&rquo; to mean <I>it,</I> as Mr Steevens has very properly explained it. When steel grows
soft as silk, let silk be <I>suddenly converted</I> to the use of war. We have many
expressions equally licentious in these plays. By &lquo;steel&rquo; Marcius means a <I>coat
of mail.</I> So, in <I>3 Henry VI:</I> &lquo;Shall we go throw away our coats of steel And wrap
our bodies in black mourning gowns,&rquo; [II, i, 160]. Shakespeare has introduced a
similar image in <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> &lquo;Thy beauty hath made me effeminate, And in
my temper soften'd valour's steel,&rquo; [III, i, 120]. &lquo;Overture,&rquo; I have observed
since this note was written, was used by the writers of Shakespeare's time in the
sense of <I>prelude</I> or <I>preparation.</I> It is so used by Sir John Davies and Philemon
Holland. So, in <I>Twelfth Night,</I> Viola says, &lquo;I bring no overture of war,&rquo; [I, v, 225].
&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (ed. i.): I think, with Tyrwhitt, we should read <I>coverture.</I> Notwithstand-
ing Malone's ingenious argument, it is impossible to extract sense from the word
&lquo;overture,&rquo; which anciently, as now, meant &lquo;a motion, or offer made, an opening
or entrance.&rquo; [Singer does not, however, adopt Tyrwhitt's reading either in his

<BQ>

I' the field prove flatterers!&rquo;<LB>

<P>The difficulty increases with the received reading; for, according to this, when
drums and trumpets prove flatterers, courts and cities are to be made of false-
faced soothing. Courts and cities are precisely what a soldier would describe
as invariably so made. But Coriolanus <I>contrasts</I> courts and cities with the field;
he separates them:
<BQ>
&lquo;Let courts and cities be<LB>
Made all of false-faced soothing&rquo;;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>and he adds, as we believe,
<BQ>
&lquo;<I>Where</I> steel grows soft<LB>
As the parasite's silk!&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The difficulties with the received reading are immeasurable. <I>When</I> steel grows
soft as the parasite's silk the commentators say that <I>him</I> (the steel), used for <I>it,</I>
is to be made an <I>overture</I> for the wars; but what &lquo;overture&rquo; means here they do
not attempt to explain. The slight change we have made gives a perfectly clear
meaning. The whole speech has now a leading idea&mdash;&lquo;Let them be made an
overture for the wars.&rquo; Let them, the instruments which you profane, be the
<I>prelude</I> to our wars. Opposed as we are to editorial licence, we hold ourselves
keeping within due bounds in substituting <I>where</I> for &lquo;when&rquo; and <I>them</I> for &lquo;him,&rquo;
for there are several instances of these words having been misprinted in the original
copies. We believe that the sense of these lines has been mistaken, in some
measure, through the deviations from the metrical arrangements in the original.
Our reading follows this arrangement much more closely than that of the modern
editors.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i.): We do not think that any of the modern explanations
[of this passage] have quite arrived at the full sense of the poet. We regulate the
passage as in the First Folio, and, adhering, with a slight exception, to the words of
the original, we only adopt a different punctuation. The meaning of Coriolanus
seems to be: &lquo;Let drums and trumpets never sound more if they are to be pro-
faned by you into flatterers; leave it to courts and cities to be made of false-faced
soothing, when steel grows soft as the parasite's silk; but let them (drums and

<P>The meaning is: When drums and trumpets in the field shall prove flatterers

to war; the steel-clad soldiers shall resign the work of war to the silken clad parasite.

understood as personified.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (ed. ii.): Various attempts have been made to

elsewhere. I have left the passage as it stands in the Folio. The leading thought
seems to be: &lquo;When drums, trumpets, and warlike instruments are profaned,

<P>and &lquo;as the <I>parasite,</I> silk.&rquo;) The only objection to the reading of the Folio text
(and it is a great one) is its rhythm, which is, in my judgment, both un-
Shakespearian and unsuited to the mood of Coriolanus. There must be a pause
after &lquo;Never sound more&rquo;; and it would be in Shakespeare's manner of versifica-
tion and especially appropriate to Coriolanus that the exclamation should come
there to a full period. The prolongation of the first sentence of the speech, by
an accessory clause, into the middle of the next line enfeebles both the protest
and the verse. And the next sentence is measurably open to the same objection.
But the rhythm of the whole speech with any arrangement is far from being
unexceptionable. In the Folio we have a hemistich of seven syllables and three
accents, followed by a line of ten syllables and four accents, which certainly indi-
cates corruption of the text or derangement of the verse.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I>
p. 361): By &lquo;him&rquo; in l. 59 can only be meant the parasite, and what is the meaning
of his being &lquo;an overture for the wars&rquo;? I feel convinced that it is a printer's
error for a noun; and I read <I>pipes,</I> which might be thus mistaken. The meaning
then would be, when things are so, let pipes and tabors, not trumpets and drums,
be used in our armies grown thus effeminate. &lquo;My throat of war be turn'd
Which quired with my drum, into a pipe Small as a eunuch's,&rquo; etc., III, ii, 138.&mdash;
<SC>Verplanck</SC> gives Knight's remarks on this passage in full, adding in conclusion,
&lquo;Thus the whole sum is: &ldquo;Let trumpets and drums cease to sound when they
become flatterers in the field. Let falsehood and flatterers have the rule in courts
and cities, where even steel becomes soft as the parasite's silk. But let martial
music be the prelude only to war.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. i.): That is, let the instruments
of music be used as a prelude to battle. The passage has caused a great deal of
discussion, and as commonly given it seems impossible to make any sense out of
it. The only tolerable explanation of the Folio reading is that &lquo;him&rquo; is used for
<I>it,</I> referring to &lquo;silk,&rquo; and that &lquo;overture&rquo; is a misprint for <I>coverture;</I> so that the
meaning is, &lquo;when <I>steel</I> grows soft as <I>silk,</I> let armors be made of <I>silk</I> instead of
<I>steel.</I>&rquo; We keep to the metrical arrangement of the original, and adopt the pointing
of Knight, as we also do the changes of &lquo;When&rquo; into <I>Where</I> and of &lquo;him&rquo; into
<I>them, where</I> being a relative adverb referring to &lquo;courts and cities&rquo; and <I>them</I> refer-
ring to &lquo;instruments.&rquo; Everyone experienced in proof-reading knows how apt
<I>where</I> and <I>when</I> and <I>him</I> and <I>them</I> are to be mistaken for each other, so that the
changes in this case need not be greatly scrupled. Touching the whole passage
as here given, we may observe that Marcius is referring to the &lquo;long flourish&rquo;
which has just been made by the musical instruments in honour of his stout and
valiant action. This he regards as a profanation; a using of that which was
meant as an incitement to do, for the purpose of glorifying what has been done.
And he wishes not simply, as it is in the common reading, that those instruments
may never sound more, but that they may never sound more when thus abused
to the end of sounding compliments and flatteries on the battlefield. All such
&lquo;fale-fac'd soothing&rquo; he would have confined to &lquo;courts and cities,&rquo; where steel
itself is used for ornament, not for fighting. That Marcius, with his all-devouring
passion for war, should speak of courts and cities as made up of false-faced soothing
is quite characteristic; but, as he thinks they <I>are</I> so already, he would not wish they
might <I>become</I> so when drums and trumpets leave prompting and turn to com-
plimenting feats of arms.&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): We give
this passage as worded in the Folio, excepting that we substitute <I>them</I> for &lquo;him&rquo;

&lquo;silk,&rquo; supposing also that &lquo;him&rquo; is used as frequently in early writings instead of
the neuter <I>it.</I> But we do not feel that the right sense of &lquo;overture&rquo; has been found.
We suspect the meaning is very simple, &lquo;overture&rquo; being used merely in its ety-
mological sense of <I>opening</I> akin to that in <I>All's Well,</I> V, iii, 16, &lquo;she had made the
overture.&rquo; The complexity and hence the difficulty consists in the figurative idea
attaching to the use of the word here in this simple sense. Marcius was thinking
not of anything in the least abstract, but of an embodied opening, or overture
for war, such an opening as he himself had just been in broaching the way of
battle into Corioli; and again in constituting himself an opening or overture for
the war against the foe in the field when he had desired, as Shakespeare puts it,
to be made into a sword opening the way into the Volscian forces. As Plutarch
says: &lquo;he made a lane through them and opened a passage into the battell of the
enemies.&rquo; Now he is being praised for all this, and while really knowing more
than anyone how essential the service was, he deprecates such praise of it as would
tend to make any less hardihood in men than such deeds require. That is why he
is so fierce about it. He loves valor and would have it a matter of course, not
exceptional, to be made a fuss over. He is sensitively apprehensive of any soften-
ing by praise of the mettle war needs. Therefore he cuts the clamor short. May
these war-trumpets, which you profane by sounding in praise of what is merely
as it ought to be, sound not a tone more. When war-trumpets and battle-drums
flatter on the battlefield (instead of being used for their legitimate purpose to
incite to deeds there) let there be nothing in Courts and Cities but &lquo;false-fac'd
soothing.&rquo; When Steele grows soft as the silk of the parasite, <I>i. e.,</I> the <I>dependent
upon other men,</I> who does not stand alone and take the initiative, then let him be
the one, and open out a path for warfare to follow in, <I>i. e.,</I> &lquo;an Overture for the
Warres.&rquo; He ends thus in proud, grim irony of the inadequacy for such an office,

Shakespeare uses this in the sense of <I>disclosing,</I> not of beginning or prelude; and

of making known. Cotgrave has: &lquo;<I>Ouverture:</I> an overture or opening, beginning
made, path begun or beaten unto; also manifestation, discovery, uncovering.&rquo;
In Bullokar's <I>Dict.</I> (1616) the word appears in this sense, &lquo;<I>Overture,</I> an opening
entrance or way made unto; a motion or offer made.&rquo; [See note by Malone,
<I>ante.</I> This definition does not appear either in the ed. 1616 or 1621.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] The
word, then, might be used by Shakespeare in any of these meanings, and this sense
of opening or prelude is the only one that can give a reasonable explanation of the
passage. . . . The preceding part of the passage is in the same strain. Drums and

the error lies much more probably in &lquo;him,&rquo; which may very likely be a mistake
for some word indicative of the behaviour of the parasite as distinguished from
the warrior. &lquo;Smiles&rquo; are the mark of the courtier, as in <I>Love's Labour's,</I> V, ii,
331: &lquo;This is the flower that smiles on every one.&rquo; I would accordingly suggest
with diffidence: &lquo;Let <I>smiles</I> be made an overture for the wars.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>G. Joicey</SC>
(<I>N. &amp; Q.,</I> 28 Nov., 1891, p. 423): In l. 57 if &lquo;Made all&rquo; were changed to <I>made
well,</I> and the words were understood to mean <I>healed</I> or <I>cured,</I> the sentence would
very well express the soldier's idea that courts and cities corrupt men. In the
second clause the confusion may have arisen through the compositor or transcriber
mistaking the words <I>wear</I> and <I>coverture</I> for &lquo;wars&rquo; and &lquo;overture,&rquo; and then other
changes may have been made in an attempt to rectify the passage. How would
it do to read somewhat as follows: &lquo;When steel grows soft as the parasite's silk
Let <I>it</I> be made <I>a coverture</I> for <I>his wear!</I>&rquo; This reading, although it takes great
liberty with the text, and is open to objection, would give a proper antithesis:
War having turned flatterer, let courts and cities cast off their false-faced soothing,
and steel having grown soft as silk, let it be spun into clothing for parasites to
wear. The word <I>coverture</I> is most like &lquo;overture&rquo; or the last line might read &lquo;into
<I>vesture</I> for his wear.&rquo; The spirit of the speech would tend to cause <I>wear</I> to be read
&lquo;wars.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>H. Ingleby</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Q.,</I> 6 Feb., 1892, p. 103), unaware apparently that he
was anticipated, proposes to arrange and point these lines identically as they appear
in Dyce, ed. ii.; he, however, retains the Folio reading &lquo;overture&rquo; where Dyce fol-
lows Tyrwhitt. Ingleby thus paraphrases: &lquo;Away with these instruments, which
you profane! When war-like instruments prove flatterers, then shall our courts
and cities be all composed of flatterers too! and when our steel becomes as soft as
the flatterer's silk, then send him (the flatterer) to deliver our messages of war!
Let us have no more of these instruments (which are unsuitable to us)!&rquo; In sober
prose we should have expected &lquo;When our drums prove flatterers, then will our
courts,&rquo; &amp;c. But in declamatory verse expressive of indignation the imperative
is much more effective though less grammatically accurate. It has generally
been objected that a soldier would always describe courts and cities as &ldquo;made of
false-faced soothing.&rdquo; But surely not a citizen of Rome! &ldquo;Him&rdquo; is usually

(<I>N. &amp; Q.,</I> 6 Feb., 1892, p. 104): With no change save in the punctuation, and the

reading in the Folio, [Spence places a full stop after &lquo;flatterers,&rquo; after &lquo;silk,&rquo; and
after &lquo;wars,&rquo; with an exclamation point after &lquo;I say&rquo;] presenting it thus: &lquo;May I
never more hear trumpet or drum if you are to profane them thus. Flattery may
well dominate courts and cities when steel-clad warriors thus act like silken para-
sites. Keep these instruments for their proper use, to sound the battle charge.
No more of this fulsome adulation!&rquo; [In <I>N. &amp; Q.</I> for 3 June, 1899, seven years
later than the foregoing note, Spence proposes &lquo;further emendations of the original
text,&rquo; viz.: <I>them</I> for &lquo;him,&rquo; which he now refers to &lquo;silk&rquo; and therefore proposes
that this be changed to <I>silks.</I> The patient reader who has journeyed thus far
through this long note will be aware, as Spence was not, that in both these con-
jectures the proposer had long since been anticipated.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>A. E. Thiselton</SC>
(<I>N. &amp; Q.,</I> 28 Jan., 1899, p. 63): If &lquo;him&rquo; is regarded as the dative instead of the
objective case the difficulty in this much-discussed line will, I think, disappear.
What would be then expressed would be: &lquo;Let an overture for the wars be made
to him,&rquo; meaning, &lquo;Let a proposal be made to the parasite with a view to engaging
his services for the wars. The bribes and flatteries you offer will be congenial to
him, and when steel has become soft as the silk he wears, he will make your best
soldier.&rquo; The words are spoken with infinite scorn, and no doubt contain, in
addition, a suggestion that the Romans would like to have a general who would
flatter them to their hearts' content, as a parasite flatters his patron. The word
&lquo;overture&rquo; is peculiarly appropriate in connexion with bribes and flattery. Corio-
lanus has just refused what he regards as a bribe to pay his sword, and, in the
lines which immediately precede, has pictured a world whose ruling principle was
flattery. &lquo;Overture&rquo; would thus appear to be far more in keeping with the spirit
of the context than <I>coverture,</I> which has generally supplanted it, while <I>armature</I>
owes its introduction merely to the manifest deficiency of <I>coverture.</I> Besides,
when steel has become soft as silk what need of either <I>coverture</I> or <I>armature</I> for
the wars?&mdash;<SC>G. S. Gordon</SC>: &lquo;Him&rquo; probably refers to &lquo;steel&rquo; by a freedom common
in Elizabethan writers. <I>Coverture,</I> which is a modern correction, means <I>covering</I>
or <I>dress,</I> so that Coriolanus may be supposed to be ironical: &lquo;When steel grows
as soft as the parasite's silk, then let it be made a covering for the wars (and a
fine covering it will make!).&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): I retain the Folio reading, and
explain it by regarding &lquo;him&rquo; as referring to &lquo;the parasite&rquo; and as a dative. Staun-
ton alone, if I am not mistaken, has done so [see note by Thiselton, <I>ante.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>],
but he rashly thought that &lquo;overture&rquo; was a misprint for <I>ovation,</I> or had that sense.
. . . Had l. 59 run &lquo;Let him be made an offer,&rquo; etc., the sense would have been
unmistakable; and as it stands, it seems to me (whether the line be correct or a
misprint, and whatever its artistic demerits as an expression of thought) to admit
readily of the following meaning: Let him (the parasite) be made a proposal for
the wars. The thought of the passage in this case is: When your drums and
trumpets flatter, when the soldier's garb is accommodated to the soft limbs of the
parasite, why not complete the round and get the man to match? . . . If <I>coverture</I>
is read instead of &lquo;overture,&rquo; the only proposal commanding attention is that which
refers it to silk or steel soft as silk, <I>without further alteration. Coverture</I> has not

<P>been found = armor, but it is used for clothes and comes pretty near the sense
of protective covering in Nashe, <I>Summer's Last Will</I> (Haz.-Dods., viii, 77), cited
by an anonymous MS. annotator of Deighton's ed. of <I>Coriolanus:</I> &lquo;Will'd that his
body spoiled of coverture Should be cast furth into the open fields.&rquo; The objec-
tion is that it necessitates imputing to Shakespeare a lax use of &lquo;him&rquo; for <I>it</I> (ac-
cusative), which he has not elsewhere employed, in a passage where it especially
leads to ambiguity. In the only illustration actually offered from other writers
there can be no doubt of the meaning, and the use otherwise fits in more naturally
with the thought. See (as quoted by Wright, <I>ante</I>) Bacon, <I>Advancement of
Learning,</I> ii, 22, &sect; 11. Obviously <I>coverture</I> could be read with dative <I>him</I> referring
to the parasite, but <I>coverture</I> has not the claims of a Folio reading.&mdash;<SC>Tucker
Brooke</SC> (<I>Yale Sh.</I>) retains the Folio reading, &lquo;overture,&rquo; since he considers that
Tyrwhitt's alteration does not much assist the interpretation of l. 59. His own
interpretation is substantially the same as Staunton's, that &lquo;him&rquo; is in the dative,
not the objective case, and thus refers to the parasite. &lquo;When soldiers adopt the
effeminate ways of courtiers let us recruit our armies among the latter class.&rquo;

<P>63. <B>shoot</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: See I, i, 228 and V, v, 6, where &lquo;Vnshoot&rquo; is found
for <I>Unshout.</I> This variation of spelling perhaps represents the current pronuncia-
tion, and if so it illustrates a passage in <I>Henry V:</I> III, vi, 81, &lquo;a horrid suit of
the camp,&rquo; where for &lquo;suit&rquo; the Folios have &lquo;sute,&rquo; and the Quartos of the imperfect
play &lquo;shout.&rquo; There is evidence that in Shakespeare's time <I>suit</I> was pronounced
<I>shoot,</I> and the present passage shows that &lquo;shoot&rquo; might have been represented by
<I>shout,</I> so that the Quartos do not really point to a different reading.
<P>64. <B>dieted</B>] Compare &lquo;Ile watch him Till he be dieted to my request,&rquo; V, i,
66.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.,</I> s. v.) furnishes other examples of this form of the verb.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>66. <B>Com. Too modest,</B> etc.] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): Cominius has a difficult
part to play, and it is noticeable how well he keeps his temper. As general, it is
his duty to praise Marcius; as a subordinate, it is Marcius's duty to be &lquo;grateful&rquo;
for his general's praise instead of parading his superiority to it.
<P>68. <B>giue</B>] <SC>Bradley</SC> (<I>N. E. D.,</I> s. v. 25): To represent, describe, portray, report.
Now <I>rare.</I> [The present line quoted as earliest example. <SC>Abbott</SC> compares
<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> I, iv, 40: &lquo;Men's reports give him much wronged.&rquo; According to
<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) these are the only examples in Shakespeare wherein the word is
used in the above sense.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>testimonie that he had wonne that day the price of prowes above all other, a
goodly horse with a capparison, and all furniture to him.&rquo; This Shakespeare does
not omit. [The present lines quoted.] But the same episode furnishes Titus
Lartius with his imagery as he points to the wounded and victorious hero, &lquo;O
general Here is the steed, we the caparison,&rquo; ll. 17, 18. This illustrates the sort
of sea-change that always takes place in the language of North under the hands
of the magician, though it may not always be equally perceptible. But it is never
entirely lacking even where we are at first more struck by the amount that Shake-
speare has retained without alteration.
<P>78. <B>Marcus . . . euer</B>] As will be seen by the <I>Text. Notes</I> this long line was
divided into two, first by Johnson, ending &lquo;<I>Coriolanus . . .</I> euer&rquo;; secondly, by
Steevens, ending &lquo;Beare . . . euer.&rquo; <SC>Walker</SC>, having evidently the text of the
Variorum of '21 only at hand wherein Johnson is followed, remarks, &lquo;A catalectic
line is a discord in Shakespeare.&rquo; To remedy this he suggests that the lines end
as in Steevens's arrangement, apparently unaware that therein he is anticipated
by that meticulous prosodist.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>, following Theobald's rearrange-
ment of the name, says: &lquo;The first is the <I>pr&aelig;nomen</I> peculiar to the individual;
the second, the <I>nomen,</I> or <I>nomen gentilicium</I> or name of the clan to which he be-
longed; the third the <I>agnomen,</I> or name, or title, added on (the &ldquo;addition&rdquo; as here),
given as an honorary distinction. Such <I>agnomina</I> were sometimes given by one
general to another, sometimes by the army and confirmed by the general-in-chief,
sometimes by the people assembled in public, and sometimes assumed by the
person himself. Here the <I>i</I> in &ldquo;Coriolanus&rdquo; must be pronounced short.&rquo;
<P>81. <B>Martius</B>] <SC>R. G. White</SC>: It has been the general custom to invest Marcius
immediately with his cognomen, and to prefix this and his following speeches,
<I>Coriolanus</I> [see <I>Text. Notes</I>]. But in the Folio this, with some propriety, is not
done until the arrival of the hero in Rome and the proclamation and confirmation
of his honors.

<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 413): I understand the meaning to be, to illustrate this honourable
distinction you have conferred on me by fresh deservings to the extent of my power.
To &lquo;undercrest,&rquo; I should guess, signifies properly to wear beneath the crest as a
part of a coat of arms. The name or title now given seems to be considered as
the crest; the promised future achievements as the future additions to that coat.&mdash;
<SC>Johnson</SC>, justly dissenting to Warburton's interpretation of &lquo;to the fairness&rquo; as
meaning <I>to the utmost,</I> remarks: &lquo;I know not how &ldquo;fairness&rdquo; can mean <I>utmost.</I>
When two engage on equal terms we say it is <I>fair;</I> &ldquo;fairness&rdquo; may, therefore, be
<I>equality; in proportion equal to my power.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: &lquo;To the fairness of my
power&rquo; is, as fairly as I can.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.,</I> s. v. Fairness, 2.): Spotlessness, un-
stained honour. [The present line quoted.] Alluding to l. 82.&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Coriolanus,</I>
p. 121): If &lquo;undercrest&rquo; is the word of the poet, this must be the sense: In his
modesty Marcius is not of opinion to have already merited &lquo;the good addition,&rquo;
the name of honour, Coriolanus; he promises to merit it by other deeds; for him
it is nothing more but a hollow name until he has &lquo;undercrested&rquo; it, adorned it
by new heroical actions, and to the &lquo;fairness of his power.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's
Sh.</I>): That is, And always to support, to the best of my ability, the title you have
graciously conferred on me. &lquo;To undercrest&rquo;; not simply &lquo;to wear as on the crest,&rquo;
but &lquo;to support as if it were my crest,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> to act up to it and so justify its be-
stowal on me, just as a man feels that he must act up to some great family motto.
The metaphor from heraldry may be preserved by using the word &lquo;support,&rquo;
which is a technical heraldic term. The whole utterance is a piece of &lquo;irony.&rquo;
It is significant of the man that he does not refuse <I>this</I> reward like the material
reward offered him.
