<P>140; and again, <I>Ibid.,</I> 97, &ldquo;poorly rich.&rdquo; It is strange that no editor, so far as
I have seen, has noticed the discrepancy between Shakespeare and his authority,
Plutarch, in the description of the Coriolan host.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 581): The
postponement of pity to wrath is a new characteristic detail which shows how these
gentler impulses in Coriolanus must yield to his ruling passions. On the other
hand, his host is transformed from a rich to a poor man, and thus his humanity
acquires a wider range, and we see how it can extend beyond his own class if only
there is a personal claim on it. Above all, there is the new illuminating touch of
the lapse of memory. Sometimes this has been taken as betraying the indiffer-
ence of the aristocrat for an inferior whose name he does not think it worth while
to remember. Surely not. Coriolanus is experiencing the collapse that follows his
superhuman exertions, the exhaustion of body and mind when one cannot think
of the most familiar words, but he rallies his strength for a last effort, and is just
able to intercede for his humble guest-friend ere he succumbs.&mdash;<SC>Prolss</SC> (p. 102):
Plutarch, by making the host of Coriolanus a rich man, directly bases the leader's
request upon the contrast between the former wealth and the present pitiable
condition of his host. Shakespeare by making Marcius forget the name of his
host seeks not only to exalt the purity of the pity and complete lack of self-
seeking in the gratitude of his hero but also that he knows how to value good
qualities even in a poor man.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): Shakespeare's variation
of the man's status [as given by Plutarch] tells in two ways: by heightening our
admiration of the hero who, at such a moment, remembers his humble befriender,
and by emphasizing the aristocratic, exclusive temper to which the name of a
mere man of the people had been of no account.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Some critics
believe that Shakespeare's purpose in inventing the circumstance of Coriolanus's
<I>forgetfulness</I> is to represent him as being so selfish that he does not care to take the
trouble to remember the name of his poor host and makes his request &lquo;entirely
out of a sense of what his own magnanimity requires of him&rquo; (Deighton, [MS.]).

<P>3. <B>The Towne is ta'ne</B>] <SC>Bayfield</SC> (191): Is it within the remotest bounds of

sound of the syllables is unchanged. What should we think of a modern poet who
wrote: &lquo;The Seine is seen,&rquo; or &lquo;The lane is lone,&rquo; or &lquo;The main doth moan,&rquo; or
&lquo;The sullen tarn awaked her teen&rquo;? Yet we are quite ready to assign to Shake-
speare the most preposterous of the Folio's vagaries. It is hardly too much to
say that, if the various phenomena we are considering were genuine, he must,
as he wrote his plays, have been subject from moment to moment to recurrent
fits of lunacy.

whose edition appeared almost contemporaneously with Capell's <I>Notes,</I> likewise

phrase &lquo;in mercy&rquo; in the same sense occurs in <I>Lear,</I> I, iv, 350: &lquo;He may enguard his
dotage with their powers And hold our lives in mercy.&rquo; In Cowel's <I>Law Dictionary</I>
&lquo;Misericordia&rquo; is defined as &lquo;an Arbitrary Amerciement imposed on any for an
Offence; for where the Plaintiff or Defendant in any Action is amerced, the Entry
is <I>Ideo in</I> Misericordia.&rquo;

<P>14-18. <B>Mine Emulation . . . may get him</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> (<I>Supplemental Observa-

to have subdued him in equal combat, our swords being fairly opposed to each

[For examples of &lquo;where&rquo; in this sense, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 134.]&mdash;<SC>Coleridge</SC>, in his
Notes on this play, commenting on this and the next speech of Aufidius, says:
&lquo;I have such deep faith in Shakespeare's heart-lore that I take for granted that
this is in nature, and not as a mere anomaly; although I cannot in myself discover
any germ of possible feeling which could wax and unfold itself into such senti-
ment as this. However, I perceive that in this speech is meant to be contained
a prevention of shock at the after-change in Aufidius's character.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Verplanck</SC>:
Such a criticism from Coleridge is worthy the reader's consideration, but I cannot
myself perceive its justice. The varying feelings of Aufidius are such as may
be often observed to arise in the contentions of able and ambitious men for honour
or power, and are just such as would, under these circumstances, be natural in
a mind like that of Aufidius&mdash;ambitious, proud, and bold, with many noble and
generous qualities, yet not above the influence of selfish and vindictive emotions
and desires. The mortification of defeat embitters his rivalry to hatred. When
afterwards his banished rival appeals to his nobler nature, that hatred dies away
and his generous feeling revives. Bitter jealousy and hatred again grow up as
his glories are eclipsed by his former adversary; yet this dark passion too finally
yields to a generous sorrow at his rival's death. I think that I have observed very
similar alternations of such mixed motives and sentiments in eminent men in
the collisions of political life.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (<I>Sh's Life, Art,</I> etc., ii, 487), after quoting
in part the foregoing remark by Coleridge, says: &lquo;The speech is hard indeed; but
I do not take it as a fair index of the speaker's real mind; it seems to me but one
of those ebullitions of rage in which men's hearts are not so bad as their tongues;
the impulsive extravagance of a very ambitious and inconstant nature writhing
in an agony of disappointment. In such cases dark thoughts often bubble up
from unseen depths in the mind, yet do not crystallize into character. Still it
must be owned that Aufidius comes pretty near putting the thought of the speech
into act at last.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 586): It seems strange that Coleridge should
say this, for it is proved by not a few examples that baffled emulation may issue
in an envy which knows few restraints. Peril was the avowal rather than the
temper which struck him as verging on the unnatural or abnormal. Those who

<P>deliberately adopt such an attitude do not usually admit it to themselves, still
less to their victims, and least of all to a third party, which may admonish us
that Aufidius's threats were not deliberate, but mere frantic outcries wrung from
him in rage and mortification. Yet they spring from authentic impulses in his
heart, and though they may for a time be hidden by his superficial chivalry, yet
they will spread and thrive if the conditions favour their growth. When they
have over-run his nature and choked the wholesome grain, he will not point to
them so openly and will name them by other names. But they are the same
and differ from what they were only as the thorny thicket differs from its parent
seeds. They have always been there, and it is well that we should be aware of
their presence from the first. . . . In short, it is not to be taken as his definite pro-
gram from which he inconsistently deviates when the opportunity is offered at
Antium for carrying it out, but as the involuntary presentment, which the reveal-
ing power of anguish awakens in his soul, of the crimes he is capable of committing
for his master passion, a presentiment that in the end is realised almost to the
letter.&mdash;<SC>T. Page</SC>: We do not feel Coleridge's difficulty here; we regard the words,
awful as they are, as scarcely to be taken seriously; they represent simply a tem-
porary furious outburst of anger couched in the wildest language Aufidius can
discover on the spur of the moment.

<P>22. <B>sanctuary</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.,</I> p. 163): &lquo;Sanctuary&rquo; is very often a dissyllable.
In old times the word, like the thing itself, was in frequent use, and, like other
familiar terms, became shortened for convenience sake. In Sir Henry Ellis's
Letter's Illustrative of English History, as quoted, <I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> No. 973, p. 625,
col. 3, letter from Lawrence Stubbs to Cardinal Wolsey, <I>the sanctuary men</I> are
called in three places <I>Sentuary men,</I> Ib. <I>the Sentuary.</I> <I>Santry</I> still exists as a family
name; so, by the way, does <I>Sanctuary.</I> [Walker furnishes several examples,
among them the present line, wherein, for the sake of the metre, &lquo;Sanctuary&rquo; is
to be pronounced <I>sanct'ry.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>23. <B>Being naked, sicke</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): That is, &lquo;Nor nakedness, nor
sickness.&rquo; Compare <I>Matthew,</I> xxv, 35, 36, &lquo;I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me,&rquo; etc. [Beeching is
possibly right, but at the same time it is to be remembered that Shakespeare, and
other writers of his time, frequently use &lquo;naked&rquo; in the sense of <I>defenseless, un-
armed.</I> See <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex., s. v.</I> 3) for examples. On the other hand, that &lquo;sick&rquo;
is here coupled with &lquo;naked&rquo; is in favour of Beeching's comparison.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>25. <B>Embarquements</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: The dramatic art of this speech is great.
For after Aufidius had so generously received Coriolanus in exile, nothing but the
memory of this speech, which lets one so well into Aufidius's nature, could make
his after perfidy and baseness at all probable. But this line [l. 25] is corrupt.
For tho', indeed, he might call the <I>assaulting</I> Marcius at any of those sacred seasons
and places an <I>embarkment</I> of fury; yet he could not call the <I>seasons and places
themselves,</I> so. We may believe, therefore, that Shakespeare wrote: &lquo;<I>Embarrments</I> all
of fury,&rquo; &amp;c., <I>i. e.,</I> obstacles. Tho' those seasons and places are all obstacles to
my fury, yet &amp;c. The Oxford Editor [Hanmer] has, in his usual way, refined upon
this emendation in order to make it his own; and so reads <I>Embankments,</I> not con-
sidering how ill this metaphor agrees with what is said just after of their lifting
up &lquo;their rotten privilege&rquo; which evidently refers to a wooden <I>bar,</I> not an earthen
<I>bank.</I> These two generals are drawn equally covetous of glory: But the Volscian
not scrupulous about the means. And his immediate repentence, after the as-
sassinate [<I>sic</I>], well agrees with such a character.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 413): As <I>Embarr-
ments</I> is a word quite new from Mr Warburton's own coinage, from whence he
hath so plentifully besprinkled our poet's works with terms of base alloy, I am not
much inclined to accept it for current. The reading of the former editions was
<I>embarkments.</I> Why may not this word have the same meaning as <I>embargo,</I> derived
from the Spanish, <I>embargar,</I> to arrest, stop, or stay; whence also in the same
language, <I>embaracion,</I> an arresting or stopping? Or if the reader should think a
new word should be coined for the occasion, why not as well <I>embargments?</I> Mr
Warburton's cavil about the uniformity of the metaphor is mere trifling. For
an <I>embarrment</I> made with a wooden bar, as he chooses to have it, unless the said

<P>28. <B>Brothers Guard</B>] <SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 361): With the fullest convic-
tion I read for &lquo;brother's guard&rquo; <I>household hearth;</I> for that was the very place
where he did find him. &lquo;He got him up straight to the chimney hearth, and sate
him down&rquo; (North's <I>Plutarch</I>). Besides, we never hear that Aufidius had a
brother; and it should be <I>under,</I> not &lquo;upon,&rquo; the guard; a man is, or stands, on his
own, not on another's guard. In <I>Rich. II:</I> IV, i, [282] we have &lquo;under his house-
hold roof&rquo;; and <I>household hearth</I> occurs in Campbell's <I>Gertrude of Wyoming,</I> iii,
17. [In both his editions, 1864 and 1865, Keightley records this reading, which
later, in his <I>Expositor</I> (1867), became of &lquo;fullest conviction,&rquo; merely as a <I>conjectural</I>
reading. As to Keightley's objection that this should be <I>under,</I> not &lquo;upon&rquo; guard,
of which he says there are no examples, Wright, following Johnson's interpretation
of the foregoing words, quotes in illustration: &lquo;The messenger Came on my guard,&rquo;
<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> IV, vi, 23, <I>i. e.,</I> while I was on guard. The quotation given by
Steevens, &lquo;The lieutenant watches tonight on the court of guard,&rquo; is not, I think,
apposite; &lquo;the court of guard&rquo; means the <I>court where the guard is placed,</I> as is shown
by Othello's words in a later scene, &lquo;In night and on the court of guard and safety&rquo;
(II, iii, 216).&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>34. <B>attended</B>] That is, <I>waited for.</I> Compare I, i, 74; I, i, 265.
<P>35. <B>'Tis South the City Mils</B>] <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>: But where could Shakespeare have
heard of these <I>mills</I> at Antium? I believe we ought to read, &lquo;'Tis south the city
a <I>mile.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Shakespeare is seldom careful about such little improprieties.
Coriolanus speaks of <I>our divines,</I> and Menenius, of <I>graves in the holy churchyard.</I>
It is said afterwards that Coriolanus talks like a <I>knell;</I> and <I>drums,</I> and <I>Hob,</I> and
<I>Dick</I> are, with as little attention to time or place, introduced in this tragedy.&mdash;
<SC>Malone</SC>: Shakespeare frequently introduces those minute local descriptions
probably to give an air of truth to his pieces. So in <I>Romeo &amp; Juliet,</I> &lquo;&mdash;under-
neath the grove of sycamore, That westward rooteth from the city's side,&rquo; [I, i,
128]. Again, &lquo;Nightly she sings on yon pomegranate tree,&rquo; [<I>Ibid.,</I> III, v, 4].
Mr Tyrwhitt's question may be answered by another question: Where could
Lydgate hear of the mills near Troy? &lquo;And as I ride upon this flode On eche syde
many a mylle stode, When nede was their graine and corne to grinde,&rquo; <I>Auncient
Historie,</I> &amp;c., 1555.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: It is worth while observing, as an indication
that in such cases of local colouring Shakespeare had probably London in his
mind, that in the year 1588 the Mayor and Corporation of the City petitioned the
Queen that they might build four corn mills on the river Thames near the Bridge,
and the Masters of the Trinity House certified that the erection of these mills
&lquo;on the south side of the Thames upon the Starlings above the bridge&rquo; would breed
no annoyance. The &lquo;city mills,&rquo; therefore, in Shakespeare's time were close to the
Globe Theatre.
<P>38. <B>I shall sir</B>]: For this use of &lquo;shall,&rquo; see note by <SC>Abbott</SC>, I, ix, 93, <I>ante.</I>&mdash;
<SC>Raleigh</SC> (p. 102): The whole First Act of <I>Coriolanus</I> is so full of alarums and ex-
cursions and hand-to-hand fighting, with hard blows given and taken, that it is
tedious to Shakespeare's modern admirers, but it gave keen pleasure to the patrons
of the Globe. <I>The Comedy of Errors</I> is noisy with beatings and the outcries of the
victims. All these things, though it discolour the complexion of his greatness to
acknowledge it, were imposed upon Shakespeare by the tastes and habits of his
patrons and by the fashions of the primitive theatre. It was on this robust stock
that his towering thought and his delicate fancy were grafted.

<P>1. <B>Actus Secundus</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): The first part of this scene is an
amusing study in manners. Notice the superior tone Menenius adopts towards
the Tribunes, soon passing into downright rudeness, which they hardly resent,
while he loses his temper at once when they in turn only hint at a home-truth.
The entry of the ladies makes us forget plebeian Rome, and leads up to the tri-
umph. The last part of the scene is a reminder that to ridicule or ignore the
Tribunes is not to draw their sting.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): The purpose of
this prelude is to show that Coriolanus's brilliant exploits and services to his
country have not affected the causes of dissension between the patricians and the
people (represented by the Tribunes) nor the popular feeling of grievance against
Coriolanus himself.&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): The subject of the first
act was the nobility of Coriolanus; for all his faults he is lifted before our eyes to
an heroic level. The subject of the second act is his inherent weakness, leading
up to and explaining the tragic crisis of his fate in the third act. The first need
for a would-be leader of men is a certain sympathy with average every-day hu-
manity. Of this Coriolanus has nothing; he is too completely self-centered and
self-absorbed. It is the function of the second act to bring this out, and to show
how irreconcilable is the hostility between him and the plebeians. The crucial
test of this is the canvassing for the consulship in which Coriolanus's insolent
demeanor gives occasion to his enemies the Tribunes to destroy the momentary
popularity which he has won by his valour.&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>):
This scene passes on the fore-stage. At l. 98 the stage-direction of the Folio shows
that Brutus and Sicinius go <I>Aside,</I> not off the stage. Since the rest, after Corio-
lanus enters in triumph, pass in procession following him across the stage, it may
be that the Tribunes pass way out upon the projecting fore-stage, and, standing
with their backs to the audience and at one side, at the back of the procession,
come forward after it has passed out at the opposite side, presumably on its way
to the <I>Capitoll.</I> After the Messenger comes to summon them they follow in the
same direction.

can, by authority, be discriminated from the corruptions of the stage, the tran-
scriber, or the printer. It is scarcely credible that in the expression of a common
idea, in prose, our modest Shakespeare should have advanced a phraseology of his
own in equal defiance of customary language and established grammar. As, on
the present occasion, the word &lquo;in&rquo; might have stood with propriety at either end
of the question, it has been casually, or ignorantly, inserted at both. [By way of
reply to the foregoing remarks by Steevens, Malone merely refers to a note on a
line from the <I>Chorus</I> preceding Act II. of <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> &lquo;for which love groan'd
for,&rquo; in vol. vi. of <I>Variorum 1821,</I> wherein Malone justifies the redundant prepo-
sition as a grammatical peculiarity of the time, instancing the present line in
<I>Coriolanus,</I> and also, &lquo;The scene wherein we play in,&rquo; <I>As You Like It,</I> II, vii,
139. Steevens refuses to accept these as valid examples, since both are taken from
the Folio text and therefore &lquo;stand on no surer ground than that of copies pub-
lished by ignorant players and printed by careless compositors.&rquo; He adds: &lquo;I
utterly refuse to admit their accumulated jargon as the grammar of Shake-
speare or of the age he lived in.&rquo; Malone in support of his statement and
in answer to Steevens's challenge quotes in answer the following examples of
this redundancy in contemporary writers: Lyly's Prologue at Court, to <I>Cam-
paspe:</I> &lquo;So are we enforced upon a rough discourse to drawe on a smooth
excuse.&rquo; <I>Job,</I> ch. xli, vers. ii, Barker's Bible, 1599: &lquo;Out of his nostrils cometh
out smoke.&rquo; Letter from Lord Burghley to the Earl of Shrewsbury, Jan.
23, 1587-8, Weymouth MSS: &lquo;I did earnestly enqre of hym, in what estate he
stood in for discharge of his former debts.&rquo; In another letter from the same to
the same, October 26, 1586: &lquo;To the which it is ment that we all should put to
our names.&rquo;&mdash;For other examples from Shakespeare see, if needful, <SC>Abbott</SC>,
&sect; 407.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>25. <B>censured</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, what opinion is formed of you, how you

am censured.&rquo; And <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> III, ii, 16, &lquo;Censure me in your wisdom.&rquo;
<P>25, 26. <B>right hand File</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): That is, men of rank who are
the right hand of the state. The parliamentary sense of right and left is here
quite untenable.&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: That is, by us of the conservative ranks. The &lquo;left-
hand file,&rquo; by the same token, would be radical opposition represented by the
Tribunes. [On this point Schmidt is undoubtedly correct; the use of Right and
Left in the parliamentary sense is too modern for application here.&mdash;<SC>Fortescue</SC>
(<I>Shakespeare's England,</I> vol. i, ch. iv, <I>The Army,</I> p. 114) says: &lquo;A file in these days
consists of two men. In the sixteenth century it numbered at least ten. . . . Again,
the place of honour to military men has always been the right of the line, and
accordingly a captain always drew up his best and choicest men in the right-hand
files of his company.&rquo; Fortescue quotes this present line in illustration.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>31, 32. <B>theefe of Occasion</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: &lquo;Of&rquo; is used frequently to connect
two nouns in apposition, as &lquo;city of London.&rquo; Compare <I>Richard II:</I> I, iii, 196,
&lquo;Banish'd this fair sepulchre of our flesh.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: You are a mighty impatient
pair, Menenius means to say; a very little occasion will put you out. To convey
this meaning it would have been enough to say &lquo;a very little occasion will rob you,&rquo;
&amp;c. But if &lquo;occasion&rquo; can be said to &lquo;rob,&rquo; why not complete the metaphor and
call it a &lquo;thief&rquo;? There is nothing active or possessive about the &lquo;of&rquo; [in the
phrase &lquo;city of London&rquo;], it merely connects in apposition. The meaning is
that London is a city. The meaning of &lquo;thief of occasion&rquo; is that occasion is a
thief.

<P>41. <B>eyes toward . . . your neckes</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: With allusion to the fable which

&AElig;sop, reproduced by Ph&aelig;drus, IV, 10, [Bk IV, <I>Fable</I> ix, ed. Dyche, 1713.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
was that Jupiter has furnished every man with two wallets, one hanging down on
his breast and containing his neighbor's faults, which are always before his eyes,
and the other hanging down his back out of sight, and filled with his own faults.
This is referred to by Horace (<I>Sat.</I> II, iii, 299) and by Catullus (xxii, 21), who
seems to speak of one wallet with two parts. Persius (iv, 24) slightly varies the
image by giving every one a single wallet to hang behind him, and making each
neglect his own, and look exclusively on his neighbor's wallet (variously called
<I>pera</I> and <I>mantica</I>).&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;[All of which is excellent as a note on Johnson's note, but
has little if anything to do with the present line in <I>Coriolanus.</I> In spite of the fact
that Johnson's note has been accepted by many commentators, I am quite in
accord with Delius that the context will not admit of any reference to this fable
here. The very next words should have shown Johnson that as Menenius asks
them &lquo;to make but an interior survey&rquo; of themselves there could be no thought
of an <I>exterior</I> wallet either front or back. <SC>Tucker Brooke</SC> (<I>Yale Sh.</I>) says:
&lquo;A variation of the fable is found in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> III, iii, 145, where Ulysses says,

<P>50, 51. <B>not a drop of alaying Tiber in't</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Lovelace, in his <I>Verses
to Althea from Prison,</I> has borrowed this expression: &lquo;When flowing cups run
swiftly round, With no allaying Thames,&rquo; &amp;c. See Percy, <I>Reliques,</I> &amp;c. (3d ed.),
ii, p. 324.&mdash;<SC>Halliwell</SC>: Mr Fairholt sends me this note: &lquo;A remarkable illustra-
tion of the allusion here made to the use of warm drinks by the Romans is fur-
nished from the discoveries made at Pompeii. Under the staircase of a shop in
that city where warm decoctions were sold a bronze urn of beautiful workmanship
was discovered which is now deposited in the Museo Borbonico at Naples. [Fair-
holt gives a sectional drawing of this urn, which shows a spherical receptacle for
the wine, surrounding an inner chamber for hot coals. The wine was poured in
at one side and drawn off by a cock at the lower opposite side. I give this note
for what it may be worth. Shakespeare's antiquarian knowledge as regards warm
drinks among the Romans could hardly have been obtained through the discovery
made at Pompeii, as Fairholt insinuates, since such had not been made until at
least one hundred and fifty years after Shakespeare's death. The allusion here is,
of course, to the popular mulled wine of Shakespeare's day.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>W. A.
Wright</SC>: Compare V, iii, 94, and <I>Mer. of Ven.,</I> II, ii, 195, &lquo;&mdash;allay with
some cold drops of modesty Thy skipping spirit.&rquo; Baret (<I>Alvearie,</I> s. v.) has,
&lquo;Alaied: tempered with water. Dilutus. . . . He alaieth wine with water. Lympha
temperat merum.&rquo; See also Huloet's <I>Abcedarium</I> (1552): &lquo;Alaye wyne. Diluo. . . .
Alayd wyne. Aquaticum Vinum.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Henry Irving Sh.</I>): There were
originally two verbs of this form, one being purely English and meaning <I>to put
down, reduce;</I> the other through French, from Latin <I>alligare,</I> now written <I>alloy,</I>
after the modern French form, and meaning <I>to mix.</I> The senses very much ran
into each other, and were in time referred to a single verb. The metaphor here
might be either that of <I>reducing</I> (as in <I>Paradise Lost,</I> x, 566, &lquo;Fondly thinking to
allay their appetite&rquo;) or that of <I>mixing with alloy.</I>

which Mr Singer remarks [as in the foregoing note]. Come, come, Mr Singer,

accepting that of Collier's MS. Corrector &lquo;as it makes both the sense and the humour
perfect.&rquo; This note Hudson repeats unchanged in his ed. ii.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M.
Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): &lquo;The first complaint&rquo; appears to us clearly to refer
to the first clause of Menenius's speech, his being &lquo;a humourous patrician,&rquo; which is
the first complaint made against him, while his being &lquo;one that loves a cup of
hot wine,&rquo; &amp;c., is the second complaint made against him. He goes on to explain
what is &lquo;the first complaint&rquo; by adding &lquo;hasty and too tinder-like upon too trivial
motion,&rquo; which exactly interprets the word &lquo;humourous&rquo; as used by Shakespeare
in one of the senses it bore in his time.&mdash;Rev. <SC>John Hunter</SC>: That is, somewhat
weak in at once showing by my looks when I am displeased.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus,</I>
p. 86) quotes at some length two interpretations of this passage: the first, that
which is commonly accepted, viz., Menenius is too apt to give judgment in the
case of an appeal without due deliberation; second, that some commentators
have understood by &lquo;the first complaint&rquo; the sin of Adam and Eve, symbolised
by the eating of the apple; Georg Herwegh, who edited this play for Ulrici's ed.,
is responsible for this; he has had no followers, but, as Schmidt objects, Menenius
is represented as an old man, and besides he is not given to speaking so euphemis-
tically. Schmidt is quite in agreement with those editors who hold that the text
is here corrupt, but maintains that no emendation thus far proposed is acceptable
(Leo's &lquo;<I>feast of lent</I>&rquo; he only refers to as &lquo;a curiosity&rquo;). In conclusion he offers his
own solution of the difficulty, which as an original emendation is even more of
&lquo;a curiosity&rquo; than Leo's; it is that we here read <I>thirst-complaint.</I> No reference is
made to the fact that this is the reading of Collier's MS. Corrector or that any
other editor so reads following that correction. Schmidt na&iuml;vely explains that <I>f</I>
and <I>th</I> are near allied in sound and that as the Tribunes speak of hunger Menenius
confesses to a sympathy with the thirsty ones. This is, however, but one of many
indications in Schmidt's notes to this play that he had not consulted&mdash;perhaps
even did not know of&mdash;the MS. corrections in Collier's Folio.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>:
That is, in hastily judging a case without waiting to hear the other side; not wast-
ing time upon trifles like the Tribunes. It has been objected to this reading that
Menenius would not speak of himself in such depreciatory terms, and justify the
Tribunes&rquo; attack. But it is his humour to say of himself the worst that popular
opinion says of him, and so to disarm his opponents; that he is quick of temper
and hasty of tongue, that his bark is worse than his bite, that he never stops to
think whether his outspokenness will give offense. There appears to be no neces-
sity for change, and certainly none for reading with Collier &lquo;the thirst complaint&rquo;
or with Leo &lquo;savouring the feast (or fish) of Lent.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Rolfe</SC>: That is, somewhat
faulty as a magistrate in forming an opinion of a case before hearing the other
side.&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: Somewhat imperfect because of a way I have of favouring the
first complainant. I suppose this means that he gave the impression, when he
was on the bench, of being keener to get through and away than to hear both
sides and give deliberate judgment. [The majority of modern editors is in favour

<P>56, 57. <B>I cannot call you Licurgusses</B>] <SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>):
This fleer of the old patrician has doubly humorous force of allusion; since it not only
refers to the renowned Spartan lawgiver, Lycurgus, who was a man that banished
luxury and possessed large wisdom with utmost severity of morals, but it also includes
reference to a King of Thrace, named Lycurgus, who abolished the worship of
Bacchus from his dominions, and ordered all the vines therein to be cut down, in
order to preserve himself and subjects from the temptations and consequences of
a too free use of wine.&mdash;<SC>Orger</SC> (p. 61): This passage has been left without al-
teration by the editors, when the suppression of the parenthesis is, I think, evi-
dently demanded by the sense. Menenius is piquing himself on his frankness,
and declares that he cannot call such politicians as these Lycurgusses on any oc-
casion when he falls in with them. I think it clear we should read, &lquo;Meeting
two such wealsmen as you are I cannot call you Lycurgusses. If the drink,&rquo; etc.

not find in your talk the ass as an ingredient (in compound),&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> if it is not all
pure asininity. That the alteration <I>cannot</I> renders the phrase more easily in-
telligible may not be gainsaid.

<P>60. <B>the Asse in compound</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Shakespeare was thinking of the

the syllable.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): Possibly Menenius means that the Tribunes

to kill so capital a calf there,&rquo; III, ii, 110.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>63. <B>you haue good faces</B>] <SC>Gordon</SC>: This jest has not been understood. To

After &lquo;ass&rquo; and <I>as</I> in l. 60 it was easy to think of <I>ace. Ass</I> and <I>ace</I> were pronounced
alike, and Shakespeare had been very guilty of the pun about twelve years before
in <I>Mid. N. Dream,</I> V, i, 315-317 (&lquo;Less than an <I>ace,</I> man, for he is dead; he is noth-
ing.&rquo; &lquo;With the help of a surgeon, he might yet recover, and prove an <I>ass</I>&rquo;). It
was this <I>ace</I> that suggested &lquo;faces.&rquo; &lquo;Faces&rquo; was a regular word for &lquo;face-cards&rquo;
(<I>i. e.,</I> king, queen, knave), and &lquo;face&rquo; and <I>ace</I> ran naturally together. Compare
Cotton's <I>Complete Gamester</I> (1674): &lquo;If you have neither ace nor face you may
throw up your game&rquo; (<I>N. E. D.</I>). On this and the ordinary meaning of &lquo;faces&rquo;
Menenius puns. You are worthy &lquo;asses,&rquo; he says, and speaking of &lquo;aces,&rquo; they
are deadly liars that report you have good &lquo;faces.&rquo; This is not easy punning, but

Menenius, 'tis plain, is abusing the Tribunes, and bantering them ironically. By
&lquo;Conspectuities&rquo; he must mean their <I>sagacity, clearsightedness;</I> and that they

explains this word, <I>Caecus:</I> vox agro Lincoln usitatissima. Ray concurs, in his
<I>North and South Country Words.</I> And our author gives us this term again in
his <I>Hamlet,</I> where the sense exactly corresponds with this interpretation: &lquo;Run
barefoot up and down, threatning the flames With bisson rheum,&rquo; [II, ii, 528],
i. e., <I>blinding.</I> It is spoken of Hecuba, whose eyes o'erflow and are blinded both
with tears and the rheums of age. [<SC>Malone</SC>, in elucidation of the word <I>bisson,</I>
quotes the above passage from <I>Hamlet</I> without any notice that both explana-
tion and quotation are Theobald's.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Halliwell</SC> (<I>Folio Edition</I>) quotes
from Boucher's <I>Glossary of Archaic &amp; Provincial Words,</I> s. v. <I>Bisson,</I> as follows:
&lquo;That is, blind. Skinner's explanation and etymology of this word are almost
beneath notice, owing, I imagine, to his having too hastily taken it for granted
that <I>bisson,</I> in Shakespeare's time, did really signify positive blindness. It has
long appeared to me that <I>bisson</I> is fairly deducible from the Saxon verb, of which
the literal import is <I>respicere;</I> and <I>respicere,</I> exactly translated, means <I>to look
back upon.</I> Shakespeare may be thought to have this idea in his mind when in
a speech by the same personage, just before that in which <I>bisson</I> occurs, he says:
&ldquo;You talk of pride; oh, that you could turn your eyes towards the napes of your
necks, and make but an interior survey of your good selves.&rdquo; And it is still more
probable that this idea, having taken possession of his mind, led him immedi-
ately after to use the word <I>bisson,</I> which, I conceive, is its true sense, notwith-
standing its having acquired, in process of time, a somewhat different one in
provincial speech. <I>Bisson rheum</I> it would be harsh, and forced beyond all prece-
dent, to interpret into blindness occasioned by rheum or a defluxion; nor would
it add much, if anything, to the sense and meaning of the passage, even if the
context would admit of such an interpretation. The whole speech has, and was
intended to have, an air of obscurity and mysteriousness, that it might with the
more effect, as well as with greater safety, convey more than met the ear. The
passage in <I>Coriolanus,</I> in which we have the odd phrase of &ldquo;bisson conspectuities,&rdquo;
is also, with the same view, dark and ambiguous, that its ironical severity might

&lquo;blynde Longeus&rquo; of the <I>Cursor Mundi,</I> 16,385. Richardson quotes from Udal's
translation of Erasmus's Paraphrase on <I>Mark,</I> viii. (fol. 52 <I>b</I>): &lquo;This man was not
poreblynd, or a litell appayred, and decayed in sight, but as bysome as was possyble
to be&rquo;; where the Latin is &lquo;sed profundissima caecitate obrutus.&rquo; See also Huloet's
<I>Abcedarium,</I> &lquo;Blynde or besom borne. C&aelig;cigenus.&rquo; The analogy of the Dutch
<I>bijziend,</I> near-sighted, is apparently accidental, although it is referred to by Ett-
m&uuml;ller (<I>Lexicon Anglo-Saxonicum,</I> p. 294), who regards &lquo;bisen&rquo; as equivalent to
&lquo;b&iacute;se&oacute;nde.&rquo;

bowing to you. To make a leg was the phrase of our author's time for a bow,
and is still used in ludicrous language.

<P>72, 73. <B>Forset-seller</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, a seller of faucets or taps. Pals-
grave (<I>Lesclarcissement de la langue Francoyse</I>) gives: &lquo;Faucet to drawe wyne&mdash;
<I>faucet z,</I> m.; <I>broche a estouper le uin.</I>&rquo; And Cotgrave, &lquo;Guille: f. The quill, or
faucet of a wine vessell.&rquo; The French forms of the word given in Cotgrave are
<I>Faulset</I> and <I>Fausset.</I> See Massinger, <I>New Way to Pay Old Debts,</I> IV, ii, &lquo;They
are good souls As ever drew faucet.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Originally <I>faucet</I> had
the meaning of the peg or screw, as opposed to <I>spigot,</I> the tube with which it
makes up the tap, and it has still this meaning in the Sheffield dialect. Compare
Lyly, <I>Mother Bombie,</I> II, v. (ed. Fairholt, ii, 101): &lquo;<I>Memp.</I> I'll teach my wag-
halter to know grapes from barley. <I>Pris.</I> And I mine to discerne a spigot from a
faucet.&rquo; But <I>fauset,</I> rarely <I>fosset,</I> was early used for the whole tap. See instances
in <I>N. E. D.,</I> which include the spelling in the text. Mr A. P. Paton has shown
that <I>forseta</I> = little chest or coffer (<I>cistella, arcella</I>) in Gouldman's <I>Latin Dict.,</I>
and <I>forset</I> (and also <I>forser</I>) occurs much earlier; see Furnivall's <I>Earliest English
Wills,</I> E. E. T. S., p. 70, l. 31, and p. 91, l. 20, and note &lquo;<I>Ital. forziere,</I> a chest, a
forcet, . . . <I>Florio,</I> 1598.&rquo; But a seller of taps is more likely to be coupled with
an orange-seller than a seller of caskets.

<P>76, 77. <B>Mummers</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, <I>maskers</I> or <I>masqueraders.</I> See Cot-
grave (<I>Fr. Dict.</I>): &lquo;Mommeur: m. A Mummer; one that goes a mumming. Mom-
mon, as Mommeur; Also, a troupe, or companie of mummers; also, a visard, or
maske.&rquo; Brand (<I>Popular Antiquities,</I> i. 461, Bohn's ed.) says, speaking of Christ-
mas, &lquo;Mumming is a sport of this festive season which consists in changing clothes
between men and women, who, when dressed in each other's habits, go from one
neighbour's house to another, partaking of Christmas cheer, and making merry
with them in disguise.&rquo; The etymology of the word is uncertain. The Germans
have <I>mumme, mummen, mummer,</I> and <I>mummerei;</I> the Dutch, <I>mommen,</I> &amp;c.; and
in consequence a Teutonic origin has been assigned to the word. But, on the other
hand, the French <I>mommeur, mommerie,</I> the Italian <I>mommeo, mommea, mommeare,</I>
and the Spanish <I>momeria,</I> seem all to point to the Latin <I>momus</I> as the origin of
the word. In Minsheu's <I>Spanish Dictionary</I> an explanation occurs which illus-
trates the present passage: &lquo;hazer M&oacute;mios, to make mops and mowes with the
mouth, to make visages and foolish faces.&rquo;
<P>77. <B>set vp the bloodie Flagge</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, declare war against pa-
tience. There is not wit enough in this satire to recompense its grossness.&mdash;
<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The red flag was the signal of battle. See <I>Henry V:</I> I, ii, 101:
&lquo;Stand for your own, unwind your bloody flag.&rquo; And <I>Jul C&aelig;s.,</I> V, i, 14: &lquo;Their
bloody sign of battle is hung out.&rquo; The famous Dr Sacheverall, in his sermon at
Oxford in 1702, on <I>Proverbs,</I> viii, 15, denounced as apostates and traitors to the
Church of England those of her members who were favourable to the dissenters:
&lquo;Against Whom every Man, that Wishes Its Welfare, ought to hang out the
Bloody Flag, and Banner of Defiance.&rquo;

<P>108. <B>Take my Cappe</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Tho' Menenius is made a prater and a
boon-compainon, yet it was not the design of the poet to have him prophane, and
bid Jupiter <I>take his cap.</I> Shakespeare's thought is very different from what his
editors dreamed of. He wrote, Take my <I>cup,</I> Jupiter, <I>i. e.,</I> I will go offer a liba-
tion to thee for this good news, which was the custom of that time. There is
a pleasantry, indeed, in his way of expressing it, very agreeable to his convivial
character. But the editors, not knowing the use of this <I>cup,</I> alter'd it to &lquo;cap.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 414): Mr Warburton's religious zeal is alarmed at the common read-
ing, &lquo;my cap,&rquo; which he therefore alters to <I>my cup,</I> but it unfortunately happens
that, being in the street, he hath no cup at hand to make the libation out of;
and though Mr Warburton understands this to be an engagement, that he will
go home and offer the libation aforesaid, yet he seems in no great haste to acquit
himself, but tarries on the stage until the procession is ended. In truth this gen-
tleman's religion needed not have been so immoderately scrupulous. Here was
no prophaneness intended. Menenius, on hearing the good news of Marcius,
his return with victory, throws up his cap into the air as a token of his exultation;
and at the same time that he thanks Jupiter offers him his cap, being the first
thing that came to hand, as an acknowledgement of his protection of the republic.
This is followed by a huzza in the usual form: &lquo;Hoo, Marcius coming home!&rquo;
Now what reason can be given why our poet might not have imagined a cap
thrown up into the air with thanks as acceptable an offering to Jupiter as a liba-
tion, at least till an opportunity of offering the latter should present itself? But
be this as it will, the libation is certainly out of the case for the reasons already
given.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: Shakespeare so often mentions throwing up caps in this play
that Menenius may be well enough supposed to throw up his cap in thanks to
Jupiter.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC> remarks that Warburton's proposed change is an indication
of how little Warburton knew of Shakespeare.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: He throws his
cap into the air, Jupiter being especially the god of the sky.

<P>119. <B>Galen</B>] <SC>Grey</SC>: An anachronism of near 650 years. Menenius flourished
Anno U. C. 260, about 492 before the birth of our Saviour. Galen was born in
the year of our Lord 130, flourished about the year 155 or 160, and lived to the
year 200.
<P>120. <B>Emperickqutique</B>] <SC>Ritson</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> p. 141): &lquo;The most sovereign pre-
scription in Galen (says Menenius) is to this news but empiricutick,&rquo; an adjective
evidently formed by the author from empirick (<I>empirique</I>), a quack.&mdash;<SC>Coleridge</SC>
(<I>Notes on Coriol.</I>): Was it without, or in contempt of, historical information
that Shakespeare made the contemporaries of Coriolanus quote Cato and Galen?
I cannot decide to my own satisfaction.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emend.,</I> etc., p. 351):
Emperickqutique was not, if we are to believe the old Corrector, formed from
&lquo;emperick,&rquo; [as Ritson suggests], but was a blunder of the printer for two words
which he absurdly combined in one, namely, &lquo;empirick&rquo; and &lquo;physique,&rquo; as physic
was then often spelt: we ought, therefore, to read, &lquo;the most sovereign prescrip-
tion in Galen is but empiric physic,&rquo; etc. &lquo;Empiric <I>physic</I>&rquo; is, of course, only
quack medicine.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> p. 213): The proposed reading, <I>em-
pirick physique,</I> is plausible. The Corrector of my second Folio has effaced six
letters in the middle of the word, leaving it <I>empirique,</I> which answers every pur-
pose. The third Folio made a step toward it by printing <I>empiricktique.</I>&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>
(ed. i.): There can be little doubt that &lquo;empirickqutique&rquo; is a misprint for em-
pirick physique, the correction in Collier's Folio.

<P>134. <B>fiddious'd</B>] <SC>Wordsworth</SC> (<I>Historical Plays,</I> i, 120): This is explained to
mean treated as Coriolanus treated Aufidius. And if this be correct the word
may be compared with, &lquo;<I>Master Fer.</I> I'll fer him,&rquo; &amp;c., <I>Henry V:</I> IV, iv, 27;
with the use of the participle &lquo;mousing&rquo; in <I>King John,</I> II, i, 371; and with the
verb &lquo;to badger&rquo;=to annoy, as dogs do a badger. . . . It occurs to me that the word
here may possibly be formed from &lquo;Fidius,&rquo; the Volscian and Sabine name of the
god Hercules&mdash;&lquo;trounced by him as by another Hercules!&rquo; (there is a reference
to Hercules below, IV, i, 22, and again IV, vi, 126); not, however, without allusion
to Aufidius's name, which may have been derived from Fidius. Respecting this
Volscian Hercules see Ovid, <I>Fasti</I> vi, 213.
<P>138. <B>the whole Name of the Warre</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, the whole credit or
glory of the war. Compare <I>1 Henry VI:</I> IV, iv, 9: &lquo;York set him on to fight and die
in shame, That, Talbot dead, great York might bear the name.&rquo; [It is, I must admit,
with hesitation that I question any interpretation by Dr Wright, but may not this
phrase refer to the fact that Cominius bestowed upon Marcius the title Coriolanus
from the siege of Corioles? In I, ix, 71-73 Cominius says: &lquo;Therefore be it known
. . . That Caius Martius wears this war's garland . . . and from this time For
what he did before Corioles, call him . . . Marcus Caius Coriolanus.&rquo; It is the ac-
count of this incident that Cominius includes in his report to the Senate.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>153, 154. <B>there's nine that I know</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Seven,&mdash;one,&mdash;and two,
and these make but nine? Surely we may assist Menenius in his arithmetic.
This is a stupid blunder, but wherever we can account by a probable reason for the
cause of it, that directs the emendation. Here it was easy for a negligent tran-
scriber to omit the second <I>one</I> as a needless repetition of the first, and to make
a numeral word of <I>too.</I>&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>, after quoting the substance of Warburton's
explanation and proposed changes, adds this comment: &lquo;It is not without reluc-
tance that I encumber my page by even mentioning such capricious innovations,
but I am sometimes obliged to do so to introduce the true explanation of passages.&rquo;
&mdash;This note Boswell did not include in the <I>Variorum</I> of 1821. Malone does not
provide any explanation, evidently preferring that that task be undertaken by
<SC>Upton</SC>; see next note.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>Upton</SC>: The old man, agreeable to his character,
is minutely particular: &lquo;Seven wounds? let me see; one in the neck, two in the
thigh&mdash;Nay, I am sure there are more, there are nine that I know of.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Coriolanus</I>): Menenius concludes aloud an enumeration he has made to him-
self, and according to which Coriolanus has nine wounds, following the incidents
just related by Volumnia.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): Menenius probably has no reference
to the wounds Volumnia was speaking of, but is probably trying to reckon up
and locate those already known to himself; he therefore specifies three, and then,
in his haste, merely states the gross number.&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>):
Menenius is not adding three to Volumnia's seven and making nine of them.
He corrects her number by adding up all the Tarquin wounds, first aloud, then to
himself, and finds there were nine.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): The usual explanation is
that Menenius silently completes a reckoning of the wounds and arrives at a
total of nine. I believe he supplements by opposing <I>neck</I> and <I>thigh</I> to <I>body,</I> and
then he, or the poet, hastily claims nine instead of ten.

<P>163, 164. <B>Death, that darke Spirit . . . men dye</B>] <SC>R. G. White</SC>: For reasons

subject, I cannot accept this couplet as Shakespeare's. The second line might
be even poorer in thought, and yet have the external semblance to Shakespeare's
work, in which it is now utterly deficient. I believe the lines to have been added
to the prompter's book to please the actor of <I>Volumnia</I> with a round, mouth-filling
speech.&mdash;<SC>Herwegh</SC> (<I>Erl&auml;uterungen und Bemerkungen,</I> ed. <SC>Ulrici</SC>, p. 163): My

of them. I quite agree with Grant White. [Herwegh is, I think, to be commended

<P>ovation in honour of the victor was introduced with great and imposing effect
by John Kemble. On reference to the stage directions of my father's inter-
leaved copy I find that no fewer than 240 persons marched, in stately procession,
across the stage. In addition to the recognised <I>dramatis person&aelig;,</I> thirty-five in
number, there were vestals, and lictors with their fasces, and soldiers with the
spolia opima, and sword-bearers, and standard bearers, and cup-bearers, and
senators, and silver eagle-bearers, with the S. P. Q. R. upon them, and trumpeters,
and drummers, and priests, and dancing girls, &amp;c., &amp;c. Now, in this procession,
and as one of the central figures in it, Mrs Siddons had to walk. Had she been
content to follow in the beaten track of those who had gone before her she would
have marched across the stage, from right to left, with the solemn, stately, almost
funereal, conventional step. But at the time, as she often did, she forgot her
own identity. She was no longer Sarah Siddons tied down by the conventions of
the prompter's book; she broke through old traditions&mdash;she recollected that, for
the nonce, she was Volumnia, the proud mother of a proud son and conquering
hero. So that, when it was time for her to come on, instead of dropping each foot
at equi-distance in its place, with mechanical exactitude and in cadence subservient
to the orchestra; deaf to the guidance of her woman's ear, but sensitive to the
throbbings of her haughty mother's-heart, with flashing eye and proudest smile,
and head erect, and hands pressed firmly on her bosom, as if to repress by manual
force its triumphant swellings, she towered above all around, and rolled, and
almost reeled across the stage; her very soul, as it were, dilating and rioting in its
exultation; until her action lost all grace, and yet became so true to nature, so
picturesque, and so descriptive that pit and gallery sprang to their feet, electrified
by the transcendent execution of the conception.
<P>166. <B>Titus Latius</B>] <SC>P. A. Daniel</SC> (<I>Time Analysis,</I> etc., New Sh. Soc. Trans.,
1877-79, p. 185, foot-note): The introduction of Titus Lartius in this scene is
an oversight which has hitherto been unnoticed, but which modern editors might
take on themselves to correct. Lartius does not speak, nor is he mentioned in
the dialogue as being present. In I, ix. Cominius places him in charge of Corioli.
In II, ii. he is supposed to be still there, for Menenius says, &lquo;Having determined
of the Volsces and <I>To send for Titus Lartius,</I>&rquo; etc. He does not make his appearance
in Rome till III, i, and there we should understand that he has returned from
Corioli without waiting to be recalled. In answer to Coriolanus, who says,
&lquo;Tullus Aufidius then had made new head?&rquo; he replies: &lquo;He had, my lord; and
that it was which caused Our swifter composition.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Henry Irving
Sh.</I>), in answer to the foregoing objection by Daniel, says: &lquo;Possibly Lartius was
allowed to join the triumph upon the stage without the question being raised
whether he had come to Rome on purpose.&rquo;&mdash;This Beeching repeats in his notes
in the later <I>Falcon Sh.,</I> adding thereto the significant remark that the words &lquo;be-
tween them,&rquo; in the stage-direction, and later &lquo;You are three,&rquo; l. 202, show that
the slip was probably Shakespeare's.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>177. <B>No more of this</B>] Mrs <SC>Griffith</SC> (p. 438): In the first scene of the first
Act one of the discontented citizens charges Marcius with paying himself for
his services, &lquo;with being proud&rquo;; and his reproach was just. But yet here he seems
to appear in a light the very reverse of such a character; for when the herald, in
the voice of Rome, is proclaiming his merits, he stops him short by crying out,
&lquo;No more of this; it does offend my heart.&rquo; He manifests the same modesty
also in the scene following this. Again, when he is pressed to harangue the
people in order to get himself elected Consul, he answers in the same style and
spirit of character. But these seeming contradictions form in effect but one char-
acter still. The overvaluing his merits, and the undervaluing the applause of
them, are both equally founded in pride, fierceness, and impatience. Plutarch

<P>draws a comparison of Coriolanus with Alcibiades; but I think he more resembles

<P>181. <B>Kneeles</B>] <SC>Wordsworth</SC> (<I>Sh's Knowledge and Use of Bible,</I> p. 201): Nicholas
Ferrar was born when Shakespeare began to write, viz., in 1592; and we are told
of him, when he was twenty-seven years old, and his mother came to visit him at
Little Gidding, that &lquo;though he was of that age, and had been engaged in many
public concerns of great importance, had been a distinguished member of parlia-
ment, and had conducted with effect the prosecution of the Prime Minister of the
day, at first approaching his mother, he knelt upon the ground to ask and receive
her blessing&rquo;; and he kept up the same practice in his family; as did also, we read,
Mr Philip Henry, who died in 1696; so that we have evidence of the existence of
the custom during two centuries. Bishop Sanderson in 1657 mentions it as
one of the observances which, in that disordered and distempered time, were
cried down as &lquo;rags of popery.&rquo; And there can be no doubt that during the Crom-
wellian usurpation our old English manners suffered not a little, and &lquo;many prac-
tices, which were themselves part and instruments of piety, were exploded and lost
by being branded under that odious name&rquo; (<I>Eccles. Biog.,</I> iv, 180). There could
not be a more striking illustration of the custom of which I have been speaking,
than that Caius Marcius, on his return from the capture of Corioli and victory
over the Volscians, should be made, as he is, to kneel and beg his mother's blessing.

<P>human heart upon the most sacred writing of its folded and golden leaves. Shake-
speare himself could not find words to tell what was in these women. [Few, I
think, realize how profound was the influence of Shakespeare upon the poetic
soul of John Ruskin. In Cook &amp; Wedderburn's definitive edition of his writings
the Shakespearian references occupy ten columns of the Index; that is, five
large 8vo pages.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): This name
for his wife, who, while the others are receiving him with loud rejoicings, meets
and welcomes him with speechless silence looking out from her swimming eyes, is
conceived in the very fulness of poetical and Shakespearian perfection. It com-
prises the gracefulness of beauty which distinguishes her, and the gracious effect
which the love-joy has upon him who shrinks from noisy applause and even from
merely expressed approbation; and it wonderfully concentrates into one felicitous
word the silent softness that characterizes Virgilia throughout. She is precisely
the woman&mdash;formed by nature gentle in manner, and rendered by circumstances
sparing in speech&mdash;to inspire the fondest affection in such a man as Coriolanus;
and we accordingly find him a passionately attached husband. The few words
he addresses to her in the course of the play are among the most intense utter-
ances of spousal enamouredness that even Shakespeare has written. The dramatic
portrait of Virgilia we have always considered to be one of the very finest of the
poet's sketch-productions. It is put in with the most masterly touches; it paints
her by very few strokes, very few colours; but they are so true, so exquisitely
artistic that they present her to the life. She is supremely gentle, and, like most
women whose gentleness is their chief characteristic, singularly immoveable, not
to say obstinate, when once resolved; she is habitually silent, as the wife of such
a man as Coriolanus and the daughter-in-law of such a woman as Volumnia would
undoubtedly become, being naturally of a gentle disposition; and this combination
of gentleness and silence is wonderfully drawn by Shakespeare throughout the
character-portrait, and as wonderfully condensed here into one expressive name.&mdash;
<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Abstract for concrete is common, though, as given to the

<P>209, 210. <B>Euer right . . . euer</B>] <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>: Cominius means to say that
&lquo;Menenius is always the same&mdash;retains his old humour,&rquo; [see <I>Text. Notes</I>]. So in
<I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> V, i, upon a speech from Cassius, Antony only says, &lquo;Old Cassius
still.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: By these words, as they stand in the Folio, I believe Coriolanus
means to say, &lquo;Menenius is still the same affectionate friend as formerly.&rquo; So, in
<I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> &lquo;for always I am C&aelig;sar,&rquo; [I, ii, 212].&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC>
(<I>Shakespeare</I>): Cominius, assenting to their old friend's cheerfully philosophic way
of taking the old &lquo;crab-trees'&rquo; sourness, exclaims &lquo;Ever right&rquo;; and Coriolanus
seconds his general's assent by adding, &lquo;Menenius, ever, ever&rquo;; meaning &lquo;our old
friend always takes the right view of these fellows' crabbedness.&rquo; We explain
this because the passage has been altered as if it were incorrect.

pression, and communicates but a very poor idea. I have ventur'd to substitute

for each other. So, afterwards, in this play: &lquo;And yet to change the sulphur with
a bolt,&rquo; [V, iii, 164]. For here we must likewise read <I>charge;</I> and so in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I>
&lquo;Oh that I knew this husband, which, you say, must change his horns with gar-
lands!&rquo; [I, ii, 5]. In the <I>Maid's Tragedy</I> (Beaumont &amp; Fletcher) <I>Charge</I> is <I>vice
vers&acirc;</I> printed instead of <I>change,</I> &lquo;For we were wont to charge our souls in talk,&rquo;
[III, ii, p. 373, ed. Dyce]. This, 'tis evident, is nonsense; but friends, by the
communication of their thoughts to each other, are finely said to <I>exchange souls</I>
in talk.&mdash;<SC>Warburton</SC>: Mr Theobald had better have told the plain truth, and
confessed that &lquo;change of honours&rquo; <I>communicated</I> no idea at all to him. However,
it has a very good one in itself, and signifies <I>variety of honours;</I> as <I>change of raiment,</I>

<P>foreshadowing. <I>Coriolanus</I> is, to a singular degree, a tragedy of premonitory
hints and casual utterances which the after-course of events makes terribly
momentous.
<P>225. <B>sway with them</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): That is, &lquo;Be king amongst
them.&rquo; This is a note of character. Coriolanus did not aim at tyranny as the
Tribunes thought; he preferred helping the state to hurting it; but, above all, he
preferred his own will.
<P>227. <B>Exeunt, etc.</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Henry Irving Sh.</I>): Mr Daniel [<I>Time Analysis</I>]
would mark a new scene here and a new day, thinking it improbable that Corio-
lanus should be made to arrive in Rome, stand for the Consulship, and be ban-
ished in one day. But such a criticism shows a misconception of the nature of
time in tragedy, which is ideal, concerning itself only with the stages of an action.
<P>229. <B>Bru.</B>] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): The discourse of the Tribunes shows
that, at the very moment of Coriolanus's triumph, he is near an unsuspected
downfall. This elaborate description would be out of place in a modern play,
because the increased capabilities of stage-effect would allow the scene to be repre-
sented more effectually to the eye. But for the rudimentary condition of the
Elizabethan theatre we should have lost some of Shakespeare's finest descriptive
passages.&mdash;<SC>S. Brooke</SC> (p. 230): The Tribunes are not carried away by the triumph
of Coriolanus. They see in it a fresh danger to the liberty of the People for which
they are contending; they lay a plot for his destruction as the enemy of the Peo-
ple, and it is just that they should do it. Coriolanus deserved death. The talk
of Sicinius and Brutus, admirably conceived by Shakespeare, proves them masters
of the situation. It is marked by that pitilessness towards the oppressing class
which has characterised, in all revolutions of the people, the leaders of the people;
and at the back of which is the long hatred of years, sometimes of centuries, as it
was in the French Revolution. The enemy must be annihilated. And the way
to destroy Coriolanus is clear&mdash;to work on his choleric pride till he insults the
people.

<P>follows: &lquo;Stay! Stay! Shrink not away at the sound of his name, to meet whom ye
were wont to press forward so joyously! When rumour announced his approach,
when the cry arose, &ldquo;Egmont comes! he comes from Ghent!&rdquo; then happy were

neighing of his steed was heard, did not every one throw aside his work, while a
ray of hope and joy like a sunbeam from his countenance, stole over the toil-worn
faces which peered from every window. Then as ye stood in doorways ye would
lift up your children and, pointing to him, exclaim, &ldquo;See! that is Egmont! he who

your poor fathers have known!&rdquo;&rquo; Lewes says in his general criticism of <I>Egmont</I>
that it &lquo;was conceived in the period when Goethe was under the influence of
Shakespeare; it was mainly executed in the period when he had taken a classical
direction. It wants the stormy life of G&ouml;tz and the calm beauty of <I>Iphigenia.</I>&rquo;

(<I>Student's Sh.</I>) compares this present passage with the above lines in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> adding:
&lquo;In either case the street-architecture seems that of Elizabethan London. Another
example of Shakespeare's power of suggesting to the mind's eye some crowded, mov-
ing pageant is that wonderful picture (praised so by Dryden) of Bolingbroke's state-
entry into London with King Richard in his train, <I>Richard II:</I> V, ii, 1-40. No
doubt the use of these long passages of description was due to the lack of scenery
on the Elizabethan stage, <I>i. e.,</I> of means to appeal to the physical eye. The
classical example is the scene in <I>King Lear</I> (IV, vi, 11-22), where the blind Glou-
cester wishes to throw himself from what he supposes to be Dover Cliff. Compare
also the description of the cliff at Elsinore, <I>Hamlet,</I> I, iv, 70-78. The same thing
is felt in the prologues of <I>Henry V,</I> especially <I>Prol.</I> iv. (describing the camp-scenes
on the eve of Agincourt).&rquo;
<P>230. <B>spectacled</B>] <SC>Halliwell</SC> gravely tells us that Mr Fairholt has communicated

of these aids to vision is, therefore, an anachronism.

examples of such are unfortunately quite frequent, but in no case with such cir-

<P>238. <B>Flamins</B>] <SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Flamens were priests devoted to the service

The <I>N. E. D.</I> gives only one example earlier than that in the text, from Bellenden's

diall.&rquo; The form <I>flamin,</I> reflecting the <I>i</I> of the oblique cases and nominative plural
of the Latin word, is also Shakespeare's, and common.

<P>Our author means, though he has expressed himself most licentiously, he cannot
carry his honours temperately from where he should begin <I>to where he should end.</I>
The word &lquo;transport&rquo; includes the ending as well as the beginning. He cannot
begin to carry his honors, and conclude his journey, <I>from</I> the spot <I>where he should
begin, and</I> to the spot where he should <I>end.</I> I have no doubt that the text is right.
The reading of the old copy is supported by a passage in <I>Cymbeline,</I> where we find
exactly the same phraseology: &lquo;&mdash;the gap That we shall make in time, from our
hence going And our return, to excuse,&rquo; [III, ii, 64]. Where the modern editors
read &lquo;<I>Till</I> our return,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>: That is, He will make shipwreck by the
way, for he will begin by claiming too much, and he will not know where to
stop. &lquo;From where he should begin and end&rquo; is usually explained as, from where
he should begin, to where he should end; and a similar expression is quoted from
<I>Cymbeline.</I> The passage in <I>Cymbeline</I> admits of no other explanation, but here
it seems better to connect &lquo;transport . . . and end&rquo;&mdash;He will not know how
to advance temperately, step by step of honour, from a modest and wise begin-
ning&mdash;and so temperately end.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> in his ed. i. accepts without question
Malone's interpretation; in his ed. ii. he adopts, however, a conjectural reading
by Seymour, &lquo;to th' end,&rquo; acknowledging that at the time of receiving this into the
text he was not aware that he had thus been anticipated; as his reason for mak-
ing this change he says: &lquo;I have tried in vain to make any sense out of the Folio
reading; and the strained yet futile attempts which have been made at explain-
ing it are, to me, strong argument of its being wrong; for by the same methods
almost any words may be made to yield almost any sense. Another reading has
occurred to me, &ldquo;<I>'Tween</I> where he should begin and end.&rdquo; This would give the
same sense, or nearly the same, as the reading in my text. And as the capitals
F and T are commonly written, either might easily be mistaken for the other;
under which mistake the rest of the word would naturally be assimilated accord-
ingly.&rquo;&mdash;[That the capitals F and T are somewhat alike in modern script is quite
true, but they did not resemble one another in the handwriting of Shakespeare's
time. Capital F was represented by simply doubling the minuscule <I>f,</I> while T
was a crescent-shaped curve opening to the right with a cross mark and dot
on the upper part.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Tucker Brooke</SC> (<I>Yale Sh.</I>): That is, He cannot, as a
self-restrained man could, derive honor from both the beginning and the com-
pletion of his performances. He cannot go an equable pace and conclude with the
same honors with which he begins.

<P>259. <B>As he is prowd to doo't</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: I should rather think the author
wrote <I>prone,</I> because the common reading is scarce sense, or English.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC>
(p. 415): I own the contruction is a little embarrassed, which is occasioned by the
omission of the particle, <I>that,</I> in the last line, whereas in compleat construction the
text should have been, &lquo;As <I>that</I> he is proud to do't.&rquo; But this is a peculiarity not
uncommon in Shakespeare's phraseology. This irregularity, however, is not in
the least helped by Mr Warburton's alteration, which, besides, teaches the reader
nothing, whereas the common reading informs him of the ground of the speaker's
assurance, to wit, the known pride of Coriolanus. For the sense is, Which cause
I make as little question that he will give, as I do, that he hath pride enough to
do so.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 86): &lquo;As <I>that</I> he is proud to do't&rquo; or has pride
enough to do't; and, indeed, 'twere advisable, and no breach of the rules of
severest criticism, to suppose a printer's omission, and let the particle stand where
it does, [<I>i. e.,</I> in Capell's own text.&mdash;The <SC>Cowden Clarkes</SC> accept Warburton's
interpretation, adding as comment on this and the preceding line: &lquo;This sentence
affords an instance of Shakespeare's using a pronoun in reference to a not last-
named antecedent, and of his elliptical mode of making a comparison.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>263. <B>The Naples Vesture</B>] <SC>J. M. Robertson</SC> (<I>Baconian Heresy,</I> p. 191): It is
now perfectly established that Shakespeare drew for his Roman plays mainly on
North's translation of Amyot's <I>Plutarch;</I> that where North errs, following Amyot,
Shakespeare errs, following North; that at no point does he supplement him;
and that, in his ignorance or disregard of chronology, he makes additional mis-
takes of his own. The blunder of making Lartius speak of Cato as a contempo-
rary or predecessor is one of these. The blunder about &lquo;the napless vesture of
humility&rquo; is another, made through following North, who took Amyot's &lquo;<I>robbe
simple</I>&rquo; to mean &lquo;a poor gown.&rquo; The Baconians and the critics who persist in
assigning <I>Titus Andronicus</I> to Shakespeare have alike failed to realize that the
writer of the &lquo;<I>Candidatus</I>&rquo; passage in that play knew the fact that public men
seeking office in Rome wore a white toga, whereas the writer of <I>Coriolanus</I> knew

<P>271, 272. <B>then haue . . . to put</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 350): With the infinitive the <I>to</I> is

<P>274. <B>as our good wills</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>, in a letter to Warburton, dated Feb. 12,
1729, says: &lquo;I read, &ldquo;As our good <I>will is,</I>&rdquo;&rquo; but does not so read either in his
first or second editions.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC> has &lquo;<I>will's,</I>&rquo; which is also the reading of the
<I>Variorum</I> of '78, and '85; and <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC> in a note in the former edition says &lquo;this
should be written <I>will's</I> for <I>will is.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC> explains the passage thus, &lquo;It should
be to him of the same nature as our dispositions towards him: <I>deadly.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Mason</SC>:
Neither Malone nor Tyrwhitt have justly explained this passage. The word
&lquo;wills&rquo; is here a verb, and &lquo;as our good wills&rquo; means &lquo;as our advantage&rquo; requires.
[It is somewhat unusual to find three commentators apparently independently
proposing the same emendation. The Cambridge Edd. assign the reading <I>will's</I>
to Johnson, but Theobald is entitled to priority, while Tyrwhitt seemingly was
unaware that he had been ancitipated.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>an end&rquo; has here the meaning which they attribute to the phrase <I>in short</I> or

<P>ment is necessary. Brutus means to say that Coriolanus thought the people as

<P><SC>Steevens</SC>: The word &lquo;teach,&rquo; though left in the text, is hardly sense, unless it
means &lquo;instruct the people in favour of our purposes.&rquo; I strongly incline to
the emendation of Mr Theobald.&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: We do not alter the text, but we in-
cline to think that <I>touch</I> is the word, as in <I>Othello,</I> &lquo;Touch me not so near,&rquo; [II,
iii, 220.&mdash;Hanmer has, however, anticipated Knight in this; it is also the read-
ing of Collier's MS. Corrector. Of Knight's proposed change Collier was as un-
aware, as Knight was unaware, of Hanmer's reading.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: No altera-
tion is necessary if &lquo;teach&rquo; be taken in the sense of <I>instruct,</I> and if we understand
that the inserted parenthesis has, as so frequently with Shakespeare, confused
the construction: If we, at some time, suggest to the people wherein Coriolanus's
insolence shall teach them&mdash;what is to be done, should follow&mdash;instead of which
the inserted clause follows: which time shall not lack, if one incites him to it, that
is, to such insolence, and that is as easy as to set dogs on sheep&mdash;then, without
concluding the sentence, &lquo;teach the people,&rquo; the first clause is resumed; this sug-
gestion will be as a fire to Coriolanus to set the stubble of the people in a blaze.&mdash;
<SC>W. S. Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.,</I> iii, 210): What can &lquo;teach&rquo; mean? Possibly <I>touch,</I> i. e.,
<I>annoy, provoke. Reach</I> (which was suggested to me by <I>soaring</I>) seems still less
unlikely. [Lettsom, Walker's editor, remarks in a foot-note that neither of these
conjectural readings is original. It is, however, well to remember that Walker's
facilities for consulting the work of his predecessors were of the meagrest.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;
<SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): If the Tribunes must &lquo;suggest to the people&rquo; they cannot
hope that &lquo;teaching&rquo; would do for the purpose; only <I>touching</I> will teach the peo-
ple, whose mental power is not very great.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 362): There
is, perhaps, an aposiopesis here; otherwise I should incline to read <I>touch,</I> as
Knight and Collier's Folio also read.&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>: &lquo;Teach&rquo;; that is, what man-
ner of man he is; open their eyes. Or, perhaps, as Gideon &lquo;taught&rquo; the men of
Succoth, [<I>Judges,</I> viii, 16].&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): &lquo;Teach&rquo; may be explained
through a logical anacoluthon, which is caused by the following parenthesis.
The infinitive which should follow is thereby forgotten by the speaker. At the
same time it is to be remembered that &lquo;to teach&rquo; is used by Shakespeare at times
in wider sense for, <I>incite, prevail upon,</I> as in &lquo;If thou teach thy spleen to do me
shame,&rquo; <I>King John,</I> IV, iii, 97; &lquo;His false cunning taught him to face me out
of his acquaintance,&rquo; <I>Twelfth Night,</I> V, i, 91.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: If &lquo;teach&rquo; be the
true reading, the sentence is perhaps abruptly broken off. Sicinius was perhaps
an early believer in the mob, and regarded it as an act of insolence to presume
to teach them.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Mr Craig left in the text the emendation
<I>reach,</I> which he had recently adopted in <I>The Little Quarto Sh.,</I> but his collections
for a note show that he had come to prefer <I>touch,</I> as do many editors. He cites
for its meaning (<I>sting, hurt</I>), <I>Cymbeline,</I> IV, iii, 4: &lquo;Heavens, how deeply you
at once do touch me!&rquo; and concludes, &lquo;The reading of Folio is &ldquo;teach,&rdquo; which
can hardly be right.&rquo; For this reason I place <I>touch</I> in the text, but record my own
opinion strongly against any alteration. I take the intended meaning to be:
&lquo;When his insolence shall teach the people their mistake, and the danger of put-
ting this present hero in authority.&rquo; His insolence is to begin their enlighten-
ment, and the Tribunes will continue the instruction and better it by their in-
sinuations.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): Hanmer's reading, <I>touch,</I> gives the right
sense. Cf. Bacon's <I>Essay</I> 32, &lquo;Speech of touch towards others.&rquo; If &lquo;teach&rquo; be
read, the sentence may be regarded as unfinished; supply &lquo;his true disposition,&rquo;

<P>should be deleted from the direction in <I>Coriolanus:</I> &ldquo;Enter officers, to lay cushions,

<P>3. <B> 1. Off. Come, come, etc.</B>] <SC>Delius</SC> (<I>Jahrbuch,</I> v, 269): The judgment of the
two Officers on Coriolanus and his attitude towards the people is, in relation to
the vicious party-standpoints of the Patrician as well as the Plebeians, the expres-
sion of a temperate, impartial discretion, and is therefore set forth in simple prose.
&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): The officers are in sympathy by birth with the
plebeians, and by office with the patricians. They are not, therefore, extreme on
either side, and their judgment of Coriolanus has the more weight.

<P>Johnson's paraphrase appears in his own and subsequent editions until that of
<SC>Steevens</SC>, 1793, where it is given, &lquo;he would have waved indifferently,&rquo; and is so
repeated in the following <I>Variorum</I> editions. This is, perhaps, due to confusion
with Monck Mason's paraphrase which is given in his <I>Comments,</I> published in
1785, and from which Steevens frequently quotes.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 361): The
subjunctive (a consequence of the old inflectional form) was frequently used, not
as now with <I>would, should,</I> etc., but in a form identical with the indicative, where
nothing but the context (in the case of past tenses) shows that it is the subjunctive,
as, &lquo;But if my father had not scanted me . . . Yourself, renowned prince, then
stood as fair.&rquo; [The present passage, also IV, vi, 141, 142, quoted in illustra-
tion.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>22-24. <B>to seeme to affect . . . their loue</B>] That is, to appear to desire or aim
at their malice is as bad as to flatter them for their love.&mdash;<SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 604)
quotes from Plutarch's <I>Comparison of Alcibiades with Martius Coriolanus,</I> &lquo;he is
lesse to be blamed, that seeketh to please and gratifie his common people: then he
that despiseth and disdaineth them, and therefore offereth them wrong and injurie,
bicause he would not seeme to flatter them, to winne the more authoritie. For
it is an evill thing to flatter the common people to winne credit; even so it is besides
dishonesty, and injustice also, to atteine to credit and authoritie, for one to make
him selfe terrible to the people, by offering them wrong and violence.&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;This
passage,&rquo; says MacCallum, &lquo;has inspired the criticism of the Officer of the Capitol,
who, however, impartially holds the scales. With this temper it is natural that
the arrogance of success, lack of nous, and want of adaptability&mdash;which is often
merely another form of self-will&mdash;should bring about Coriolanus's ruin; and it is
these characteristics, or a modicum of them, to which Aufidius, in point of fact,
attributes his banishment (IV, vii, 39-47).&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>Sherman</SC> (<I>Tudor Sh.</I>) also calls
attention to this passage from North's <I>Comparison</I> in connection with the present
passage.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Perhaps it is unnecessary to look beyond the
ordinary meaning of &lquo;seem to&rquo; here, although, from what we have just been told,
there is no doubt about the fact that Coriolanus affects the malice of the people.
It is, however, right to note the peculiar use of <I>seem</I> in Shakespeare's time. The

meaning, &lquo;think fit,&rquo; which would suit the passage under consideration, quoting
Jonson's <I>Alchemist</I> (1610), I, iii, &lquo;The rest they'll seem to follow.&rquo; [Case gives
