<P>26. <B>as those</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: That is, the ascent of those. [For other examples of
this ellipsis after &lquo;as,&rquo; see <SC>Abbott</SC> &sect; 384.]
<P>27, 28. <B>supple and courteous . . . Bonnetted</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The sense, I think,
requires that we should read <I>unbonnetted.</I> Who have risen only by <I>pulling
off their hats to</I> the people. &lquo;Bonnetted&rquo; may relate to people, but not without
harshness.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. i, pt i, p. 87): The Oxford editor's removing the comma
from &lquo;people&rquo; gives a meaning that could not be intended; namely&mdash;standing
cover'd, <I>videlicet</I> when address'd by the candidates for their favour: the proper
sense of it seems to be,&mdash;bonnetted by them, meaning&mdash;those candidates; who
were &lquo;supple and courteous to the people&rquo; and did them the honours of the cap
&lquo;without any further deed.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: <I>Bonneter,</I> Fr., is to pull off one's cap.
See Cotgrave. So, in the academic style, to <I>cap</I> a fellow is to take off the cap
to him.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I have adhered to the original copy in printing this very obscure
passage, because it appears to me at least as intelligible as what has been sub-
stituted in its room. [See <I>Text. Notes,</I> ll. 27, 28.] &lquo;Bonnetted&rquo; is, I apprehend, a
verb, not a participle, here. They humbly took off their bonnets, without any
further deed whatsoever done in order to <I>have</I> them, that is, to insinuate them-
selves into the good opinion of the people. To <I>have them,</I> for to have <I>themselves</I>
or to wind themselves into, is certainly very harsh; but to <I>heave</I> themselves,
&amp;c., is not much less so.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I continue to read&mdash;<I>heave.</I> &lquo;Have&rquo; in
<I>Henry VIII:</I> II, ii, 83, was likewise printed instead of <I>heave</I> in the First Folio,
though corrected in the Second. The phrase in question occurs in Hayward,
&lquo;The Scots heaved up into high hope of victory,&rquo; &amp;c. Many instances of Shake-
speare's attachment to the word <I>heave</I> might be added on this occasion.&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>:
The context appears to us to give exactly the contrary meaning [to that given by
Malone]. That is: &lquo;His ascent is not by such easy degrees as those who, <I>having</I>
been supple and courteous to the people,&rquo; <I>put on</I> their bonnets &lquo;without any further
deed.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: &lquo;To bonnet,&rquo; a verb not previously appearing, which evidently
could mean to take off the cap, must here mean to obtain something by off-
capping, as in V, i, &lquo;knee the way into his mercy.&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;Bonnetted&rquo; would then be
connected with &lquo;into their estimation and report,&rquo; and thus explains the paren-
theses &lquo;without any further deed to have them&rquo; (<I>i. e.,</I> their estimation and report).
Those who complimented themselves into the estimation and report of the people,
without any further act, to win the same. [This somewhat novel interpretation
is dependent upon the punctuation which Delius has adopted, for which see <I>Text.</I>

<P><I>Notes.</I> Schmidt, both in text and interpretation, follows Delius without referring,
however, to his predecessor.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>):
We believe that &lquo;bonnetted&rquo; here means saluted with the cap, made a gesture of
salutation with the cap. &lquo;Have&rquo; seems here to be used idiomatically, as we use
it in such phrases as, &lquo;I'll have them into the basket in no time&rquo;; &lquo;He'll have them
into the post before five,&rquo; where &lquo;have&rquo; has the force of <I>get, put,</I> or <I>place.</I> It
has the effect of a rapid action, which is precisely the effect here required.&mdash;
<SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;Bonnetted&rquo; is accepted as meaning took off the cap, but it may sig-
nify invested with the badge of consular office.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: If the reading
of the whole passage be right, the meaning must be that given by Malone. But
I cannot help suspecting that something is lost. [Referring to Staunton's sugges-
tion Wright says: &lquo;A cap or bonnet was not among the insignia of a consul, nor
is there any evidence that Shakespeare thought it was.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii,
p. 338) transposes the order of these lines thus: &lquo;bonnetted into their estimation
and report, without any further deed to have them at all&rquo;; and thus comments:
&lquo;The right construction is, I think, clearly that given in this text; but it is, to say
the least, not easy to get the sense of that construction from the old order of the
words. Nor is the transposition which I have made a whit more free or bold than
a great many others that are commonly thought needful, as indeed most of them
are.&rquo;&mdash;J. D. (<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I> 7 May, 1881, p. 362): The phrase [<I>to have thern</I>]
was commonly used in the west fifty years ago, and is probably used still. It
meant to be in, or more fully to come into, a certain state. If some persons who
had become embarrassed had recovered their position, it would be said of them,
&lquo;They hau (have) themsels neaw aw reet,&rquo; and sometimes, though more rarely,
&lquo;They hau them aw reet.&rquo; . . . It is a genuine Teutonic idiom. The German
ironical pbrase, &lquo;Es hat sich wohl,&rquo; answers to our vulgar English &lquo;That is a good
one.&rquo; The meaning, I think, is that Coriolanus was not like those &lquo;supple and
courteous&rquo; men, who took off their bonnets to the people in order to come into
their estimation, and (good) report, but by his deeds had deserved worthily of his
country.&mdash;<SC>Kinnear</SC> (p. 311): &lquo;Having been thus supple,&rquo; having given their hats,
having been off to the people, these <I>popular men,</I> &lquo;without any further deed,&rquo;
&lquo;bonnetted,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> resumed the hats <I>they had given,</I> and went their way. Compare
Marcius's speech on this point, II, iii, 97-102; and also Volumnia's instructions to
her son, III, ii, 92, 93: &lquo;I prithee now my son Go to them with this bonnet in thy
hand.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): To &lquo;bonnet&rquo; has been taken to mean <I>put on the
hat,</I> as though this were the insignia of a consul; but the use of &lquo;unbonneted&rquo; in
<I>Othello</I> I, ii, 22, where it plainly means <I>without taking off the bonnet,</I> is against this
interpretation. &lquo;<I>Heave,</I>&rquo; Pope's reading, gives the right sense, but compare
<I>Tam. of Shrew,</I> Ind., ii, 39, &lquo;Or wilt thou sleep? We'll have thee to a couch.&rquo;
The preposition &lquo;into&rquo; seems to be constructed with both verbs, &lquo;bonneted&rquo; and
&lquo;have them.&rquo; &lquo;They bowed themselves into estimation with the people, doing
nothing else that could lift them into their good report.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>):
That is, merely took off their bonnets, their caps, by way of compliment to the
people, and <I>did</I> nothing that might deservedly get them the people's good will.
He means a cheap and easy popularity, won by flattering the mob, not by rendering
the State solid services like those of Coriolanus. There is no need to change
&lquo;have&rquo; to <I>heave.</I>&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): That is, merely took off their caps and
nothing more. [Among the many interpretations of this much-discussed passage

<P>61. <B>Treatie</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emendations,</I> &amp;c., p. 353): The Corrector of
the Folio, 1632, directs us to substitute <I>treatise</I> for &lquo;treatie,&rquo; a change supported
by &lquo;theme,&rquo; which immediately follows.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> &amp;c., p. 215):
That the old copy is right in reading &lquo;treatie,&rquo; and that the Corrector's <I>treatise</I> is
wrong, will appear from the poet's own use of the latter word twice only, and
then in the sense of a <I>dissertation,</I> which is not the meaning here required. <I>Treaty,</I>
according to Huloet, is, &lquo;Traictement de quelque matiere,&rquo; which is exactly what
is wanted. The same authority has, &lquo;To <I>treate</I> and <I>debate</I> some matter, Traicter
quelque matiere et la debattre.&rquo; There can be no doubt, therefore, that the old
reading is what the poet intended, and that the corrector's substitution would be
mischievous. The Senators were assembled to <I>discuss</I> the meritorious actions of
Coriolanus, and what honour should be conferred upon him; he was the <I>theme</I> of
the assembly.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (ed. ii.) calls attention to the spelling of this word in The
Folio as <I>Treatic.</I> It is plainly &lquo;Treatie&rquo; in the Verner and Hood reprint of 1807,
in the Staunton lithograph, and in the Booth reprint of 1864, and also in my own
copy of the Folio, but in the Lee Facsimile of the Devonshire Folio it is quite as
plainly <I>Treatic</I> as Singer gives it. This, I think, points to the copy which Singer
had before him, and is but another example of variations in different copies of the
First Folio.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>64. <B>blest to doe</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emend.,</I> &amp;c., p. 353): The scribe clearly
misheard the word, and wrote &lquo;blest&rquo; for <I>prest,</I> i. e., ready&mdash;of perpetual occurrence

reason why they should state that they should be &lquo;blest&rquo; in doing so.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC>
(<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> p. 215): The substitution of <I>prest</I> for &lquo;blest&rquo; is a good and legitimate
emendation, which I also find confirmed in my corrected copy of the second folio.&mdash;
<SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Blackwood's Maga.,</I> Sep., 1853, p. 322): We cannot approve of the change
<I>prest</I> for &lquo;blest.&rquo; . . . Sicinius has just remarked that the Senate has assembled
to do honour to Coriolanus, on which Brutus says: &lquo;Which the rather We shall be
blest to do if he remember,&rquo; etc. Does not this mean&mdash;Which honour we shall be
<I>most happy</I> to do to Coriolanus, if, etc.? Why then change &lquo;blest&rquo; into <I>prest?</I>
a very unnatural mode of speech.&mdash;<SC>Mommsen</SC> (<I>Der Perkins-Sh.,</I> p. 96): &lquo;Blest&rquo;

right.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. i.): That <I>prest</I> (i. e., ready) suits the present speech very well
there is no denying, but &lquo;bless'd&rquo; (<I>i. e.,</I> most happy) is supported by a passage in
<I>King John,</I> III, i, 251, &lquo;And then we shall be blest To do your pleasure and con-
tinue friends.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Keightly</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 363) refers to the MS. correction, but
considers that &lquo;no change is needed&rquo;; in support of the Folio he quotes the line
from <I>King John</I> as given above by Dyce, remarking that &lquo;blest&rquo; is &lquo;the same as
<I>happy</I> of the present day.&rquo;

<P>67. <B>That's off</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, that is nothing to the purpose.&mdash;J. D.
(<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I> May 7, 1881, p. 362): This explanation is not in accordance
with the meaning of the phrase as it was and is still used in the west of England.
It refers to something that has passed away, and ought not to be referred to now.
If a man were reproached for some past fault that had been condoned or put
away he would say: &lquo;That's off, that's off; yo munna bring that agen me.&rquo; It
will be seen that Shakespeare uses the phrase in this sense. Brutus has alluded
to the contempt that Coriolanus had formerly shown for the people, and intimates
that he would be more readily honoured &lquo;If he remember A kinder value of the
people than He hath hereto prized them at.&rquo; Menenius does not deny the fault,
but pleads that it belongs to the past and ought not now to be recalled. He gives
a rebuke, as Brutus calls it, to a charge that seemed to him ill-timed.
<P>84. <B>weigh</B>] <SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Times Literary Supplement,</I> July 27, 1922, p. 482): For some
inscrutable reason the dash of the Folio has been replaced by a full stop [see <I>Text.
Notes</I>]. Dashes to mark interruption are not so plentiful in the Folio that we
can afford to throw them away. Menenius, as ever, tries to stop Coriolanus
from his furious outburst. We could supply Coriolanus's unspoken words from
this very play. Probably they were, &lquo;That's lesser than a little!&rquo;

avoid confusion with the hard sound of <I>ch</I> as in <I>chronicle?</I> <SC>Ellis</SC> (<I>Early Eng.
Pronunciation,</I> ch. vi, s. v. CH.) says: &lquo;Not used in Anglo-Saxon period, but in

<I>ch</I>aise it is (sh) in 19<SUP>th</SUP> cent., but for French words introduced before 18<SUP>th</SUP> cent.

<P>104, 105. <B>he bestrid An o're-prest Roman</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: This was an act of similar
friendship in our old English armies, but there is no proof that any such prac-
tice prevailed among the legionary soldiers of Rome, nor did our author give
himself any trouble on that subject. He was led into the error by North's
translation of Plutarch, where he found these words: &lquo;The Roman souldier being
thrown unto the ground even hard by him, Martius straight <I>bestrid</I> him, and
slew the enemy.&rquo; The translation ought to have been: &lquo;Martius hastened to
his asisstance, and <I>standing before him,</I> slew his assailant.&rquo; See note l. 108 where
there is a similar inaccuracy.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Shakespeare may on this occasion
be vindicated by higher authority than that of books. Is it probable that any
Roman soldier was so far divested of humanity as not to protect his friend who
had fallen in battle? Our author (if unacquainted with the Grecian <I>Hyperaspists</I>)
was too well read in the volume of nature to need any apology for the introduction
of the present incident, which must have been as familiar to Roman as to British
warfare.

&sect; 20, p. 30.

<P>112. <B>seuenteene Battailes</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (ed. i.): I cannot help making a remark
upon this circumstance of our Author's conduct, whether casual or designedly.
It is said, and the fact is true, that he has followed Plutarch very closely in this
story, but he deviates from him in one point, by which he seems to decline a strange
absurdity in the calculation of time. Shakespeare tells us that at sixteen years
old, Coriolanus began his soldiership, when Tarquin made head to regain his
kingdom; and that in <I>seventeen battles</I> he distinguished himself with exemplary
bravery and success. Plutarch likewise says that our Hero set out in arms a
youth, that his first expedition was when Tarquin made this push, and that he
signalized himself in war for seventeen years successively. Now it happens a
little unluckily for Plutarch's account that this attempt of Tarquin was made
A. U. C. 258, and Coriolanus was banished, nay, and killed within the period of
eight years after his first Campaign, A. U. C. 266. There is something again lies
cross on the other side, that if Coriolanus was so young when he commenced
soldier, and if the interval was so short between that and his banishment, he was
too young to have been admitted a candidate for the Consulship. The compli-

<P>113. <B>He lurcht . . . the Garland</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Ben Jonson has the same ex-
pression in <I>The Silent Woman:</I> &lquo;&mdash;you have lurch'd your friends of the better
half of the garland,&rquo; [V, i.; ed. Gifford, p. 495]. <SC>Malone</SC>: To &lquo;lurch&rquo; is properly
<I>to purloin;</I> hence Shakespeare uses it in the sense of <I>to deprive.</I> So, in <I>Christ's
Teares over Jerusalem,</I> Thomas Nashe, 1594, &lquo;I see others of them sharing halfe
with the bawdes, their hostesses, and laughing at the punies they have lurched,&rquo;
[ed. McKerrow, p. 150, l. 36]. I suspect, however, I have not rightly traced the
origin of this phrase. To &lquo;lurch,&rquo; in Shakespeare's time, signified to win a maiden
set at cards, &amp;c. See Florio's <I>Italian Dict.,</I> 1598: &lquo;<I>Gioco Marzo.</I> A maiden set,
or lurch, at any game.&rquo; See also Cole's <I>Latin Dict.,</I> 1679: &lquo;A lurch, <I>Duplex palma,
facilis victoria.</I>&rquo; &lquo;To lurch all swords of the garland,&rquo; therefore, was to gain from
all other warriors the wreath of victory with ease and incontestable superiority.&mdash;
<SC>Pye</SC> (p. 248): Did Mr Malone never play, or sit by when others have played, at
whist, picquet, or cribbage? He must then have known what a &lquo;lurch&rquo; is, and
also that what he calls &lquo;a maiden game,&rquo; though it is a &lquo;lurch,&rquo; is distinguished
from a common lurch by the appellation of a <I>love</I> game. I wish the critics would
think that a little acquaintance with the common language and habits of life is
<I>almost</I> as necessary as black letter reading to a commentator on Shakespeare.
Having said this, I must add that the drift of the whole sentence cannot be better
explained than it is in the conclusion of Malone's note.&mdash;<SC>W. S. Baynes</SC> (<I>Shake-
spearian Glossaries,</I> Edinburgh Review, July, 1869; reprinted in <I>Sh. Studies,</I>
p. 251): Although the noun, &lquo;lurch,&rquo; is found in this technical sense [&lquo;to win a
maiden set at cards&rquo;] in most European languages, there is no proof that the word
existed in English, nor, if it did, would it suit the context. Shakespeare evidently
uses the English verb &lquo;lurch&rquo; literally, to devour eagerly, &lquo;ravin up,&rquo; gulp down, and
in the secondary sense to seize violently upon, rob, engross, absorb. Both noun
and verb were in use among the Elizabethan writers in the sense of seizure, rob-

<P>bery, and it is the more important to illustrate this meaning, as the noun is wholly
unknown to our lexicographers. An instance of its use occurs, however, in the
poems prefixed to <I>Coryat's Crudities,</I> where one of the author's friends commemo-
rates his achievements abroad, and amongst others the robbery of a waxen image
from the Virgin's shrine in a church at Brixia: &lquo;Briefly for trial of a religious lurch
Thou nimbd'st an image out of Brixia's church,&rquo; [lines by Richard Badley].
Again the verb is used more than once, in precisely the same sense, by Warner,
and an example or two will sufficiently bring out its special meaning. In reference
to the rage of the vulgar wealthy for titles and territorial distinction he says:
&lquo;Hence country louts land-lurch their lords, and courtiers prize the same,&rquo; [<I>Albion's
England,</I> Bk ix, ch. 46, ed. 1602, p. 217.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]. And again, referring to the grasping
ambition of Spain as the nominal champion of the Romish Church, &lquo;For these
elsewhere, and ever Spayne when Spayne would sceptres lurch,&rquo; [<I>Albion's England,</I>
Bk x, ch. lx, ll. 15, 16]. In the sense of engrossing, of seizing and carrying off with
a high hand, &lquo;lurch&rquo; is also used amongst others by Bacon and Milton. To
&lquo;lurch all swords of the garland&rquo; means, therefore, not only to rob all swords of the
garland, but to carry it away from them with an easy and victorious swoop. [The
foregoing in regard to this word &lquo;lurch&rquo; was seriously questioned, among other

<P>117-119. <B>as Weeds . . . his Stem</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: The editor of the second Folio
for &lquo;weeds&rquo; substituted <I>waves,</I> and this capricious alteration has been adopted in
all the subsequent editions. In the same page of that copy, which has been the
source of at least one-half of the corruptions that have been introduced in our
author's works, we find <I>defamy</I> for &lquo;destiny,&rquo; <I>sir</I> Coriolanus, for &lquo;sit Coriolanus,&rquo;
<I>trim'd</I> for <*>tim'd,&rquo; and <I>painting</I> for &lquo;panting&rquo;; but luckily none of the latter sophis-
tications have found admission into any of the modern editions except Mr Rowe's.
<I>Rushes</I> falling below a vessel passing over them is an image as expressive of the
prowess of Coriolanus as well can be conceived. A kindred image is found in
<I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> &lquo;&mdash;there the strawy Greeks, ripe for his edge, Fall down before
him, like the mowers swath,&rquo; [V, v, 24].&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: <I>Waves,</I> the reading of the
second Folio, I regard as no trivial evidence in favour of the copy from which it
was printed. &lquo;Weeds&rquo; instead of <I>falling below</I> a vessel under sail cling fast about
the <I>stem</I> of it. The justice of my remark every sailor and waterman will confirm.
But were not this the truth, by conflict with a mean adversary, valour would be
depreciated. The submersion of <I>weeds</I> resembles a Frenchman's triumph over a
<I>soupe aux herbes;</I> but to rise above the threatening billow, or force a way through
the watery bulwark, is a conquest worthy of a ship, and furnishes a comparison
suitable to the exploits of Coriolanus. Thus in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> &lquo;The strong-ribb'd
bark through liquid mountains cuts, Bounding between the two moist elements,

<P>Like Perseus' horse,&rquo; [I, iii, 41]. If Shakespeare originally wrote <I>weeds,</I> on finding
such an image less apposite and dignified than that of <I>waves,</I> he might have intro-
duced the correction which Mr Malone has excluded from his text. The <I>stem</I>
is that end of the ship which leads. From &lquo;<I>stem</I> to <I>stern</I>&rquo; is an expression used by
Dryden in his translation of Virgil, &lquo;Orontes&rquo; bark . . . From stem to stern by
waves was overborne,&rquo; [Bk i, ll. 162-164].&mdash;<SC>Boswell</SC>: &lquo;Weeds&rquo; is used to signify
the comparative feebleness of Coriolanus's adversaries.&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: Of the correct-
ness of the original [&lquo;weeds&rquo;] we think there can be no doubt. <I>Waves</I> falling before
the stem of a vessel under sail is an image which conveys no adequate notion of a
triumph over petty obstacles; a ship cuts the waves as a bird the air; there is
opposition to the progress, but each moves in its element. But take the image of
weeds encumbering the progress of a vessel under sail, but with a favoring wind
dashing them aside, and we have a distinct and beautiful illustration of the prowess
of Coriolanus. Steevens says: &lquo;<I>Weeds,</I> instead of falling below a vessel under
sail, cling fast about the stem of it.&rquo; But Shakespeare was not thinking of the
weed floating on the billow; the Avon or the Thames supplied him with the image
of weeds rooted at the bottom.&mdash;<SC>Verplanck</SC>: The <I>weeds</I> of the flats of the Hudson
and the inlets of Long Island Sound have so often furnished the American editor
with a practical illustration of this image, that he has no hesitation in adopting
this as the true reading.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: The reading of the Folio is here undoubtedly
correct. As the weeds bend before the stem of the advancing ship, so do the
enemies fall together before Coriolanus. The word &lquo;stem,&rquo; particularly applic-
able to a vessel, is here not so particularly applied to Coriolanus or his sword.&mdash;
<SC>Singer</SC> (ed. ii.): I think, with Steevens, that a vessel <I>stemming the waves</I> is an image
much more suitable to the prowess of Coriolanus than the displacing of weeds.&mdash;
<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): We think that the original word gives
the effect of contemptible impediments overcome better than the substituted
word, which presents the idea not of opposers or opposition, but of due medium,
waves being the natural upbearers of a ship, and forming its path or course.&mdash;
<SC>Lettsom</SC> (ap. <SC>Dyce</SC> ii.): Read <I>waves</I> with the Second Folio. The sense requires
a circumstance that happens usually, <I>not exceptionally,</I> to ships under sail.&mdash;
<SC>Whitelaw</SC>: The reading of the 1<SUP>st</SUP> Folio is more appropriate, expressing in the
helplessness of the Volscians before Coriolanus his heroic and superhuman prowess,
whereas the image of a ship stemming the waves would rather suggest that his
courage triumphed over superior strength. Again, &lquo;waves&rquo; could hardly be said
to fall under the vessel's stem.

<P>122, 123. <B>alone . . . The mortall Gate</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 87): &lquo;Mortal&rquo;

us, which is mangl'd in very strange sort in the Oxford edition, [Hanmer's, see

<P>123. <B>The mortall Gate</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The gate that was made the scene of death.&mdash;

Johnson explains it. Compare the sense of &lquo;mortal&rquo; in III, i, 360 <I>post</I> (&lquo;Mortal,
to cut it off&rquo;). Shakespeare has &lquo;mortal engines&rquo; (<I>Othello,</I> III, iii, 355); &lquo;mortal
drugs&rquo; (<I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> V, i, 66).

been closed on him. In <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> II, v, [16], we have the same change of <I>ar</I>
to <I>ain.</I> [This last is Keightley's own reading of the line, which is obelised in the
<I>Globe Sh.,</I> &lquo;But old folks many faine as they were dead,&rquo; Keightley reading <I>fare;</I>
he has thus far had but one follower, viz., <SC>R. G. White</SC>.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>:
The inevitable doom of the city was as it were portrayed on the gates in the blood

<P><SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): &lquo;Which&rquo; is here commonly related to gate, but perhaps
it is to be related to &lquo;city,&rquo; and &lquo;painted&rquo; a word falsely read by the compositor,
conformably <I>haunted.</I> Shakespeare is fond of using <I>to haunt</I> as applied to a cease-
lessly hostile follower.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The figure of his sword being death's
stamp and marking his victims is here carried on. Coriolanus set his bloody mark
upon the gate, or upon the city, indicating that it was his by an inevitable fate,
as plague-stricken houses were painted with a red cross.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>):
&lquo;Shunless destiny&rquo; may be simply blood destined to flow, the blood of men for
whom there was no escape at his hands.&mdash;<SC>Sherman</SC> (<I>Tudor Sh.</I>) refers to Wright's
remark on the sign placed on a plague-stricken house, and adds: &lquo;Possibly there is
a reminiscence also of the blood-painted doors by which the Israelites avoided the
&ldquo;shunless destiny&rdquo; of the first-born of the Egyptians.&rquo; [Shakespeare was, I
think, too well versed in Old Testament History to have been unmindful of the
fact that the blood was struck upon the lintels and was to be a sign of immunity
to the dwellers, not a mark of doom.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Orger</SC> (<I>Sh's Histories and Tragedies,</I>
p. 62): As the author calls Coriolanus's sword &lquo;Death's stamp,&rquo; I can hardly con-
ceive he would so soon change his metaphor and speak of his &lquo;<I>painting</I>&rquo; the gate
with death; but he may more consistently be said to have <I>printed</I> it with ruin, as
he left on it the <I>mark</I> of inevitable fate. We may compare <I>Tit. And.,</I> III, i, 170,
&lquo;Writing destruction on the enemies castle.&rquo;
<P>125, 126. <B>strucke . . . like a Planet</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: So in <I>Timon,</I> &lquo;Be as a planet-

posed malignant influence of the planets, which was a subject of popular belief in
his time. Compare I, i, 162. See also <I>Othello,</I> II, iii, 182, &lquo;As if some planet had
outwitted men.&rquo; The word &lquo;moonstruck&rquo; for <I>lunatic</I> still remains in the language
as an evidence of this belief.&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): The idea of &lquo;destiny&rquo;
is continued. But I am not sure that Shakespeare has not before him the visual
image of a building physically struck not by a planet, but by a thunderbolt.&mdash;

the use of <I>planet-stricken</I> &lquo;for any sudden attack for which the physician could

<P><I>Notes.</I>] The implication of the words that are quoted is, Now he thought all was
his own, and his task done; &lquo;<I>When by and by,</I>&rquo; etc.
<P>127. <B>by and by</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Henry Irving Sh.</I>): It is interesting to note as a
point of morals that not only &lquo;by and by&rquo; but also <I>presently</I> and <I>anon,</I> all of which
formerly meant <I>at once,</I> have come to mean <I>after an interval.</I>
<P>129. <B>fatigate</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, wearied, fatigued. In Sherwood's <I>English-
French Dictionary,</I> printed as a supplement to Cotgrave (ed. 1632), we find &lquo;to
fatigate,&rquo; &lquo;fatigated,&rquo; and &lquo;a fatigating.&rquo; Minsheu (<I>Guide into Tongues,</I> 1617) gives:
&lquo;To fatigate or make wearie,&rquo; and this was the earlier form of the word, &lquo;fatigue&rquo;
being subsequently introduced. For the participial termination compare &lquo;articu-
late,&rquo; <I>1 Henry IV:</I> V, i, 72; &lquo;suffocate,&rquo; <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> I, iii, 125, and many others.
<P>131, 132. <B>Runne reeking o're . . . spoyle</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Coriolanus is com-
pared to a stream of reeking blood, which marked the course of his slaughtering
sword. &lquo;Spoil&rquo; appears here to be a term of the chase as it is in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> III, i,
200, &lquo;Here thy hunters stand Sign'd in thy spoil,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Bayfield</SC> (p. 195): Editors
correct by beginning the second line with &lquo;'Twere,&rquo; but &lquo;if&rquo; and &lquo;'twere&rquo; get in-
tolerable emphasis and the rhythm is ruined. Clearly the second line must begin
with &lquo;It were,&rquo; so that the words may run, &lquo;as &verbar; if it &verbar; were a per &verbar; petual &verbar; spoil.&rquo;
<P>136. <B>He cannot . . . Honors</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, no honor will be too great
for him; he will show a mind equal to any elevation.&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>, in reference to
Johnson's paraphrase, says: &lquo;This is what the speaker meant, but the irony of
&ldquo;measure&rdquo; is unmistakable. To observe &ldquo;measure&rdquo; in his course of honour was
precisely what Coriolanus could never do.&rquo;
<P>137, 138. <B>which we . . . kickt at</B>] For those whose hypersensitive metrical ears
are offended by the lack of a syllable in this compound line, <SC>Hanmer's</SC> addition will
doubtless afford relief; <SC>Abbott's</SC> cure is less drastic: &lquo;our&rquo; is here a dissylable as
in many other cases. It is, however, to be noticed that l. 137 is printed as prose
in the Folio, and l. 138 is a short isolated line. Rowe is responsible for the verse,
and it is his, not perhaps Shakespeare's, verse that is at fault.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P><SC>Whitelaw</SC>: That the time should pass, and the end come, bring no reward&mdash;
no more to be said of it than that, the time having passed, the end has come&mdash;
to this he is contented to look forward.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>) dissents to White-
law's interpretation. &lquo;It is much better,&rquo; he says, &lquo;to take only the first infinitive,
&ldquo;to spend the time,&rdquo; as directly dependent on &ldquo;content&rdquo;; he is satisfied to bring
the time to an end, to have a pastime; &ldquo;to end it,&rdquo; while he is bringing the time,
or also his &ldquo;doing his deeds, to an end&rdquo;; compare II, iii, 201, 202, and such a passage
as, &ldquo;I fly not death, to fly this deadly doom,&rdquo;&rquo; <I>Two Gentlemen</I> (III, i, 185), while
I fly, etc.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: To spend the time for the mere purpose of bringing it
to an end, and without any object of an ulterior reward. All his achievements
are a pastime, a means of killing time.&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: In all that Coriolanus does he
has no ulterior motives. Great action, to him, is its own reward, an end in itself.
He does great deeds (as Johnson puts it) for the sake of doing them, and spends
his time for the sake of spending it, content that it should end there, and lead to
nothing.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): To do great deeds is, for Coriolanus, its own
reward, and he is content so to spend his time as merely to pass it. Cominius
seems to mean by his last words that Coriolanus has no ulterior objects, cherishes
no ambitious designs, in what he does (whereas the Tribunes accuse him of aiming
at &lquo;tyrannical power,&rquo; III, iii, 1, 2, 83-86); enough for him if his time be spent in
doing, and end there, <I>i. e.,</I> lead to nothing. The use of a literary artifice, here
assonance (<I>spend . . . end</I>), often, I think, gives point to the style at the expense
of clearness.&mdash;<SC>Craig</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): And whatever expenditure of time it takes to
complete his work, he ungrudgingly gives it.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Ibid.</I>): This interpretation,
however, would make &lquo;it&rquo; refer to &lquo;deeds,&rquo; whereas with &lquo;it&rquo; referred to &lquo;time,&rquo; as
strict grammar requires, the passage is understood that, provided his time is used
up, Coriolanus is content to spend it without reward for himself.

<P><I>both</I> Consuls. And then the people, assisted by the seditious temper of the Tribunes,
got the choice of one. But if Shakespeare makes Rome a democracy, which at
this time was a perfect aristocracy, he sets the balance even in his <I>Timon,</I> and turns
Athens, which was a perfect democracy, into an aristocracy. But it would be
unjust to attribute this entirely to his ignorance; it sometimes proceeded from the
too powerful blaze of his imagination, which, when once lighted up, made all
acquired knowledge fade and disappear before it. For sometimes again we find
him, when occasion serves, not only writing up to the truth of history, but fitting
his sentiments to the nicest manners of his peculiar subject, as well to the <I>dignity</I>
of his characters or the <I>dictates</I> of nature in general.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The inaccuracy is
to be attributed not to our author, but to Plutarch, who expressly says, in his
<I>Life of Coriolanus,</I> that &lquo;it was the custom of Rome <I>at that time,</I> that suche as dyd
sue for <I>any</I> office, should for certen dayes before be in the market-place, only with
a poor gowne on their backes, and without any coate underneath, <I>to praye the
people to remember them at the daye of election.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: It is not difficult
to trace the origin of the mistake. Plutarch in his <I>Life of Coriolanus</I> (c. 14) merely
says that it was usual for candidates for an office to stand in the Forum dressed
in a toga (<G>i(ma\tion</G>) only, without the <I>tunica</I> (<G>xitw/n</G>) or close-fitting garment under-
neath. In the <I>Qu&aelig;stiones Roman&aelig;,</I> 49, he makes the same statement on the
authority of Cato. Now Amyot in his French translation, which is the original
of North, renders the expression correctly enough, &lquo;une robbe simple, sans saye
dessoubs,&rquo; and the whole appears in North as [given above by Malone].
<P>155. <B>stand naked</B>] <SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): &lquo;Naked&rquo; is often equivalent to <I>unarmed,</I>
but here, no doubt, the display of wounds and the single garment suggests the
word, as it does in the passage from <I>Roman Questions,</I> [cited by Wright]: &lquo;To the
end, therefore, that such scarres might be better exposed to their sight whom they
met or talked withall, they went in this maner downe to the place of election,
without inward coats in their plaine gownes. Or haply, because they would seem
by this nuditie and nakednesse of theirs, in humilitie to debase themselves, the
sooner thereby to curry favor, and win the good grace of the commons,&rquo; etc.
[Case quotes but a part of the foregoing extract as in <I>Bibl. de Carabas,</I> pp. 78, 79;
the passage as here given is from Holland's translation of <I>The Philosophie or
Morals of Plutarch,</I> ed. 1603, p. 867.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>179. <B>he wil require them</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, he will ask them. Generally
&lquo;require&rquo; is used with the accusative of the thing asked, and now has the sense of
asking with authority, like <I>demand;</I> but formerly both &lquo;require&rquo; and <I>demand</I> were
equivalent to the simple <I>ask.</I> Compare <I>Henry VIII:</I> II, iv, 144, &lquo;In humblest
manner I require your highness.&rquo;

now on the &lquo;Market place,&rquo; but in the Capitol. The pointing only wants to be
rectified, and we shall know what this Magistrate would say, viz., Come, I know
the people attend us in the Forum; we'll go and inform them what proceedings
have been here in the Senate. [See <I>Text. Notes.</I>]

<P>2. <B>1 Cit. Once if he do require,</B> etc.] <SC>Delius</SC> (<I>Sh's Use of Prose, Jahrbuch,</I>
v, p. 269): The several citizens to whom Coriolanus must sue for their votes for
the consulship speak in Plebeian prose. Coriolanus, who on his entrance in
converse with Menenius had still spoken in blank verse, likewise becomes one of
the people, since he addresses the Citizens in their own manner when he sets out
to get their voices. He is not able to play this irksome part long. After he has
happily answered the first voices he again resumes his blank-verse for the suing
of the later voices. Blank-verse is likewise used by the Tribunes in announcing
to the three Citizens the craftily determined plot to render null the choice of
Coriolanus in the end. The political interests which there come into play justify
the use of fluent verse by the higher-standing Tribunes, as well as the three Citizens.
<P>2. <B>Once</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: &lquo;Once&rquo; here means the same as when we say <I>once for
all.</I>&mdash;<SC>Farmer</SC>: This use of the word &lquo;once&rquo; is found in <I>The Supposes,</I> by Gascoigne,
&lquo;Once, twentyfour ducattes he cost me,&rquo; [Act V, sc. v, p. 236, ed. Cunliffe.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>].&mdash;
<SC>Steevens</SC>: Again in <I>Com. of Errors,</I> &lquo;Once this, your long experience of her wis-
dom,&rquo; [III, i, 89].&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I doubt whether &lquo;once&rquo; here signifies <I>once for all;</I>
I believe it means &lquo;if he do but so much as require our voices,&rquo; as in the following
passage in Holinshed's <I>Chronicle:</I> &lquo;&mdash;they left many of their servants, and men
of war behind them, and some of them would not once stay for their standards.&rquo;
[This note appears first in Malone's own edition; it is not repeated in the <I>Variorum</I>
of 1821.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 57) besides the present line gives three other examples
wherein &lquo;once&rquo; is used in the sense <I>once for all.</I> Under the sense <I>in a word</I> <SC>Abbott</SC>
quotes the line from <I>Comedy of Errors</I> given by Steevens. Pope's unfortunate
emendation <I>Oons!</I> for &lquo;Once&rquo; drew forth from Theobald the following note, which
he omitted, however, in his ed. ii, &lquo;What, more anachronisms, and more than
ever the Poet design'd or slipt into! But this, like the boiled Pig and Colliflower
in the <I>Farce,</I> is of Squire Somebody's own bespeaking, and 'twill be but kind to
let him have the dish to himself. Mr Pope, I presume, hardly thinks that <I>Blood</I>
and <I>Wounds</I> ever came into an oath till after the Crucifixion of our Saviour.
But, to set that question apart, our citizens here are no such blustering blades.
They say honestly, in all other editions, no more than this: &ldquo;Once, if he do require
our voices,&rdquo; &amp;c., <I>i. e.,</I> In a word, once for all, I've said it once and I'll stand to it.&rquo;
[See <I>Appendix: Shakespeare and the Masses,</I> <SC>R. W. Chambers</SC>, p. 712.]
<P>5, 6. <B>We haue power . . . to do</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: I am persuaded this was in-

<CC>
<P>the schools.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: A ridicule may be intended, but the sense is clear enough.
<I>Power</I> first signifies <I>natural power</I> or force, and then <I>moral power</I> or <I>right.</I> Davies
has used the word with great variety of meaning: &lquo;Use all thy <I>powers,</I> that heavenly
<I>power</I> to praise, That gave thee <I>power</I> to do.&rquo;&mdash;[Johnson was evidently trusting to
his memory; this quotation is from Sir John Davies' <I>Nosce Teipsum,</I> the concluding
lines, and in Arber's reprint (<I>English Garner,</I> vol. v, p. 202) runs thus: &lquo;Use all
thy powers that Blessed Power to praise! Which gives thee power to Be, and
Use the same.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 416): I am as well persuaded, as Mr Warburton
can be of the contrary, that &lquo;this was <I>not</I> intended as a ridicule on the Augustine&rquo;
(it should be the Augustinian) &lquo;manner of defining free-will at that time in the
schools.&rquo; The present expression, indeed, is no other than the natural dictate of
an honest heart, which Shakespeare felt in its full force. The sense is, We have
indeed a power by law to do it if we think proper, but this power amounts to the
same as no power at all, because we should offer the greatest violence to our very
natures if we should exert it. Thus much I thought it right to say in justification
of this sentiment, which considered as Shakespeare intended it, as a moral senti-
ment, is a very fine one, and a very serious one; not a ludicrous one, as Mr War-
burton, wrapped up in his verbal metaphysics, would represent it. But to consider
it in the metaphysical light in which he hath chosen to place it, I would beg leave
to ask him one question. Doth he know what was the Augustinian definition of
free will, which in Shakespeare's time, or at any time before, or since, obtained
in the schools? I am persuaded he doth not, or he could never have thought
the ridicule, he hath gone out of his way to fasten upon it, would suit it. But
I believe the truth of the case is this, Mr Warburton had formerly read the
<I>Provincial Letters,</I> in the first of which the <I>pouvoir prochain</I> of the Dominican
Thomists . . . is very finely and very strongly ridiculed, and that in a manner
which bears a distant resemblance to the text of our poet. This probably might
give the hint to his confused imagination to transfer a misunderstood ridicule
upon a doctrine to which it is no way applicable. For let me ask him another
question. Had he himself the power while he was writing this note to throw up
the sash of his study window and leap out of it? I suppose he will scarce deny
that he had the power to do so; but that power being under the control of another
power, which belonged to him as a moral agent, I suppose too he will as little
deny, that, upon the result of the combination of those two powers, he had not,
as then circumstanced, the power to exert the physical power. If he should deny
it, the common sense of mankind will bear witness against him. This is the very
case in our poet's text. The man had in himself the power to do it, but it was
a power he had no power to exert. But thus it will always be with people who
affect to know everything. They are at every turn betraying their ignorance of
the very rudiments of what they will be talking about.

<P>59. <B>thinke vpon you</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): To &lquo;think upon,&rquo; in the mouth
of a suppliant, has the special sense of &lquo;to remember <I>with compassion,</I>&rquo; as in <I>Jonah,</I>
i, 6, &lquo;If so be God will think upon us&rquo;; so that there is a touch of epigram in Corio-

<P>61, 62. <B>like the Vertues . . . lose by em</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: I wish they would forget
me as they do those virtuous precepts which the divines preach up to them, and
lose by them, as it were, by their neglecting the practice.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i,
p. 88): &lquo;Virtues&rquo; are put poetically for precepts of virtue, which divines are
properly enough said to lose by hearers upon whom they have no influence.&mdash;
<SC>Badham</SC> (<I>Criticism,</I> p. 13): Anyone who can seriously maintain that there is a
meaning in this passage as it now stands has much false ingenuity to unlearn.
The following passage in North's <I>Plutarch</I> (<I>Life of Romulus,</I> p. 26, ed. 1579) may
perhaps afford us some clue: &lquo;Moreover other birdes are allwayes (as a man would
saye) before our eyes, and doe daylie shewe themselves unto us: where the vulter
is a very rare byrde and hardly to be seene, and men do not easily finde their
ayeries. Which hath geven some occasion to holde a false opinion that the vulters
are passagers, &amp;c. The prognosticators also thincke that such things which are not
ordinarie and but rarely seene, be not natural, but miraculously sent by the gods

<CC>
<C>[61, 62. <B>like the Vertues Which our Diuines lose by em</B>]</C>
<P>to prognosticate something.&rquo; Now we have no doubt that Coriolanus here wishes
that his dealings with the people were as transitory and rare as the visits of vultures
are to the gaze of the soothsayers. He never wishes to encounter them more, not
even to hear their praises. But then how is this passage to be moulded according
to this view? Shall we read, &lquo;I wish they would forget me like the vultures
Which our diviners lease by&rquo;; or, Which our divines lose sight of? Let the judicious
determine or, rather, let them propose some more satisfactory way of introducing
this word thus strangely corrupted into <I>virtues.</I> [It is, I think, doubtful that
Badham's extravagant emendation or explanation will appeal to any thoughtful
reader. He himself would very likely have somewhat modified his view had he
consulted the several passages wherein Shakespeare refers to the Vulture. In
no instance is this bird taken except as the emblem of voracity, which honor it
seems to share with the cormorant. The words &lquo;virtues&rquo; and <I>vultures</I> in the
handwriting of the time do not in the least resemble each other.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Verplanck</SC>:
&lquo;I wish they would forget me, as they do the moral teachings of our divines.&rquo; This
(repeat a dozen critics) is &lquo;an amusing instance of anachronism.&rquo; I do not see why
the priestly teachers of morals in a heathen land may not well be termed &lquo;divines&rquo;
by an English poet without implying that he supposed them to be doctors of
divinity of Oxford or Geneva. [As far as I know Verplanck himself is the first
to call attention to the anachronism&mdash;his edition appeared in 1847&mdash;the &lquo;dozen
critics&rquo; are all named John Doe.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: This use of the term &lquo;divines&rquo;
has been set down as another anachronism. No doubt it is so. And so in North's
<I>Plutarch</I> we often find that the ancient Greeks and Romans had <I>bishops</I> among
them. The poet simply uses the language of his time to represent what has been
done at all times.&mdash;<SC>Wellesley</SC> (p. 26): None of the commentators have informed
us what were the precepts by which Coriolanus imagines that the Roman divines
of his day are as much losers as he is by his example. I should rather suppose that
he borrowed his simile from the Faculty, and that we should read, &lquo;Which <I>medicines</I>
lose by <I>time,</I>&rquo; the compositor having read <I>our divines</I> for <I>medicines</I> and <I>them</I> for <I>time.</I>
&mdash;<SC>Jabez</SC> [<SC>C. M. Ingleby</SC>] (<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I> 11 Aug., 1877, p. 105): Undoubtedly
<I>time</I> may have been read &lquo;them,&rquo; which, in its turn, was contracted into &lquo;em.&rquo;
But if &lquo;our divines&rquo; be a corruption, its place can hardly have been occupied by
<I>medicines;</I> for men do not cease to care for the lost virtues of their drugs, but throw
physic to the dogs when it is found to have survived its efficacy. On the contrary,
men do not throw away their <I>old wines,</I> not even their tawny port, but they set
store by them, prizing them for the very reason that their former virtues, have
departed. I therefore propose to read, &lquo;Like the virtues Which <I>old wines</I> lose
by <I>time,</I>&rquo; conceiving that <I>our d</I> is a misprint for <I>old, ivines</I> for <I>wines.</I> Coriolanus
might fitly compare himself (as valued by the plebs) to the virtues of a wine, which
men think they do well to dispraise and forget. [In Cam. ii. another emendation
is accredited to Ingleby, &lquo;Which dry wines lose by time&rquo;; it is, however, marked
as withdrawn. May we not add, <I>wisely?</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>R. M. Spence</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I>
1 Sep., 1877, p. 163): In a reverent and diffident spirit I venture to suggest that
Shakespeare's words may possibly have been, &lquo;I would they would forget me,
like the victims Which our diviners toss by 'em.&rquo; <I>I. e.,</I> as haruspices, having ex-
amined the <I>exta,</I> toss the carcases of the victims aside, as having served their
purpose, so wish I that the <I>profanum vulgus</I> of Rome, having got what they wanted
from me&mdash;victory over their foes and security for themselves&mdash;may ever forget

<P>66. <B>Enter three of the Citizens</B>] There is, it will be noticed, a discrepancy be-

&lquo;a brace&rquo; editors have altered the &lquo;three&rquo; of this stage-direction to &lquo;<I>two,</I>&rquo; but it
may be remarked that &lquo;brace,&rquo; like the German ein Paar, is frequently used for a

the other, and at first only two be seen by Coriolanus.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>):
The Cambridge Edd. make a third citizen enter alone. This is possible, as the
citizens had agreed to come &lquo;by ones, by twos, and by threes&rquo; (l. 45). In that case
he must step ahead of the &lquo;brace,&rquo; as he is first to reply (Folio). On the other hand,
in l. 85, Coriolanus says, &lquo;There's in all <I>two</I> voices begg'd&rquo;; which the Cambridge
Edd. do not alter!

<P>68. <B>a brace</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.,</I> s. v. III, 15. D.) gives several examples wherein
&lquo;brace,&rquo; meaning <I>couple,</I> applied to persons is used in a slightly humorous or con-
temptuous sense, its usual application being to designate a pair of dogs, from the
strap or <I>brace</I> which holds them together. The word thus used by Coriolanus on
this occasion is quite in character.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>69. <B>You know the cause</B> (<B>Sir</B>)] <SC>Dyce</SC>: Rowe's alteration (<I>sirs</I>) is perhaps right,
for Coriolanus may now be speaking to the &lquo;brace,&rquo; though he presently asks them
for their voices one by one. In the more recent editions (Mr Knight's excepted)
the dialogue between Coriolanus and these two Citizens is arranged in a sort of
verse, but the Folio gives it as prose; nor does it seem to have been intended by
the author for verse any more than the dialogue between Coriolanus and the
&lquo;two other Citizens,&rquo; of which no editor has attempted to make verse.
<P>70. <B>3 Cit.</B>] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): The Citizen insists on all the

<P>85. <B>A match Sir</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC>: The meaning we take to be this: Coriolanus
having won the voice of one Citizen, turns to the other with the enquiry,
Will you match it? and then proceeds: &lquo;There's in all two worthy voices begged,&rquo;
&amp;c.
<P>87. <B>But . . . odde</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: As this hemistich is too bulky to join with its
predecessor, we may suppose our author to have written only, &lquo;This is something
odd&rquo;; and that the compositor's eye had caught &lquo;But&rquo; from the succeeding
line.&mdash;[Shakespeare is in nowise responsible for this halting verse into which his
prose has been ruthlessly measured out; any errors in the prosody must be ascribed
to Capell, as Steevens doubtless knew.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>88. <B>And 'twere . . . no matter</B>] <SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>):
The naturalness of the writing here, with this break in the speech, and with the
half expressed but most expressive sentences of puzzled annoyance and grudged
consent, is inimitable. There is no one like Shakespeare for conveying perfect

<P>96-98. <B>You haue . . . Common people</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): This repre-
sents the sole effort of the Citizens to put in practice the &lquo;lessoning&rquo; of the Tribunes.
And it is more than enough to stir the resentment of Coriolanus.&mdash;<SC>MacCallum</SC>
(p. 527): It is all very well for the candidate to turn this off with a flout, but it is
the sober truth. That the despised plebeian should see both sides of the case
shows in him more sanity of judgment than Coriolanus ever possessed; that he
should nevertheless cast his vote for such an applicant shows more generosity as
well. And the generosity, if also the simplicity, of the electors is likewise made
more pronounced than in Plutarch by their persevering in their course despite the
scorn with which Coriolanus treats them; of which Plutarch, of course, knows
nothing. Even that they forgive till the tribunes irritate the wounds and predict
more fatal ones from the new weapon that has been put into such ruthless hands.
All these instances of right feeling and instinctive appreciation of greatness are
in Shakespeare's picture, while they are not at all, or in a much less degree, in
Plutarch's.

<P>101. <B>my sworne Brother</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: In the middle ages &lquo;fratres jurati&rquo;
were persons who had taken an oath to share each other's fortunes. Cowel in
his <I>Law Dictionary</I> says: &lquo;Fratres conjurati Are sworn Brothers or Companions.
. . . Sometimes they are so called who were sworn to defend the King against
his Enemies.&rquo; Compare <I>As You Like It,</I> V, iv, 107, &lquo;They shook hands and swore
brothers.&rquo; Again <I>Much Ado,</I> I, i, 73, He hath every month a new sworn brother.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Gordon</SC>: As if he and the people had sworn, according to the old custom of
comrades-at-arms, to stand by each other in everything. Coriolanus is bitterly
ironical, for flattery in such a compact is the unpardonable sin. That the people
are willing to be flattered shows that they are not fit for such comradeship.

<P>102. <B>'tis . . . gentle</B>] <SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): &lquo;Condition&rquo; is disposition, and also
quality, trait. Either sense will serve here, according as we understand Corio-
lanus to insinuate that the flatterer's disposition is gentle in the people's eyes, or
that they regard flattery as a gentle trait. Compare <I>Henry V:</I> V, ii, 314, &lquo;Our
tongue is rough, coz, and my condition is not smooth; so that, having neither the
voice nor the heart of flattery about me, I cannot,&rquo; etc. See also <I>Mer. of Ven.,</I>
I, ii, 143, &lquo;the condition of a saint.&rquo;
<P>113. <B>Seale your knowledge</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I will not strengthen or complete your
knowledge. The seal is that which gives authenticity to a writing.
<P>118-129. <B>Better it is . . . will I doe</B>] <SC>Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): Heroic verse
is not common in the play, but here it is used to express the excited, overstrained
condition of Coriolanus. The Citizens have got upon his nerves, and he relieves
himself in a moment's interval with this angry outburst.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>):
An example of Shakespeare's surviving use of rhyme for sententious reflection and
emotional self-expression, both of which are united in this passage.

ludicrous interpretation, he would probably have admitted it to be a natural

the Latin, which he does not understand. The very same mistake has happened
in <I>Othello,</I> where we find &lquo;<I>tongued</I> consuls&rquo; for &lquo;<I>toged</I> consuls.&rquo; The particle &lquo;in&rquo;

difficulty as usual by substituting <I>gown</I> without any regard to the word in the
original copy.&mdash;<SC>Douce</SC>: Mr Steevens has, in his note on this passage, cited the
romance of Howleglas to show that a husbandman's gown was called a <I>wolf,</I> but

is literally translated from the French, where the word &lquo;loup&rquo; certainly occurs, but
I believe it has not the same signification in that language. The French copy also
may be <I>literally</I> rendered from the German. [Douce is probably correct in saying

the coarse skin of the wolf, or the dress of the wolf in sheep's clothing; the former
(though good and formative in itself) requires that we lay greatest stress upon
<I>coarse;</I> the latter, as both Steevens and Malone rightly note, is the more natural.
But with this last interpretation, which depends upon the general acquaintance
with the language of the Bible and fable, it is necessary that not the classic word
(<I>toge</I>), but the popular word <I>gown</I> be read. And this word, so thoroughly appro-
priate, is not supplied by the original text. Thus we are constrained to decide in
favor of the MS. Corrector, since <I>woolless</I> corresponds most closely with the poet's
idea of the classic dress of the candidate. The copyist and reader were most
wofully at fault not only with the two words &lquo;hire&rquo; and &lquo;toge,&rquo; but also with a third,
<I>woolless,</I> since they did not understand <I>togue</I> and took it for <I>tongue,</I> thus &lquo;woolvish
tongue&rquo; seemed to them a much better sense than &lquo;woolless tongue&rquo;; thus they
tinkered with the (oldest) texts. Perhaps also the handwriting here was some-
what illegible.&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC> (<I>Sh. Scholar,</I> p. 360): Where is the propriety, espe-

ceased to be a disguise, and lost all significance; and besides, &lquo;wolfish&rquo; means not
&lquo;belonging to a wolf,&rquo; but &lquo;like a wolf.&rquo; Unquestionably, Shakespeare would

(i, 491): The train of thought in this speech shows Coriolanus already to have
abandoned the single indispensable rule of life of the conservative aristocracy.
His own subjective consciousness he turns against sacred custom. He forgets
that every prerogative becomes, and must become, a bond for him who enjoys it;
that unconditional personal freedom leads to isolation, and is incompatible with
the struggle for power. And thus he is driven to his fate before the wind of passion.
In this scene the drama easily displays its highest skill.&mdash;<SC>Snider</SC> (ii, 229): Corio-
lanus cannot submit to an institution&mdash;his individual will is supreme. This first
discipline of office&mdash;the suppression of his personal caprice and the submission to
the established custom&mdash;cannot be endured by him. Hence on this side he is
as revolutionary as the plebeians. The two parties thus reach the same point&mdash;
the destruction of the institutions which restrain their tendencies. The patricians,
however, as the true conservative element of society seek to conciliate both sides
and to retain the ancient laws and customs of the nation.&mdash;<SC>J. C. Collins</SC> (<I>Studies
in Sh.,</I> p. 82): A sentiment peculiarly characteristic of the Greeks was their
superstitious reverence for what was popularly accepted and become custom.
This continually finds expression in the Greek dramas, and is, indeed, woven into
the very fabric of their ethics. We need go no further than a line in Sophocles,
as it is typical of innumerable other passages, &lquo;what custom establishes outmasters
truth,&rquo; <I>Frag.</I> 84, and Euripides, <I>Bacch&aelig;,</I> 894, &lquo;What has long been custom, is
divine.&rquo; This is exactly Shakespeare's philosophy, [the present line quoted],
&lquo;Our virtues Lie in the interpretation of the time&rquo; (IV, vii, 51, 52), but illustration
would be endless.&mdash;<SC>Brandes</SC> (ii, 253): Coriolanus is utterly unaware that this
speech of his strikes at the very root of that ultra-conservatism which he affects.
The very thing he has refused to understand is, that if we invariably follow cus-
tom the follies of the past would never be swept away, nor the rocks which hinder
our progress be burst asunder. To Coriolanus, what is customary is right, and
he never realises that his disdain for the Tribunes and people has led him into a
politically untenable position. We are by no means sure that Shakespeare's
perceptions in this case were any keener than his hero's, but, consciously or un-
consciously, it is this very inconsistency in Coriolanus's character which makes it
so vividly lifelike.&mdash;<SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 601): It is characteristic of this spirit [of
self-centred confidence and egotism] which really makes a man a law unto himself
and the measure of all things, that though by all his training and prejudices inclined
to the traditional and conservative in politics, yet, if use-and-wont presses hard
against his own pride, he shows himself an innovator of the most uncompromising
kind. Coriolanus objects once and again to the prescriptive forms of election.
[In this and the following lines] he blossoms out as the reddest of radicals, though
a radical of the Napoleonic type.

some of the thrice six battles he had not so much seen, as heard of.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.):
Here &lquo;heard of&rquo; seems to mean <I>famous,</I> and to refer either to the battles or to the
speaker. Mr Collier's explanation is a strange one.&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC>:
Taking into consideration Coriolanus's scoffing manner of speaking here, we think
this means, &lquo;eighteen battles I have seen something of, and heard something of.&rquo;
He has just before sneeringly said he would remind the voters of a time &lquo;when some
certain of your brethren roar'd, and ran from the noise of our own drums,&rquo; and
he may well have here in his mind the sounds as well as the sights of a battle field.
If the expression &lquo;I have seen and heard of&rquo; include&mdash;as we think it does&mdash;the
elliptically conveyed effect of &lquo;I have seen and <I>made</I> heard of,&rquo; or caused to be
heard of, it is thoroughly in Shakespeare's comprehensive style.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed.

<P>ii.): This, if the text be right, must mean, apparently, &lquo;I have taken part in eighteen
battles, and those so considerable that I have since heard them talked about.&rquo;
The words &lquo;and heard of&rquo; seem, to say the least, rather odd and out of place.
Perhaps it should be &lquo;and <I>shared</I> of,&rquo; which is a modest equivalent for <I>been a
part of,</I> and is good English for <I>had a share of;</I> therewithal it accords with what
Cominius says in the preceding scene, where, after describing the hero's first
exploit, he continues, &lquo;And in the brunt of seventeen battles since.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Rolfe</SC>:
This must be thrown in contemptuously, like the &lquo;some less, some more&rquo; in the next
line. The Plebeians do not see at the time that he is <I>mocking</I> them (l. 171) while
begging their voices.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Henry Irving Sh.</I>): One would have thought
that this passage required no annotation, but Dyce's note shows how the simplest
things may be hidden from the wise and prudent. . . . Of course Coriolanus is
quizzing the people by affected magniloquence, from which he occasionally lapses
into irony. The effect on the people would be to puzzle them, which would be
partly Coriolanus's intention. It is perhaps allowable to call attention to the
excellent development of this scene. At first Coriolanus is simply cross and speaks
shrewishly to the citizens; then he recovers his good temper and is chiefly bored
by them; then when they refer to his wounds he becomes angry again and almost
resolves to give up the consulship; finally he reflects that as the ceremony is half
over he may as well finish it, and for the remainder of the time throws himself
into the part with exaggerated urbanity.&mdash;<SC>Kinnear</SC> (p. 313) proposes that &lquo;<I>you</I>
heard of&rquo; be read in the preceding line and &lquo;<I>I</I> have&rquo; in this. In both of which
readings he is, however, anticipated; the former by Farmer and the latter by
Keightley.&mdash;<SC>Ed</SC>.

<P>213. <B>Tying</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Versification,</I> p. 119): Words in which a short vowel is
preceded by a long one or a diphthong, among the rest may be particularly
noticed such present participles as <I>doing, going, dying, playing,</I> &amp;c., are frequently
contracted; the participles almost always. [Walker gives a large number of
examples in illustration.]
<P>217. <B>free Contempt</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, with contempt open and unrestrained.
<P>221. <B>Heart</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): &lquo;Heart&rquo; here used with the idea of &lquo;mind
intelligence&rquo; rather than &lquo;courage&rquo;; &lquo;had you tongues,&rquo; were you given tongues
that you might use them against the guidance of judgment?&mdash;<SC>Case</SC>, in reference
to the foregoing, says, &lquo;It is more likely that, though the expression is condensed,
spirit, action in speech, judgment are all involved: Were you quite spiritless?
Had you judgment and yet voted against its dictates? The <I>N. E. D.</I> cites this
passage under sense &ldquo;The seat of courage: hence Courage, spirit,&rdquo; and not under
&ldquo;Mind,&rdquo; where III, i, 311 <I>post</I> is given. It cannot be repeated too often that
precise correspondence in thought must not be demanded from Elizabethans
when they do not appear to give it.&rquo;
<P>222-225. <B>Against . . . Tongues</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC> alone of all the editors retains the
arrangement of these lines as in the Folio. See <I>Text. Notes.</I>
<P>223-225. <B>deny'd . . . Bestow</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 382): The Elizabethans seem to have
especially disliked the repetition which is now considered necessary in the latter
of two clauses connected by a relative or a conjunction. Here in strictness we
ought to have &lquo;bestowed&rquo; or &lquo;do you bestow.&rquo;
<P>224. <B>againe</B>] Here used metaphorically for, on the other hand; compare, &lquo;The
one is my sovereign, . . . the other again Is my kinsman,&rquo; <I>Rich. II:</I> II, ii, 113.
See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 27.

<P>244-246. <B>Lay a fault . . . on him</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): Here the Tribunes
break with truth; their office is new, and they dislike taking its responsibility.
They have every confidence that their end is wise, but in the choice of means
display the moral cowardice of a despised race. No doubt personal pique mingles
with their motives, but there is nothing to show it to be paramount.
<P>245, 246. <B>That we . . . on him</B>] <SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): The meaning seems to be:
&lquo;we labour'd, or took pains, that there might be no obstacle or hindrance to excuse
you from voting for him.&rquo; Endeavored to have, or to leave, &lquo;no impediment
between.&rquo; The language is somewhat obscure. Here we have a right piece of
demagogical craft; the sneaking &lquo;wealsmen&rquo; trying to creep, underhand, into the
good graces of the patricians while setting the dogs to worrying them.

</CC>
<PB N=276>
<HE>276 <I>THE TRAGEDIE OF</I> [<SC>act ii, sc.</SC> iii.</HE>
<FHL>
<CC>
<C>[259, 260. <B>hither . . . twice being Censor</B>]</C>
<P><I>Text. Notes</I>), a line having been certainly left out in this place, as will appear to any
one who consults the beginning of Plutarch's <I>Life of Coriolanus,</I> from whence this
passage is directly translated.&mdash;<SC>Theobald</SC>: I have taken notice, in the course of
these notes, of many anachronisms knowingly committed by our Author. I can-
not help observing that he is guilty of more than one here through an inadvert-
ence and desire of copying Plutarch at all hazards. This passage, as Mr Pope
rightly informs us, is directly translated from that Greek biographer; but I'll
tell Mr Pope a piece of history, which, I dare say, he was no more aware of than
our Author was. Plutarch, in the entrance of Coriolanus's life, tracing the origin
of the Marcian family, blends his account not only with ancestors but the descend-
ants of that great man; and Shakespeare in his haste (or perhaps his inacquaintance)
with this particular point not attending to Plutarch's drift; but, taking all the
persons named to be Coriolanus's ancestors, has strangely tripped in time, and
made his Tribune talk of persons and things not then in being. For instance, he
is made to talk of Censors. Now Coriolanus was killed in the year 266, A. U. C.,
but no Censors were ever created at Rome till 46 years after that period, in the
year 312. Again, here is mention not only of a Censor, but of Censorinus. Now
Caius Marcius Rutulus, when he came a second time to that office, on account
of the known law propounded by him, was dignified with that additional name,
in the year 487. But this was not until 220 years after the death of Coriolanus.
And then again here is mention of the Marcian waters being brought into Rome.
But we have the positive testimony of Julius Frontinus that they had no Aqueducts
at Rome till the year 441, and that the Marcian water was not introduced till the
year 613, so that the Tribunes are made to talk of a fact 347 years later in time
than the period of Coriolanus. I would not be supposed to found any merit on
this discovery, much less to be desirous of convicting my Author of such mis-
takes, but I thought it proper to decline a charge of ignorance that might have
been laid at my door had I passed this affair over in silence. Mr Pope, 'tis plain,
tho' he took the pains to add the conjectural line about Censorinus, was not aware
of this confusion in point of chronology, or of our Author's innocent trespass.
<I>Non omnia possumus omnes.</I>&mdash;<SC>Warburton</SC>, without referring to Theobald's note,
calls attention to the anachronism of a mention of a Censor here, and to the con-
fusion between the ancestry and posterity of Coriolanus; he adds: &lquo;Another in-
stance of Shakespeare's inadvertency, from the same cause, we have in <I>1 Henry
IV,</I> where an account is given of the prisoners took on the plains of Holmedon,
&ldquo;Mordake the Earl of Fife, and eldest son To beaten Douglas,&rdquo; [I, i, 71]. But
the Earl of Fife was not son to Douglas, but to Robert, Duke of Albany, governor
of Scotland. He took his account from Holinshed, whose words are: &ldquo;And of
prisoners among others were these, Mordack, Earl of Fife, son to the governor
Arkimbald Earl Douglas,&rdquo; etc. And he imagined that the governor and Earl
Douglas were one and the same person.&rquo; [This note Warburton did not repeat,
or make reference to this appearance of it, in his notes on <I>1 Henry IV.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;
<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 89): Here, indeed, are anachronisms with a witness;
for Censorinus and Quintus and Publius were descendants, not ancestors, of
Coriolanus, and that many generations beneath. The source of this mistake of
the poet's sprung from too hasty a transcript of a passage in his Plutarch. As a
drama his play is not much the worse for it; and yet it strikes the editor's fancy
that he saw the fault while 'twas in making, and meant to have mended it; and
</CC>
<PB N=277>
<HE><SC>act ii, sc.</SC> iii.] <I>CORIOLANUS</I> 277</HE>
<FHL>
<CC>
<C>[259, 260. <B>hither . . . twice being Censor</B>]</C>
<P>that the gap was a gap in his own copy caus'd by this intention, and not a slip
of the printer's, as usual.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC> gives the passage from Plutarch which was the
cause of this confusion; and, without reference to Theobald's note, gives the dates
of the first Censorship and the introduction of the Marcian waters. He thus
concludes his note: &lquo;Can it be supposed that he who would disregard such an-
achronisms, or rather he to whom they were not known, should have changed
Cato, which he found in his Plutarch, to Calves, from a regard to chronology?&rquo;
See I, iv, 82.&mdash;<SC>Verplanck</SC>: Shakespeare misunderstood the biographer, and sup-
posed that he meant to give the genealogy of his hero, when he intended merely
to speak of the illustrious men who had at different times sprung from the Marcian
family, some before Coriolanus, and the last named long after him. Yet it is a
singular circumstance, which shows the little real value of such minute criticism,
that Niebuhr and the modern school of critical Roman historians, while they
allow the story of Coriolanus to be substantially true, yet maintain that he must
have lived much later than the date assigned to him by the popular histories.
If they are correct in this theory, the Poet is accidentally much nearer to the
chronological truth than many of the learned critics who have been so precise in
marking the number of years he has gone astray.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: The &lquo;darling of the
people&rquo; of Pope's addition has but little of the true Shakespearian ring; it is,
moreover, not to be found in Plutarch, whom Shakespeare is here somewhat closely
following, without noticing that Plutarch is mentioning not alone ancestors but
descendants of Coriolanus.&mdash;<SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 487, foot-note): The addition by
Delius seems preferable to the reading of the Cambridge Editors. In the first
place, it is closer to North, and agrees with Shakespeare's usual practice of keeping
to North's words so far as possible. In the second place, it is closer to the Folio
text, involving only the displacement of a comma. In the third place, it is simpler
to suppose that a whole single line has been missed out than that parts of two have
been amputated, and the remainders run together.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emenda-
tions,</I> etc., p. 354): Pope's line respecting Censorinus was not wanted, inasmuch
as this portion of the speech of Brutus was struck out by the old Corrector,
possibly, because he saw the defect, and was not in a condition to remedy it.
Nevertheless, something was at one time written in the margin, but it is so
erased as not now to be legible.&mdash;<SC>Lettsom</SC> (Walker's <I>Shakespeare's Versification;
Preface,</I> p. xxi.): It is worth observing that though Collier's old Corrector has
inserted nearly a dozen lines in the text, while Walker has pointed out several
places where lines appear to be missing, and in some instances has attempted to
supply the deficiencies, their opinions in this respect never coincide. On the pas-
sage in <I>Coriolanus,</I> where Pope has inserted the line, &lquo;And Censorinus darling of
the people,&rquo; they are both silent. This is the more to be regretted, as scarcely
any supplementary verse could be less satisfactory than Pope's. However the
lost verse may have begun, it must have ended with the words &lquo;nam'd Censor-
inus,&rquo; as is clear from what immediately follows.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I>
etc., p. 216), in reference to the foregoing comment on the omission by the MS.
Corrector, exclaims: &lquo;A pretty argument truly! What then becomes of his
&ldquo;authorities,&rdquo; which we are led to believe he consulted on other occasions? I
undertake to say that Pope's line is a much more judicious addition to the text,
as evidently necessary and warranted by the passage in Plutarch, than any of the
uncalled for interpolations of the correctors so triumphantly dwelt upon by Mr

<P>Collier!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Tycho Mommsen</SC> (<I>Der Perkins Folio,</I> p. 437), on this same head, asks:

to line 260; and in justification of my text cite the lack of the two syllables in the
Folio, and the presence of the word in the above passage from Plutarch. [Singer,
ed. ii., has herein anticipated White.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Cambridge Edd.</SC> (<I>Note</I> V.): The
reading we have given in the text leaves the words of the Folios still in their order,
and introduces what must have been the significant fact that Censorinus was
chosen &lquo;by the people.&rquo; A stain or rent in the copy might have rendered parts
of two lines illegible, the remainder being unskilfully pieced together by tran-
scriber or printer.&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): Our unwillingness
to disturb a generally received reading makes us adopt Pope's line as it is, else
we should have preferred to give the line thus, &lquo;The darling of the people, Cen-
sorinus,&rquo; as then not only the rhythm would be better, but the surname would be
brought more immediately in connection with the words, &lquo;and nobly nam'd so.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>) marks here a line omitted, offering as one to supply its
place, &lquo;And he that was surnamed Censorinus.&rquo; [This version, according to
Wright (<I>Clarendon Sh.</I>), was also proposed by Dr Brinsley Nicholson.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;
<SC>R. M. Spence</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I> 9 June, 1894, p. 443): Perhaps with no other
passage in Shakespeare has conjectural emendation taken greater liberties; while,
as I shall demonstrate, the wholesale emendation is altogether unnecessary,
emendation is needed, but it consists only of the correction of a common misprint
and the addition of a single word, the omission of which can be easily accounted
for. The misprint is &lquo;so&rquo; for <I>as.</I> This &lquo;so,&rquo; if I mistake not, was what put Pope
and others on the wrong scent, backwards instead of forwards. Had they ob-
served the punctuation in the Folio (the comma between &lquo;nam'd&rquo; and &lquo;so&rquo;),
the misprint would have become self-evident. The word <I>Censor</I> has been omitted
from a cause which is often a source of mistake&mdash;inattention on the part of the
printer to the consecutive repetition of the same word. Again the punctuation
of the Folio (the comma at the end of the line) might have guided the critics
aright. As indubitably the true reading I give with confidence: And nobly
nam'd, <I>as</I> twice being censor, <I>Censor</I> Was his great ancestor. First we have
censor, the official title, and then Censor, the abbreviated English form of Cen-
sorinus, the honorable name conferred on C. Marcius Rutilus, in recognition of
the fact that he had held the censorship twice. As to the scanning of the line now
restored, it is a regular line of five accents with an additional syllable. [The
title at the head of this paragraph runs, &lquo;The Solution of the Long-standing
Crux in &ldquo;Coriolanus.&rdquo;&rquo; Whether this be the author's own, or one supplied by
the Editor of <I>N. &amp; Q.,</I> it is, I think, in either case injudicious. Modest or defer-
ential introduction of a purely conjectural emendation inspires acquiescence,
whereas assertion is apt to beget hostility. In proof of this it may be said that
but two of the subsequent editors or commentators (Cholmeley and E. K.
Chambers) have shared Spence's &lquo;confidence&rquo; in this &lquo;indubitable&rquo; addition, or
have even taken any notice of it.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Herford</SC> (<I>Eversley Sh.</I>), discarding all
emendations, leaves these lines as in the Folio. He adds: &lquo;Professor Littledale
proposes a comma at &ldquo;being,&rdquo; which gives a harsh but possible sense.&rquo;

<P>260. <B>twice being Censor</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: For the sake of harmony I have arranged
