&mdash;&lquo;the people had chosen him censor twice.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC>: Shakespeare seems to have
entertained a different notion; and what Steevens calls &lquo;harmony&rquo; Shakespeare
probably considered <I>monotony.</I> His great object, as regards versification, seems
from the first to have been to free it from the weighty words constantly recurring
at the ends of lines, which gave such a burdensome dulness to the delivery of
the verse of his immediate predecessors. Steevens, by his alteration, introduced
the very fault which Shakespeare seems anxious to avoid. [Collier is, I think,
unjust. By &lquo;harmony&rquo; Steevens apparently refers, not to the versification, but
to the <I>agreement</I> with Plutarch. Steevens was an offender on many occasions
in the manner Collier mentions, but this is not one of them.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>266. <B>Skaling</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, <I>weighing</I> his past and present behaviour.&mdash;
<SC>Schmidt</SC>: This is the usual explanation, but, according to the view of Sicinius,
there is no difference between the past and present behaviour of Coriolanus, but
rather both the former and the latter show him to be the constant enemy to the
people. With reference to I, i, 40, we should have to take it in another sense:
<I>reviewing</I> his present by his past behavior.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, <I>weighing,</I>
and so comparing, not contrasting. Coriolanus had been uniform in his behaviour
to the people, their &lquo;fixed enemy.&rquo; The word is used probably in the same sense
in <I>Meas. for Meas.,</I> III, i, 266, &lquo;The poor Mariana advantaged and the corrupt
deputy scaled&rquo;; that is, weighed in the balance and found wanting.

<P>a true leader, or if he had been willing, like the rest of the Senators, to affect a

Brutus and Sicinius from the opposite side enter to stop them. As the mutiny
grows against Coriolanus he is urged &lquo;home to thy House&rquo; (l. 287), and thither he
goes (at l. 310), passing into the rear-stage, now imagined to be his house. Scene ii.
follows in the rear-stage, where Coriolanus takes his mother's advice and says he
is &lquo;going to the Market place&rquo; (l. 159), and there in the fore-stage scene iii. is placed.
With the call &lquo;Go see him out at Gates&rquo; (iii, 171) the Act ends, all making their
<I>Exeunt</I> together in a tumult through the central exit. [This reconstruction of the
stage-business is certainly plausible, yet it is, I think, open to several objections.
In the first place, account is not taken of the disposition of the stage at the close
of Act II. The scene of Coriolanus's ordeal, since it requires but little space for
the few actors taking part, was doubtless played on the fore-stage, the curtains
being drawn between the columns, thus cutting off the middle and inner stage.
Another reason for the use of this fore-stage may be found in the fact that both
scenes i. and ii. of Act II. are scenes requiring the use of the full stage (the triumphal
return of Coriolanus and the Senate House). At the opening of this Act the cur-
tains between the columns are drawn aside and the full stage is made available
for the crowded scene of the tumult and mutiny; when Coriolanus returns to his
house it is more natural for him to make his exit by the same door through which
he entered instead of through the doorway to the small inner stage. At the end
of this scene the curtains between the columns are closed after the departure of all
the participants, and the scene at Coriolanus's house is then played on the fore-
stage. The use of the small inner stage for this important scene is hardly practical
on account of the number of actors taking part. For scene iii, the market place
again, the curtains are drawn aside and the full stage is used for the final scene of
the banishment.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>10. <B>Lord Consull</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Shakespeare has here, as in other places, attributed
the usage of England to Rome. In his time the title <I>lord</I> was given to many officers
of state who were not peers; thus <I>lords</I> of the council, <I>lord</I> ambassador, <I>lord</I>
general, &amp;c.&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): In reference to Malone's

he knew would be instantly comprehended by the public for whom he wrote, and
he wished to give the immediate impression of Coriolanus's having attained his
new dignity: that dignity striven for in the last Act, assumed and recognised at
the commencement of the present Act, and forfeited before the conclusion of its
first scene. This is just one of the poet's touches of dramatic art; with apparent
carelessness, but really nicest forethought, marking a point which, as the action
progresses, is essential to be well borne in mind.&rquo;

in one of the most striking chapters (xvi.) of <I>Kenilworth:</I> &lquo;Thou art a knave&mdash;
an ungrateful knave; but he that hath done, can undo&mdash;thou shalt not prank thee
in thy authority long.&rquo; <I>Kenilworth</I> is permeated with Shakespearian words and
allusions, which add greatly to its Elizabethan colouring. The Shakespearian
touches are introduced so naturally as to form part of the very texture of the
diction of the novel. They witness to a remarkable degree of familiarity with
Shakespeare's plays. One of the most interesting of Scott's <I>Miscellaneous Essays</I>
is on the drama. [In <I>Quarterly Review,</I> April, 1826.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>64. <B>Com. You are . . . businesse</B>] <SC>Knight</SC>: This interposition of Cominius

sequel of the dialogue clearly shows that it was uttered by Coriolanus.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC>:
The prefixes could not have been very easily mistaken by the printer, as that of
Coriolanus in this part of the scene is <I>Corio.,</I> and that of Cominius, <I>Com.</I> We
adhere to the ancient authorities, for the later folios make no change. [In his

to Cominius as identified with the interests of Coriolanus: the <I>business of your
party.</I>

to &lquo;business,&rquo; not &lquo;way.&rquo; That is: I am the man to better your business in every
way. He compares, &lquo;What you do Still betters what is done.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Wint. Tale,</I> IV,

<P>78. <B>Rub, layd falsely</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Falsely&rquo; for &lquo;treacherously.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The

passes lightly over the mockery of the people and revives an old grievance. Corio-
lanus responds to this only and admits it. Cominius, then, in saying that he had
not deserved the rub, could not consistently mean to deny the charge which con-
stituted it and to urge that it was therefore <I>untruly</I> made; but he could say that
this base and undeserved opposition was a mere pretext and false or untrue in
that sense. This may be called hair-splitting, but it illustrates the difficulties
that confront the commentator, and, after all, even the presence or absence of
consistency is not a conclusive test.

<P>unsuccessful candidature has, except as it adds to his private irritation, no im-
mediate result; and only some time later does his banishment follow on quite
another occasion. Corn had come from Sicily, and in the dearth it was proposed
to distribute it gratis; but Marcius inveighed against such a course and urged
that the time was opportune for the abolition of the Tribunate in a speech which,
in the play, he &lquo;speaks again&rquo; when his election is challenged. But the <I>Life</I>
reports it only as delivered in the Senate; and the Tribunes, who are present, at
once leave and raise a tumult, attempt to arrest him, and are resisted. The Sen-
ators, to allay the commotion, resolve to sell the corn cheap, and thus end the dis-
content against themselves, but the Tribunes persist in their attack on the ring-
leader, hoping, as we have seen, that he will prove refractory and give a handle
against himself. When he does this and the death-sentence is pronounced, there
is still so much feeling of fairness that a legal trial is demanded, which the Trib-
unes consent to grant him, and to which he consents to submit on the stipulation
that he shall be charged only on the one count of aspiring to make himself king.
But when the assembly is held the Tribunes break their promise and accuse him
of seeking to withhold the corn and abolish the Tribunate, and of distributing the
spoils of the Antiates only among his own followers. . . . So the unexpectedness
of this last indictment throws him out. Now there are several things to notice in
Shakespeare's very different version. The first is the tact with which he compresses
a great many remotely connected incidents into one. He antedates the affair
about the corn with Marcius's speech against the distribution and the Tribunate,
and only brings it in as a supplementary circumstance in the prosecution. The
real centre of the situation is Coriolanus's behaviour when a candidate, and round
this all else is grouped; and this behaviour, it will be remembered, is altogether a
fabrication on Shakespeare's part.

<P>90. <B>Cockle</B>] <SC>Beisley</SC> (p. 129): The cockle of modern botanists (Lychnis
Githago) is a tall handsome plant with purplish flowers, growing mostly in corn-
fields, the seeds of which are black; . . . but the plant meant by Shakespeare is
the Lolium temulentum, in his time called <I>darnel,</I> as well as <I>cockle</I> and cockle
weed.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The two plants [&lquo;cockle&rquo; and <I>darnal</I>] are clearly distin-
guished by Lyte and Gerarde. The latter says (p. 926, ed. 1597): &lquo;Cockle is a
common or hurtfull weede in our Corne, and very well known by the name of
Cockle.&rquo; And in the next page: &lquo;Some ignorant people haue vsed the seede
heereof for the seede of Darnell, to the great danger of those who have receiued
the same.&rquo; If any further proof were needed that the two plants are quite dis-
tinct, and were known to be so in the 16<SUP>th</SUP> century, it would be supplied by the
following passage from Latimer's <I>Sermons</I> (p. 72, Parker Society ed.): &lquo;Who is
able to tell his diligent preaching, which every day, and every hour, laboureth to
sow cockle and darnel?&rquo;

<P>100. <B>Meazels</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: In Early English <I>misel</I> is a leper, from the Old

scurvy wretch. See Wiclif, <I>Matt.</I> x, 8, &lquo;Clense the mesels,&rquo; for &lquo;cleanse the
lepers.&rquo; And <I>Promptorium Parvulorum,</I> &lquo;Mysel, or mesel, or lepre, Leprosus.&rquo;
In Chaucer, <I>Parson's Tale,</I> &lquo;meselrie&rquo; is leprosy. But by the middle of the 16<SUP>th</SUP>
century the word &lquo;measles&rquo; had acquired its modern sense. Huloet, <I>Abcedarium,</I>
has &lquo;Mesiles disease, <I>Variol&aelig;,</I>&rquo; and Cotgrave gives &lquo;Rougeolle: f. The Mazles.&rquo;
Shakespeare uses it here with a reference also to the contemptuous sense which it
had acquired when applied to persons.&mdash;<SC>Moyes</SC> (p. 26): The exact meaning of
&lquo;meazels,&rquo; its spelling, and its relationship to leprosy, elephantiasis, smallpox,
and our present-day measles, constitute a very confused subject. The infectious
nature of the disease, however, is clearly implied. According to Creighton, a
word &lquo;meseles&rquo; is used in the poem <I>Piers Plowman,</I> meaning <I>lepers,</I> but John of
Gaddesden uses the word &lquo;mesles&rquo; in his description of &lquo;morbilli&rquo; (or our present-
day measles). Again, &lquo;Ye Maysilles&rquo; is given in Levins' <I>Manipulus Vocabulorum</I>
as meaning &lquo;Variol&aelig;&rquo; (our present-day smallpox), and in Baret's dictionary the
word <I>measles</I> is defined as &lquo;a disease with manie reddish spottes or speckles in the
face and bodie, much like freckles in colour.&rquo; It must be remembered that the
confusion was one not merely of words and names, but that smallpox (variola)
and measles (morbilli) were constantly confused, and their distinction was due to
the Arabian physician and made known in England by John of Gaddesden. We
may fairly suppose that &lquo;meazels&rquo; in the text refers to our present-day measles.

<P>112. <B>Triton of the Minnoues</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC> and <SC>Johnson</SC> both explain, some-
what unnecessarily, that a minnow is a very small fish; and Steevens quotes in
illustration the only other passage wherein the word is used by Shakespeare&mdash;
<I>Love's Labour's,</I> I, i, 250: &lquo;there did I see that low-spirited swain, that base minnow
of thy mirth.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: The high and mighty Tribune with his absolute <I>shall</I> con-
trols the swarming mass of the people, just as a Triton controls the swarming fish
of the smallest kind. Likewise there is an alliteration between Triton and Tribune.
[Possibly also between &lquo;Triton of the minnows&rquo; and Tribune of the many.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;
<SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh. Illustrated by Old Authors,</I> p. 29): The contrast between Triton,
the son of Amphitrite, and Neptune, and the minnows, which are very small fish,
is apparent; and although it may be truly said that Triton, as a deity of the sea,
would rule over the minnows with his &lquo;absolute&rquo; or peremptory &lquo;shall,&rquo; which
Coriolanus calls &lquo;the horn and noise of the monster,&rquo; yet, when it is remembered
that Triton used to announce the approach of Neptune by blowing his horn,
which was a large conch or sea-shell, it may be considered probable that Shake-
speare plays upon the word &lquo;shall&rquo; in this passage, using it in a double sense;
for the words &lquo;shall&rquo; and <I>shell</I> do not differ more from each other in sound than
the words &lquo;sheep&rquo; and &lquo;ship,&rquo; which Speed plays upon in <I>Two Gentlemen,</I> I, i,
72, 73; and it may also be considered probable that Shakespeare, further on in
this passage [ll. 130, 131], plays upon the word &lquo;shall,&rquo; using it again in a double
sense. For the reader will perceive that Coriolanus speaks of &lquo;such a one as he,
who puts his <I>shall</I> against a graver bench than ever frown'd in Greece&rquo;; and Shake-
speare, using the word in a double sense, may refer to the practice in ancient Greece
of banishing persons considered dangerous to the state by ostracism, where the
votes were given by shells, each man marking upon his <I>shell</I> the name of the person
he would have banished. [This last suggestion is, I think, of very doubtful likeli-
hood. See ll. 130, 131 and note by <SC>Case</SC>, <I>supra.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>113. <B>His absolute Shall</B>] <SC>R. G. White</SC>: The recognition of the compulsory sense
of &lquo;shall,&rquo; and the difference of signification between that auxiliary and &lquo;will&rquo;
could not be more strongly marked than it is in the outbreak of the newly chosen
Consul against the Tribune's use of the former instead of the latter. But upon
this point there can hardly be any misunderstanding, and need be no remark.
No one who is acquainted with our early literature will dispute for a moment
that very long before the Elizabethan period &lquo;shall&rquo; emphatically applied by a
speaker to a second or third person expressed obligation, or that &lquo;will&rquo; was used in
the same manner, or, again, that &lquo;shall,&rquo; used with regard to a coming event, had a
prophetic force, and implied either the ability to bring it about, or the well assured
belief that it would happen. It is the restriction of &lquo;shall,&rquo; in the first person, to
the expression of simple futurity, and of &lquo;will&rquo; to that of &lquo;volition,&rquo; which is a mark

<P>114. <B>'Twas from the Cannon</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Was contrary to the established rule;
it was a form of speech to which he has no right.&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc.,
p. 252): These words appear to me to imply the very reverse. Cominius means
to say &lquo;that what Sicinius had said was according to the rule,&rquo; alluding to the
absolute veto of the Tribunes, the power of putting a stop to every proceeding;
and, accordingly, Coriolanus, instead of disputing this power of the Tribunes,
proceeds to argue against the power itself and to inveigh against the Patrician
for having granted it.&mdash;<SC>Pye</SC> (p. 249): I am rather inclined to the last opinion if
&lquo;canon&rquo; is meant for <I>rule;</I> but it is very probable that Shakespeare (considering
his little attention to this sort of propriety) might mean that the absolute <I>shall</I>
of the Tribune came as loudly as if from the mouth of a cannon.&mdash;[Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC>
(<I>First Folio Sh.</I>), without reference to the foregoing remark, characterises &lquo;Cannon&rquo;
here as &lquo;an anachronism which has lacked notice because commonly explained in
the sense of canon as rule or law.&rquo; An interpretation which, to me at least, is
inconsistent with the dignified language of this scene.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>C. &amp;. M. Cowden
Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): We hold with Mason's explanation, because it consists
with Sicinius's speech at the commencement of the last scene of this Act, &lquo;When
they hear me say, &ldquo;It <I>shall</I> be so, i'the right and strength o'the Commons,&rdquo; . . .
insisting on <I>the old prerogative and power,</I>&rquo; &amp;c.; but the present passage affords a
remarkable instance of the directly opposite sense which the word &lquo;from&rquo; may
give to a sentence, according to the sense in which the word is used and taken.&mdash;
Rev. <SC>John Hunter</SC>: Imitated from the decalogue, in which the word &lquo;shall&rquo;
occurs so frequently, &lquo;Or that the Everlasting had not fixed His canon 'gainst
self-slaughter,&rquo; <I>Hamlet,</I> I, ii, 131.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>), in support of the inter-
pretation given by Johnson that &lquo;from the canon&rquo; here means contrary to law,
quotes <I>Hamlet,</I> III, iii, 22, &lquo;For anything so overdone is from the purpose of
playing&rquo;; and <I>Twelfth Night,</I> I, v, 201, &lquo;But this is from my commission.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Wright</SC>
likewise follows Johnson, and to the two examples given by Schmidt adds: &lquo;Why
birds and beasts from quality and kind,&rquo; <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> I, iii, 65.&mdash;<SC>Orger</SC> (p. 62):
If Cominius interrupts the speech with the words &lquo;'Twas from the Canon,&rquo; they
can only mean, as Mason paraphrases, &lquo;it was according to law.&rquo; But such a
declaration is little calculated to assuage Coriolanus's violence, and the meaning
of &lquo;canon&rquo; in all other places is &lquo;Divine Law,&rquo; the language of the Ten Command-
ments. The imperious &lquo;shall&rquo; Coriolanus might naturally declare belonged to
a law with heavenly sanction, not to mortal voice; and the force of the term will
be preserved if we continue the speech to him without interruption, &lquo;His absolute
&ldquo;shall,&rdquo;&mdash;'Twas from the canon, &ldquo;Shall&rdquo;!&rquo;&mdash;[Johnson's, rather than Mason's,
interpretation is adopted by the majority of modern editors.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>121-123. <B>If he . . . Lenity</B>] <SC>Hanmer</SC> transposes l. 125 (&lquo;Let them have
cushions by you&rquo;) to follow &lquo;If he have power,&rquo; reading the latter line &lquo;If they,&rquo;
etc. On this change Capell (vol. I, pt i, p. 89) remarks: &lquo;It requires no ex-
traordinary reasoning to see that the speaker's conclusions follow right, in the
present arrangement, and in their due order, which cannot be said of the old one;
nor can any good reason be given why one Tribune only should be mentioned in
the first member of this rhetorical period, and both in the last; a further argument
in favour of both changes. Transpositions are frequent in printing; and the reader
will see very signal ones pointed out to him in the course of these notes, some of
which have the authority of other old copies for their rectification.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>:
If this man have power, let the ignorance that gave it him vail or bow down before
him.&mdash;<SC>Collier's</SC> MS. Corrector for &lquo;Ignorance&rquo;; &lquo;awake&rquo;; &lquo;Lenity&rquo; reads <I>im-
potence; revoke; bounty.</I> Of these changes Collier says: &lquo;The meaning is, that if
the Tribune have power, let the <I>impotence</I> (not &ldquo;ignorance,&rdquo; which is not the
proper antithesis to power) of the Senate submit to it; but if he have none, let the
Senate <I>revoke</I> the <I>bounty</I> by which such a dangerous privilege had been conceded
to the populace. The &ldquo;lenity&rdquo; of the patricians was not to be &ldquo;awakened.&rdquo;
Coriolanus calls upon them to <I>revoke</I> the <I>bounty</I> which had caused them to re-
linquish a power properly belonging only to themselves. What the hero says
afterwards is in entire consistency with this view of the passage: &ldquo;At once pluck
out the multitudinous tongue; let them not lick The sweet which is their poison,&rdquo;&rquo;
[ll. 184-186].&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> etc., p. 218): This is a sweeping liberty to
be taken with the old text. &lquo;<I>Ignorance</I>&rquo; could hardly be a misprint for <I>impotence,</I>
nor is the change requisite, for the next sentence proves that ignorance is the
right word, &lquo;If you are learned be not as common fools&rquo;; <I>revoke</I> for &lquo;awake&rquo;
may have been, and seems a likely, substitution; but <I>bounty</I> for &lquo;lenity&rquo; is not
required; the concession of power to the plebs and the indulgence given to the
Tribune was ill-judged <I>lenity,</I> not <I>bounty.</I> [See Collier: <I>Trilogy,</I> in <I>Appendix,</I>
p. 589.]&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: To &lquo;vail&rquo; means to <I>lower,</I> and Coriolanus would hardly call
upon his brother patricians <I>to lower</I> their <I>impotence.</I> The genuine word was far
more probably <I>signorie</I> or <I>signories,</I> i. e., <I>senatorial dignity, magistracy, sway.</I>
The emendation &lquo;<I>revoke</I> your <I>. . . bounty</I>&rquo; is an emendation, however clever, of
very questionable propriety; for &lquo;lenity&rquo; in this place does not, perhaps, mean
mildness, but <I>lenitude, supineness.</I> So in Plutarch's <I>Life of Coriolanus:</I> &lquo;For he
(Marcius) alledged that the creditors losing their money they had lost, was not
the worst thing; but that the lenity (<I>i. e.,</I> the inaction of the people when sum-

<SC>Hudson</SC>, reading with Collier's MS. Corrector <I>revoke,</I> says: &lquo;It seems clear enough
that <I>awake</I> reverses the drift of the argument. But the following clause, &ldquo;if you
are learn'd,&rdquo; makes against <I>impotence,</I> as it is evidently meant to be antithetic
to &ldquo;your ignorance.&rdquo; As to the substitution of <I>bounty</I> for &ldquo;lenity,&rdquo; it is to be
observed that Coriolanus is here speaking not against the Senate's bounty in
letting the people have corn <I>gratis,</I> but against the Senate's indulgent temper, or
<I>lenity,</I> in letting them have Tribunes as their own special magistrates.&rquo;&mdash;[In his
ed. ii. Hudson remarks: &lquo;I adopt Hanmer's reading as the simplest and most
satisfactory way of setting both the logic and the language in order. Collier's
Folio substitutes <I>impotence</I> for &ldquo;ignorance,&rdquo; and thus gets a fitting antithesis to
<I>power;</I> but does nothing towards redressing the other difficulties of the passage.
&ldquo;Awake your dangerous lenity,&rdquo; it seems to me, cannot be made to yield any con-
sistent sense.&rquo; This last statement, in view of Hudson's usual perspicacity, is
somewhat surprising. The figure is a little involved, but depends upon the mean-
ing of &lquo;lenity,&rquo; which here is stretched to mean <I>torpor, slothfulness.</I> It is, in fact,
practically the same figure as used by Buckingham in his simulated address to
Richard urging him to take upon himself the royal seat; he says: &lquo;&mdash;the mild-
ness of your sleepy thoughts Which here we waken to our country's good&rquo; (III,
vii, 123). In effect Coriolanus says: &lquo;If this officer have no power then arouse
your dangerous torpor, and let what was inactive become active.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC>
(<I>Coriolanus</I>): In <I>All's Well,</I> V, iii, the words, &lquo;Oft our displeasures, to ourselves
unjust, Destroy our friends, and after weep their dust,&rquo; are to be understood as
follows: &lquo;<I>In</I> our displeasures <I>we</I> often destroy our friends, and after <I>we</I> weep their
dust.&rquo; In the same manner the words &lquo;awake your dangerous lenity&rquo; are to be
understood, &lquo;<I>you must</I> awake <I>out of</I> your dangerous lenity.&rquo; Perhaps the best
reading would be <I>away</I> instead of &lquo;awake,&rquo; though <I>with</I> after <I>away</I> is wanting.&mdash;
<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.): &lquo;Awake <I>out of</I>&rquo; is not English.&mdash;<SC>Cartwright</SC> (p. 30): Read,
&lquo;vail your <I>arrogance;</I> if none <I>away,</I>&rquo; etc. Compare, &lquo;Would the nobility lay aside
their ruth And let me use my sword,&rquo; I, i, 210. And, &lquo;This too much lenity And
harmful pity must be laid aside,&rquo; <I>3 Henry VI:</I> II, ii, 9. &lquo;Away&rquo; seems preferable
to &lquo;away with,&rquo; as a more probable misprint, and the following passage appears to
confirm the &lquo;Well, I must do't Away, my disposition,&rquo; III, ii, 136. And &lquo;Away
thy hand,&rquo; says <I>Hamlet;</I> or &lquo;with&rquo; may be understood as in <I>Othello:</I> &lquo;What con-

not wholly apposite, as Cartwright has omitted a line following &lquo;magic&rquo;: &lquo;For

its fitness to the context, or the probability of the typographical errors which it
presupposes.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Johnson's paraphrase gives a sufficient, if not an
exact, sense for this expression, &lquo;vail your ignorance.&rquo; Ignorance of consequences
has betrayed the &lquo;good but most unwise patricians,&rquo; and it is, therefore, more
cutting to say they must stoop their ignorance than their pride, whether we take
the act to signify submission or shame. The Prayer Book (Litany) uses <I>ignorance</I>
for a fault ignorantly committed, &lquo;to forgive us all our sins, negligences, and
ignorances.&rquo;

<P>When the <I>taste</I> of the <I>great,</I> the patricians, must <I>palate,</I> must <I>please,</I> [or must <I>try</I>]

<SC>Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc., p. 253): Neither Johnson nor Steevens appear to me to
have rightly conceived the meaning of this passage; nor would Johnson's amend-
ment render it intelligible. That which I should propose, is to read <I>the general
taste,</I> instead &lquo;of the greatest taste,&rquo; and then the meaning will be thus: &lquo;You are
Plebeians,&rquo; says Coriolanus, &lquo;and they are no less, if, when both of your opinions
are blended together; that is, are put upon an equal footing, the opinions of the
Tribunes shall be most relished by the multitude.&rquo; He calls the taste of the
multitude <I>the general taste,</I> as in l. 175 he calls the ignorance of the multitude &lquo;the
general ignorance.&rquo; Volumnia, in scene ii, calls the people &lquo;our general louts.&rquo;
And Hamlet says a certain speech was &lquo;caviare to the general.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I
think the meaning is, the plebeians are no less than senators, when the voices
of the senate and the people being blended together, the predominant taste of the
compound smacks more of the populace than the senate.&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>: &lquo;The
prevailing flavour of the whole smacks rather of their voice (their authority) than
of yours.&rquo; Judged by results (the taste it leaves in the mouth) this dualized
government of compromise gives expression to the popular, rather than to the
patrician, will; the tribunicial nay is stronger than the consular yea. <I>To palate</I>
elsewhere of the person who tastes; here, of the thing, or flavour, which affects
the palate. [Thus also, substantially, W. A. Wright.]&mdash;<SC>Herford</SC> (<I>Eversley Sh.</I>):

<P>130, 131. <B>a grauer Bench . . . in Greece</B>] In Plutarch, Coriolanus, speaking
against giving corn gratis, refers to &lquo;the cities of Greece, where the people had
more absolute power.&rquo; Hence probably the comparison.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>132. <B>my Soule akes,</B> etc.] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): Coriolanus is an aristocrat
in principle. In these speeches, from l. 85, however mistimed they may be, he
is expressing his serious political convictions. It may be worth noting what was
actually the issue of the strife between these two &lquo;authorities,&rquo; the whole Roman
people with their Consuls on the one hand, and the plebeians with their tribunes
on the other. The Senate, originally merely a consulting body, gradually super-
seded both. It is not hard to see how, when magistracies were annual, knowledge
of affairs, and so responsibility, and so power, came to lie with a permanent body.
And to this both patricians and plebeians were eligible by serving certain magis-
tracies.

<P>pressed.&mdash;<SC>Herford</SC> (<I>Eversley Sh.</I>): It has been remarked that there was never a con-
stitution which looks more unworkable on paper than the Roman. But the Romans
had a genius for government which prevented deadlocks.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>):
In no nation was the &lquo;sense of the State&rquo; more developed. And this sense told them
what the State needed, and regulated the working of its political machinery to that
end. Much the same might be said of the English and the English constitution.
<P>135, 136. <B>take . . . by th'other</B>] <SC>Case</SC>: That is, seize the one by means of the
other. The commentators [Beeching and Chambers] say <I>destroy,</I> but their author-
ity to go so far is questionable. Seizure is an idea which naturally follows that
of entry through a gap. Compare IV, iv, 26, <I>post.</I>
<P>138. <B>Who euer gaue that Counsell,</B> etc.] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>):
Coriolanus in his excitement goes back to an old grievance. So far from wishing
to conciliate, he picks up the challenge thrown down by Brutus in ll. 56, 57 above.
According to Plutarch this episode of the distribution of the corn took place after
Coriolanus's rejection as Consul. Shakespeare leaves us to infer that it took
place at some undefined time before the action of his play begins. But he works
into the present scene part of the speech against the distribution put by Plutarch
in Coriolanus's mouth.

we must understand &lquo;our recompense to them.&rquo; [Dyce likewise thus interprets
the Folio reading.]

<P>156. <B>could neuer be the Natiue</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: &lquo;Native&rquo; for <I>natural birth.</I>&mdash;
<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 418): It is evident from the scope and drift of the whole context that
the word &lquo;native&rquo; cannot signify here &lquo;<I>the natural birth.</I>&rquo; Coriolanus had enumer-
ated several reasons why the donation of corn could not be interpreted as a recom-
pense, given in recognition of any meritorious service done by them: &lquo;They ne'er
did service for it, and when pressed to the war refused to stir out of the gates; when
in the war their mutinies and revolts could be no arguments in their favour; their
frequent and causeless accusations of the senate could not be the inducement
which prevailed with that body.&rquo; This being the sense of the context, it neces-
sarily follows either that we must understand the word &lquo;native&rquo; to denote the
native cause or inducement that gave birth to the donation, which is a sense I
am afraid the word will scarcely bear; or we must read <I>motive</I> instead of it.&mdash;
<SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Native&rquo; is here not <I>natural birth,</I> but <I>natural parent</I> or <I>cause of
birth.</I>&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 90) refers the reader to his <I>Glossary</I> for his inter-
pretation of this word, wherein he gives, with reference to this passage&mdash;<I>native
cause,</I> remarking that he was led to this meaning by the word &lquo;unborn&rquo; just pre-
ceding it.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: So, in a kindred sense, in <I>Henry V:</I> &lquo;A many of our bodies
shall no doubt Find native graves,&rquo; [IV, iii, 96].&mdash;<SC>Mason</SC>: I cannot agree with
Johnson that &lquo;native&rquo; can possibly mean <I>natural parent</I> or <I>cause of birth;</I> for if
the word could bear that meaning it would not be sense here, as Coriolanus is
speaking not of the consequence, but the cause, of their donation. Malone's

<P>158. <B>this Bosome-multiplied</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: This <I>multitudinous</I> bosom; the bosom
of that many-headed monster, the people.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emendations,</I> etc.,
p. 356): &lquo;Bosom multiplied,&rquo; a misprint most evident now it is pointed out [see
<I>Text. Notes</I>], has always been retained in the text. It can never be reprinted;
and is it too much to infer that the old corrector had somewhere seen or heard the
above passage, and others, represented with undoubted improvement? In II, i,
59 we have had <I>bisson</I> printed &lquo;beesome,&rquo; and here it is printed &lquo;bosome&rquo;; it is
very clear that the compositor did not understand the meaning of the word, which
then, perhaps, was becoming somewhat obsolete; this consideration can, however,
afford him no excuse for converting <I>multitude</I> into &lquo;multiplied.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC>, in <I>Notes

<P>corrections must still be looked upon as conjectural, the volume will be of high

alterations that no conjectural ingenuity could have suggested. The volume has

doubt that that particular correction was made on authority.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>A. E. Brae</SC>
(<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I> 10 July, 1852, p. 26): I cannot perceive anything in the proposed
alteration [<I>bisson multitude</I>] to exalt it above the common herd of conjectural
guesses; on the contrary, with the example of &lquo;bisson conspectuities&rquo; in the same
play, nothing appears <I>more obvious</I> than the extension of the same correction to
any other suspected place to which it might seem applicable. Dealing with it,
therefore, merely as conjectural, I reject it: (1) Because the apologue of &lquo;the
belly and the members,&rquo; in the first scene, gives its tone to the prevailing metaphor
throughout the whole play. Hence the frequent recurrence of such images as
&lquo;the many-headed multitude,&rquo; &lquo;the beast with many heads,&rquo; &lquo;the horn and noise
of the monster,&rquo; &lquo;the <I>tongues</I> of the <I>common mouth,</I>&rquo; &amp;c.; and hence the strong
probability that in any given place the same metaphor will prevail. (2) Because
in <I>Coriolanus</I> there are three several expressions having a remarkable resemblance
in common, viz., &lquo;multiplying spawn,&rquo; &lquo;multitudinous tongue,&rquo; &lquo;bosom multi-
plied,&rquo; and the concurrence of these three is strongly presumptive of the authen-
ticity of any one of them. (3) Because in the speech wherein &lquo;<I>bosom multiplied</I>&rquo;
occurs&mdash;the matter in discussion being the policy of having given corn to the people
<I>gratis</I>&mdash;when Coriolanus exclaims, &lquo;Whoever gave that counsel, <I>nourished</I> dis-
obedience, <I>fed</I> the ruin of the state&rquo;; these two words, of themselves, seem intended
to be metaphorical to the subject; but when he goes on to enquire, &lquo;how shall
this bosom multiplied <I>digest</I> the senate's courtesy,&rquo; it becomes manifest that
&lquo;digest&rquo; continues the metaphor which &lquo;nourished&rquo; and &lquo;fed&rquo; had begun, and if, in
addition, it can be shown that &lquo;bosom&rquo; was commonly used as <I>the seat of digestion,</I>
then the inference appears to be irresistible that &lquo;bosom multiplied&rquo; is a phrase
expressly introduced <I>to complete the metaphor.</I> Now, that <I>bosom</I> was so used, and
by Shakespeare, is easily proved. Here is one example from <I>2 Henry IV:</I> &lquo;Thou
beastly feeder . . . disgorge thy glutton bosom,&rquo; I, iii, 98. But I shall go still
further: I assert that Shakespeare has nowhere used <I>digest</I> in the purely mental
sense; that is, without some reference real or figurative, to the animal function
of the stomach. . . . (4) Because, since digest is thus invariably used by Shake-
speare, &lquo;bosom multiplied,&rquo; having close relation with that function, is in strict
analogy with the prevailing metaphor of the play; while, on the other hand, <I>bisson
multitude</I> has no relation with it at all; and therefore, had the latter been the
genuine expression, it would have been associated not with &lquo;digest,&rquo; but with
some verb bearing more reference to the function of sight than to that of degluti-
tion or concoction. (5) Because I cannot perceive why there should be any greater
difficulty in the metaphorical allusion to <I>the bosom multiplied digesting the senate's
courtesy</I> than to <I>the multitudinous tongue licking the sweet which is their poison.</I>
There is, in fact, such a close metaphorical allusion between the two expressions that
one can scarcely be doubted as long as the other is received as genuine.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC>
(<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I> July 24, 1852, p. 85) regrets that this &lquo;very elaborate and in-
genious argument&rquo; has failed to convince him. &lquo;I still think,&rquo; he continues, &lquo;that had
Mr Collier's second folio only afforded this one very happy correction, it would
have done good service to the text of a play in which the printer's errors are numer-

<SC>Perring</SC> (p. 298): The critics convert &lquo;this bosom multiplied&rquo;&mdash;by what process
I know not&mdash;to &lquo;this bissom multitude!&rquo; The latter being the harsher expression,
is thought perhaps to accord better with Coriolanus's temper. As a matter of
fact, however, for this particular passage the other phrase bears off the palm. It is
not the blindness of the multitude which is here glanced at, but the dangerous
knowledge bosomed up by them and sure in time to be thoroughly digested, that
they had wrung gratuities and concessions from a reluctant oligarchy. Multiply
the bosom, and you augment the danger. <I>Bissom multitude</I> is just the phrase
that an unwary critic would catch at; and how triumphantly might he point to
&lquo;bissom conspectuities&rquo; in another part of the play! But &lquo;bosom multiplied&rquo; is the
phrase for the place, original, unique, and strikingly apposite, bearing the stamp
of discerning judgment and originating genius. It may be matched with the
&lquo;multitudinous tongue&rquo; which occurs a little further down; only there <I>speech,</I>
here <I>thought,</I> is the dominant idea. By all means read, therefore, &lquo;How shall this

with our eyes. But can a bosom digest? No; but it is the bosom which first
feels the load of repletion and indigestion. Had Shakespeare's idea been simply
digestion he would have used <I>belly.</I> It is because the courtesy-crammed multitude
<I>cannot</I> digest, can indeed do nothing more than gorge what the senate gives it,
that he uses &lquo;bosom.&rquo; This is confirmed by the only other passages in Shakespeare
where &lquo;bosom&rquo; occurs in this connexion. They are <I>2 Henry IV:</I> I, iii, 95-98,
and <I>Macbeth,</I> V, iii, 44. In both of these passages, as in ours, the bosom suffers
from repletion, and is the seat not of digestion, but of indigestion. The first is
a striking parallel in more than language; that &lquo;beastly feeder,&rquo; the insatiate
multitude, is precisely the subject of Coriolanus's thoughts. The second is a
description of ordinary dyspepsia. Editors have been accustomed to defend

<P><I>i. e.,</I> No, I will still proceed, and the truth of what I shall say may be sworn to.
And may both divine and human powers (<I>i. e.,</I> the Gods of Rome and Senate)
confirm and support my conclusion.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 419): I would gladly be informed
how <I>sworn by</I> came to signify <I>sworn to.</I> Mr Warburton complains that the
common reading as pointed in the former editions &lquo;is unintelligible.&rquo; If it is so,
it can be only so to those who are ignorant that the Romans commonly swore by
what was Human as well as by what was Divine: by their own head; by the head
of others, of their parents, of their children; by their eyes; by the dead bones and
ashes of their parents; by the conscious knowledge of their own minds, &amp;c. See
Brisson. de Formulis, pp. 808-817. The sense is, No, let me add this further; and
may everything Divine and Human which can give force to an oath bear witness
to the truth of what I shall conclude with.&mdash;<SC>Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> &amp;c., p. 254):
Warburton's explanation is not admissible; the <I>What may be sworn by</I> cannot possibly
mean <I>What may be sworn to;</I> and, according to his manner of pointing, the words
<I>divine</I> and <I>human</I> have no substantive to which they can refer; but according to
the present pointing Coriolanus invokes everything in heaven and on earth, of
reverence sufficient to be sworn by, to confirm what he says. So in Fletcher's
<I>Coxcomb,</I> Antonio says to Mercury: &lquo;By this light I cannot; By all that may be
sworn by,&rquo; [I, i; ed. Dyce, iii, p. 125.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>].

<P>174. <B>yea and no</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: According to Sir Thomas More's rule, yea
and nay go together, and yes and no; the former being answers to questions framed
in the affirmative, and the latter to those framed in the negative. But this was a
rule not strictly observed, and Shakespeare neglected it both here and elsewhere.
Compare <I>Lucrece,</I> 1340, &lquo;Receives the scroll without or yea or no.&rquo; And <I>Merry
Wives,</I> I, i, 88, &lquo;By yea and no I do.&rquo;
<P>177. <B>vnstable Slightnesse</B>] <SC>Whitelaw</SC>: That is, feeble vacillation.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Coriolanus</I>) dissents to this, saying that &lquo;slightness&rquo; here rather means, &lquo;A bearing
which earns for one the adjective <I>slight.</I> Nothingness, an attitude of mind that
means nothing, and for which nothing has meaning, so that it is unstable, without
hold on anything.&rquo; [See <SC>Badham</SC>, Note on 177, 178&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>177, 178. <B>Purpose . . . to purpose</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This is so like Polonius's
eloquence, and so much unlike the rest of Coriolanus's language, that I am apt
to think it spurious.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 420): &lquo;Purpose so barr'd&rquo; is only the same thing,
recapitulated in three words, which had been before expressed more at large in
ll. 173-175. Wherever this is done, Coriolanus concludes, nothing is done to
purpose. If Mr Warburton had given himself the leisure to understand this, I
suppose he would scarce have disgraced this passage, notwithstanding a play on
the words not unusual to Shakespeare, by comparing it to Polonius his eloquence,
or rejected it as spurious.&mdash;<SC>Badham</SC> (p. 7): The sense and metre in this passage
alike indicate that it is corrupt; for to what does senatorial wisdom have recourse
when its wiser purposes are barred their execution by popular ignorance? not
slightness&mdash;though slightness will certainly be the quality of whatever fabric
they rear, but <I>sleights,</I> i. e., shifts, tricks, expedients. [Read therefore] &lquo;To unstable
<I>sleights;</I> purpose so barred, it follows,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): That is,
where a deliberate and continuous course is precluded there can be no successful
policy; all is from hand to mouth and unsatisfactory. There is, I think, a per-
sonal note in this passage which suggests that it expresses Shakespeare's own
indictment of democracy. Want of continuity of policy has ever been the char-
acteristic weakness of popular government.
<P>180, 181. <B>That loue . . . change on't</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, Who are so
wedded to accustomed forms in the administration that, in your care for the
</CC>
<PB N=307>
<HE><SC>act iii, sc.</SC> i.] <I>CORIOLANUS</I> 307</HE>
<FHL>
<CC>
<C>[180, 181. <B>That loue . . . change on't</B>]</C>
<P>preservation of those, you overlook the danger the constitution incurs by strictly
adhering to them. This the speaker, in vindication of his conduct, artfully rep-
resents to be his case; yet this pertinent observation the Oxford Editor [Hanmer],
with one happy dash of his pen, in amending &lquo;doubt&rquo; to <I>do,</I> entirely abolishes.&mdash;
<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 420): That is, You whose love for the fundamental part of the state
(or, which in the language and sentiments of Coriolanus amounts to the same
thing, the supreme authority of the Senate) is not overpowered by your appre-
hensions, that the steps necessary to support it may possibly hazard the change of
it. That this is the sense of the passage is evident from what immediately
precedes and follows it (l. 179 and ll. 181-184). All which lines express the very
same sentiment under various illustrations. Instead of this, Mr Warburton hath
given us a sense which the words do by no means express, and which counteracts
the very scope and intention of the speaker; a sense which insinuates that it is
more prudent to yield in points of form than hazard the safety of the constitution.
Whereas the advice of Coriolanus is, That it is better to put the whole to the
hazard at once than to temporize, while the authority of the Senate is thus gradu-
ally subverted.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: To &lquo;doubt&rquo; is to <I>fear.</I> The meaning is: &lquo;You whose
zeal predominates over your terrors; you who do not fear so much the danger of
violent measures, as wish the good to which they are necessary, the preserva-
tion of the original constitution of our government.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 90):
That is, stand in fear of the consequences attending a change of it, have <I>doubts</I>
about them. &lquo;The fundamental part of state&rquo; is, in the speaker's estimation,
that government which subsisted before the people had any great share in it,
and especially before the institution of tribunes; whom he would have them set
aside and fear no consequences, reverting to a rule by themselves; assigning for
cause of his advice their present <I>dishonourable</I> dependence, which hinder'd them
from doing anything rightly, or the state any service, while the tribunes had a
<I>veto</I> in everything. This short gloss conveys a true idea of the tendency of all
this long speech, some part of which is wrapped up in a purposed obscurity, the
speaker being more set on fire; in his next he is more open.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> takes objection
to the first part of Johnson's paraphrase on the ground that &lquo;<I>zeal</I> is not <I>discretion.</I>&rquo;
He thus interprets: &lquo;You that will show less fear than prudence (or foresight),
<I>or</I> that will rather be prudent (or foreseeing) than afraid.&rquo; And continues: &lquo;&ldquo;Vio-
lent measures,&rdquo; as advocated in lines 183 <I>et seq.,</I> may affect &ldquo;the state,&rdquo; as Corio-
lanus wishes, by their success, or &ldquo;the fundamental part of state,&rdquo; as he does
not wish, by their failure. In the one case, change is the action of the senators
(and = changing) and &ldquo;on't&rdquo; refers to &ldquo;state&rdquo; only; in the other, change is the
result of the failure of that action and &ldquo;on't&rdquo; refers to &ldquo;the fundamental part
of state.&rdquo; The two senses (which, after all, are involved in Johnson's expression,
&ldquo;the danger of violent measures&rdquo;) could be put in this way: (a) You that fear
not to change the constitution in order to preserve its foundations; (b) You that
so love the fundamental part of state that you will risk it to make it sure. The
fundamental part of the state is affected in Coriolanus's eyes already, but there is
room for greater loss, so that this cannot be urged against (b), which has also a cor-
respondence with the alternatives that follow in ll. 181-183.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon
Sh.</I>): &lquo;Whose love for what is really and originally the State outweighs any fear
of the revolution that might follow making the change&rquo;; <I>i. e.,</I> abolishing the
tribunate.

<P>183. <B>To iumpe a Body</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: To &lquo;jump&rquo; anciently signified to <I>jolt,</I> to
give a rude concussion to anything. &lquo;To jump a body&rquo; may, therefore, mean
&lquo;to put it into a violent agitation or commotion.&rquo; Thus Lucretius, III, 452&mdash;
<I>quassatum est corpus.</I> [This assertion by Steevens, without any example to sup-
port it, is not borne out by fact. The <I>N. E. D.</I> does not give any such transitive
meaning to the verb <I>jump;</I> his quotation from Lucretius is nothing to the purpose;
<I>quassatum</I> is used tropically for <I>enfeebled, weakened.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] So in Phil. Holland's
translation of Pliny's <I>Natural History,</I> bk xxv, ch. v, p. 219, &lquo;If we looke for good
successe in our cure by ministring ellebore, &amp;c., for certainly it putteth the patient
to a jumpe or great hazard.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: From this passage in Pliny it should
seem that &lquo;to jump a body&rquo; meant to <I>risk</I> a body; and such an explication seems
to me to be supported by the context in the passage before us. So in <I>Macbeth,</I>
We'd jump the life to come,&rquo; [I, vii, 7]. Again in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> &lquo;&mdash;our fortune
Lies upon this jump,&rquo; III, viii, 6. [Also <I>Cymbeline,</I> &lquo;or jump the after enquiry
on your own peril,&rquo; V, iv, 188.]&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I> 24 July, 1852, p. 85):
I read (meo periculo), &lquo;To <I>impe</I> a body,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> restore or increase its power. This
term from falconry was familiar to the poet.&mdash;[In his <I>Shakespeare Vindicated</I>
(published a year later) Singer repeats this emendation, remarking of the word
&lquo;jump&rquo; that &lquo;all attempts to give it a reasonable meaning have failed&rquo; and &lquo;nothing
can be made of it.&rquo; In illustration of Shakespeare's use of the word <I>imp</I> as a
term of falconry, used metaphorically, Singer quotes, &lquo;Impe out our country's
broken wing,&rquo; <I>Richard II:</I> II, i, 292, and thus concludes: &lquo;The word originally
signified to insert, and, in falconry, to insert a feather into an injured or deficient
wing of a hawk; but its general meaning is to mend by artificial means; this is the
sense required here&mdash;to patch up.&rquo; Thus, in <I>The Pilgrim,</I> Beaumont and Fletcher,
I, i, &lquo;None of your pieced companions, pined gallants That fly to flitters, with
every flaw of weather; None of your imped bravadoes.&rquo;&mdash;Singer's statement, that
the general meaning of <I>imp</I> &lquo;is to mend by artificial means&rquo; and hence &lquo;to patch
up,&rquo; is only partly correct. The original meaning is <I>to engraft,</I> from the Greek <I>em-
phenein,</I> to implant; Shakespeare was undoubtedly familiar with the term in fal-
conry, and certainly understood it sufficiently to preclude his using it in connection
with a dose of physic. Medicine is not used to patch up a sickened body; but
may often be used, as Malone says, even at the risk, or hazard, of a cure. The
Anonymous writer in <I>Blackwood's Magazine</I> (Sep., 1853, p. 322), who reviews
Collier's MS. Corrections, turns aside for a moment to speak with special com-
mendation of this emendation by Singer; but, misled by him, also asserts that
&lquo;there is an old word <I>imp,</I> which signifies to patch,&rquo; and, since no sense can be made
of the words &lquo;to jump a body,&rquo; <I>imp</I> &lquo;is the word which ought to stand in the
text.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. i.): Malone's explanation of this rank corruption has,
I am sorry to see, misled Dr Richardson to cite the passage in his <I>Dictionary</I> under
&lquo;Jump.&rquo; Mr Singer would read &lquo;To <I>imp.</I>&rquo; But I have no doubt that <I>vamp</I> (Pope's
emendation) was Shakespeare's word; &lquo;<I>vamp,</I>&rquo; in fact, comes nearer to the <I>ductus
literarum</I> of the old lection than does <I>imp;</I> &lquo;<I>va</I>&rquo; was more likely to have been mis-
taken for &lquo;in&rquo; than &lquo;i&rquo; for &lquo;in.&rquo; The proneness of printers to blunder in words
beginning with <I>v</I> is very remarkable.&mdash;<SC>Ibid.</SC> (ed. ii.): In my former edition I read

<P>under the editorship of Alexander Chalmers, has failed to verify this. All other
readings proposed by Kinnear are recorded in this second Cambride ed.; it would
seem, therefore, that, in this case, the Editors regarded the reading by Chalmers
as anticipating that by Kinnear.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): That is, <I>witless.</I>
The literal meaning <I>bare</I> leads easily to the figurative idea <I>destitute</I> of force, <I>meagre,
paltry,</I> and so <I>destitute</I> of sense. Similarly, Shakespeare often has <I>barren</I> = barren
of wits, empty-headed, stupid; cf. <I>Richard II:</I> I, iii, 168, &lquo;dull, unfeeling, barren
ignorance.&rquo; Or does &lquo;bald&rquo; imply &lquo;in their dotage&rquo;?&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: The jest of youth
at middle age. It is difficult to be at once bald and majestic, as Julius C&aelig;sar found.
Ordinarily Shakespeare takes the other side, and suggests, according to the prov-
erb, that bushy headed people have more hair than wits. This is a touch of
nature. He was prematurely bald himself.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): With more respect
Cominius calls Sicinius &lquo;Ag'd sir&rquo; in l. 212 below, but possibly &lquo;bald&rquo; is more than
a mere taunt of youth against age on the part of Coriolanus, and figuratively im-
plies <I>contemptible</I> or <I>bald-witted.</I> The figurative use of &lquo;bald&rquo; was as common then
as now: <I>Comedy of Errors,</I> II, ii, 110, &lquo;I knew 'twould be a bald conclusion&rquo;; <I>1
Henry IV:</I> I, iii, 65, &lquo;This bald unjointed chat of his.&rquo; References to the use of
<I>barren</I> by Shakespeare and others (as in <I>Mid. N. Dream,</I> III, ii, 13, &lquo;The shallowest
thick-skin of that barren sort&rquo;) do not seem much to the point, as there is no diffi-
culty in the application of an adjective meaning unproductive or sterile, and very
little metaphor.

which is unavoidable, was law.&rquo;
<P>200. <B>Let what . . . be meet</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Let it be said by you that what is meet

propriety, directed the legislature. [For other examples of this confusion of two

<P>time with the Tribuneship of the Plebs, as servants of the Tribunes, and at first
probably nominated by them till 471, when, like them and under their presidency,
they began to be elected by the whole body of the Plebs. They took their name
from the temple (<I>&aelig;des</I>) of the plebeian goddess Ceres, in which their official archives
were kept. Besides the custody of the <I>plebi-scita,</I> and afterwards of the <I>senatus-
consulta,</I> it was their duty to make arrests at the bidding of the Tribunes; to carry
out the death-sentences which they passed, by hurling the criminal down from the
Tarpeian rock; to look after the importation of corn; to watch the traffic in the
markets; and to organise and superintend the Plebeian and Roman Games. Like
the Tribunes, they could only be chosen from the body of the Plebs, and wore no
badge of office, not so much as the <I>toga pr&aelig;texta,</I> even after they became an au-
thority independent of the Tribunes.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Dictionary of Classical Antiquities,</I> <SC>Seyffert</SC>

<P>211, 212. <B>Wee'l Surety him. Ag'd sir, hands off</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 484): Monosyllables
containing diphthongs and long vowels, since they naturally allow the voice to
rest upon them, are often so emphasized as to dispense with an unaccented syl-
lable. [In the present instance Abbott suggests that the emphasis falls on &lquo;<I>We,</I>&rquo;
and &lquo;Ag'd&rquo; is to be pronounced as a dissyllable, <I>Aged,</I> thus the metre is made regular;
but are not these two short lines by their very irregularity highly expressive of the
vehemence and haste of the dialogue? See <I>Text. Notes,</I> l. 212, for Hanmer's and
Capell's attempts to regulate the metre here. <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.) queries as to whether
&lquo;surety&rquo; is a trisyllable for the same purpose.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>He desires the tribunes to speak to the people because he was not able; and at the
end of the speech repeats the same request to Sicinius in particular.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>:
I see no need of any alteration. [<SC>Rann</SC> is Mason's sole follower in this arrange-
ment.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: Editors connect &lquo;tribunes to the people,&rquo; although &lquo;to
the people&rquo; would be better connected with &lquo;Speak&rquo; (l. 229), separated therefrom
by the parenthesis &lquo;Coriolanus, patience.&rquo; The Tribunes should ask silence of the
people, since Menenius knows not how to obtain a hearing for himself, as in an
earlier case (cf. I, i.).&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): &lquo;<I>You,</I>&rquo; i. e., do <I>you</I> speak (Menenius
himself being unable). Some would read &lquo;You, tribunes, Speak to the people!&rquo;
But abruptness seems more suitable to the context.&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC> (p. 299): Menenius,
who all along endeavors to maintain amicable relations with the commons, and
to act as a sort of peacemaker between the two rival factions, would surely not,
when the populace were all afire, deliberately blow the flames and insence the
Tribunes by crying out insultingly &lquo;You, tribunes to the people!&rquo; Rather does
he do his utmost to check the conflagration and prevent the flames from spreading,
appealing to each one of the opposing parties in turn; admonishing first the Trib-
unes, then Coriolanus; exhorting <I>them</I> to speak to, to restrain, pacify the people;
exhorting <I>him</I> to have patience. Such being the case, the passage should be
stopped thus:

<P>To have upbraided the popular magistrates at such a critical juncture would have
been as impolitic as it would have been alien to the part which Menenius assumed.
But perhaps I shall be told that the interpretation which I have given is the inter-
pretation contemplated, <I>stops notwithstanding.</I>
<P>233. <B>at point to lose</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, on the point of losing. See
V, iv, 67, and <I>Cymbeline,</I> III, i, 30, &lquo;The famed Cassibelan, who was once at
point . . . to master C&aelig;sar's sword.&rquo;
<P>234. <B>Martius . . . Martius</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect;&sect; 475, 476): A word repeated twice in a
verse often receives two accents the first time, and one accent the second, when it
is less emphatic the second time than the first. Or the word may occupy the
whole of a foot the first time, and only part of a foot the second. On the other
hand, when the word increases in emphasis, the converse takes place. Even at
the end of the verse Marcius has but one accent as a rule. But here it is unusually
emphasized.
<P>239. <B>What is the Citie, but the People?</B>] <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh's Legal Maxims,</I> ed.
ii, p. 53): In this passage Shakespeare probably refers to the maxim: Civitas et
urbs in hoc differunt, quod incol&aelig; dicuntur civitas, urbs vero complectitur &aelig;dificia
(Mirror, cap. 2, sect. 18, Brit. fol. 87, Co. Litt. 109 b). A city and a town differ in
this, that the inhabitants are called the city, but the town comprises the buildings.
<P>244. <B>And so are like to doe</B>] <SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Coriolanus,</I> p. 123): Menenius speaks this to
himself. Since there is the question who will prevail, Coriolanus or the Tribunes,

<P>Menenius fears the latter: &lquo;I fear you will remain in your place, and Coriolanus
will lose his new-won consulship.&rquo; [Leo is perhaps right; but at the same time it
is to be remembered that Menenius is acting the part of conciliator, and by this
remark he means to assure the Tribunes that there is no danger of their losing
their offices under the Consulship of Coriolanus.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>245. <B>Com. That is the way,</B> etc.] <SC>Knight</SC>: We give this speech, as in the orig-
inal, to the calm and reverend Cominius. Coriolanus is standing apart, in proud
and sullen rage; and yet the modern editors put these four lines in his mouth, as
if it was any part of his character to argue with the people about the prudence of
their conduct. The editors continue this change in the persons to whom the
speeches are assigned, without the slightest regard, as it appears to us, to the
exquisite characterisation of the poet. Amidst all this tumult the first words
which Coriolanus utters, according to the original copy, are, &lquo;No, I'll die here.&rquo;
He again continues silent; but the modern editors must have him talking; and so
they put in his mouth the calculating sentence, &lquo;We have as many friends as
enemies,&rquo; and the equally characteristic talking of Menenius, &lquo;I would they were
barbarians.&rquo; We have left all these passages precisely as they are in the original.&mdash;
<SC>Staunton</SC>: It is usual, though in opposition to the old copies, to assign this speech
to Coriolanus on account of what Sicinius says immediately after it, &lquo;This de-
serves death.&rquo; But the speech is not at all characteristic of Coriolanus; and the
observation of the Tribune refers to what he had previously spoken, &lquo;Marcius
would have all from you.&rquo; [The <SC>Cowden Clarkes</SC>, following the Folio reading,
give substantially the same reason as has Staunton for retaining this speech as
in the original text.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.), after quoting Staunton's note, adds: &lquo;Staunton
is, in my opinion, mistaken.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (ed. ii.): In the old copies this
speech is given to Cominius, but it evidently belongs to Coriolanus, as the rejoinder
of the Tribunes as well as the tenor of speech itself shows.&mdash;Rev. <SC>John Hunter</SC>:
The speech is not in keeping with the proud sullenness of Coriolanus; and the fol-
lowing words of Sicinius refer to his previous accusation. [Thus also <SC>Rolfe.</SC>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>247. <B>which yet distinctly raunges</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, which has as yet
a clearly recognised position, occupies a prominent rank.
<P>247. <B>distinctly</B>] That is, <I>separately.</I> <SC>Abbott</SC> compares: &lquo;&mdash;on the topmast,
The yards and bowsprit, would I flame distinctly, Then meet and join,&rquo; <I>Tempest,</I>

<P>292-295. <B>Mene. I would they were . . . Be gone</B>] <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>: The beginning
of this speech (attributed in the Folio to Menenius) I am persuaded should be
given to Coriolanus. The latter part only belongs to Menenius, &lquo;Begone, put not
your worthy rage,&rquo; etc. [In the <I>Variorum of 1773</I> this note is misplaced; it there
follows Warburton's note on l. 284, to which it manifestly cannot refer.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;
<SC>M. Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc., p. 255): The word &lquo;Begone&rquo; certainly belongs to
Menenius, who was very anxious to get Coriolanus away. In l. 281 he says,
&lquo;&mdash;be gone, away.&rquo; And in l. 306, &lquo;Pray you be gone.&rquo; [See also l. 290, &lquo;be gone,
'beseech you.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Badham</SC> (<I>Text of Sh.; Cambridge Essays,</I> p. 277): In <I>Corio-
lanus,</I> Act III, the second (<I>sic</I>) scene is one of the most corrupt in Shakespeare,
where, by the consent of modern editors, Menenius, the peacemaker, is made to
call his countrymen barbarians, and after abusing them, to tell Coriolanus, who
has been perfectly <I>silent,</I> &lquo;not to put his worthy rage into his tongue,&rquo; to offer to
fight the Tribunes (which clearly belongs, as well as what follows, to Cominius),
and, in pleading for his friend, to admit that he is a mortified limb indeed, but one
that should be left on the body out of regard for its previous service.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Coriolanus</I>): The giving of l. 291 to Coriolanus as in the Folio is plainly an error;
but that is not sufficient reason for modern editors to give ll. 292-294 to Coriolanus
instead of Menenius as in the Folio. There the speech of Menenius continues down
to &lquo;another,&rquo; l. 296, but evidently with the words &lquo;Begone,&rquo; etc., another interlocutor
is introduced, who can be no other than Cominius. The admonition thus appro-
priately applies to Menenius, who is heatedly advising, while it comes too late to
Coriolanus.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Line 295 (&lquo;&mdash;put not your worthy rage into your
tongue&rquo;) implies that Coriolanus has just spoken, and justifies the arrangement of
the speeches proposed by Tyrwhitt.

<P>294. <B>calued i'th' . . . Capitoll</B>] Was there perhaps lingering in Shakespeare's
memory a faint echo of his line in <I>Hamlet,</I> &lquo;It was a brute part of him to kill so

<P>296. <B>One time will owe another</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I know not whether &lquo;owe&rquo; in this
place means <I>to possess by right</I> or to be <I>indebted.</I> Either sense may be admitted.
<I>One time,</I> in which the people are seditious, will <I>give us power</I> in some <I>other time;</I>
or, <I>this time</I> of the people's predominance will <I>run them in debt;</I> that is, will lay
them open to the law, and expose them hereafter to more servile subjection.&mdash;
<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 421): The sense is, If we give way now, our present moderation will
entitle us to expect a more favourable opportunity, when we may be able to set
everything right again.&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc., p. 255): I believe Menenius
means, &lquo;This time will owe us one more fortunate.&rquo; It is a common expression to
say, &lquo;This day is yours, the next will be mine.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The meaning seems to
be, &lquo;One time will compensate for another. Our time of triumph will come here-
after; time will be in our debt, will <I>owe</I> us a good turn, for our present disgrace.
Let us trust to futurity.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC>: I think Menenius means to say, &lquo;Another
time will offer when you may be quits with them.&rquo; There is a common proverbial
phrase, &lquo;One good turn deserves another.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: One time of mis-
fortune will owe us another of retribution. The people have it all their own way
now; our time will come.&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>: Our time will come. &lquo;Non si male nunc,
et olim Sic erit.&rquo; Today's reverse will give us a claim to another day of better
fortune.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): Yielding today will owe us victory tomorrow.
&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): I take the meaning to be, &lquo;What you say now will
have to be accounted for later&rquo;; Menenius being afraid that Coriolanus may say
something, in his present anger, which will compromise his position beyond
redress.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Your turn will come, Fortune will owe you a good
turn for a bad one.
<P>297. <B>fortie of them</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): Elizabethans often use <I>forty</I> to
imply an indefinitely large number. Cf. <I>Merry Wives,</I> I, i, 205, &lquo;I had rather
than forty shillings I had my Book of Songs and Sonnets here&rquo;; and <I>Sonnet</I> ii,
&lquo;When forty winters shall besiege thy brow.&rquo; Other numbers, <I>e. g.,</I> 3 and 13, have
become significant through some ancient belief or historical event; and perhaps
40 gained some mysterious import through the Scripture. Thus the wanderings
of the Israelites lasted forty years, the fast of our Lord forty days. [The flood

<P>and quotes Sir Thomas Browne's <I>Vulgar Errors,</I> III, 16, &lquo;That young vipers force
their way through the bowels of their dam . . . is a very ancient tradition . . .
affirmed by Herodotus, Nicander, Pliny, Plutarch.&rquo; One of the characteristics of
Euphuism was a mighty parade of unnatural natural history, hence it is not sur-
prising to find more than one reference in <I>Euphues</I> to this popular superstitition;
compare the <I>Epistle Dedicatory,</I> &lquo;lest . . . I should with the viper lose my blood
with mine own blood&rquo; (ed. Bond ii, 5), and <I>Euphues,</I> p. 177. See <I>Absalom and
Achitophel,</I> 1012-15. To Sicinius, Coriolanus is a viper, in seeking to prey upon
the city that bore and reared him. This interpretation seems to me favoured by
&lquo;viperous traitor,&rquo; l. 353 below. The unnatural young viper, but not Lernean
Hydra, might be so described. [<SC>Case</SC> also interprets &lquo;viper&rquo; in the sense of un-
natural offspring; yet, in spite of Verity's excellent note, I am inclined to think
that here Shakespeare uses &lquo;viper&rquo; as the symbol of treachery or a traitor&mdash;the
words &lquo;viperous traitor&rquo; seem to point to this.&mdash;<SC>Craigie</SC> (<I>N. E. D.,</I> s. v. Viper, 3. b.):
In allusion to the fable of the viper reared or revived in a person's bosom. One
who betrays or is false to those who have supported or nourished him; a false or
treacherous person. 1596. <I>Edward III:</I> I, i, 105, &lquo;Degenerate Traytor, viper to
the place Where thou was fostered in thine infancy.&rquo; Under section 2. A venomous,
malignant, or spiteful person, a villain or scoundrel, Craigie quotes the present
line.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>328, 329. <B>he hath resisted Law . . . further Triall</B>] <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh's Legal
Maxims,</I> ed. ii, p. 58): Merito beneficium legis amittit, qui legem ipsam sub-
vertere intendit (2 Inst. 53). According to Sicinius, Coriolanus had resisted law
and therefore lost the benefit of the law.&mdash;<SC>E. J. White</SC> (p. 410): Sicinius declares
that one who has scorned the forms of law should be dealt with in a summary
manner as an outlaw, and in this instance that Coriolanus was entitled only to a
trial by the <I>Comitia,</I> or the vote of the people, whose power he had spurned. This
verse shows the Poet's respect for law, in the abstract, as the medium through
which the rights of the citizens are enjoyed. &lquo;He hath resisted law&rquo; as presented
here is a serious charge, and one that the speaker believes entitles the party guilty
of such offence to no legal protection. Like poor Shylock's plea, when he &lquo;stands
for law,&rquo; this illustrates the deep insight into the world of law, as the only correct
medium through which the proper ideals of equality and justice can be attained,
and shows the lawyer's respect for the law in the abstract that ought to be un-
derstood by all citizens.

<P>333. <B>and we their hands</B>] That is, The Tribunes are the mouths of the people,
and we, the people, are the hands of the Tribunes.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>334. <B>He shall sure ont</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 91): Meaning out of the house
(either his own or some other) where they supposed he had taken shelter [see
<I>Text. Notes</I>]. The four later moderns [Pope, Theobald, Hanmer, Warburton]
give us: He shall be sure on't, without any authority for <I>be,</I> or, in fact, any for
<I>on't;</I> for the &lquo;ont&rquo; of the First Folio is a printer's mistake, a (<I>u</I>) inverted; nor would
the rabble have expressed themselves so if they had intended to say, He shall
certainly know it.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The meaning of these words is not very obvious.
Perhaps they mean, He shall, that's sure. I am inclined to think that the same
error has happened here and in a passage in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> and that in both places
&lquo;sure&rquo; is printed instead of <I>sore.</I> [See <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> II, v, 133, this ed.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] He
shall suffer for it, he shall rue the vengeance of the people. The editor of the Second
Folio reads, He shall sure <I>out;</I> and <I>u</I> and <I>n</I> being often confounded, the emendation
might be admitted, but there is not here any question of the expulsion of Corio-
lanus. What is now proposed is to throw him down the Tarpeian rock. It is
absurd, therefore, that the rabble should, by way of confirmation of what their
leader Sicinius had said, propose a punishment he has not so much as mentioned,
and which, when he does afterwards mention it, he disapproves of&mdash;&lquo;to eject
him hence Were but one danger.&rquo; I have, therefore, left the old copy undisturbed.
[This note, which appears first in Malone's ed. 1790, is not included among the
notes on this passage in the <I>Variorum</I> of 1821.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Perhaps our
author wrote, with reference to the foregoing speech, &lquo;He shall, <I>be</I> sure on't,&rquo;
<I>i. e.,</I> be assured that he shall be taught the respect due to both the Tribunes and
the people. [Rather an unfortunate betrayal of the fact that Steevens had not
examined the texts of some of his predecessors (see <I>Text. Notes</I>); and doubly
unfortunate inasmuch as this note evidently misled Dr W. A. Wright, who, in the
<I>Clarendon Ed.,</I> credits this reading to Steevens.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>336. <B>cry hauocke</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, Do not give the signal for unlimited
slaughter, &amp;c.&mdash;<SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>: &lquo;To cry havoc&rquo; seems to have been the signal for gen-
eral slaughter, and is expressly forbid in <I>Les Ordinances des Battailles,</I> 9 R. ii,
art. 10: &lquo;Item, que nul soit si hardy de crier havok sur peine d'avoir la test coupe.&rquo;

<P>353-355. <B>to eiect him . . . one danger . . . death</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Letter to</I> War-
burton, Feb. 12, 1729, in Nichols, <I>Illustrations,</I> etc., ii, p. 485): <I>Were</I> is the verb both
to <I>danger</I> and <I>death;</I> which <I>wards,</I> as you conjecture, will not be. I had corrected
it, dear Sir, a long while since, in this manner: &lquo;To eject him hence, <I>Were</I> but
<I>our</I> danger, etc., <I>i. e.,</I> to banish him will be hazardous to us; to let him remain
at home, our certain destruction; therefore he must die tonight.&rquo; [This is, I be-
lieve, the only record of Warburton's conjecture <I>wards</I> for &lquo;were&rquo; in l. 354; he did
not repeat it in his own edition, and Theobald, whose note in his own edition four
years later is substantially as above, did not refer to this conjecture.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;
<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 421): I can see no reason for altering the common reading, &lquo;Were but
one danger&rquo;; that is, as I apprehend, the danger from the enemy, if they deprive
themselves of so able a champion. Mr Theobald objects, that hereby the climax,
which seems evidently designed, is destroyed. I can see no climax even in his
emendation, but an antithesis only, which is equally preserved in both readings.&mdash;
<SC>Keightly</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 366): I read <I>our</I> for &lquo;one&rquo; as Theobald proposed. In
<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> (I, iv, 3) we have &lquo;<I>One</I> great competitor,&rquo; where the sense demands
<I>our;</I> and in <I>Sonnet</I> xcix, &lquo;Our blushing shame,&rquo; where editors, as sense requires, read
<I>One.</I>&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): It appears to us that the sentence
means: &lquo;To banish him from hence were but to encounter one danger; and to allow
him to remain in Rome would be to encounter another&mdash;the certain destruction
of our offices as tribunes.&rquo; We think the word <I>another</I> is ellipitically understood
after &lquo;here,&rquo; as thus: &lquo;To eject him hence were but one danger; and to keep him
here, another&mdash;our certain death.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): That is, one unbroken,
complete danger. Compare <I>Macbeth,</I> &lquo;Making the green, one red,&rquo; II, ii, 63;
also <I>2 Henry IV:</I> I, i, 157, &lquo;But let one spirit of the first-born Cain Reign in all
bosoms.&rquo; See also IV, vi, 172 <I>supra.</I>&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: If this be the true reading,
it must mean one all-pervading constant source of danger.&mdash;<SC>Rolfe</SC>: If this be
what Shakespeare wrote, we must accept the Cowden Clarkes' explanation. Per-
haps it would be better to read (with Theobald) &lquo;our danger.&rquo; The Cambridge
Edd. conjecture &lquo;<I>moe</I> danger&rquo;; but <I>moe</I> (as one of these editors has himself else-
where noted) is used only with a plural or a collective noun.&mdash;<SC>T. Page</SC>: That is,
Would be nothing but one all-absorbing cause of danger. Compare <I>Macbeth,</I>
II, ii, 63. Theobald's conjecture of <I>our</I> for &lquo;one&rquo; is highly probable.&mdash;[The majority
of commentators are in favor of the interpretation of &lquo;one&rquo; here in the sense
<I>constant, perpetual,</I> though just how the expulsion of Coriolanus would be a con-
tinual danger is not made evident. This interpretation, moreover, renders the
rest of Sicinius's remarks meaningless, or without the needed antithesis. I am
therefore inclined to think the explanation by the Cowden Clarkes is the more
rational: To expel this traitor is only one danger; to let him remain is a double
danger&mdash;our destruction. The one danger being, as Heath interprets, the loss of
such a champion. The adversitive &lquo;but&rquo; is also against the meaning <I>constant.</I>
Sicinius would hardly say, The expulsion of this traitor is only a continuous
danger, as an antithesis to the destruction of the Tribunate. One is almost as

previous speech and argument. By adopting Steevens's interrogation point placed
at its conclusion the consecution is not only rendered obvious, but the same
interrogatory form is kept up as in the line, &lquo;What has he done to Rome that's
worthy death?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): Here Menenius is probably to be understood

are, however, all somewhat stirred, and a touch of verbal irregularity seems to
fit the context.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Ellipse confuses the grammar and the precise
sense, but whether it is the foot or the service of the foot that is no longer regarded
when the disease of the one terminates the other, signifies little. Either [Warbur-

country it honoured him, not now; and he or Sicinius would continue: when the
foot serves it is regarded, not when mortification has set in, inferring that it must
then be cut away, as Sicinius said in l. 362. In Menenius's mouth the speech is
bitterly ironical and recurs to l. 363, but there is this inconsistency in the metaphor,
that &lquo;a limb that has but a disease; Mortal to cut it off,&rquo; is now a limb that has a
disease; mortal not to cut it off.
