<P>385. <B>Proceed by Processe</B>] <SC>E. J. White</SC> (p. 411): This is lawyer-like advice,
to enjoy only the rights which the law guarantees through the remedial pro-
cedure of the courts, which crystallized into fundamental or organic law, in this
country, by our provision that no one should be denied his rights except upon
&lquo;due process of law.&rquo; &lquo;Process&rquo; is a word used to convey the means of compelling
a defendant to appear in court after suing out the original writ in a civil suit,
or after indictment found in a criminal case.
<P>388. <B>If it were so?</B>] <SC>Badham</SC> (<I>Sh. Criticism,</I> p. 11) adds the line &lquo;And he would
prove obedient&rquo; after &lquo;so?&rquo; &lquo;as necessary both for the sense and the metre.&rquo; Ten
years later, in his essay on <I>The Text of Shakespeare,</I> Badham amplified on this,
saying (p. 278): &lquo;I have not the least doubt that Brutus's speech has been mutilated;
for Sicinius's remark is applicable to nothing that precedes, nor are the words
&ldquo;If it were so&rdquo; grammatically correct, supposing &ldquo;if&rdquo; referred to Menenius's fear of
civil war; for in that case we should require <I>It is be so.</I> I believe that Shakespeare
gave proof in this case of his dramatic skill by making the yielding of Brutus
preparatory to that of Sicinius, and that the missing words were to the following
effect.&rquo; [Badham then repeats the line as given in his former work, without refer-
ring to his previous conjecture.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>393. <B>a could</B>] <SC>Bayfield</SC> (p. 198): Here and in V, iii, 137 are the only two
places where the vulgarism <I>a</I> for <I>he</I> occurs in the verse. In the prose the one

<P>396. <B>bring him in peace</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: The words &lquo;in peace&rquo; were probably in
the MS. placed at the beginning of the next line, and caught by the transcriber's
eye glancing on the line below. [See <I>Text. Notes.</I>]&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i.): Pope left
out &lquo;in peace&rquo; because the same words occur just below; but Menenius may be
reasonably supposed to repeat them, by way of emphasis, and to show the
Tribunes in what condition of mind he will undertake to bring Coriolanus.&mdash;<SC>Ibid.</SC>
(ed. ii.): We think Pope was right; it was probably a printer's error.&mdash;<SC>Badham</SC>
(<I>Text of Sh.,</I> p. 274): The absurd repetition in lines 396 and 398 is well worth
attention, as showing those faults which transposition alone remedies. The most
natural, I should almost say, the only way of accounting for such a blunder is to
suppose that the person who dictated the passage to a transcriber, having reached
the end of one line, skipt the next, and proceeded with the third, and then, upon
discovering his mistake, went back to the omitted line, and continued to dictate
without ordering an erasure. Afterwards it would often happen that when the
redundancy was discovered by a careless or unlearned person the erasure would
be made in the wrong place. It is to this cause of transcribing from dictation that
we must also attribute the endless confusions of metre by the ignorant divisions
of the lines, which some of our modern editors have so religiously restored.
Anyone who makes such a remark must prepare himself for the taunt that he counts
the verses upon his fingers. As Shakespeare wrote in numbers, and as numbers
are intended to be counted, it certainly seems wiser, in case of a deficient ear, to
count upon our fingers than not to count at all. I am very far from approving
of Sir Thomas Hanmer's or Steevens's practice, of making emendations to suit
the metre; but there is surely a wise middle course to be observed between retain-
ing what amends itself, or defending what is incurable, and attempting to repro-
duce that of which there are no vestiges to guide us. [My own complete agree-
ment with the concluding portion of the foregoing&mdash;expressed so succinctly and
admirably&mdash;must be my excuse for inserting here remarks of a character more
general than the present particular instance may warrant.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>3. <B>Death on the Wheele, or at wilde Horses heeles</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> has, on this line,
contributed a long note to the effect that neither of these punishments was known
at Rome, following this with speculations as to how Shakespeare might have
become acquainted with the latter form of death for traitors. On the question of
its being known to the Romans Malone quotes from Virgil, <I>&AElig;neid,</I> viii, 642-645,
a reference to the death of Mettius Suffetius, and from Livy, I, ch. xxviii, where
the same incident is recorded with details as to the rending apart of Mettius by
horses harnessed to chariots. As Malone remarks, since Shakespeare mentions
death on the wheel, which was certainly unknown to the Romans, it is highly
improbable that he knew anything about the fate of Mettius; he suggests, how-
ever, that: &lquo;Shakespeare had probably read or heard in his youth that Balthazar
Gerard, who assassinated William Prince of Orange in 1584, was torn to pieces
by wild horses; as Nicholas de Salvedo had been not long before, for conspiring to
take away the life of that prince.&rquo; Malone also refers to the infliction of this same
punishment upon John Chastel in 1594 for his attempt on the life of <I>Henri IV.</I>&mdash;
<SC>Steevens</SC>: Shakespeare might have found mention of this punishment in our
ancient romances. Thus, in <I>The Sowdon of Babylone,</I> p. 55: &lquo;&mdash;Thou venomouse
serpente With wilde horses thou shalt be drawn to morowe And on this hille be
brente.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>), in reference to any objection to
the mention of these punishments as violating historic accuracy, say: &lquo;With almost
as much justice might it be gravely objected that to &ldquo;pile ten hills on the Tarpeian
rock&rdquo; was never known to be done in Rome as a means of punishing by death.
For poetic and dramatic purpose Shakespeare putting these words into Corio-
lanus's mouth has a truth of appropriateness far beyond that demanded by the
accuracies of chronological fact.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): It has not been observed that
the expression &lquo;at wild horses' heels&rquo; (notwithstanding the plural <I>horses</I>) would
apply equally well or better to the different punishment inflicted, for example,
upon Brunhault (or Brunhilda) in 613, under Clotaire II, who was put to death
by being dragged at the heels of a wild horse. See Beard, <I>The Theatre of God's
Iudgements,</I> 1597, Ch. xiii, Of Queenes that were Murderers, p. 281 (<I>sic,</I> really
293): &lquo;shee was adjudged to be tyed by the haire of her head, one arme and one
foot to the taile of a wild and untamed horse, and so to bee left to his mercy to
bee drawen miserably to her destruction; which was no sooner executed, but her
miserable carkasse (the instrument of so many mischiefes) was with mens feet
spurned, bruised, trampled, and wounded after a most strange fashion; and this
was the wofull end of miserable <I>Brunchild.</I>&rquo; See also <I>ibid.,</I> xviii, p. 349: &lquo;some he
tied to the tailes of wild horses, to be drawne ouer hedges, ditches, thornes and
briers.&rquo; Case compares, with the present line, Dekker, <I>Olde Fortunatus,</I> 1600:

<P>&lquo;Thou shalt be tortured on a wheele to death, Thou with wild horses shalt be
quartered&rquo; (ed. Pearson, I, 170). [Inasmuch as Dekker's comedy and <I>Coriolanus</I>
are nearly contemporaneous and &lquo;the wheel&rquo; and &lquo;wild horses&rquo; are mentioned in
both, small room is left for doubt that we have here the main source of Shakespeare's
reference. Either of the quotations from Beard's volume are, to my mind, much
more likely sources than any of those incidents cited by Malone, if historic refer-
ence is sought.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>5. <B>precipitation</B>] <SC>Whitelaw</SC>: That is, <I>precipice.</I>&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): Not
precipice, but rather <I>downfall.</I> &lquo;Might&rquo; instead of <I>may,</I> required by sequence of
tense, may be referred to other cases, and is here better to elucidate the purely
hypothetical character of the expression.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Precipitousness, the
space through which anything is precipitated.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Not apparently
as Schmidt (<I>Lex.</I>) explains it, &lquo;the throwing or being thrown headlong,&rquo; but the
precipitousness, the precipice. The whole expression means: so that no man,
standing at the top, however keen-eyed, could see the bottom.
<P>6. <B>the beame of sight</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, farther than the eye could pierce.
Compare <I>Merry Wives,</I> I, iii, 68: &lquo;Sometimes the beam of her view gilded my
foot,&rquo; like a ray of light proceeding from a luminous body.
<P>8. <B>Enter Volumnia</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes and Emendations,</I> etc., p. 357): A rather
noticeable change is made by the old annotator in the entrance of Volumnia:
in print, she is made to come in just before the Patrician's speech, &lquo;You do the
nobler,&rquo; standing by and saying nothing, while Coriolanus speaks of her in the
third person. A manuscript emendation fixes her arrival on the scene, more
naturally perhaps, at the words of Coriolanus addressed expressly to her, &lquo;I talk
of you,&rquo; &amp;c. We may suppose that this arrangement represents the practice of
our old stage in this respect.
<P>9. <B>You do the Nobler</B>] <SC>Badham</SC> (<I>Criticism Applied to Sh.,</I> p. 10): What a strange
jumble is here!&mdash;&lquo;You do the nobler!&rquo; Can any critic produce a passage from
Shakespeare to justify such an expression as this? or if he could, shall we believe
that the Patrician is intended to encourage him in his contumacy? If so, why does
Coriolanus bring in the mention of his mother, and justify himself, as he is here
made to do, by her example? And then what a gross contradiction to the general
economy of the play, that Coriolanus whose respect for his mother is stronger
than his ambition or his revenge,&mdash;who is to him the single object of his deepest
passion, family pride,&mdash;should talk <I>at her,</I> and then turn round and tell her so;

<P>and a pretty character he gives of her. She, a high born, calls the plebeians by
the vilest names; as if the coarseness, which political animosity barely excuses in
a man, was becoming in a Roman matron. And then observe how the ingenious
editors distort the plain meaning of words. &lquo;I muse&rquo; is <I>I think,</I> but here, forsooth,
it <I>must mean</I> I wonder. The truth is, Volumnia does not enter until the words
&lquo;I talk of you,&rquo; as the very words declare; for had she been on the scene that
information would have been superfluous. But Volumnia's name was there, no
doubt, and the nearest approximation to the original passage which we have to
offer is this:

<P>12. <B>Wollen Vassailes</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 92): What shall we say is the sense
of the epithet &lquo;Woolen&rquo;? <I>Clothed in wool</I> does not satisfy; and the editor rather
inclines to think it has some particular meaning which does not occur to him; or
else, that the word is not right, and yet he does not think it is&mdash;<I>wooden.</I>&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M.
Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): The way in which &lquo;them&rquo; is used here, alluding
to the common people, affords a fine instance of Shakespeare's dramatic way of
abruptly commencing a scene, as well as of using a pronoun in reference to an
unnamed but thoroughly understood antecedent. The term &lquo;woolen vassals&rquo;
here shows Shakespeare's intention to convey the circumstance that the garment
worn by the Plebeians was of wool; and this lends support to our interpretation of
the word &lquo;woolvish&rquo; as given in our note on II, iii, 115. At the same time the
epithet &lquo;vassals&rquo; affords confirmation to our surmise that <I>slavish</I> may have been
the word for which the Folio printers mistakenly substituted &lquo;wooluish.&rquo;&mdash;
Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): So the &lquo;rude Mechanicals&rquo; of <I>Mid. N. Dream</I>
(III, i, 79) are called &lquo;hempen home-spuns.&rquo; The &lquo;woolen statute cap,&rquo; by English
law worn by commoners whose income was under 20 marks, has perhaps influenced
this reference to coarse clad vassals or dependents. [All sumptuary laws were
repealed in the first year of King James I. (1603); six or seven years before the date
of composition of this present play.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>15, 16. <B>When one but . . . stood vp To speake</B>] <SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC>
(<I>Shakespeare</I>): When one of my rank did but stand up to speak, &amp;c. As we inter-
pret this sentence, the construction is transposed here; but the line so runs that
it will admit of three different interpretations: first, the one we have given; second,
when but a single man of my rank stands up, &amp;c.; third, when a man but of my
rank in the state stands up, &amp;c. &lquo;Ordinance&rquo; is here used in the sense of <I>order,
rank.</I> [This is the only passage wherein Shakespeare uses the word in just this
sense; elsewhere it means <I>established rule</I> or <I>divine dispensation,</I> as is shown by
<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) from several examples. In his edition of this play, which appeared
subsequently, Schmidt dissents at interpreting &lquo;ordinance&rquo; in the sense of <I>rank,</I> for
the very reason that it is not thus used elsewhere, and is disposed to accept the
alternative meaning given by Delius, <I>Authority, power,</I> paraphrasing thus: Except,
indeed, one who is not, as I am by my authority, ordained to speak of peace or
war. &lquo;We should notice,&rquo; adds Schmidt, &lquo;that Coriolanus speaks the words for
himself and drops the ordinarily accepted modesty.&rquo; <SC>Case</SC> notes that no other
instance of &lquo;ordinance&rquo; in the sense of <I>rank</I> appears to be known.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>18, 19. <B>Rather say . . . I am</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Sir Thomas Hanmer supplies the
defect in this line [l. 19] very judiciously, in my opinion, by reading: &lquo;<I>Truly</I>
the man I am.&rquo; <I>Truly</I> is properly opposed to &lquo;False&rquo; in the preceding line.&mdash;
<SC>Badham</SC> (<I>Text. of Sh.; Cambridge Essays,</I> p. 278): This defectiveness of the line
[18] would not appear, to many competent judges, a matter of suspicion. I will
freely confess that the line of eight syllables occurs so often in Shakespeare that
in any less corrupt text it would be ridiculous to retain the least misgiving about it;
but to my ear, at least, it sounds as unrhythmically abrupt as the dramatic Alex-
andrine is abrupt and yet rhythmical, or as the six-syllable line is well suited to an
harmonious pause; but in the passage before us, if there is any meaning, it is at
least very obscurely expressed; I venture, therefore, to propose an insertion: . . .
Rather say <I>you are glad</I> I play the man I am.
<P>20. <B>Oh sir, sir, sir</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes and Emendations,</I> etc., p. 357): The alter-
ation of the MS. Corrector is certainly the more proper.&mdash;<SC>T. Mommsen</SC> (<I>Der
Perkins Folio,</I> p. 181): Either reading is acceptable, yet <I>son</I> is more dignified.
&lquo;Sir&rquo; said to a child is, now at least, somewhat trivial.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Strictures,</I> etc.,
p. 156): Here the MS. Corrector's &lquo;improvement&rquo; entirely does away with one
of Shakespeare's touches of nature. In the reiterated &lquo;sir&rquo; Volumnia testifies
her displeasure at Coriolanus. [Dyce later, in his ed. ii, repeats the foregoing
objection to the change of the MS. Corrector; and records the fact that W. N.
Lettsom makes the same change.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 366): The
<I>son, son, son!</I> of Collier's Folio is much better. She never elsewhere says <I>Sir</I> to
him. [See <I>Appendix:</I> <SC>Collier's</SC> <I>Trilogy,</I> p. 595.]
<P>23. <B>Let go</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC> commends the alterations of Hanmer and Ritson as
proper to complete the metre, adding: &lquo;Too many of the short replies in this and
other plays of Shakespeare are apparently mutilated.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC>
(<I>Shakespeare</I>): Various alterations have been proposed to supply the two addi-
tional feet in the line, which metre-mongers suppose it to require, but which we
think Shakespeare's dramatic judgment and poetic taste caused him occasionally
and purposely to omit. &lquo;Let go&rquo; is an idiomatic use of the words (as the French
employ their phrase &lquo;<I>laissez donc</I>&rquo;) to express dissent from a last spoken opinion,
and to signify prohibition of further discussion.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The usual form
of this expression is &lquo;Let it go,&rquo; that is, let it pass, never mind. See <I>King John,</I>
III, iii, 33, &lquo;I had a thing to say, but let it go.&rquo;

<P>26. <B>The things</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: A few letters replaced, that by some carelessness
dropped out, restore us the poet's genuine reading, &lquo;The <I>thwartings</I> of,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC>:
A most certain correction.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: Mr Theobald only improved on Mr Rowe's
correction. [See <I>Text. Notes.</I>]&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC>: It would be difficult to find a better
word [than <I>thwartings</I>], considering either the sense or the probability that the
compositor misread the manuscript from which he printed.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>):
&lquo;The things,&rquo; that is, the Plebeians (compare II, ii, 117; III, i, 212; III, ii, 12).
They would have been less of your disposition, had you but shown yourself less
like yourself, and like the man you played, if, etc. This is intelligible, and yet
editors have conjectured about the passage, and almost unanimously adopted
Theobald's correction. The plural &lquo;dispositions&rquo; is favorable (if not quite con-
clusive) for the Folio reading, besides the fact that &lquo;them&rquo; and &lquo;they&rquo; according to
the new reading have no expressed connection. Furthermore, the tone of the speech,
which through the remark that the despised Plebeians, the things, could equally
extol their manhood, retains its pointed character.&mdash;[<SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Jahrbuch,</I> xv, 1880,
p. 52), in a review of Schmidt's edition of this play, singles out the foregoing note
for special notice. He refuses to accept the three passages cited by Schmidt as
proof that the word &lquo;things&rquo; is necessarily used by Shakespeare in a technical
sense for the Plebeians. These passages are: &lquo;a thing of blood,&rquo; where Cominius
thus speaks of Coriolanus; &lquo;hence rotten thing,&rquo; where Coriolanus thus addresses
Sicinius; and &lquo;woolen vassals, things created,&rquo; etc. In these two latter examples
Leo points out that &lquo;things&rquo; is not a contemptuous epithet, so much as a term
equivalent to <I>creature.</I> Leo, in fact, does not agree to any one of Schmidt's argu-
ments in favor of the intelligibility of the Folio reading. As this is, however,
but an interpretation of another's interpretation and not an elucidation of Shake-
speare's text I have refrained from a more detailed transcribing of Leo's remarks.
He concludes with a question for consideration as to whether with the word
<I>thwartings</I> the adjective &lquo;lesser&rquo; is not the more appropriate, while with &lquo;things&rquo;
<I>less</I> must be inserted as an emphatic adverb. An emendation which was also
proposed by an Anonymous commentator ap. Cam.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Per-
haps, having regard to what follows, we might read, &lquo;The things that cross.&rquo;
<P>26. <B>dispositions</B>] That is, <I>mood, caprice.</I> Compare <I>Lear,</I> I, iv, 242: &lquo;&mdash;put
away These dispositions that of late transform you.&rquo;
<P>27, 28. <B>them . . . they</B>] <SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): The intro-
duction of &lquo;them&rquo; here, which in strict grammatical construction refers to <I>thwart-
ings,</I> but which really and in Shakespearian construction refers to the Plebeians,
admirably serves to maintain the characteristic effect of the dialogue, both mother
and son alluding to the unmentioned but perfectly comprehended theme of their
wrathful antipathy by the same pronoun. See l. 2 above.

<P>28. <B>Ere they lack'd</B>] <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 371): Theobald, by substituting <I>thwartings</I>
for &lquo;things,&rquo; restored both significance and rhythm to l. 26; but, strange to say,
he took no notice of the equally obvious defect in this line, expressing a sense
exactly the reverse of that which the context requires. The genuine reading is
doubtless &lquo;<I>when</I> they lack'd,&rquo; etc. It is probable that <I>when</I> was first perverted
into <I>where,</I> and the latter, not suiting the sense, was abbreviated to &lquo;ere,&rquo; or shrank
perhaps to the same dimensions from being misheard.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>):
That is, before they lost the power, while they still had it in their power (by refusing
to assent to his nomination to the Consulship). With verbs signifying a negative
idea, <I>e. g.,</I> &lquo;lack,&rquo; &lquo;want,&rquo; there is often some ambiguity of expression due to the
general tendency to duplicate the negative. A striking instance is <I>Macbeth,</I>
III, vi, 8: &lquo;Who cannot want the thought? = Who <I>can want</I> (i. e., &lquo;lack&rquo;) the
thought?&rquo; [An interpretation more rational than Bailey's, since it does not
involve a change of the text.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>30. <B>Volum. I, and burne too</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.): The Cambridge Editors (<I>Globe
Shakespeare</I>) give this speech to &lquo;<I>A Patrician.</I>&rquo; I can only say that whoever re-
collects Mrs Siddons in this scene will, I am sure, allow that the words &lquo;<I>Ay, and
burn too</I>&rquo; seemed to come quite naturally from the lips of Volumnia as a sudden
spirt of contempt for that rabble whom, however, she saw the necessity of her son's
endeavoring to conciliate.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: In the Folios this speech is given to
Volumnia, but as it seems strange in the mouth of one who is counselling modera-
tion, the editors of the Globe edition gave it to &lquo;A Patrician.&rquo; Dyce says that no
one who had heard it spoken by Mrs Siddons could doubt its appropriateness, but
surely it ought to be &lquo;<I>Aside.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Page</SC>: Perhaps this is said sarcastically: Yes, but
what if they take to rioting and <I>burning.</I> Compare <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> III, ii, 208: &lquo;Re-
venge! About! Seek! Burn! Fire!&rquo; Though, of course, it may simply be expressive
of her hearty wish that they may be burned as well as hanged.&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC>
(<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): The Globe editors transfer this to &lquo;<I>A Patrician,</I>&rquo; but we may take
it as an outburst of Volumnia's inmost personal feeling, and hardly inconsistent
with the policy she is urging.&mdash;<SC>Herford</SC> (<I>Eversley Sh.</I>): The Folios give this
speech to Volumnia, but modern editors, arguing that she is advising patience,
take it from her. Yet her point of view is quite clear. She despises and hates
the plebeians as much as Coriolanus can, but she would choose her own time to
show her wrath. Compare ll. 37, 38, and 79-81. Compare also Menenius in
III, i, 322.&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Volumnia says this with a skill
peculiar to her creator, the Poet. She does not contrary her son by mollifying
him. She is as completely of his opinion as to unworthiness as he can be, she vir-
tually thus reminds him. She makes her point of policy the clearer and the more
effective with him by agreeing with him here. Menenius is not so wise and not
so effective as Volumnia. [Wright would make this an <I>Aside.</I>] This, of course,
would make it useless as a challenge of her son's attention to her on just the point
she raises and no other. The part Volumnia plays in this scene is all Shake-
speare's.&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: I think, with Aldis Wright, that this should be an Aside.&mdash;

<P><SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): It is clear that the strange feeling of scorn which the noble
Coriolanus nourished for the commons of Rome had been sucked in with his very
milk. In North's <I>Plutarch</I> we get nothing of this side of the character of Volumnia.
See also ll. 37 to 40 below, and what follows.
<P>34-36. <B>There's no remedy . . . and perish</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, there's no
help for it; it cannot be helped. Compare <I>Meas. for Meas.,</I> II, i, 295: &lquo;It grieves
me for the death of Claudio; But there's no remedy.&rquo; We should have &lquo;Lest&rquo;
[in place of &lquo;Unless&rquo;]. The construction is loose, and perhaps Shakespeare meant
to say: &lquo;Unless you would have our good city cleave in the midst,&rquo; &amp;c., or &lquo;Unless
our good city is to cleave,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: There's no way out of it; you must
eat humble pie, unless, by your not doing so, you are content that our city should
go to wrack and ruin. I owe this explanation to Mr W. J. Craig. [Case does
not, however, include this among Craig's notes on this play in the <I>Arden Shake-
speare.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>38. <B>I haue a heart as little apt as yours,</B> etc.] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes and Emenda-

<I>To brook control without the use of anger.</I>&rquo; The line in Italics is written in a blank
space, and a mark made to where it ought to come in. The compositor was,
doubtless, misled by the recurrence of the same words at the ends of the two lines,
and carelessly omitted the first. From whence, if not from some independent

the superfluous and tautologous line interpolated, &lquo;I have a heart as little <I>soft</I>

<SC>Staunton</SC>: Mr Collier's annotator here indulges in one of his most daring flights&mdash;
the intercalation of a whole line!&mdash;rendering the passage thus, &lquo;<I>To brook reproof
without the use of anger.</I>&rquo; This interpolation (which, by the way, has been corrupted
or corrected since its publication in Mr Collier's <I>Notes and Emendations,</I> and in
his Mono-volume Shakespeare, where it reads, &lquo;brook <I>control</I>&rquo;) we hold to be quite
superfluous, and, if even a <I>lacuna</I> were manifest, to be altogether inadmissible.
For admitting, which we are not guilty of, the antiquity claimed by Mr Collier for
the marginal annotations of his copy of the Second Folio, we agree with Mr R. G.
White (<I>Shakespeare's Scholar,</I> p. 76) that &lquo;the interpolation of an entire line by one
man in 1662 is as little justifiable as the entire interpolation of an entire scene by
another man in 1762 or 1853.&rquo; That there is a difficulty in the construction of the
speech as it stands in the ancient text nobody can deny. But it is surely one sus-
ceptible of a solution less perilous and arbitrary than the insertion of a new line.
Our own impression, long before the Perkins Folio came to light, was that the
transcriber or compositor had slightly erred in the words &lquo;as little,&rquo; and that the
poet probably wrote, <I>of mettle,</I> i. e., of temper, &amp;c.&mdash;&lquo;I have a heart <I>of mettle</I> apt
as yours,&rquo; which naturally enough led to &lquo;But yet a brain,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;[The reading
&lquo;reproof&rquo; instead of &lquo;control&rquo; in the interpolated line, to which Staunton calls atten-
tion, appears in the text of Collier's ed. ii.; it is, I think, due to inadvertence on
Collier's part, as it is not thus printed in his subsequent lists; and in the text of
his ed. iii, 1878, the error&mdash;if such it be&mdash;is corrected without remark. See also

as yours,&rquo; etc. Many instances of this use of the word <I>lightly</I> are to be found in
<I>Johnson Richardson</I> (R. of Brunne, Chaucer, Gower, Holland, Plinie), and

The &lquo;well said&rquo; of Menenius, who repeats the most important word &lquo;<I>stoop,</I>&rquo; apply-

used by Shakespeare in a sense appropriate here. [Had Kinnear but consulted
a Concordance or Schmidt's <I>Lexicon</I> he would, I am sure, have seen fit to modify
this last assertion. See following note.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Desdemona,
according to Iago (<I>Othello,</I> II, iii, 326), &lquo;is of so free, so kind, so <I>apt,</I> so blessed a
disposition, she holds it a vice in her goodness not to do more than she is requested.&rquo;
Volumnia has as little apt a disposition (heart) as Coriolanus. The use of <I>apt</I>
is essentially the same in both plays, and the context in <I>Coriolanus</I> makes its mean-
ing as plain within certain limits as if Volumnia had proceeded to define it ex-
tensively. We may take it as <I>impressible,</I> or <I>flexible</I> (&lquo;as little apt&rquo; = inflexible),
or <I>compliant,</I> or <I>docile,</I> or (with closer reference to the context demanded), <I>ready,
willing</I> (to return and mend a roughness, or eat humble pie). Shakespeare uses
the word many times for receptive, teachable, prone, either alone (<I>Hamlet,</I> I,
v, 31, &lquo;I find thee apt; And duller shouldst thou be,&rquo; etc.) or with extension (<I>Lear,</I>
II, iv, 309, &lquo;And what they incense him to, being apt To have his ear abused,&rquo; etc.).
No commentator has objected to the word in <I>Othello,</I> but the text has been
tampered with here. Mr Craig seems to have felt a difficulty in interpreting
&lquo;apt,&rquo; and believing that &lquo;anger,&rquo; l. 39, pointed to Staunton's <I>mettle,</I> intended to
suggest &lquo;<I>to</I> mettle apt as yours,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> as prone to anger as yours. [This last refers
to the notes prepared by W. J. Craig for the edition of this play in the <I>Arden Sh.,</I>
and left unfinished by his untimely death. Case undertook the task of arranging
and completing the work. It is noteworthy, I think, that up to the time of the
unnecessary interpolation by the MS. Corrector neither editors nor commentators
had been conscious of any corruption or difficulty in this passage. The meaning
of the word &lquo;apt&rquo; was perfectly understood apparently. It is not included in the
<I>Glossaries</I> of either Hanmer or Capell. Neither Collier nor Singer suggest a
change; but with the appearance of the MS. interpolation the whole pack is at
once in full cry. Singer is the one who, unconsciously perhaps, metaphorically
drew a herring across the trail and started them all on a false scent, hunting a
substitute for the word &lquo;apt,&rquo; a word which Shakespeare uses in many other places,
and which, as Case says, has not been elsewhere suspected. The latter's excellent
note is a fitting finish to the discussion.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>54. <B>But when extremities speake</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: Volumnia leaves her sentence
unfinished, the conclusion of which must be, You must accommodate yourself
accordingly. The editors place a period after &lquo;speak&rquo; and connect the sentence
with what has preceded it: Though therein you can never be too noble, except
when necessity prompts&mdash;which gives a very dull meaning to the passage.

<P>71. <B>Which your heart prompts you</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Perhaps the meaning is, which
your heart prompts you <I>to.</I> We have many such elliptical expressions in these
plays. So in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> &lquo;Thy honourable metal may be wrought From that it is
dispos'd [<I>to</I>],&rquo; I, ii, 313. But I rather believe that our author has adopted the
language of the theatre, and that the meaning is, which your heart suggests <I>to</I>
you; which your heart furnishes you with, as a prompter furnishes the player with
the words that have escaped his memory. So afterwards, &lquo;Come, come, we'll
prompt you.&rquo; The editor of the Second Folio, who was entirely unacquainted with
our author's peculiarities, reads, &lquo;prompts you <I>to,</I>&rquo; and so all the subsequent
copies read.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I am content to follow the Second Folio; though perhaps
we ought to read, &lquo;which your heart prompts <I>in</I> you.&rquo; So in <I>A Sermon Preached
at St. Paul's Crosse,</I> &amp;c., 1589, &lquo;&mdash;for often meditation prompteth in us goode
thoughtes, begettyng therein goode workes,&rquo; &amp;c. Without some additional
syllable the verse is defective.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC>: We can scarcely doubt that the earlier
part of this speech has suffered from the transcriber or the printer; with the
present text, whatever arrangement of the lines be adopted, the verse halts miser-
ably.&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>: The 2<SUP>nd</SUP> Folio has &lquo;prompts you <I>to,</I>&rquo; making &lquo;heart&rquo; much

<P>72. <B>but roated in your Tongue</B>] <SC>Boswell</SC>: Perhaps we should read <I>rooted.</I>
[<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> p. 161) makes the same conjecture, apparently as unaware as
Boswell that he had been therein anticipated [see <I>Text. Notes</I>], and later adopts
this reading in his text.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): Dyce proposes an emendation here,
which seems to show that he did not understand the drift of the passage: he wishes
&lquo;roted&rquo; to be printed <I>rooted,</I> but the words were to be said by <I>rote</I> by the tongue,
and not to be <I>rooted</I> in it. Besides, Dyce's proposal is not novel, since Boswell
formerly hinted at <I>rooted,</I> but did not venture to print it. [Naturally he did not;
he was printing Malone's text, not Shakespeare's.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Strictures on
Collier's Shakespeare,</I> p. 157): The whole of this passage is very obscure because
corrupted. As I cannot believe with Mr Collier that &lquo;words roted <SC>in</SC> your tongue&rquo;
could mean &lquo;words said by rote <SC>by</SC> the tongue,&rquo; I continue to think that here
&lquo;roated&rquo; should be &lquo;<I>rooted.</I>&rquo; (Richardson, in his <I>Dictionary,</I> quoting the passage
<I>sub</I> &lquo;Rote,&rquo; observes, &lquo;<I>Roated</I> in Shakespeare is, perhaps, rooted, fixed, infixed,
impressed,&mdash;no deeper than your tongue.&rquo;)&mdash;[In his ed. Dyce adds to this quota-
tion from Richardson, &lquo;That it is so I make no question.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden
Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): Out of the four passages where &lquo;rote&rquo; occurs in Shake-
speare's plays, the Folio twice spells it, as here, &lquo;roate.&rquo; We are thus particular
in stating this point, because Johnson and others change &lquo;roted&rquo; to <I>rooted</I> here.
&lquo;Such words that are but roted in your tongue&rquo; appears to us to mean &lquo;Such words
as are but retained by rote in your tongue&rquo;; mere words acquired by rote and held
ready for conventional utterance. Shakespeare uses the expression &lquo;by rote&rquo;
to convey the idea of &lquo;without real meaning,&rquo; as well as &lquo;by a routine process of
memory,&rquo; in the passage, &lquo;Oh she knows well Thy love did read by rote and could
not spell,&rquo; <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> II, iii, 88; and Bacon (in the <I>Essay on Atheism</I>) employs
it in this comprehensive sense when observing, &lquo;He rather saith it by rote himself,
as that he would have, than that he can thoroughly believe it, or be persuaded
of it.&rquo; We think that to throw out a word like &lquo;roted&rquo; merely because there has
been no instance of its use prior to Shakespeare's is to reject the advantage afforded
by having such a genius to create expressive words for the language.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC>
(<I>Arden Sh.</I>): <I>Rooted</I> gets rid of any difficulty about the preposition, and gives the
sense that the words suggested go no deeper than the tongue. Reading &lquo;roted&rquo;
we must interpret memorized, learnt by rote, and (recollecting also the freer use
of prepositions in Shakespeare's time) explain &lquo;in&rquo; as due to preoccupation with
place, the thought of words which are in or on the tongue with nothing to prompt
them in the heart. <I>Roat</I> is used = to repeat or sing (Skeat and Mayhew's
<I>Tudor and Stuart Glossary</I>) by Drayton, e. g., <I>The Muses Elizium,</I> Nymphal vi.
(<I>Melanthus,</I> 8):
<BQ>
&lquo;I to my Bottle straight, and soundly baste my Throat<LB>
Which done, some Country Song or Roundelay I roate<LB>
So merrily.&rquo;<LB>

at least have examined other works on the same subject.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>no allowance, <I>i. e.,</I> approbation to your bosom's truth,&rquo; appeared to me unintelli-
gible. But &lquo;allowance&rquo; has no connection with the subsequent words, &lquo;to your
bosom's truth. The construction is, though but bastards to your bosom's truth,
<I>not the lawful issue of your heart.</I> The words, &lquo;and syllables of no allowance,&rquo; are
put in opposition with &lquo;bastards,&rquo; and are, as it were, parenthetical.&mdash;<SC>Mason</SC> (<I>Com-
ments,</I> etc., p. 255): The word <I>alliance</I> differs so little from &lquo;allowance,&rquo; it makes
the meaning of the sentence so clear, and corresponds so well with the word &lquo;bas-
tards,&rquo; in the line preceding, that I should not hesitate in adopting this amendment
of Johnson's. Steevens very roundly asserts that &lquo;allowance&rquo; is the right reading,
but he offers nothing in support of that assertion except a line from <I>Othello,</I> which
is nothing to the purpose. &lquo;A pilot of very expert and approved allowance&rquo; means
only a <I>pilot,</I> acknowledged and approved to be an expert one; and I don't see how
the word &lquo;allowance,&rquo; in this sense, will apply to the present passage. There can
be no doubt that &lquo;allowance&rquo; was used in Shakespeare's time in the sense of <I>ap-
probation.</I> So Lear says, &lquo;O Heavens! If you do love old men, if your sweet sway
Allow obedience,&rquo; [II, iv, 194]. And Johnson, I believe, is right in asserting that it
means legal right, established rank, or settled authority; but none of these words
would make sense of the present passage if substituted in the place of &lquo;allowance&rquo;
unless we alter it by reading &lquo;<I>from</I> your bosom's truth&rquo; instead of <I>to;</I> and if the
passage is to be amended, the most natural amendment is to read <I>alliance.</I>&mdash;
<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Though they (the syllables) are not acknowledged as the legit-
imate issue or genuine expression of your inmost thoughts. For &lquo;allowance&rquo;
in the sense of <I>acknowledgment, recognition,</I> which keeps up the figure suggested
by &lquo;bastards,&rquo; compare <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> II, iii, 146, &lquo;A stirring dwarf we do allow-
ance give Before a sleeping giant.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): &lquo;Allowance&rquo; is here used
in the old sense to <I>allow,</I> that is, to <I>justify</I> or <I>approve,</I> as in <I>Psalm</I> xi. of the Psalter,
&lquo;The Lord alloweth the righteous.&rquo; Also in many other places of the English
Bible. Shakespeare has &lquo;allowance&rquo; repeatedly in the same sense; as in <I>Lear,</I>
I, iv, 228, &lquo;that You protect this course and put it on By your allowance.&rquo; The
best explanation of the passage in the text that I have met with is furnished me
by Mr Joseph Crosby: &lquo;Truth sits enthroned on your bosom, to sanction your
thoughts and language; but in the present case your words will be but illegitimate
offspring, not born of your heart, having no approval or justification from that
truth, but merely roted in your <I>tongue</I>&mdash;spoken, as a parrot or child talks, <I>by
rote.</I>&rquo; A verse from <I>Psalm</I> cxxxix. is not irrelevant here, &lquo;There is not a <I>word
in my tongue,</I> but Thou, O Lord, knowest it altogether.&rquo; I was once led to favour
<I>alliance,</I> but am now thoroughly satisfied that &lquo;allowance&rquo; is right.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC>
(<I>Student's Sh.</I>): That is, utterly disavowed by the real feelings in your heart.&mdash;
<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): Not allowed as true in your secret heart.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC>
(<I>Arden Sh.</I>): That is, of no acceptance to your heart's truth, <I>i. e.,</I> to your real
feelings. &lquo;Allowance&rquo; is used with various shades of meaning by Shakespeare,
such as acknowledgment, approbation, etc., but <I>acceptance</I> (as in <I>Isaiah,</I> lx, 7,
&lquo;they shall come up with acceptance on mine altar&rquo;) best accounts for the use
of the preposition &lquo;to,&rquo; in which a difficulty is sometimes found.

<P>81. <B>in Honor</B>] <SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): The interpretation occasionally found (&lquo;as far as

obvious one. It could hardly have been suggested if the text had read, &lquo;I should in
honour do so,&rquo; and Volumnia has already said that dissembling does not dishonour.
<P>81, 82. <B>I am in this Your Wife . . . the Nobles</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Volumnia is
persuading Coriolanus that he ought to flatter the people, as the general fortune
was at stake; and says, that in this advice, she speaks as his wife, as his son; as
the senate and body of the patricians, who were in some measure link'd to his
conduct.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I rather think the meaning is, &lquo;I am in their <I>condition,</I> I
am at stake, <I>together with</I> your wife, your son.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc., p.
256): &lquo;I am in this&rquo; means I am in this predicament.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I think the
meaning is, In this <I>advice,</I> in exhorting you to act thus, I speak not only as your
mother, but as your wife, your son, &amp;c., all of whom are <I>at stake.</I>&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>:
I am involved in this, I am of those whose lives and fortunes are at stake.&mdash;
<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): Some explain, &lquo;I speak for&rquo;; but the point is
rather, &lquo;I am at stake in this; so are your wife and the rest, for we are in danger
of losing you.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Probably everyone at first reading under-
stands as Malone, for it is natural to read putting stress on &lquo;<I>this.</I>&rquo; But if &lquo;<I>I</I>
is stressed Johnson's interpretation, and of a successive naming of the friends at

may (as an alternative to the &lquo;pause-accent&rquo;) be regarded as quasi-trisyllabic.

<P>96, 97. <B>wauing thy head, Which . . . thy stout heart</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: But do
any of the ancient or modern masters of elocution prescribe the &lquo;waving the head&rquo;
when they treat of action? Or how does the waving the head correct the stout-
ness of the heart, or evidence humility? Or, lastly, where is the sense or grammar
of these words, &lquo;Which often thus,&rquo; &amp;c.? These questions are sufficient to show that
the lines are corrupt. I would read, therefore, &lquo;&mdash;waving thy <I>hand,</I> Which <I>soften</I>
thus, correcting thy stout heart.&rquo; This is a very proper precept of action suiting
the occasion: Wave thy hand, says she, and soften the action of it thus&mdash;then strike
upon thy breast, and by that action show the people thou hast corrected thy stout
heart. All here is fine and proper.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: The correction is ingenious, yet
I think it not right. <I>Head</I> or <I>hand</I> is indifferent. The <I>hand</I> is <I>waved</I> to gain
attention; the head is shaken in token of sorrow. The word <I>wave</I> suits better to
the hand, but in considering the author's language too much stress must not be
laid on propriety, against the copies. I would read thus, &lquo;&mdash;waving thy head
<I>With</I> often, thus, correcting thy stout heart.&rquo; That is, <I>shaking thy head,</I> and <I>striking</I>
thy breast. The alteration is slight, and the gesture recommended not improper.&mdash;
<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 92): This most admirable speech has been misinterpreted,
mangl'd, and (by dint of false pointing) render'd scarcely intelligible; the only

from being written contractedly, for that very word [<I>And</I>] which has now taken

<SC>Malone</SC>: I am persuaded these lines are printed exactly as the author wrote them,

&lquo;&mdash;&mdash; This your son-in-law<LB REND=RIGHT>
And son unto the king, (whom heavens directing),<LB>
Is troth-plight to your daughter,&rquo; [V, iii, 151].<LB>

<P>Again in <I>King John:</I>
<BQ>
&lquo;Who having no external thing to lose<LB>
But the word maid,&mdash;cheats the poor maid of that,&rquo;<LB>

<P>[II, i, 571]. In the former of these passages, &lquo;whom heavens directing,&rquo; is to be
understood as if Shakespeare had written, <I>him</I> heavens directing (<I>illum deo ducente</I>);
and in the latter, &lquo;<I>who</I> having,&rquo; has the import of <I>They</I> having. <I>Nihil quod amittere
possint, praeter nomen virginis, possidentibus.</I> This mode of speech, though not
such as we should now use, having been used by Shakespeare, any emendation of
this contested passage becomes unnecessary. Mason says that there is no verb
in the sentence, and therefore it must be corrupt. The verb is <I>go,</I> and the sentence
not more abrupt than many in these plays. Go to the people, says Volumnia,
and appear before them in a supplicating attitude,&mdash;with thy bonnet in thy hand,
thy knees on the ground (for in such cases action is eloquence, &amp;c.), waving thy
head; <I>it,</I> by its frequent bendings (such as those that I now make), subduing thy
stout heart, which now should be as humble as the ripest mulberry; or, if these
silent gestures of supplication do not move them, add words, and say to them, &amp;c.
Whoever has seen a player supplicating to be heard by the audience when a tumult,
for whatever cause, has arisen in a theatre will perfectly feel the force of the
words &lquo;waving thy head.&rquo; No emendation whatever appears to me to be neces-
sary in these lines.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: All I shall observe respecting the validity of the
instances adduced by Mr Malone in support of his position is that as ancient
press-work seldom received any correction, the errors of one printer may frequently
serve to countenance those of another without affording any legitimate decision
in matters of phraseology.&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: This passage has been a stumbling-block
to the commentators; and they want to know how the waving of the head corrects
the stout heart. They have forgotten the maxim which Volumnia has just
uttered, &lquo;Action is eloquence.&rquo; She is explaining her meaning by her action:
waving thy head, which often wave&mdash;thus&mdash;(and she then waves her head several
times). She adds, &lquo;correcting thy stout heart,&rquo; be &lquo;humble as the ripest mulberry.&rquo;
We owe this interpretation to a pamphlet printed at Edinburgh in 1814: &lquo;Ex-
planations and Emendations of Some Passages in the Text of Shakespeare,&rquo; [by
R. Morehead, who wrote under the pseudonym <I>Martinus Scriblerus.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>].&mdash;

from the former to the latter syllable of the word &lquo;bussing,&rquo; and so make the

<P>It is to be remarked that, except in the parenthesis [l. 93], the sense and con-
struction of the sentence are kept suspended by participles until the word &lquo;say,&rquo;
which renders our removal of the phrase &lquo;here be with them&rquo; still more probable;
perhaps Shakespeare had written &lquo;here bends,&rquo; describing the action of Volumnia.
<I>Vailing</I> is to be understood as in the passage &lquo;Then vail your impotence,&rquo; where
all the editions we have seen absurdly retain &lquo;ignorance.&rquo; Nothing can be more
easy or simple than the transposition of the initial words, &lquo;Now humble&rquo; and
&lquo;Which often.&rquo; In the introduction of the letter <I>s</I> we find that Warburton has
anticipated us, but, as he did not see the necessity of the transposition, his emenda-
tion is worse than useless, as it makes Volumnia recommend her son to soften his
head, or perhaps his hand (for that is another reading), instead of his heart.&mdash;
<SC>R. G. White</SC>: &lquo;Which, often,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> which <I>do</I> often; by this repeated act of courtesy
correcting thy stout heart. The difficulty seems to have resulted from a failure
to perceive the elision in &lquo;which often,&rquo; and that &lquo;thus&rquo; belongs to &lquo;correcting.&rquo;
The whole passage is difficult.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. i.): That is, &lquo;which often <I>do</I>&mdash;thus&mdash;
correcting thy stout heart.&rquo; Of course at the word <I>thus</I> she waves her head several
times, acting out the verb while omitting it in her speech, and so making a practical
illustration of what she would have him do. Commentators have stumbled much
at the passage from not knowing what to do with &lquo;which.&rquo; All becomes clear
enough when we thus make &lquo;which&rquo; to be governed not by the verbal sign of the
action, but by the action itself.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 367) proposes and adopts
in his text, &lquo;Often thus; which correcting thy stout heart,&rquo; and the omission of
&lquo;or,&rquo; l. 99, remarking: &lquo;By these slight corrections this place gains sense&mdash;a thing
it never had before. All through the speech, it may be observed, Volumnia acts
the part she would have her son perform. The transposition he had made in the
first line&mdash;where the folio has &ldquo;Which often thus,&rdquo;&mdash;having perplexed the printer,
he took &ldquo;humble&rdquo; for a verb, and so introduced &ldquo;or&rdquo; to try to make sense.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The two lines describe two different gestures&mdash;one indicated by

heart. Having curbed his pride he is to lower his head to the people in token of

construction, &lquo;Which&rquo; is used loosely, as the relative often is in Shakespeare,
and is either redundant or equivalent to the personal pronoun. Compare V,

<P>The folio has &ldquo;waving thy head,&rdquo; but Ophelia, [<I>Hamlet,</I> II, i, 93], considered the

print; <I>so</I> naturally follows, &ldquo;And thus far having stretch'd it, &amp;c.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC>
(p. 301): When expositors make such a fluster about the government of the
relative &lquo;which,&rquo; are they oblivious of the verb &lquo;<I>do</I>&rquo; and of its occasional ellipse,
specially in conversation, supplemented by gesticulation? I can only suppose that
they shrink from this explanation because of the simplicity of it; but the simplicity
of an explanation, if common sense go along with it, should recommend it rather
than otherwise.

the forces of these leaders mercilessly to the sword after having persuaded them
to lay down their arms upon terms, and a full pardon, secured by his princely
honor&mdash;a like perfidy to that perpetrated against the forces of Jack Cade and Wat
Tyler (also with the approbation of the poet) after they had been induced to dis-
band on the most solemn promises of amnesty from the king.

<P>123. <B>vnbarb'd Sconce</B>] <SC>Hawkins</SC>: &lquo;Unbarbed&rquo; is <I>bare,</I> uncovered. In the
times of chivalry, when a horse was fully armed and accoutred for the encounter,
he was said to be <I>barbed;</I> probably from the old word <I>barbe</I> which Chaucer uses for
a veil or covering.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The suppliants of the people used to present them-
selves to them in sordid and neglected dresses. &lquo;Unbarbed sconce&rquo; is <I>untrimmed</I>
or <I>unshaven head.</I> To <I>barb</I> a man was to shave him. [True to form, Steevens
follows up this interpretation with an apt quotation from <I>Promos and Cassandra,</I>
1578, wherein &lquo;barbe&rquo; is used in this sense. He also remarks that &lquo;to <I>barbe</I> the
field was to cut the corn,&rquo; giving as an example of this, &lquo;The labring hunter tufts
the thick unbarbed grounds,&rquo; Drayton, <I>Polyolbion,</I> Song xiii. Steevens quotes
an objection by Dean Milles' in his comment on the Pseudo-Rowley, p. 215, &lquo;But
would that appearance have been particular at Rome in the time of Coriolanus?&rquo;
The Puck of Commentators was for once caught napping; he answered that
&lquo;Every one but the Dean understands that Shakespeare gives to all countries the
fashions of his own,&rquo; apparently forgetting that he had begun his note with the
remark that this custom was peculiar to Rome. He concludes his note with a
grudging admission that the signification given by Hawkins may be, perhaps,
correct. All of which seems to justify the comment of W. A. Wright that &lquo;it is
doubtful whether Steevens is serious in this interpretation&rquo; of &lquo;unbarbed&rquo; as
<I>untrimmed.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;Professor <SC>T. S. Baynes</SC>, in an article in the Edinburgh Review
for October, 1872 (p. 369), gives so clear an exposition of the matter in dispute as
between these two interpretations that I gratefully avail myself of his remarks:
&lquo;Curiously enough, of the two explanations [of unbarbed], that by Hawkins, the
more correct, has been almost unanimously rejected by modern editors and critics.
Thus Mr Dyce explains unbarbed, &ldquo;unshorn, untrimmed,&rdquo; [<I>Glossary, s. v.</I>]; the
Cambridge Editors give the same meaning in the Globe Edition; while Todd in his
edition of Johnson, Richardson in his Dictionary, and Nares in his Glossary give
&ldquo;unbarbed&rdquo; as unshorn, each quoting this passage in <I>Coriolanus</I> as the example.
Mr Staunton, it is true, adopts Hawkins' more correct interpretation, but he does this
without a word of explanation or defence. Now, with an erroneous rendering in
almost undisputed possession of the ground, this is hardly sufficient. It is neces-
sary to indicate at least the reasons that make the one interpretation right, and
the other wrong. It may be stated at the outset that the words &ldquo;barbed&rdquo; and
</CC>
<PB N=363>
<HE><SC>act iii, sc.</SC> ii.] <I>CORIOLANUS</I> 363</HE>
<FHL>
<CC>
<C>[123. <B>vnbarb'd Sconce</B>]</C>
<P>&ldquo;unbarbed&rdquo; are used both literally and figuratively for shaven and unshorn.
But in this speech of Coriolanus the term cannot be interpreted in this sense, as
it would then have no real meauing or relevancy at all. So far as mere personal
appearance is concerned, Coriolanus had just presented himself in the most public
and official manner, both in the Capitol and the Forum before the senate and the
citizens, with the confidence of a proud nature, and the indifference to mere
pouncet-boxes and curling-irons proper to a soldier and a hero. There could
thus be no possible reason against his returning, on the ground of mere personal
appearance. If he really were somewhat rough and unkempt, he would surely,
under the circumstances, be the better pleased. Least of all would he think of
calling in the barber before presenting himself to the greasy multitude. The speech
obviously refers not to mere personal appearance, but to the accredited signs of
deference, humility, and respect. One of these&mdash;and that the most eloquently
submissive&mdash;was uncovering, standing bareheaded, and bowing in a lowly manner
to the assembled citizens. This the proud spirit of Coriolanus could not stomach,
and he had the greatest difficulty in forcing his stubborn will into even momentary
and simulated acquiescence. This was the bitterest element in the partial and
mocking ceremony he had just gone through. When urged by his friends to speak
to the citizens and ask their suffrages, according to established usage, he replies,
<BQ>
&ldquo;I cannot<LB REND=RIGHT>
Put on the gown, stand naked, and entreat them.&rdquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>Here &ldquo;stand naked&rdquo; cannot, of course, be taken literally, though it might be sup-
posed to refer indirectly to showing his wounds. This, however, Coriolanus did
not do, and the phrase must be understood as referring primarily to the fact that
he was obliged to stand uncovered, bare-headed, before the &ldquo;bisson multitude.&rdquo;
But his gall so rises at the degradation, that while going through the form he cannot
help flouting the citizens to their face, &ldquo;since the wisdom of their choice is rather
<I>to have my hat</I> than my heart, I will practise the insinuating nod.&rdquo; Again, Volumnia,
well knowing what the chief difficulty was, addresses herself most earnestly to this
point, detailing to her son in eager gestures the submissive actions by which he
must at once seek to regain the popular favour. In her excited and intensely
dramatic address [ll. 91-105] we see Volumnia pointing to her son's bonnet, and
showing by her own action the way in which he should use it in addressing the
citizens. At last, in reply to the reiterated and united entreaties of mother and
friends, Coriolanus impatiently exclaims, &ldquo;Must I go show them my unbarb'd
sconce?&rdquo; It may be easily shown that &ldquo;unbarbed&rdquo; has the meaning which the
context thus requires. A war-horse protected by head- and chest-pieces of de-
fensive armour was technically said to be <I>barbed, barded,</I> or <I>bard,</I> these being all
different forms of the same word derived from the French <I>bard&eacute;,</I> which Cotgrave
renders, &ldquo;barbed or trapped as a great horse.&rdquo; . . . To show an unbarbed sconce
is thus to show an uncovered, unprotected sconce; in other words, to appear bare-
headed. That the word in this connection cannot possibly refer to shaving is
evident from the fact that <I>sconce</I> means head, and is never applied to the face by
Shakespeare or his contemporaries.&rquo; [This article appears also in Baynes's
volume, <I>Shakespeare Studies, and Other Essays,</I> p. 301. Since this exposition by
Baynes modern editors uniformly adopt this explanation of the word &lquo;unbarbed&rquo;;
Steevens's explanation, though frequently mentioned, has been discarded.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>123. <B>Sconce</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: &lquo;Sconce&rquo; is a half-comic word for <I>head,</I> used with
intentional contempt by Coriolanus. See Cotgrave: &lquo;<I>Teste:</I> f. A head, pate,
skonce, nole, costard, noddle. [The original meaning of &lquo;sconce&rquo; is a <I>small fort</I>
or <I>bulwark,</I> thence applied to a helmet, and thus to the head itself.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>124, 125. <B>Must I . . . that it must beare</B>] <SC>F. C. Sharp</SC> (p. 70): In the entire range
of Shakespeare's plays there is but a single record of a genuine conflict between
the impulse to speak the truth, at whatever cost, and the desire to dissemble for
what, apart from the deception, would be recognised as a worthy purpose. Corio-
lanus, having ruined his cause with the people by his plainness of speech, is urged
by his friends to return to the Forum and disown his insulting epithets. At
first he cannot bring himself to consent. But the ground of his refusal is no more
an objection to deceit as such than it is a regard for social veracity. It is solely
the aversion of the proud patrician to the humiliation of bending his uncovered
head before the despised mob, of admitting to himself and to them that he dare
not say what he pleases. His mother understands him perfectly. Determined
that he shall yield, her last move is to appeal to his love for her, the appeal that
had never failed. Coriolanus has within him the spirit of the Spartan prisoners
who, rather than bear the name of slaves, took their lives. Like the medi&aelig;val
knight, the lie was disgraceful in his eyes primarily, if not solely, because the sign
of a cowardly spirit.
<P>126. <B>this single Plot</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, piece, portion; applied to a piece
of earth, and here elegantly transferred to the body, carcase.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: Coriolanus
means the spot of ground upon which he is directly standing, and from that proceeds
to the consideration of his own body. &lquo;They to dust should grind it&rquo; refers to
&lquo;this mould&rquo; alone.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): By &lquo;this single plot&rquo; Coriolanus
certainly does not mean the spot of ground upon which he is standing, but rather
his own person. This same mode of expression appears in the <I>Sonnets:</I> &lquo;Why
should my heart think that a several plot? Which my heart knows the wide
world's common place,&rquo; [<I>Sonnet</I> cxxxvii, l. 9]. The elucidating apposition in the
next line&mdash;&lquo;this mould of Marcius&rquo;&mdash;precludes any other interpretation.&mdash;<SC>W. A.
Wright</SC>: Coriolanus speaks of his own person, not of the ground upon which he
stands, as Delius interprets. The words which follow, &lquo;This mould of Marcius,&rquo;
make this clear.

one and the same thing; and mean no more than the flesh and substance of Marcius's

<P>129, 130. <B>You haue put me . . . toth' Life</B>] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>):
As Coriolanus's fate becomes too much for him, our sympathies swing to his side,
and his position, at least when he is not angry, becomes charged with pathos.&mdash;
<SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 603): He was justified in objecting to methods of dissimulation
and flattery, but, if only he had been reasonable, a middle would not have been
hard to find which should safeguard his self-respect while pacifying the populace.
It is because his self-respect is of passion, not of reason, that he is so unconciliatory,
and therefore almost as culpable as if he were guilty of the opposite fault. Plutarch,
indeed, thinks he is more so. In his comparison between him and Alcibiades he
is in this matter more lenient to the latter. [See note by MacCallum, II, ii, 22-24,
where the passage from the comparison is given.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>129. <B>such a part, which neuer</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: So in <I>3 Henry VI:</I> II, vi, 66, &lquo;&mdash;he
would avoid such bitter taunts Which in the time of death he gave our father.&rquo;
Again, above, ll. 71, 72; also V, iii, 8; also, V, iii, 155. This phraseology was intro-
duced by Shakespeare in the first of these passages, for the old play on which
<I>3 Henry VI.</I> was founded reads, &lquo;<I>As</I> in the time of death,&rquo; &amp;c. The word <I>as</I>
has been substituted for &lquo;which&rquo; by the modern editors in the passage before us.&mdash;
[The words, &lquo;the passage before us,&rquo; seem to refer to this passage in <I>Coriolanus,</I>
but Malone means that from <I>3 Henry VI,</I> where, as a matter of fact, the Folio
reads, &lquo;Which,&rquo; and Pope, following the older play, reads <I>As,</I> thus also the editors
down to Malone, who restores the Folio reading. This ambiguous wording misled
the meticulous Cambridge Edd., who, in their <I>Note VIII,</I> give this last sentence of
Malone's note alone, adding: &lquo;We have been unable to find it [the reading <I>as</I> for
<I>which</I> in this line in <I>Coriolanus</I>] in Rowe, Pope, Theobald, Hanmer, Warburton,
Johnson, Capell, or Steevens. It is probably a printer's emendation in some of
the numerous reprints of the play.&rquo; Their own <I>Text. Notes</I> on the passage in
<I>3 Henry VI.</I> would have settled the point in question.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>130. <B>discharge</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, <I>perform;</I> a technical word for playing

either your straw-coloured beard,&rquo; &amp;c. And IV, ii, 8, &lquo;You have not a man in
all Athens able to discharge Pyramus but he.&rquo;

<P>141. <B>That Babies lull a-sleepe</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The folios read, and Shake-

<I>Hamlet,</I> I, ii, 38, &lquo;More than the scope Of these deleted articles allow.&rquo; Again,
<I>Love's Labour's Lost,</I> IV, iii, 345, &lquo;And when Love speaks, the voice of all the gods

was plural, but this is unnecessary.&mdash;[In assigning this supposition to Walker

the supposition that &lquo;voice&rquo; is here the plural, giving, as his authorisation for this,
Walker's <I>Versification,</I> art. LI, where is recorded a number of examples wherein
nouns ending in <I>s, ss, ce,</I> etc., take a plural verb; but neither Walker nor
Lettsom quote the present line as such. In any case the supposition is Lettsom's,
not Walker's.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;Miss C. <SC>Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): An inversion made

<P>&lquo;it is my more dishonor,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>, accepting Johnson's interpretation
as correct, remarks on Schmidt's, &lquo;But Volumnia is quite sincere in her desire
to induce Coriolanus to yield to the people, and such an argument [as Schmidt's]
would be a strange one to employ for the purpose.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Thiergen</SC> (p. 206): Schmidt's
taking of &lquo;fear&rquo; as the imperative seems to me quite impossible by reason of the
construction of the passage.&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC> (p. 302): Let it be observed that almost
in the same breath that Volumnia avows a feeling of pride of some sort, <I>she dis-
avows the pride which stiffened Coriolanus</I> (l. 157), as not derived from her, nor
appertaining to her, <I>but of his own begetting.</I> And secondly, it is evident that
Coriolanus felt that his mother had <I>chidden him,</I> and had not come round to his
view of her own free will, but rather because she felt that she could not do other-
wise. Her surrender to her son, then, was not a cheerful and spontaneous, but a
half-hearted and compulsory one. Thus much generally; and now to come to
particulars: in what terms does Volumnia describe her own feelings? Certainly
not as one who <I>feared</I> the consequences; for (to use her own words) she mocked at
death with as big a heart as Coriolanus did. How then? As one who felt pride,
but not exactly the pride which Coriolanus felt; but a rational pride akin to what
we sometimes call self-respect&mdash;a feeling that she had gone as far in entreating her
son as a mother, or at least as Coriolanus' mother, should. <I>He</I> would be too proud
to be continually suing, and continually denied; well then&mdash;<I>that</I> pride of his she
too felt; she let it be as he willed; she passively permitted it, albeit it was contrary
to her wish, her counsel, her best and highest judgment. I can almost fancy that
Shakespeare had in his mind here that famous chapter in Israelitish history, when
Jehovah, finding his people were determined to have a visible and temporal king
like all the nations around them, let them have their will; allowing it rather than
approving of it, conceding what was, in reality, repugnant to his commands and
his counsel.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>) quotes Johnson's interpretation and adds.
&lquo;Better, she means apparently, <I>experience</I> the worst <I>in one's own person</I> than live
in constant <I>fear</I> of what the future may bring <I>to you and to us.</I> To know, even to
suffer, the worst is a relief, compared with constant anticipations of evil.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Deighton</SC>: If, though your mother, I must bow to your pride, that is a thing which
I can bear; to fear the dangers it may bring upon us is, to one of my nature, an
impossibility.&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): Volumnia gives up her cause,
and resigns herself to the sympathy with Coriolanus's pride, which has throughout
been competing with her alarm at his obstinacy.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC>, on the foregoing note,
says: &lquo;But his pride is just what she cannot sympathise with, and disowns in
him&mdash;&ldquo;owe thy pride thyself.&rdquo; Johnson's interpretation, though accepted by
recent editors, assumes too much, and practically identifies &ldquo;pride&rdquo; with &ldquo;stout-
ness,&rdquo; which more nearly corresponds with &ldquo;valiantness.&rdquo; The fact seems to
be that Volumnia, in her resentment, exhorts herself, not Coriolanus, saying in
effect, &ldquo;now let the sense of thy pride rather concern thy mother than fear of danger
of thy valiant obstinacy.&rdquo;&rquo;

<P>1. <B>Sicinius and Brutus</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): The Tribunes are here seen at
their worst: frankly treating the people as mere tools, exploiting the advantage which
Coriolanus's passionate temperament gives them over him, and showing themselves
with the self-importance of the demagogue in office (&lquo;us&rquo; . . . &lquo;we&rquo; . . . &lquo;our&rquo;).
<P>2-6. <B>In this point . . . ne're distributed</B>] <SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 511): The accusa-
tions brought against Coriolanus in Shakespeare are substantially just. He
may not seek to wind himself into a power tyrannical if we take <I>tyrant,</I> as Plutarch
certainly did but as Shakespeare probably did not, in the strict classical sense of
<I>tyrannus,</I> but with his disregard of aged custom and his avowed opinions of the
people, there can be no doubt that he would have wielded the consular powers
tyrannically, in the ordinary acceptation of the word. For there can be as little
doubt about his ill-will to the masses and his abhorrence of the tribunitian system.
And it is on these that he is condemned. It is very noticeable that the division
of the Antiate spoil, which in Plutarch is the most decisive and unwarrantable
allegation against him, is mentioned by Shakespeare only in advance as a sub-
ordinate point that may be brought forward, but, as a matter of fact, it is never
urged. Shakespeare makes no further use of a circumstance to which Plutarch
attaches so great importance that he dwells on it twice over and gives it the prom-
inent place in the narrative of the trial. This piece of sharp practice becomes quite
negligible in the play, and the only chicanery of which the tribunes are guilty in
the whole transaction is that, as in the <I>Life,</I> but more explicitly, they goad Corio-
lanus to a fit of rage in which he avows his real sentiments&mdash;a tactical expedient
that many politicians would consider perfectly permissible. Shakespeare, as has
often been pointed out, in some ways shows even less appreciation than Plutarch of
the merits of the people; so it is all the more significant that, at the crisis of the
play, he softens down and obliterates the worst traits in their proceedings against
their enemy. And the second thing we observe is that by all this Shakespeare
emphasises the insolence and truculence of the hero. It is Coriolanus's pride that
turns his candidature, which begins under the happiest auspices, to a snare. It is
still his pride that plays into the Tribunes' hands and makes him repeat in mere
defiance his offensive speech. It is again his pride, not any calumny about his
misapplying the profits of his raid, that gives the signal for the adverse sentence.
Just as in this respect the plebs is represented as, on the whole, less ignoble than
Plutarch makes it, so Coriolanus's conduct is portrayed as more insensate. And
this two-fold tendency, to palliate the guilt of Rome and to stress the violence
that provoked it, appears in the more conspicuous of Shakespeare's subsequent
deviations from his authority. [Both Verity and Gordon call attention to the
unfairness in bringing forward this question of the spoils of the Antiates.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>be of greater force (<I>because their voyces were numbered by the polle</I>) then the noble
honest citizens whose persons and purse did dutifully serue the common wealth
in their warres' (p. 231). The sentence &lquo;because . . . polle&rquo; is not in the Greek,
and it is not a correct explanation of the Tribunes' preference for voting by tribes.
In the case of both <I>centuries</I> and <I>tribes</I> voting was by poll, till the vote of a century
or tribe was arrived at, and then the vote of century or tribe was given as a single
one. Without going into questions of Roman constitutional history, it will be
sufficient to say that in the assembly by centuries (<I>comitia centuriata</I>) the pre-
ponderance was given to property. It is more important to notice how carefully
Shakespeare follows North, taking from him any details which may give life to
the narrative.&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>) likewise notes that the sentence
in regard to voting by the poll is an addition of the translator from the Greek.
He gives substantially the same explanation of the methods of voting by tribes
and by centuries as that by Beeching, and concludes his note thus: &lquo;Probably
Shakespeare has not quite understood the point, even if North did.&rquo; [The paren-
thetical explanation is perhaps due to Amyot and not North, who translated the
French of Amyot, not the original Greek. Langhorne's translation of this incident
is: &lquo;But the first thing they did, after the people were assembled, was to compel
them to give their voices by tribes, and not by centuries; thus contriving that the
meanest and most seditious part of the populace, and those who had no regard
to justice or honour, might out-vote such as had borne arms, or were of some for-
tune and character.&rquo; A foot-note adds: &lquo;From the reign of Servius Tullius the
voices had been always gathered by centuries. The Consuls were for keeping
up the ancient custom, being well apprised, that they could save Coriolanus if
the voices were reckoned by centuries, of which the knights and the wealthiest
of the citizens made up the majority, being pretty sure of ninety-eight out of a
hundred and seventy-three. But the artful tribunes, alleging that, in an affair
relating to the rights of the people, every citizen's vote ought to have its due
weight, they would not by any means consent to let the voices be collected other-
wise than by tribes.&rquo; (vol. ii, p. 190)&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>34, 35. <B>to haue his worth Of contradiction</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: The sense here
falls miserably. <I>He hath been used,</I> says the speaker, <I>ever to conquer</I>&mdash;And what

Off contradiction.</I>&mdash;i. e., to have his opinion carry it without contradiction. Here
the sense rises elegantly. <I>He used ever to conquer; nay, to conquer without opposi-
tion.</I>&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 422): When we say a man is used to have his word [see <I>Text.</I>
</CC>

<CC>
<C>[34, 35. <B>to haue his worth Of contradiction</B>]</C><LB>
<P><I>Notes</I>] we mean that he will still have something proper or improper to say on
every occasion that offers. What strange English too is <I>Off contradiction?</I> Yet,
in spite of the genius of our language, Mr Warburton will have it that these words
signify, &lquo;He has been used to have his opinion carry it without contradiction; nay,
to conquer without opposition.&rquo; Surely the tribunes knew better, as well from
what had just before passed, as from the other transactions mentioned in the play,
the establishment of the tribunitial magistracy, and the distribution of the corn,
both which Coriolanus had violently opposed and had been overruled in his
opposition. The latter part of Mr Warburton's interpretation, though he under-
stands it as a compliment to Coriolanus out of the mouth of his enemies, is such a
one as Coriolanus himself would undoubtedly have interpreted to be an affront.
The common reading gives us a very just and a very natural sense. [It is to be
remembered that by this Heath means the reading of Rowe, Pope, Theobald,
etc., and not the Folio text.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]: &lquo;He hath been ever used in war to conquer,
and in peace to lay hold of every opportunity to contradict the desires of the people.
The first circumstance hath blown up his pride, and the second is so habitual to
him that he cannot get the better of it; there is therefore no doubt but, if we can
once put him in passion, and off his guard, both those principles of action will
display themselves with their usual extravagance.&rquo; The source of Mr Warburton's
mistake is evident; he must needs be searching for a climax where none was intended.
&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC>, whose text reads, &lquo;to have his 'worth,&rquo; says: &lquo;Thus the folios, and
rightly; for though <I>'worth</I> be an uncommon contraction (a singular one, if you
will, for no example is met with), the word so understood fits the place and the
speaker; and that very contraction has fitted it, for <I>pennyworth</I> had not been toler-
able. The sense is, &ldquo;<I>He hath been us'd</I> to have his full swing of it.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;[In his
<I>Glossary</I> Capell cites the present passage, s. v. <I>'Worth:</I> Pennyworth.]&mdash;<SC>Malone's</SC>
note on this passage does not contain any reference to Capell; but he likewise
declares in favour of the Folio reading, and interprets &lquo;worth&rquo; in the sense of
<I>pennyworth,</I> quoting in illustration <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> &lquo;You take your pennyworth [of
sleep] now,&rquo; IV, v, 4.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emendations,</I> etc., p. 358): The following
must be allowed to be a valuable emendation of a passage which is thus given in
every edition, ancient or recent, &lquo;&mdash;to have his worth Of contradiction.&rquo; Malone
gravely says that &lquo;to have his worth of contradiction&rquo; means to have his <I>penny-
worth</I> of it; but the whole figure here is taken from horsemanship. When a restive
animal obtains his own way he is said to have his mouth given to him; to give a
horse his mouth is to free him from restraint; therefore Brutus, speaking of
Coriolanus and of his irritable spirit, remarks:

<P>48. <B>Through our large Temples</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: Though this be the reading of

emendation [see <I>Text. Notes</I>] restoring the text rightly, because Mr Warburton
started the same conjecture, unknowing that I had meddled with the passage.

reading.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>48. <B>shewes of peace</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: The &lquo;shows of peace&rquo; are multitudes of people
peaceably assembled either to hear the determination of causes or for other
purposes of civil government.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The real &lquo;shows of peace&rquo; among the
Romans were the olive branch and the caduceous; but I question if our author, on
the present occasion, had any determinate idea annexed to his words. Mr
Malone's supposition, however, can hardly be right; because the &lquo;temples&rquo; (<I>i. e.,</I>
those of the gods) were never used for the determination of civil causes, &amp;c. To
such purposes the Senate and the Forum were appropriated. The <I>temples</I> indeed
might be thronged with people who met to thank the gods for a return of peace.&mdash;
<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Shakespeare may have had in his mind some occasion like that of
Nov. 24, 1588, when Queen Elizabeth went to St Paul's to return thanks for the
victory over the Spanish Armada. See Stow's <I>Annals,</I> p. 1260 (ed. 1601).
