<P>58. <B>this present</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): Either to be taken with a reference to
time&mdash;now, today&mdash;so that no later repetition of the complaint is to be feared; or
with reference to the case now under discussion, so that there remains in reserve
other points of complaint. Grammatically the first is the more simple explana-
tion, and seems more consistent with the question &lquo;must all determine here?&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): At this present time. Some take it as meaning the present
charge, referring to the events in III, i, and the attempt to attach him &lquo;as a trait-
orous innovator, A foe to th' public weal&rquo; (ll. 207, 208). On the whole, however,
time or occasion seems to be intended. Coriolanus had been prepared by Cominius
for new and stronger accusations, and had agreed to answer &lquo;mildly,&rquo; although, in
fact, his patience breaks down as soon as he hears the old charge repeated. As
Sicinius says there was no need to &lquo;put new matter to his charge&rquo; (l. 101 <I>post</I>).
<P>61. <B>the peoples voices</B>] <SC>E. J. White</SC> (p. 413): The different departments of
government, now recognised, were not separated at this period of the world's
history; it was a fundamental principle of Roman Government that the supreme
power was inherent in the people, though it might be delegated by them to elected
or hereditary magistrates. All important matters, however, had to be brought
before the sovereign people, who could ratify or reject the proposals made to them
without discussion. The power of the people, swayed as they were by improper
appeals and motives, led to a period of moral and political corruption which was
followed by the military despotism of the C&aelig;sars.

him, and not understanding its propriety, supposed that <I>church</I> had been acci-
dentally omitted, and intruded it into the text. It would be an endless task to

<P>verb <I>season</I> occurs arise unmistakably from the idea of flavouring and the related
ideas of preserving and of qualifying or tempering [as given by Schmidt], while
the few which are usually put down under &lquo;mature,&rquo; &lquo;ripen&rquo; may quite well have
the same origin. The strongest case for &lquo;mature,&rquo; &lquo;ripen&rquo; is <I>Hamlet,</I> I, iii, 81,
where Polonius says, &lquo;my blessing season this in thee!&rquo; but even here it is possible
to regard the blessing as the preservative, or as the ingredient making all palatable.
In the same play, III, ii, 219, as ripening or preparing takes time, &lquo;And who in
want a hollow friend doth try Directly seasons him his enemy,&rquo; is better explained
by <I>flavours, qualifies;</I> and similarly in III, iii, 86, &lquo;When he is fit and season'd
for his passage,&rquo; there can be no question of maturing and ripening, but only of
being tempered and qualified at a particular time by the seasoning of repentance.
In <I>Timon,</I> IV, iii, 85, the context, with salt and tubs, the concomitants of pickling,
not of ripening, surely fix the metaphor. The <I>N. E. D.,</I> however, places the present
passage under the figurative use of <I>seasoned</I> in sense, &lquo;fitted for use, matured,
brought to a state of perfection,&rquo; etc.

<P>91. <B>hell. Fould in,</B> etc.] Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): The re-punctuation

enemy. First he growls, &lquo;The fires i' th' lowest hell.&rquo; Then blazes into fury and

<P><S>Cris.</S> O&mdash;<I>clutcht.</I>
<P><S>Hor.</S> Now it is come; <I>clutcht.</I>
<P><S>C&aelig;s. Clutcht!</S> it is well that is come up; it had but a narrow passage.&rquo;
<P>(V, i; ed. Gifford, p. 529). &lquo;Clutch&rquo; in the sense <I>to grasp</I> was somewhat unusual,
its more common meaning was to <I>clutch</I> the fist, where we now use <I>clench.</I> Gifford,
in a note on this latter expression (<I>Ibid.,</I> p. 519), says: &lquo;Steevens, with his cus-
tomary disregard of truth in everything which relates to our author [Ben Jonson],
declares, in his final remarks on <I>Hamlet,</I> that Jonson has more than once in the
<I>Poetaster</I> pointed his ridicule at some of Shakespeare's descriptions and characters,
and frequently sneered at his choice of words, of which he instances <I>clutch.</I> I will
take upon me to affirm that the play does not contain a single allusion to any
character that Shakespeare ever drew, nor an expression that can, by any inge-
nuity, however malicious, be tortured into a sneer at his language. <I>Clutch,</I> indeed,
is used by him (as well as others), and with strict propriety; which can scarcely
be said of it as employed by Marston; let the reader judge:
<BQ>
&ldquo;Tis yet dead night, yet all the earth is <I>clutch'd</I><LB>
In the dull leaden hand of snoring sleepe,&rdquo; <I>Antonio's Revenge,</I> I, i.'&mdash;<LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.,</I> s. v. <I>Clutch,</I> II, 5.) quotes the above passage from Marston as
the earliest use of the verb in the sense &lquo;To hold tightly in the bent or closed hand.&rquo;
Its novelty, as well as its offensive sound to his poetical ear, evidently caused
Jonson to hold this particular word up to ridicule. Steevens thought it might
not be generally understood, since in his own edition, 1793, he defines the word as
in the present passage, &lquo;<I>grasp'd.</I> So Macbeth, in his address to the &ldquo;air-drawn
dagger,&rdquo; &ldquo;Come let me clutch thee.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;II, i, 34.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>96. <B>Thou lyest vnto thee</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): It is almost universally
understood that &lquo;unto thee&rquo; is dependent on &lquo;say,&rquo; and so it may well be; but it
may not be impossible that it is connected with &lquo;liest&rquo;: &lquo;Thou liest before thine
own self, thou speakest this with the clearest consciousness of the lie.&rquo;

<P>119. <B>Nor checke my Courage</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emendations,</I> etc., p. 359):

for &lquo;courage,&rquo; an easy mistake, the setting right of which is an evident improve-
ment. The very same misprint has been pointed out and remedied in the same
way in <I>3 Henry VI:</I> [II, ii, 57, &lquo;And this soft courage makes your followers
faint,&rquo; where the MS. correction is &lquo;soft <I>carriage.</I>&rquo;].&mdash;<SC>Mommsen</SC> (<I>Der Perkins Folio,</I>
p. 270): Although <I>carriage</I> is assuredly the better word, and the change natural for
the ear, it is at the same time to be considered that &lquo;courage&rquo; anciently bore a
double sense, that is, boldness and character of mind, <I>e. g.,</I> Chaucer, <I>Cant. Tales,</I>
near the beginning, &lquo;So pricketh hem nature in hir corages,&rquo; i. e., <I>minds, hearts.</I>
Nevertheless in this particular passage in <I>Coriolanus</I> it would have been a rightly
conceived and a finer insertion of the MS. Corrector, to guard the hero from mis-
understanding, than had he spoken of his bravery, since his pride is customarily

<P>Here, strange as it may seem considering the context, <I>carriage</I> has always kept

passage of <I>Henry VI.</I> by changing &lquo;courage&rquo; to <I>carriage,</I> so Mr Collier corrupts the
passage of <I>The Island Princess</I> by changing &lquo;carriage&rquo; to <I>courage:</I>

<P>123. <B>Enui'd against the people</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, behaved with signs of
hatred to the people.&mdash;<SC>Andrew Becket</SC>, whose name has long since been excluded
from this edition, proposed, as far back as 1815, that we should here read, &lquo;<I>In-
veigh'd</I> against the people.&rquo; The sole reason for resuscitating Becket is, that to
him rightfully belongs, through priority, the credit for this change. In 1856
<SC>Badham</SC>, in his article <I>The Text of Shakespeare,</I> p. 289, says: &lquo;For <I>envyed against</I>
read <I>enveyed against,</I> or, as Holinshed writes it (I have unfortunately mislaid the
reference), <I>invaied,</I> which in our modern orthography would be &ldquo;inveigh'd.&rdquo; To
envy against a person or thing is foreign to the language, and there was nothing to
induce Shakespeare to adopt such a license of construction. Lyly plays upon the
resemblance of the two words (<I>Euphues,</I> p. 47): &ldquo;Although I have been bolde to
invay against many, yet am I not so brutish as to envy them all.&rdquo;&rquo; As will be
seen, Badham has no doubts as to the originality of his conjectural reading.&mdash;
<SC>Staunton</SC> in 1860, likewise with no hint as to having been anticipated, notes:
&lquo;&ldquo;Envied&rdquo; here is, perhaps, only a misprint of <I>Inveighed;</I> so in North's <I>Plutarch</I>
(<I>Life of Solon</I>), &ldquo;But Solon going up into the pulpit for orations, stoutly inveyed
against it.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Bailey</SC>, writing in 1866, is perhaps the most culpable as regards a
lack of research in the matter; he says: &lquo;There is an expression in this tragedy that
I do not find has struck any critic as corrupt,&rquo; and then quotes this present line,
adding (ii, 60): &lquo;Surely we ought to read <I>inveigh'd</I> &ldquo;against the people.&rdquo; The
verb <I>inveigh,</I> it is true, does not occur elsewhere in these plays, although the noun
<I>invective</I> is found once. But the verb seems to have been familiarly employed
by several writers of the age, such as Drayton and Holland, and the objection of
its non-appearance in Shakespeare's writings may be equally adduced against the
actual reading. I cannot, in any of them, discover the phrase &ldquo;envied against,&rdquo;
which, even if it were genuine, must be deemed harsh and unusual, if not un-
precedented.&rquo;
<P>124. <B>as now at last</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Read rather &lquo;<I>has</I> now at last.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>:
I am not certain but that &lquo;as&rquo; in this instance has the power of <I>as well as.</I> The
same mode of expression I have met with among our ancient writers.&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC>
(&sect; 113) for this passage refers to examples wherein &lquo;as&rquo; is frequently used (without
<I>such</I>) to signify &lquo;namely.&rquo; Since there is, however, a hint as to <I>time</I> here, the
phrase may, perhaps, more fitly be explained by <SC>Abbott's</SC> following section: &lquo;<I>As</I>
is apparently used redundantly with definitions of time (as <G>w(s</G> is used in Greek with
respect to motion). It is said by Halliwell to be an Eastern Counties phrase:
<BQ>
&ldquo;This is my birthday, as this very day<LB>
Was Cassius born,&rdquo; <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> V, i, 72.<LB>
&ldquo;One Lucio as then the messenger,&rdquo; <I>Meas. for Meas.,</I> V, i, 74.<LB>

was born &ldquo;on this very day,&rdquo; which is not literally true, <I>as</I> meaning &ldquo;as I may say.&rdquo;
Here, and in our Collect for Christmas Day, &ldquo;as at this time to be born,&rdquo; <I>as</I> seems
appropriate to an <I>anniversary.</I> In the second example the meaning of &ldquo;as then&rdquo;
is not so clear; perhaps it means &ldquo;<I>as far as regards</I> that occasion.&rdquo; Compare:

<P>135. <B>and it shall be so</B>] <SC>Knight</SC>: If we turn to the beginning of the scene we
shall find the directions of the Tribunes very precise as to the echo which the
people were to raise of their words. When, therefore, Sicinius here pronounces
the sentence of banishment, he terminates, as he said he should, with, &lquo;It shall
be so&rquo;; and the people, true to the instruction, vociferate, &lquo;It shall be so.&rquo; They
afterwards repeat the cry in the exact words. Perhaps, upon the whole, the common
text here presents one of Steevens's most atrocious alterations. [See <I>Text. Notes,</I>
l. 135.]
<P>139. <B>from Rome</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: How from Rome? Did he receive hostile marks
from his own Country? No such thing. He received them in the service of Rome.
So, twice in the beginning of the next Act, it is said of Coriolanus:
<BQ>
&lquo;To banish him that struck more blows for Rome.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>

<P>one example from Bacon, &lquo;Pallas her glass,&rquo; [<I>Adv. of Learning,</I> 278].&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Jahrbuch,</I>
xv, p. 55): I am quite in accord with Schmidt in his opposition to the editors, but
not because I accept his explanation, but rather because the word <I>for</I> is not needed;
&lquo;from&rquo; means here: I have received wounds from (through) Rome because I

<P>140, 141. <B>I do loue My Countries good,</B> etc.] <SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 605): To
Volumnia, despite all her maternal preference and patrician prejudice, Rome is
the grand consideration, as her deeds unequivocally prove. Nor is she singular;
she is only the most conspicuous example among others of her caste. Cominius,
too, postpones the family to the state. And this is more or less the attitude of the
rest. But Coriolanus reverses the sequence, and gives his chief homage precisely
to the most restricted and elementary, the most primitive and instinctive prin-
ciple of the three [family, State, nobility]. He loves Rome, indeed, fights for her,
grieves for her shames, and glories in her triumphs; but he loves the nobility more,
and would by wholesale massacre secure their supremacy. He loves the nobility
indeed, but when they, no doubt for the common good, suffer him to be expelled
from Rome, they become to him the &lquo;dastard nobles&rquo;; and he makes hardly any
account of his old henchman and intimate, Menenius, and none at all of his old
comrade and general, Cominius. But he loves his family as himself, and though he
strives to root out its claims from his heart, the attempt is vain.

<P>161. <B>Making but reseruation,</B> etc.] <SC>Malone</SC>: Instead of &lquo;Making but reservation
of yourselves,&rquo; which is the reading of the old copy, and which Dr Johnson very
rightly explains, I have no doubt that we should read, as I have printed, &lquo;Making
<I>not</I> reservation,&rquo; etc., which agrees with the subsequent words, &lquo;still your own foes,&rquo;
and with the general purport of the speech; which is, to show that the folly of the
people was such as was likely to destroy the whole of the republic without <I>any</I>
reservation, <I>not only others, but even themselves,</I> and to subjugate them as abated
captives to some hostile nation. If, according to the old copy, the people have the
prudence to make reservation of themselves, while they are destroying their
country, they cannot with any propriety be said to be in that respect &lquo;still their
own foes.&rquo; These words therefore decisively support the emendation now made.
How often <I>not</I> and <I>but</I> have been confounded in these plays has already been fre-
quently observed. In this very play <I>but</I> has been printed, in a former scene, instead
of <I>not,</I> and the latter word substituted in all modern editions. See II, iii, 73. [If
Malone were not aware that in this emendation he was anticipated by Capell,
he should have been. Steevens is more than usually just and properly assigns
it.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): That Capell was right we have the authority of the
old Corrector.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: This, since Capell's edition, has been invariably
printed, &lquo;Making <I>not</I> reservation,&rquo; &amp;c., to the complete destruction of the sense,
which manifestly is, Banish all your defenders as you do me, till at last, your
ignorance, having reserved only your impotent selves, always your own foes,
deliver you the humbled captives to some nation, &amp;c.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. i.): Coriolanus
imprecates upon the base plebeians that they may still retain the power of banish-
ing their <I>defenders,</I> till their undiscerning folly, which can foresee no consequences,
leave none in the city <I>but themselves;</I> so that for want of those capable of con-
ducting their defence they may fall an easy prey to some nation who may conquer
them without a struggle. If we were to read as Malone would have us&mdash;&lquo;Making
<I>not</I> reservation of yourselves&rquo;&mdash;it would imply that the people <I>banished themselves</I>
after having banished their defenders.&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>):

<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Johnson explains the reading of the Folios. But Capell's is

not keep them, but handed them over to the enemy.&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick
Sh.</I>): With the reading of the Folios Coriolanus says, &lquo;Banish your defenders, and,

The Folio's reading has been retained by some editors and variously explained.
. . . Each interpretation seems to me forced and inconsistent with the general
tenour of the passage and the particular description that follows. [Verity quotes,
with approval, Malone's reason for accepting the change of &lquo;but&rquo; to <I>not.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;
<SC>Gordon</SC>: The effect of the change of &lquo;but&rquo; to <I>not</I> is to spoil both lines. For the
point is, not that they do not spare themselves and no others, and being left to
themselves, fall a prey to the first attack. Here is the whole force of &lquo;Still your
own foes,&rquo; that they are so without knowing it. They think in their ignorance
that when they have saved themselves they have saved everything. If <I>not</I> be
read all this is lost, and &lquo;Still your own foes&rquo; becomes superfluous. If they do not
spare even themselves, it is idle repetition to add that they are their own foes.&mdash;
<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Retaining &lquo;but&rquo; the sense of the whole passage is: keep the
power to banish those who would defend you, until your ignorant policy (which
never perceives consequences till it undergoes them), reserving only yourselves
from banishment, and in so doing making you still your own enemies, hand you
over, etc. Malone argues inconsistency with the purport of the speech, &lquo;which is
to show that the folly of the people was such as was likely to destroy the whole of
the republic without <I>any</I> reservation, <I>not only others, but themselves.</I>&rquo; But the
reservation in this case is from banishment, not from destruction, a distinction
which also puts out of court his further argument. This being so, the Folio text
is here retained, but if Capell's reading had been substituted, it must have appealed
for support not to Malone's argument, but to its giving a sense supposed simplest
and most readily perceptible, <I>viz.,</I> Not even safeguarding yourselves (for you are
always your own enemies), deliver you, etc.&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC> (p. 304): There is not the
least reason for substituting <I>not</I> for &lquo;but&rquo; in this line. Coriolanus declares that

<P>1. <B>Actus Quartus</B>] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): Coriolanus's career in
Rome has ended in disaster; but he is not a man to put up with disaster content-
edly. Already a vague scheme, soon to take dreadful shape, has suggested itself
to him, whereby he may re-establish himself in his own eyes, and once more play
a brave part in new scenes and under new conditions. The attempt to carry out
this scheme forms the subject of the Fourth Act; the Fifth is concerned with its
ultimate failure. In the first three scenes, however, Coriolanus's designs are not
directly revealed. For a time our sympathies are allowed to turn towards him in
his misfortune. His departure is touched with pathos, though beneath there is
the tragic undertone of an austere and terrible intention. Shakespeare adds a
dramatic touch in making Coriolanus depart alone, and not &lquo;with three or four
of his friends,&rquo; [as in North's <I>Plutarch</I>].
<P>2. <B>Enter Coriolanus,</B> etc.] Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Shakespeare's way
to represent this on his stage was presumably to represent the group as entering
from one of the side doors, and bringing Coriolanus out the double doors in the
rear stage. These could be made to look enough like the gates in a city-wall to
be so supposed, as already they had been supposed (I, iv, v, vii.), to be the fortified
gates of Corioli.
<P>4. <B>Come leaue your teares</B>] <SC>R&ouml;tscher</SC> (p. 23): In this parting from mother
and wife the nobility of Coriolanus's character is strongly manifested. The tones
of his heart, which does not want that its innermost quivering be visible, and yet
cannot conceal the pain of separation, presage wonderfully the hero's catastrophe
in the Fifth Act. We see the heroic self-command of a great character which knows
its full worth no less than the loss which he suffers. Such scenes as this are ever
most difficult in their sensualisation, because they demand at one and the same
time the full expression of contradictory emotion. Since we wish to see the col-
lectedness and self-abnegation of an heroic nature shaken to the depths by a
powerful sorrow, the sorrow should appear without sentimentality, the pride
without stubbornness. The broken voice should tremble through this manifesta-
tion of nobility, and thus convey to us the feeling of inner woe. With this tragic
turning of fate the r&ocirc;le of Coriolanus ends in the Third Act.
<P>4. <B>leaue your teares</B>] That is, leave off weeping; compare <I>Hamlet,</I> III, iv, 34:
&lquo;Leave wringing of your hands.&rquo;
</CC>

<P>7. <B>Extreamities was</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: <I>Extremity</I> in the singular number is used by
our author in <I>Merry Wives, Comedy of Errors, Tro. &amp; Cress.</I>&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: However
often Shakespeare has used extremes [<I>sic,</I> Qu. extremity?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] in other places,
we find that he has employed the plural here; what ground, therefore, have we for
changing a word that affords perfect good sense, and is found in the only ancient
authentic copy. It is decisively confirmed and supported not only by that copy,
but by another place in this very play, where we meet with exactly the same
phraseology, III, ii, 52-54:
<BQ>
&lquo;You are too absolute,<LB>
Tho' there you can never be too noble,<LB>
But when extremities speak,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;<LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Delius</SC>: &lquo;Extremities&rquo; is here collective, equivalent to a myriad or crowd of
stresses, and has, as a single idea, both verb and predicate in the singular.&mdash;
<SC>Dyce</SC>: Malone adhered, perhaps too obstinately, to the Folio reading here; to his
citation from an earlier scene in defence of the plural, we may, however, oppose
what afterwards occurs, &lquo;Now this extremity Hath brought me to thy hearth,&rquo;
IV, v, 83.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 368): The reading of the Second Folio is,
perhaps, right; yet the First Folio reading is not wrong.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: There
is great looseness with regard to the copula when subject and predicate are of
different numbers. Compare <I>Psalm,</I> xviii, 11, &lquo;His pavilion round about him were
dark waters and thick clouds of the skies.&rquo; And <I>Richard II:</I> V, v, 55, &lquo;Now sir
the sound that tells what hour it is Are clamorous groans.&rquo; But it is most proba-
ble that &lquo;extremities&rquo; is a misprint, and one of a kind common in the First Folio.&mdash;
Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): The correction of the plural, &lquo;Extreamities,&rquo;
to the singular may be justified as the correction of a misprint, like the obviously
needed change made in the Second Folio of the period after &lquo;chances&rquo; [l. 8] into a
comma; still there is something in the way Coriolanus employs &lquo;extremities&rquo; here
that, taken together with the capitalization of the word, suggests a collective
used here in an abstract sense, a condition of things at the extreme. Notice below
&lquo;Fortunes blowes . . . craves.&rquo; Wright assumes a misprint and prints &lquo;extremity.&rquo;
Since neither the time, the poet, nor the hero represented are formalists, why efface
the signs of such combined plasticity of speech?&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): The Second
Folio needlessly changed the text to <I>extremity,</I> a reading which some editors adopt;
but Malone properly insisted on the correctness of the old text. &lquo;Extremities&rquo; has
already occurred in III, ii, 54, <I>ante.</I>&mdash;<SC>H. Cunningham</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I> 16 October,
1926): Notwithstanding the plural form in the Folio, which is supported by Malone
and Case, and notwithstanding the plural &lquo;chances,&rquo; in l. 8, I am inclined to think
that other editors (not to speak of the Second Folio) were correct in printing the
singular&mdash;Shakespeare's spelling, if he wrote the singular, being, of course, &lquo;Ex-
tremitie.&rquo; The misprinting of this letter &lquo;s&rquo; in the old editions is something por-
tentous; there are nearly a hundred examples in Qq 1, 2, and Folio in <I>Hamlet</I> alone!
Further, there are nearly thirty examples of the singular &lquo;Extremity&rquo; in the plays,
but only some three or four of the plural. &lquo;Extreme&rquo; and &lquo;Extremity&rquo; are favourite
words with Shakespeare, and occur many times in the plays. It would seem,
on the whole, that the balance is in favour of the singular form here.

<P>10-12. <B>Fortunes blowes . . . A Noble cunning</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The modern editors
have, for &lquo;gentle wounded,&rquo; silently substituted <I>gently warded,</I> and Dr Warburton
has explained <I>gently</I> by <I>nobly.</I> It is good to be sure of our author's words before
we go to explain their meaning. The sense is: &lquo;When Fortune strikes her hardest
blows, to be wounded, and yet continue calm, requires a generous policy.&rquo; He calls
this calmness <I>cunning,</I> because it is the effect of reflection and philosophy. Per-
haps the first emotions of nature are nearly uniform, and one man differs from
another in the power of endurance, as he is better regulated by precept and instruc-
tion. &lquo;They bore as heroes, but they felt as man,&rquo; [Pope, Homer's <I>Iliad,</I> Bk
xxiv, l. 646.&mdash;In the <I>Variorum</I> of 1773 and subsequent repetitions of this note
by Johnson the line is incorrectly given, &lquo;Felt as <I>men.</I>&rquo; It is actually an addition
to Homer by Pope; the original has merely, &lquo;and their moan went up throughout
the house,&rquo; l. 512. This line quoted by Johnson, without either title or author,
is not given in any of the many collections of quotations and, though repeated
by subsequent editors, has not, as far as I know, been identified. Its locating,
therefore, involved a thorough search through the poetic works of Addison, Dryden,
Cowley, and Pope (the <I>Concordance</I> to the latter's <I>Works</I> does not include the trans-
lations of either the <I>Iliad</I> or the <I>Odyssey</I>); permit me then to say, in the words of
Johnson himself in his <I>Preface,</I> &lquo;Let us hear no more of the dull duty of an editor.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 97): &lquo;<I>Gently</I>&rquo; is a very proper correction of the sec-
ond modern's [Pope]; but why he and the gentlemen after him should put <I>warded</I>
for &lquo;wounded&rquo; they have not told us, nor can the most sagacious discover a reason
for it: The apothegm is just and a fit one, and the expression of it no ways ob-
scure; <I>that</I> must be implied at the head of it, and then the meaning will be that,

<C>[10-12. <B>Fortunes blowes . . . A Noble cunning</B>]</C>
<P>when fortune strikes her most home blows, to come off with but small or slight
wounds, requires skill and address.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: &lquo;Fortunes blows&rquo; stands here in the
form of anacoluthon without an attendant verb, and can only be connected with

somewhat involved, it is far more after the manner of Shakespeare than the cor-
rection which the margins propose. <I>Gentle-minded</I> is quite uncalled for. The
meaning is: You were used to say that when Fortune's blows were most struck
home, to be gentle, <I>though</I> wounded, craves a noble cunning&mdash;that is, a high
degree of self-command.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: Every endeavor to elicit sense from this

I, ii.). &lquo;It is twice blessed&rquo; (<I>Mer. of Ven.,</I> V, i, 186); and then &lquo;gentle&rquo; will denote
that the blows were open and honorable ones. If this should not satisfy, we might,

originally meant &lquo;blows&rquo; to be the subject, and then introduced a new subject
in &lquo;being wounded.&rquo; But the sense is clear enough; it is governed by the antithesis
of &lquo;common&rquo; and &lquo;gentle.&rquo; &lquo;Being gentle wounded&rquo;=&lquo;to bear your wounds as a

servare mentem,&rquo; [<I>Carm.,</I> II, <I>Ode</I> iii, 1, 2].<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The verb &lquo;craves&rquo; is singular through attraction to the sense-subject, not the
grammatical subject; it is not the &lquo;blows,&rquo; but bearing the blows gently, that
&lquo;craves&rquo; wisdom; and the idea of bearing them is implied by the qualifying clause
&lquo;being <I>gentle</I> wounded.&rquo; The interposition of l. 11 between the strict grammatical
subject and its verb facilitates the attraction of the verb to the general sense.

<C>[10-12. <B>Fortunes blowes . . . A Noble cunning</B>]</C>
<P>(This is not a case for considering the possible influence of the &lquo;northern&rquo; plural
in <I>es</I> or <I>s.</I>) &lquo;Cunning&rquo; is a good instance of the tendency of words to deteriorate
in sense. The quality itself being so often misapplied, the word got a correspond-
ingly bad notion. (Perhaps with a strongly classical writer like Milton we should
take &lquo;noble cunning&rquo; differently, as an <I>oxymoron.</I>)&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: The construction
of the sentence (it has no grammar) is this: when fortune's blows are most struck
home, to be gentle under one's wounds craves a noble cunning. &lquo;Craves,&rquo; therefore,
is rightly singular. Its subject is not &lquo;blows,&rquo; but &lquo;being gentle wounded,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I>
gentleness under one's wounds.&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): An example
of the molten heat of Coriolanus's words that must be understood by following
the thought rather than the form. He means, &lquo;Fortune's blows when most struck
home crave a noble cunning in one, wounded, being gentle, <I>i. e.,</I> in one wounded
by them who is gentle.&rquo; The capitalization of <I>Noble</I> suggests that the nobleness
is that demanded of a Noble. Coriolanus's definition of a Noble is not external;
it is a matter of spirit and fortitude, not mere rank.&mdash;<SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Times Literary Supple-
ment,</I> 27 July, 1922, p. 482): Apart from the intolerably awkward syntax, the
use of &lquo;gentle&rquo; is unparalleled; and, after the straightforward lines that precede,
the sudden tangle brings us up with an unpleasant jar. When Shakespeare over-
rides syntax he usually makes his sense quite clear. Moreover, Coriolanus is
quoting his mother's proverbs; this one is a riddle. We cannot believe that
Shakespeare wrote the lines as they stand. The natural sense in the context is,
&lquo;Fortune's blows when most struck home, being . . . crave a noble cunning.&rquo;
The three words beginning with &lquo;being&rquo; represent a phrase in apposition to, and
explanatory of, &lquo;Fortune's blows when most struck home.&rquo; We suggest, diffidently,
that behind the meaningless &lquo;gentle&rquo; is concealed the adjective &lquo;tentles&rquo; (tentless,
<I>i. e.,</I> impossible to probe) and that the line originally read, &lquo;When most struck,
being tentless wounds, do crave A noble cunning.&rquo; They are wounds beyond the
skill of the ordinary surgeon. Shakespeare in this martial play was particularly
fond of using the word &lquo;to tent&rquo; metaphorically, see I, ix, 40, and in particular,
III, i, 285, &lquo;'Tis a sore upon us you cannot tent yourself.&rquo; [In a letter to the
Editor of <I>The Times Literary Supplement</I> for August 17, 1922, Henry Cunningham
says, &lquo;Sir: The writer of the admirable leading article on <I>Coriolanus,</I> in the issue
of July 27, advances some interesting points on the textual interpretation of the
play. His diffident suggestion on the famous <I>crux</I> &ldquo;being gentle wounded&rdquo; is
extremely ingenious. But, although making excellent sense, it introduces in
&ldquo;tentless&rdquo; a <G>a)/rac lego/menon</G> which is rather daring, besides bringing more letters
into the printed line of the Folio than could ordinarily have been included therein.
In turn I suggest:
<BQ>
&ldquo;Fortune's blows,<LB REND=RIGHT>
When most struck home, being <I><B>tender</B> wounds, do crave</I><LB>
A noble cunning,&rdquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P><I>i. e.,</I> when Fortune's blows are shrewdest, the wounds she makes are raw and
tender, and require skilful surgery. The meaning of this is plain and unexception-
able; and it will be observed that the trace and number of the letters (viz., 19) in
the above italicized words exactly correspond with those of the &ldquo;gentle wounded,
craves&rdquo; in the Folio reading. This is a matter of the utmost importance in the
criticism of a doubtful word or passage in the Folio.&rquo; Four years later Cunningham
returns to this same passage in a communication to <I>Notes &amp; Queries</I> (October 16,

I think there is an even more pertinent attribute to be found for &ldquo;wound(e)s,&rdquo;
viz., <I>tentless</I>(<I>e</I>) or <I>tentless</I> or <I>tentles,</I> however it may have appeared in Shake-

he have chosen such an epithet? Surely he meant that Fortune's blows, not be-
ing merely <I>physical,</I> would require a nobler philosophy for their endurance, since
they could not be &ldquo;tented&rdquo; after the fashion of mere physical wounds. Finally,
what reason may we assign for the corruption of the text? A glance at the Folio
may show. I think it was owing to the attempt of the printers to get the necessarily
excessive amount of type into the line without carrying over into the next. They
seldom or never carried the words of a line of MS. on to the next, as modern printers
commonly do. Hence if Shakespeare's MS. had the line in the following form,
<BQ>
&ldquo;When most strooke home, being tentlesse woundes, do crave,&rdquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>the inference may be justly drawn that the Folio printers found it impossible to
get his words into the regular lineal space, and (possibly not understanding
Shakespeare's meaning or his contractions) corrupted the text as we find it in the
Folio. &ldquo;Tent&rdquo; as a substantive, of course, means lint or other substances used
to search and cleanse a wound; and, as a verb, to probe it, or apply the &ldquo;tent.&rdquo;
See I, ix, 40, and III, i, 285 <I>ante;</I> also <I>Cymbeline,</I> III, iv, 118, &ldquo;And mine ear
Therein false struck, can take no greater wound Nor tent to bottom that.&rdquo; This
last is especially worthy of notice, since &ldquo;struck,&rdquo; &ldquo;tent,&rdquo; and &ldquo;wound&rdquo; are found
in close collocation. Be it noted also that <I>Coriolanus</I> and <I>Cymbeline</I> are not far
removed from each other in point of date.&rquo; [At first sight it would seem that
Cunningham, himself, was the author of the Anonymous article in the <I>Times

<P>plague rid you,&rquo; etc.): In the <I>General Practise of Physicke,</I> 1605, p. 675, three
different kinds of plague-sore are mentioned: &lquo;sometimes it is red, otherwhiles
yellow, and sometimes blacke, which is the very worst and most venimous.&rquo; . . .
An early MS. medical commonplace-book, in my possession, says, &lquo;the plague
and pestilence, or <I>red plage,</I> doth moste abounde from Midsomer to Autumne,&rquo; &amp;c.
The same volume prescribes blood-letting for this disease.&mdash;<SC>Moyes</SC> (p. 21): This
was doubtless typhus fever. The disease was common at the time, and in France
the name given to it was <I>La pourpre,</I> from the red eruption which accompanied
it. Some have made out the reference to be one form of the plague, but the
resemblance (if not relationship) between the plague and typhus is at times so
close that a celebrated physician from Egypt, seeing certain typhus fever cases
in London, said that if seen at home they would have been regarded as the
plague.

<P>35. <B>Like to a lonely Dragon</B>] <SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): Here
the construction allows of two meanings in the sentence&mdash;&lquo;Like a lonely dragon,
that his pestilential fen makes feared and talked of more than seen,&rquo; and &lquo;like a
lonely dragon that makes his fenny retreat feared and talk'd of more than seen.&rquo;
This duplicate meaning applies well to Coriolanus, whose withdrawal to some
unknown place causes him to be dreaded and talked of during absence, and whose
known fierce nature causes this intended place of retreat to become a subject of
fear and wondering conjecture.&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): He does not compare <I>himself</I>
with a lonely dragon (for just now there is no reason to suppose that he will be
feared), but the <I>banishment;</I> he says, &lquo;though I go alone, as if I were going
to. . . .&rquo; It is to be remembered that banishment was the hardest destiny for a
Roman. A banished Roman was lost forever, but Coriolanus assures his mother
that he will&mdash;even banished&mdash;perform deeds that will &lquo;exceed the common&rquo;:
&lquo;There is a world elsewhere.&rquo;

<P><SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Grey conjectured &lquo;<I>den</I>&rquo; quite needlessly. In Topsell's <I>History of
Serpents</I> (ed. 1658), p. 705, we read: &lquo;Of the Indian Dragons there are also said
to be two kindes, one of them fenny, and living in the marishes, which are slow
of pace and without combes on their heads like females; the other in the Moun-

which it was one of the labours of Hercules to destroy, and to which he has com-
pared the people. The Poet shows the loneliness of spirit felt by him amid the
sense of strength, the consciousness of the ability to be dangerous. Out of that
rankling sense of loneliness and unbeheld power, brooded over stoically here,
which the Poet shows as the right soil for what is to come, his revenge will grow.

Shakespeare's inclusive style, for &lquo;needer&rquo; as here employed gives the effect of
the man needing the advantage of which there is a prospect, and of the man
needed home by his friends who want him to profit by it. Moreover, what golden
wisdom and practical truth are comprised in a line or two!

<P>59-61. <B>While I remaine . . . like me formerly</B>] <SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): Corio-
lanus had probably not yet resolved upon his revenge. But the words have a
dramatic irony, inasmuch as that revenge was a legitimate birth of character.&mdash;
<SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 611): It is sometimes said that defeat and the desire for ven-
geance teach him the lessons which his mother had inculcated in vain, and that
henceforth he shows himself a master of dissimulation, flattery, and deception.
In proof of this it is usual to cite, in the first place, the farewell scene, when he
breathes no word to Cominius, Menenius, Virgilia, or Volumnia of his intention
to join the Volscians and return to overthrow Rome. But was any such intention
as yet in his mind? In Plutarch he has adopted no definite plan before he sets
out. . . . If we turn to the parting scene in the tragedy, and let it make its own
impression, without reading into it suggestions from subsequent occurrences, I
think we feel that he is not so much undecided as that the idea has not entered
into his head. We seem to hear the very accent of sincerity in his repetition of the
maxims that erewhile he learned from his mother's own lips. He seems to hint at
seeking out new adventures and a new career in new regions beyond the reach of
Rome. It was not cautelous baits and practice that he would have to fear, but
the open violence of Aufidius if he already thought of going to Antium, and the
simile of the lonely dragon more talked of than seen would be abundantly in-
appropriate if it referred to his re-appearance at the head of the Volscian forces;
but the expression would be quite apt if he meant to make his name redoubtable
by his single prowess in strange places amidst the risks of an errant life. It is in
professed anticipation of this that he rejects the companionship which Cominius
offers. Are these utterances mere pretence? And have not his last farewells
the genuine note of cordiality and good-will? If we could imagine that he would
bring himself to address those whom he afterwards called the &lquo;dastard nobles&rquo; as
&lquo;my friends of noble touch,&rquo; it would still be impossible to believe him guilty of
cold-hearted deceit to Virgilia and Volumnia. It would not be like the former
champion of Rome to return as its assailant; but we may take it that at this
moment he is expecting to carve his way to glory in a different world and perhaps
eventually be recalled to his country, but in any case to proceed merely on the
old lines insofar as that is possible, and meanwhile to be reported of, as Menenius

<P>24. <B>Are you mankinde</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The word &lquo;mankind&rquo; is used maliciously
by the first speaker and taken perversely by the second. A <I>mankind</I> woman is
a woman with the roughness of a man, and, in an aggravated sense, a woman
ferocious, violent, and eager to shed blood. In this sense Sicinius asks Volumnia
if she be <I>mankind.</I> She takes <I>mankind</I> for a <I>human creature</I> and accordingly cries
out, &lquo;Note but this fool.&mdash;Was not a man my father?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC> compares
<I>Winter's Tale,</I> &lquo;&mdash;a mankind witch,&rquo; [II, iii, 67]. Also Jonson, <I>Silent Woman,</I>
&lquo;O mankind generation!&rquo; [V, i, ed. Gifford, p. 488. Whereon the editor has
the following note: &lquo;That is, simply masculine, always a term of reproach when
applied to a female.&rquo; Upton quotes several passages to prove that it means <I>wicked,</I>
in every one of which it means <I>mannish.</I> That the word, however, is sometimes
used in an ill sense as an augmentative for violent, outrageous, &amp;c., is certain.
Cotgrave calls some fierce animal &lquo;a mankind wild beast&rquo;; and Hall (<I>Mass.,</I>
vol. iv, p. 53) speaks of &lquo;stripes for the correction of a mankind ass.&rquo;]&mdash;<SC>W. A.
Wright</SC>: Compare Fletcher's <I>Woman Hater,</I> III, i, &lquo;Are women grown so man-
kind, must they be wooing?&rquo; And as it is unnatural for women to be like men,
&lquo;mankind&rquo; came to mean generally unnatural, monstrous, and so, fierce and cruel.&mdash;
<SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): There is a malicious and low sense in these words: Volumnia
says to Brutus, &lquo;will you be gone?&rquo; Virgilia to Sicinius, &lquo;you shall stay too,&rquo;
and continues, &lquo;I would I had the power to say so to my husband.&rquo; The tribune
understands quite well the stinging pain of these words, but he prefers to com-
ment on them in a spiteful sense, as expressing the lady's <I>kind</I>ness to <I>men,</I> since
she wants to retain him and Brutus and have her husband too. And, therefore,
he asks, &lquo;Are you man<I>kind?</I>&rquo; Volumnia has too much of feminine purity to
understand the coarse quibble, and answers in the clear sense of the word, calling
him and his father a fox. [I forbear comment on the foregoing unnecessarily coarse
interpretation; it may, however, be said in passing that no such meaning of &lquo;man-
kind&rquo; is recorded in the <I>N. E. D.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): The <I>New Eng. Dict.</I>

(used chiefly of animals), fierce, savage, keen to attack men, citing for this form

&AElig;sop is largely responsible for endowing the fox with the vice of ingratitude.
As a character in the Fables he appears more often than any other of the animals
or personages. In every case it is by some subtle trick that he outwits the others,
and, in many cases, benefits himself at their expense. In the fable of the Country-
man and the Fox, where the former deceives the huntsmen in regard to the fox's
hiding-place, and thus aids him to escape, the fox departs without a word of

the countryman pointed at his place of concealment while he said that he had
not seen the fox. Topsell, in his enumeration of the epithets applied to the fox,
does not give &lquo;ungrateful&rquo; as one of them. In the many exploits and adventures
of <I>Reynard the Fox,</I> subtlety and craft are the main characteristics of his be-
haviour; of the many accusations made against him, ingratitude is not men-

This speech is by some modern editors given to Volumnia on the ground that it

Virgilia is moved to burst out to this effect sympathetically, explaining Volumnia's
words, when the smug Sicinius is too obtuse to imagine why he ought to be in Arabia.

Coriolanus. Imagine Virgilia calling the Cat who banished her husband <I>Good

anything before but a cat, and now he's a cat to me.&rquo;

<P><B>Scene III.</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): This scene illustrates a very instructive
feature of Shakespeare's dramatic method, his side-scenes (if I may so term them).
Take two other instances: first, <I>Richard II:</I> III, iv. Coleridge said of that scene:
&lquo;Shakespeare's wonderful judgment appears in his historical plays in the introduc-
tion of some incident or other, though no way connected, yet serving to give an air
of historic fact. Thus the scene of the Queen and the Gardener realizes the thing,
makes the occurrence no longer a segment, but gives an individuality, a liveliness
and presence.&rquo; As the gardener and servants talk about the unhappy state of
England, and we hear their comments on contemporary events, those events ap-
pear much nearer to us and more vivid; we slip insensibly into the feelings of an
onlooker. A somewhat similar scene is <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> II, iv, which depicts Portia,
wife of Brutus, restlessly waiting to hear how the plot against C&aelig;sar has gone.
Such side-scenes give us the impressions of those who are watching the course of
events from a little distance, and we seem to join them as spectators; there, for
instance, we cannot help feeling something of Portia's anxiety as she waits for
news and suddenly thinks that she hears a sound from the direction of the Capitol.
And the same sort of effect is produced by <I>Macbeth,</I> II, iv. The <I>rationale</I> of such
scenes&mdash;always brief scenes&mdash;is that they just mark time to estimate and forecast.
Hitherto we have been, as it were, amid the rush of tragic incidents; now we view
them retrospectively, some way off, as when one turns to look back on a plain;
now we see them as they appear to the non-actors. We learn the immediate
after-effects of the occurrences at which we have been present, and the next stage
is foreshadowed. Thus this little scene is literally &lquo;a highway between Rome and
Antium&rquo;; and the end of the way is &lquo;Antium. Before Aufidius's house&rquo; (Scene iv.).

<P>10. <B>your Fauour is well appear'd</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This is strange nonsense.
We should read, &lquo;&mdash;is well <I>appealed,</I>&rquo; i. e., brought into remembrance.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC>
(<I>Revisal,</I> p. 424): Mr Warburton might with equal propriety have said <I>appeal'd</I>
signified anything else which first came into his head; for the English language
knows it not in his signification. Possibly the poet might have written <I>supply'd.</I>
Then the sense will be, Though I do not recollect your countenance, yet it is so
well helped out by your voice that I very well remember you.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I
would read, &lquo;is well <I>affeared.</I>&rquo; That is, <I>strengthened, attested,</I> a word used by our
author in <I>Macbeth,</I> &lquo;The title is affeer'd,&rquo; [IV, iii, 34]. To <I>repeal</I> may be <I>to bring
to remembrance,</I> but <I>appeal</I> has another meaning. [Had Johnson consulted the
texts of his predecessors he would have seen that in this reading he had been
anticipated; see <I>Text. Notes.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC>: &lquo;Appear'd&rquo; is not easily vindicated,
for we have no example of that verb's being ever us'd passively; neither ought
it to have been by the poet, who might better have given us, had he been so dis-
pos'd, &lquo;<I>but your favour</I> appears <I>by your tongue,</I>&rquo; or, I see your face in your speech,
meaning, he recollected him by it.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I would read, &lquo;is well <I>approved,</I>
i. e., your tongue confirms the evidence of your face. So in <I>Hamlet,</I> &lquo;That if
again this apparition come He may approve our eyes and speak to it,&rquo; [I, i, 28].&mdash;
<SC>Malone</SC>: If there be any corruption in the old copy, perhaps it rather is in a
preceding word. Our author might have written, &lquo;your favour <I>has</I> well appeared,&rquo;
etc., but the old text may, in Shakespeare's licentious dialect, be right. So Chaucer
uses <I>dispaired:</I> Quod Pandarus, &lquo;allas! what may this be, That thou dispaired
art,&rquo; &amp;c., [<I>Troilus and Criseyde,</I> Bk i, l. 778.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]. Singer, in support of his read-
ing <I>appayed,</I> says: &lquo;No phrase is more common in our elder language than <I>well
appayed,</I> i. e., satisfied, contented. The Volcian means to say, &ldquo;Your counte-
nance is altered, but your voice <I>perfectly satisfies</I> me.&rdquo;

<C>[10. <B>your Fauour is well appear'd</B>]</C>
<P>gestion, Singer remarks: &lquo;The correctors have not done wisely, for the phrase
should be, &ldquo;well <I>appaied,</I>&rdquo; i. e., compensated for, satisfied by. The phrase is
very common in our older language&rquo; (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> etc., p. 222).&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC>:
Steevens plausibly proposed <I>approv'd;</I> but I believe the old text is right, the more
so that there seems to me to have been a jingling quibble intended between &lquo;beard&rquo;
and &lquo;appeared.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 369): The poet probably wrote <I>has,</I>
pronounced <I>as,</I> of which the printer made &lquo;is.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, is well
shown, made apparent. If &lquo;appeared&rquo; is the true reading, it must be used in this
transitive sense, but I have not met with another example.&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 296):
The predilection for transitive verbs was, perhaps, among other causes why many
verbs which are now used intransitively were used by Shakespeare reflexively.
<I>Appear</I> is, perhaps, used reflexively in, &lquo;No, no; we hold it as a dream till it
appear itself,&rquo; <I>Much Ado,</I> I, ii, 22. &lquo;If you could wear a mind . . . and but dis-
guise That which to appear itself must not yet be,&rquo; <I>Cymb.,</I> III, iv, 148, <I>i. e.,</I> that
which as regards showing itself must not yet have any existence. Though these
passages might be, perhaps, explained without the reflexive use of &lquo;appear,&rquo; yet
this interpretation is made more probable by, &lquo;Your favour is well appear'd,&rquo;
<I>Coriol.,</I> IV, iii, 9. [See note on I, ii, 19, 20, <I>Much Ado,</I> this edition.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;
<SC>Rolfe</SC>: An explanation so improbable [as that given by Wright and Abbott]
should be admitted only as a last resort. It is better, with Schmidt (<I>Lex.</I>), to take
&lquo;appear'd&rquo; as an adjective equivalent to <I>apparent, discernible</I> (cf. dishonour'd=
dishonourable, in III, i, 78 above) or to take &lquo;is appear'd&rquo; as=has appeared.
For this latter, it is true, we have only Dogberry's authority in <I>Much Ado,</I> IV, ii,
1, but on the face of it &lquo;is appear'd&rquo; is quite as allowable as <I>is arrived, is come,</I> etc.
Abbott (&sect; 295) calls these &lquo;passive verbs&rquo;; though they are simply active &lquo;perfects&rquo;
(or &lquo;present perfects,&rquo; or whatever the grammars may call them) with the auxiliary
<I>be</I> instead of <I>have,</I> as in the French <I>est arriv&eacute;,</I> the German <I>ist gekommen,</I> etc. <I>Appa-
raitre,</I> by the way, is conjugated with <I>&ecirc;tre</I> as well as <I>avoir.</I>&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Henry Irving
Sh</I>): The sense required is, &lquo;your identity is made more apparent by your tongue,
your face is helped by your tongue&rquo;; the Volsce combines these into &lquo;your favour
is well appeared (or made apparent) by your tongue.&rquo; But as this transitive use
of &lquo;appear&rquo; is unsupported, it may be a misprint. Steevens's <I>approved</I> misses the
sense.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): It is evident that the authors of the changes in &lquo;ap-
pear'd&rquo; did not understand the Poet's use of to <I>appear.</I> Mr Joseph Crosby has
satisfied me in the matter by pointing out a good many instances where that word
is clearly used as a transitive verb, meaning to <I>show,</I> to <I>manifest,</I> to <I>make apparent,</I>
to present, &amp;c. So in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> III, iii, 3, &lquo;Appear it to your mind that,
through the sight I bear in things to come.&rquo; See also III, i, 121, 122 above.&mdash;
<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): The Folio reading might possibly mean &lquo;is made
apparent,&rquo; but &lquo;appear&rquo; is not elsewhere used in this transitive sense. The point is:
my imperfect remembrance of your &lquo;favour&rquo; or countenance is &lquo;approved&rquo; or con-
firmed by my remembrance of your voice.&mdash;<SC>Kinnear</SC> (p. 325): That is, your person
has been manifested by your speech&mdash;your tongue has told me plainly who you
are. The Folio has &lquo;<I>is</I> well appeared,&rquo; evidently a misprint, as no such construc-
tion is found in Shakespeare, nor has any instance been cited from other writers.
The correction <I>has</I> is by Malone.&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC> (p. 305): Is it not possible that, in
Shakespeare's day, the participle may have been permitted to occupy the place
of the adjective? &lquo;Is entered&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;is arrived&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;is approached&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;is become&rquo; are
</CC>

is but his birth-place.

&lquo;From our infancy We have conversed and spent our hours together,&rquo; it would
suffice to indicate that &lquo;hours&rquo; was the word here intended by the author. That
&lquo;hour&rquo; occurs again in the next line but one, far from offering an objection to the
retention of &lquo;hours&rquo; previously, lends support to our belief that the Folio word
is the author's word, because it is in accordance with Shakespeare's style thus
to repeat a word where it lends force and point to his meaning. His meaning is:
&lquo;Strange that friends, whose hours have been spent perpetually together, should
within an hour break out to bitterest enmity.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Dyce follows
Collier's MS. correction. But &lquo;hours&rquo; is used for time generally. See I, v, 7,

money?&rquo; <I>Winter's Tale,</I> I, ii, 161.
<P>28. <B>inter-ioyne their yssues</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, allow their children to
intermarry. [Rolfe also thus interprets this.]&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>):
That is, unite their designs, as Coriolanus proposes he and Aufidius shall do.&mdash;
<SC>Gordon</SC>: Interjoin their destinies, throw in their lot with each other, join fortunes.
&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): And make their children intermarry. For &lquo;issues&rquo; compare
<I>Henry VIII:</I> III, ii, 191, &lquo;our issues Who, if he live, will scarce be gentlemen.&rquo;
This illustrates, probably, the commonest sense of &lquo;issue,&rquo; but besides the obvious
one of <I>consequence,</I> and the like, the word is used for &lquo;An action, a deed (in
relation to the doer)&rquo;; see <I>N. E. D.,</I> which cites <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> III, i, 294, &lquo;there
shall I try . . . how the people take The cruel issue of these bloody men,&rquo; and
<I>Cymb.,</I> II, i, 51.
<P>28-30. <B>So with me . . . if he slay me</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>, in reference to Rowe's modi-
fication of the reading of F<SUB>4</SUB>, says: &lquo;He who reads this would think he was read-
ing the lines of Shakespeare, except that Coriolanus, being already in the town,
says he <I>will enter it.</I> The intermediate line [between ll. 28 and 29] seems to be
lost, in which, conformably to his former observation, he says that <I>he has lost his
birthplace and his loves upon</I> a petty dispute, and is trying his chance in <I>this enemy
town;</I> he then cries, turning to the house of Aufidius, <I>I'll enter if he slay me.</I> I have
preserved the common reading because it is, though faulty, yet intelligible, and
the original passage, for want of copies, cannot be restored.&rquo;
<P>29. <B>My Birth-place haue I</B>] <SC>Capell</SC>, with no further comment than calling
attention to his change of text, reads, &lquo;<I>hate</I> I&rquo;; Steevens calmly appropriates this
reading, and is unduly credited with it by Malone and all subsequent editors
except Staunton, until it was restored to its rightful author by the Cambridge
Edd. Collier, whose MS. Corrector also thus reads, remarks (ed. ii.): &lquo;Precisely
the same blunder occurs in <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> III, v, 146, where, in the Folio 1623,
&ldquo;hate&rdquo; is misprinted <I>haue;</I> in the 4tos. it is, correctly, &ldquo;hate.&rdquo; In the comedy
of <I>Patient Grissil,</I> 1603, V, ii, Sir Owen is made to say, &ldquo;And all that have scolds,
as Sir Owen does,&rdquo; &amp;c.; but he ought to say, &ldquo;And all that <I>hate</I> scolds,&rdquo; &amp;c. The
error is in the original edition, but is repeated in the imprint by the Shakespeare
Society, 1841, p. 90.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): There may be a line lost, but it
looks as if the original substitution of &lquo;have&rquo; for <I>hate</I> had caused the introduction
of <I>left</I> [in F<SUB>4</SUB>].
<P>29. <B>my loues vpon</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): For this use of &lquo;upon&rquo; with &lquo;love&rquo;
compare such phrases as to <I>dote on;</I> also, &lquo;Can thy right hand seize love upon
thy left,&rquo; <I>Ven. &amp; Ad.,</I> l. 158; and, &lquo;You know the goodness I intend upon you,&rquo;
V, i, 7.

<P>followed by a resolution. &lquo;If&rquo; properly occupies a whole foot because of the pause
made after it for emphasis. Such a pause must be made in delivering the words
whatever arrangement be adopted, and since it is important, the poet naturally
so provided for it. Coriolanus, who speaks in the low and lifeless tones of a broken
man, begins very slowly and with great solemnity, his manner forming a fine
dramatic contrast to the impatiently sharp and jerky sentences of Aufidius. It is
a telling situation if well acted, and Shakespeare, even though he was Shakespeare,
must have expended some little thought upon it. I cannot forbear drawing at-
tention to the perfect rhythm of the three lines uttered by Coriolanus. But for
the trifling inversion &lquo;not yet thou know'st&rquo; for &lquo;thou knowest not yet&rquo; the sen-
tence has the balance of natural and musical prose; indeed, if it were not marked
off into lines, many would take it for prose, as did the reviser of the Folio. Yet it
is verse of Shakespeare's very best for rhythm and balance, and the art shown
in one point in particular, the quadrisyllabic &lquo;Think me for the,&rquo; is worth noting.
He might have written &lquo;Think me the &verbar; man I &verbar; am,&rquo; but he does not. With
that sense of dramatic fitness which never ceases to amaze us, just in order that
Coriolanus may not too obviously be speaking in verse at such a moment, he
modifies the ordinary rhythm by the introduction of the single syllable &lquo;for,&rquo; and
the disguise is as complete as it need be. It would be difficult to find a better
illustration of the ideal of blank verse at which he aimed in his mature work&mdash;
prose that is also verse, and verse that is not, and yet might be, prose.
<P>56. <B>Whence . . . Thy name</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 510): Apparent lines of four accents
can sometimes be explained by giving the full pronunciation to contractions, such
as <I>s</I> for <I>eth, 'd</I> for <I>ed, 'll</I> for <I>will, 't</I> for <I>it,</I> &amp;c; or they are lines of three accents with
a detached foot. [Of the present line Abbott remarks, &lquo;But the pauses between
the abrupt questions may be a sufficient explanation.&rquo;]
<P>56. <B>What . . . Thy name?</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> gives as a corrected reading of his F<SUB>2</SUB>,
<I>wouldst thou.</I> Inasmuch as F<SUB>2</SUB> reproduces the abbreviated form of &lquo;thou&rquo; as in
F<SUB>1</SUB>, both in my copy and the Methuen facsimile, it would seem that Collier's Folio,
1632, has here an omission of this symbol, and the omission was supplied by the
MS. Corrector.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.) queries: &lquo;<I>and</I> what wouldst thou? <I>say,</I> thy name?&rquo;
In this he is, however, partly anticipated by Capell. See <I>Text. Notes.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

subject of Shakespeare's obligations to Plutarch. Nowhere, as is abundantly
clear, does our English poet make any pretence of concealing these, but adopts

<P>all, even to the very words of Sir Thomas North, with only such transposition and
alteration as may be necessary to give them a rhythmical cadence and flow. He
is too rich, and conscious that he is too rich to fear the charge of endeavoring to
pass himself off for such by the laying of his hands upon the riches of others. And
here, indeed, is what properly determines whether an author should be adjudged
by us as a plagiarist or not. The question is not what he appropriates, but what
proportion these appropriations bear to that which he has of his own; whether,
if these were withdrawn and resumed by their rightful owners, they would leave
him poor. If such would be the result, then, however few and small these may have
been, we can count him no better than a daw, passing himself off for a peacock
by the aid of feathers stuck into his plumage, and not properly his own. If, on the
other hand, all revindication by others of what is theirs would leave him essen-
tially as rich as he was before, his position in the world of poetry is not affected by
the bringing home to him of any number of these appropriations. We need not
fear to allow Shakespeare to be tried by this rule; and we can only admire that
noble confidence in his own resources which left him free without scruple to adopt
and to turn to his own uses whatever he anywhere found which was likely to prove
serviceable to the needs of his art.&rquo; [See <I>Appendix: Source of the Plot,</I> p. 636.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>59. <B>thinke me for the man I am</B>] <SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>):
We believe that the present passage affords one of those instances . . . where
Shakespeare employs a usually known form of expression while introducing his
own special word into it; thus giving the effect of the usually known expression
together with the effect and the additional meaning of his own introduced word,
so that here, &lquo;think me for the man I am,&rquo; while giving the impression of &lquo;take me
for the man I am,&rquo; conveys also the impression of &lquo;recognize me in thy thought
for the man I am.&rquo; It is this skilful method of employing conventional and well-
known phrases in an unconventional and original manner which forms one of the
merits of Shakespeare's peculiar and masterly style.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Compare
<I>Meas. For Meas.,</I> V, i, 144, &lquo;I know him for a man divine and holy.&rquo; And
<I>Henry VIII:</I> II, iv, 45:
<BQ>
&lquo;The king, your father, was reputed for<LB>
A prince most prudent.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>

<P>107. <B>Auf. Oh Martius, Martius</B>] <SC>Viehoff</SC> (<I>Sh's Coriolan.: Sh. Jahrbuch,</I>
iv, 51): Aufidius recognizes Coriolanus as soon as he casts aside his disguise;
he feigns for a short time not to know him in order to bring his hated opponent
to a circumstantial declaration, and under cover of this to form his own plan as
to how he will treat him. However warm and sincere his first speech, beginning
&lquo;Oh Martius, Martius,&rquo; may sound, it is by no means honest. The superabundance
of his expressions and his bearing towards Coriolanus as the <I>3<SUP>d</SUP> Servant</I> describes
it [ll. 199-210] plainly point to dissimulation and duplicity. It is, indeed, quite
usual with Shakespeare, if he portrays love and faith in the form of hypocrisy,
to choose the most glaring colours. As regards Aufidius it is for the first time, at
the close of the play, when his hated opponent lies dead before him, that we may
trust his words when he says:
<BQ>
&lquo;My rage is gone<LB REND=RIGHT>
And I am struck with sorrow.&rquo;&mdash;<LB>

<P>This amplification is part of Shakespeare's general treatment of the Aufidius
element, which bulks far more important in the play than in the history.&mdash;
<SC>S. Brooke</SC> (p. 239): Aufidius is the instrument of the fate of Coriolanus. He
shows the bottom of his heart in his answer to his former enemy. But his envy
is only rooted out because he sees his ancient foe in the gloom of misfortune.
Envy is too subtle a devil to leave the heart so soon, and Shakespeare knows its
fashions. Moreover, with envy ever goes hate. It is envy's boon companion. And
Aufidius's hate was deep:
<BQ>
&lquo;Where I find him, were it<LB REND=RIGHT>
At home, upon my brother's guard, even there<LB>
Against the hospitable canon, would I<LB>
Wash my fierce hand in 's heart,&rquo; [I, x, 27-30].<LB>
</BQ>
<P>Such a hatred does not die; it only sleeps for a time. We have a comfortable way
of thinking that our vices have gone when the reason of them is momentarily taken
away. It was agreeable to Aufidius at first to be magnanimous to his rival, to be
able to say &lquo;Poor Coriolanus,&rquo; and to give him half his power. That flattered
his patronising pride. But the moment Coriolanus again took precedence, envy
came back with seven more devils than before; and in the resurrection of this envy
and its results lies the rest of the drama. The envy of Aufidius is deepened by the
pride of Coriolanus, who will, even in exile, have the first place; and he uses this
insolent pride, as the Tribunes used it before, to work the ruin of Coriolanus, who
had learned nothing from all his pain and follies, who was still himself his only law,
his only right.
<P>110-112. <B>Should from . . . Martius</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> opines that the metrical arrange-
ment of these lines as given in the Folio is doubtless right, though l. 110 &lquo;is cer-
tainly mutilated.&rquo; He speaks with decided disfavor of Pope's insertion (see <I>Text.
Notes</I>). In his ed. ii. he queries: &lquo;Should from out yonder cloud speak divine
things?&rquo; quoting in support of this <I>Hamlet,</I> III, ii, 392, &lquo;yonder cloud.&rquo; Both
Wordsworth and Hudson, ed. ii, adopt Dyce's conjectured emendation in their
texts.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>Lettsom</SC> (ap. Walker, <I>Crit.,</I> iii, 209, foot-note): The arrangement

<P>121-124. <B>But that I see thee . . . my Threshold</B>] <SC>F. Harris</SC> (<I>The Man Sh.,</I>
p. 242): Aufidius was not such a friend to Coriolanus that we can take his protesta-
tion seriously. The argument is evidently a stock argument to Shakespeare; a
part of the ordinary furniture of his mind; it is like a fashionable dress of the
period&mdash;the wearer does not notice its peculiarity. The truth is, Shakespeare
found in the literature of his time, and in the minds of his contemporaries, a
fantastically high appreciation of friendship with a corresponding disdain for
love as we moderns understand it. In <I>Wit's Commonwealth,</I> 1598, we find, &lquo;The
love of men to women is a thing common and of course, but the friendship of man
to man, infinite and immortal.&rquo; Passionate devotion to friendship is a sort of
mark of the Renaissance, and the words &lquo;love&rquo; and &lquo;lover&rquo; in Elizabethan English
were commonly used for &lquo;friend&rquo; and &lquo;friendship.&rquo; Moreover, one must not for-
get that Lyly, whose euphuistic speech affected Shakespeare for years, had handled
this same incident in his <I>Campaspe,</I> where Alexander gives up his love to his rival,
Apelles. Shakespeare, not to be outdone in any loyalty, sets forth the same fan-
tastical devotion in his sonnets and plays.
<P>123, 124. <B>my wedded Mistris . . . my Threshold</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Shakespeare was
unaware that a Roman bride, on her entry into her husband's house, was prohibited
from <I>bestriding</I> his threshold; and that, lest she should even touch it, she was
always lifted over it. Thus Lucan, ii, 359, &lquo;Tralata vetuit contingere limina
planta.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): So far from proving that
Shakespeare was &lquo;unaware&rquo; of the custom in question, we think that the present
passage shows that he knew the classic ceremonial of receiving a bride at the
entrance of the bridegroom's house, of her being borne across the threshold, and
of its having been thus specially marked as the barrier which separated her from
her girlhood's condition, and which introduced her to the new sphere of a wedded
home and wedded duties. We think that Shakespeare's making Aufidius advert
thus particularly to the point when first he beheld his wedded mistress cross his
threshold, betokens the poet's perfect consciousness that there was an ancient
solemn rite connected with the circumstance; and that the word &lquo;bestride&rquo; is not
to be taken literally for &lquo;step across,&rquo; but is to be taken as meaning &lquo;pass over,&rquo;
&lquo;cross over.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: A Roman bride was carried over the threshold of
her husband's house. We know nothing of the custom of Antium in this respect,
nor did Shakespeare. [As a comment on Steevens's patronising and pompous note
this, by Wright, is, I think, much better than that by the Cowden Clarkes. Wright
plainly shows that the question does not merit serious discussion.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;Miss
<SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Aufidius is in an ecstatic mood, and must use an
energetic word for the act of entering a threshold. Besides he has already passed
from his figure of speech as to his Bride crossing his threshold to this new-beloved
warrior putting the first foot over, in the act of entrance, according to Roman
custom, without touching the threshold itself, which it was unlucky to do. Hence
brides were carried over.

<P>129. <B>thy selfe</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): Shakespeare always writes <I>thyself,</I> and

world I loved,&rquo; [<I>Tempest,</I> I, ii, 68]. This will be more apparent if an adjective

<P>150. <B>ere destroy. But come in</B>] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): Various
emendations have been proposed to avoid the octosyllabic line. But Aufidius
ends his address with a dramatic pause; the rest of the speech is spoken as the
two move towards the inner door of the hall. [To the same effect <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 484,
remarks that &lquo;the last syllable of &ldquo;destroy&rdquo; seems prolonged.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>156. <B>Enter . . . Seruingmen</B>] <SC>S. Brooke</SC> (p. 240): It is characteristic of Shake-
speare's work that he introduces here, after Aufidius and Coriolanus meet, a
humorous episode in the talk of the servants. The two leaders deceive themselves
into an apparent friendship, each ignorant of what their passions of pride and
envy are sure to produce. But the servants see much further than their masters.
They see the folly of both these great men and laugh at it, especially at that of
their master. Their talk is an excellent piece of wit, of human nature; and also
of their class, when they are mere hirelings. They have not a vestige of care for
their country, only for their own interests. &lquo;Let me have war, say I; it exceeds
peace as day does night; it's sprightly, waking, full of vent. . . . The wars for
my money. I hope to see Romans as cheap as Volscians.&rquo; And it may be that
Shakespeare meant a satire on the class feeling of the nobility of Rome by noting
something of the same kind in a different and a lower class.&mdash;<SC>Bradley</SC> (<I>Shake-
spearean Tragedy,</I> p. 61): Sometimes [towards the close of a] Tragedy we find
humourous or semi-humourous passages. On the whole such passages occur
most frequently in the early or middle part of the play, which naturally grows more
sombre as it nears the close; but their occasional introduction in the Fourth Act,
and even later, affords variety and relief, and also heightens by contrast the tragic
feelings. For example, there is a touch of comedy in the conversation of Lady
Macduff with her little boy. Purely and delightfully humourous are the talk and
behaviour of the servants in that admirable scene where Coriolanus comes dis-
guised to the house of Aufidius; of a more mingled kind is the effect of the discussion
</CC>

<P>158. <B>I had thoght</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): Shakespeare uses &lquo;I had thought&rquo;
rather than &lquo;I thought,&rquo; and quite according to rule, inasmuch as the thought was
abortive, and, conformably, the infinitive perfect follows; especially in the sense:
I meant, I was about, I had a mind, where the intention has not come to fruition;
for example, &lquo;I had thought, sir, to have held my peace,&rquo; <I>Winter's Tale,</I> [I, ii, 28];
&lquo;I had thought to have yerked him here under the ribs,&rquo; <I>Othello,</I> [I, ii, 5].
<P>158. <B>stroken</B>] Compare, for this participial formation, <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> III, i, 209,
&lquo;How like a deer, strucken by many princes, Dost thou lie here.&rquo;

&lquo;heart,&rquo; mind, conscience, etc.: To suggest to one <I>that;</I> in unfavourable sense, to
misgive. Also to prompt (one) <I>to</I> do something. Also, quasi-impersonal, <I>It
gives me</I> = I have a foreboding. 1551. Robinson tr. <I>More's Utopia:</I> I. (Arber),
67, &lquo;To speke truelye as my minde geueth me.&rquo; [Compare also <I>Henry VIII:</I>
V, iii, 109, &lquo;My mind gave me, In seeking tales and informations Against this
man. . . . Ye blew the fire that burns ye.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Wright</SC> compares I, ix, 68, &lquo;To us
that give you truly&rquo;; but this, I think, is not strictly parallel to the present pas-

<P>191. <B>Come we are fellowes and friends</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: As fellows and good friends

Servant, who a short while before had asserted that Aufidius was worth six of
Marcius, now that he finds which way the wind is blowing and that he need not be
afraid of being betrayed to his master, turns round and admits that, after all, his
master was no match for Marcius.

<P>200. <B>set at vpper end o'th'Table</B>] &lquo;In an Elizabethan mansion the hall, where
the meals took place, was furnished with an upper table capable of extension,
known as a draw-table, at which the family sat, chairs being set for the master
and mistress of the house and stools for the younger members of the household
and ordinary guests; along the sides of the hall were ranged plain long tables and
forms for the servants and poorer dependents. When guests could not find room
at the high table, the upper ends of the side tables were used for their accommoda-
tion, a salt being placed where the distinction of class commenced.&rquo; Percy

If, as Malone contends, the Servant was not intended to speak absolute nonsense,

<C>[228, 229. <B>full of Vent</B>]</C>
<P>furnishes opportunity for a man to sow his wild oats.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;Vent&rquo; is
<I>voice, utterance.</I>&mdash;<SC>Baynes</SC> (<I>Edinburgh Review,</I> Oct., 1892, p. 339): The phrase
&lquo;full of vent&rquo; has so perplexed the critics that more than one has proposed to sub-
stitute for it &lquo;full of vaunt.&rquo; The Folio text is, however, perfectly accurate, and
peculiarly expressive, although it has never yet been correctly explained. The
only explanation attempted is that of Johnson, repeated by subsequent editors,
that &lquo;full of vent&rquo; means &lquo;full of rumour, full of materials of [for] discourse.&rquo; This,
however, is a mere conjecture, and not a happy one, as it altogether misses the
distinctive meaning of the phrase. &lquo;Vent&rquo; is a technical term in hunting to express
the scenting of the game by the hounds employed in the chase. Both noun and
verb are habitually used in this sense. Their exact meaning and use will be made
clear by an extract or two from Turberville's translation of Du Fouilloux, the popular
manual of hunting in Shakespeare's day. The first extract refers to the wiles and
subtleties of the hart when keenly pressed in the chase: &lquo;therewithall he wil lie flat
downe vpon his bellie in some of their layres, and so let the houndes ouershoote
him: and bicause they should have no sent of him, nor vent him, he wil trusse
all his .iiii. feete vnder his belly and wil blow and breath vpon ye grounde in some
moyst place: in such sorte y<SUP>t</SUP> I haue seene the houndes passe by such an Harte
within a yeard of him and neuer vent him,&rquo; [<I>Booke of Hunting,</I> Tudor and Stuart
Library, p. 111]. Further on the author, speaking of the hart, says again ex-
pressly, &lquo;When he smelleth or venteth anything, we say he hath this or that in the
wind.&rquo; In the same way, when the hound vents anything, he pauses to verify the
scent, and then, full of eager excitement, strains in the leash to be after the game
that is thus perceived to be a-foot. The following extract from the rhyming report
of a huntsman upon sight of a hart in pride of grease illustrates this:
<BQ>
&lquo;Then if my Prince, demaund what head he beare,<LB>
I answere thus, with sober words and cheare:<LB>
My liege I went, this morning on my quest,<LB>
My hound did sticke, and seemde to vent some beast,&rquo; [Op. cit., p. 96].<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The use of the noun is exemplified in another hunting rhyme, or huntsman's soliloquy,
entitled &lquo;The Blazon of the Hart,&rquo; which is of special interest from the vividness of
the picture it brings before us:
<BQ>
&lquo;And whiles I seeke his slotte where he hath fedde<LB>
The sweete byrdes sing, to cheare my drowsie hedde<LB>
And when my Hounde, doth streyne vpon good vent,<LB>
I must confesse, the same dothe me content,&rquo; [p. 60].<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The technical meaning and use of the word in these passages is sufficiently clear,
and it will be seen how happily Shakespeare employs it. To strain at the lyam
or leash &lquo;upon good vent&rquo; is in Shakespeare's phrase to be &lquo;full of vent,&rquo; or in
other words, keenly excited, full of pluck and courage, of throbbing energy and
impetuous desire, in a word, full of all the kindling stir and commotion of antic-
ipated conflict. This is not only in harmony with the passage, but gives point
and force to the whole description. War is naturally personified as a trained
hound roused to animated motion by the scent of game, giving tongue, and strain-
ing in the slips at the near prospect of the exciting chase. This explanation justifies
the reading of the Folios, &lquo;<I>sprightly walking,</I> audible, full of vent,&rquo; or at least

boldly, &lquo;vent is voice, utterance.&rquo; But the previous epithet, &lquo;audible,&rquo; gives this
feature of the description &lquo;vent,&rquo; referring not to sound at all, but to the quick
perception of the game, and the signs of eagerness, such as kindled eye, dilated

advance arising from the discovery of good vent as compared with the dissatisfied
