nifies &lquo;flat, insipid,&rquo; &lquo;full of vent&rquo; would seem to be either effervescent, working,
ready to burst the cask, or full of scent. Cotgrave, indeed, gives &lquo;Odorement . . .
a smell, waft, sent, vent&rquo;; but it does not appear from this that &lquo;vent&rquo; means &lquo;scent&rquo;

editors. The explanation now in favour is that &lquo;vent&rquo; is a hunting term. A
hound was said to &lquo;vent&rquo; the game when he smelt him in the wind. War would
then be likened to a pack of hounds in full cry; &lquo;audible&rquo; would express their cry;
and &lquo;full of vent&rquo; would mean &lquo;full of the spirit of the chase.&rquo; This is attractive
but far-fetched. It is obtained by (1) singling out for over-emphasis one term of
the four, and (2) entirely neglecting the antithesis in the four terms that follow

who proposed the explanation may be pardoned their over-emphasis, but not
their neglect of the whole structure of the passage. If &lquo;mulled&rquo; corresponds to
&lquo;full of vent,&rquo; as it must, then &lquo;full of vent&rquo; can have nothing to do with hunting.&mdash;

<P>funeral banquet.&rdquo; In this uncertainty as to the figures intended I have preferred

spritely, wide awake, keen of ear, so, possibly, it is full of utterance, vents much;
compare &lquo;What his breast forges, that his tongue must vent,&rquo; III, i, 316. Others
are confident of allusion to hunting in the technical term <I>vent,</I> and some trace a
personification of war as a trained hound through the series of expressions. It is
true that Shakespeare makes war a dog elsewhere, but in plain language. Mr
Craig, in the <I>Little Quarto Shakespeare,</I> combating this idea, thinks that &lquo;&ldquo;full of
vent&rdquo; may mean, very efficacious to clear the country of its surplus population,&rquo;
and refers to I, i, 243, 244. This is given here as his only recorded interpretation
of the passage, but with emphatic dissent. Wright sees an apposition in the epi-
thets given to war and peace respectively, taken in reverse order. A correspond-
ence may exist, but it may also be only apparent or accidental. Such exactitude
is in strong contrast with what follows. That which is sprightly, walking, etc.,
may indeed destroy men, but apoplexy, lethargy, or anything sleepy and insensible
may be acquitted of any activity in getting bastards.
<P>229-231. <B>Peace, is a very Apoplexy . . . of men</B>] <SC>H. Coleridge</SC> (ii, 179):
&lquo;Plague of this dead peace,&mdash;this bastard-breeding, lousy, idleness,&rquo; Fletcher,
<I>Mad Lover,</I> Act I. By these, and many other scattered allusions in the plays of
the period, we may conjecture that the long shutting of the Temple of Janus by
the <I>Rex Pacificus</I> was far from popular. Yet there can be no doubt that in pre-
serving peace, and neglecting the military, he acted most beneficially for the
people, though ruinously for his family and the regal power.&mdash;<SC>Bucknill</SC> (<I>Medical
Knowledge,</I> etc., p. 210): The activity and vigour of a state of war is paradoxically
preferred to peace, as if the former were a state of health, and the latter a disease.
Hamlet makes peace the time of health, though of plethoric health which ripens
into war. Apoplexy is here confounded with lethargy, which is described as pro-
ceeding by the degrees&mdash;mulled, deaf, sleepy, insensible. The term &lquo;apoplexy&rquo; is
used rather loosely by Shakespeare in many places, but always to signify an
affection of the brain; whereas modern physicians have most absurdly used the
same term for sudden diseases of other organs, and thus speak and write of apo-
plexy of the lungs and apoplexy of the liver.&mdash;Br. <SC>Nicholson</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I>
16 Oct., 1886, p. 305): The phrasing [Peace is a very apoplexy, lethargy] does not
seem to me idiomatic English. To make it ordinary idiomatic English we must,
I think, do one of two things. Either with Walker insert <I>a</I> before &lquo;lethargy,&rquo;
and also punctuate <I>apoplexy;</I> this makes the clause from &lquo;lethargy&rquo; an explanation
of &lquo;apoplexy&rquo;; and it may be remarked that such an explanation agrees very exactly
with Falstaff's, &lquo;This apoplexy is, I take it, a kind of lethargy; . . . a kind of
sleeping in the blood&rquo; (<I>2 Henry IV:</I> I, ii, 104-5). Or we might read <I>apoplexy-
lethargy,</I> the lethargy consequent on an apoplectic attack. And with reference to
either suggestion it should be remembered that in those days &lquo;apoplexy&rquo; did not
bring to mind those ideas with which it is now associated. Thus Andrew Boord,

<P>229. <B>mull'd</B>] <SC>Hanmer</SC>: That is, softened and dispirited, as wine is when burnt
and sweetened. Latin: <I>Mollitus.</I>&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): The only instance in Shake-
speare where this word is used, and I agree, therefore, with Walker's emendation,
<I>mute.</I> [Leo does not, however, adopt it in his text.&mdash;<SC>Ed.]</SC>&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>):
That is, <I>softened, drowsified</I> like mulled wine, which is heated, spiced, and sweetened.
So, perhaps, especially if contrasted with &lquo;full of vent,&rquo; but the <I>N. E. D.</I> cites this
passage under a rare obsolete verb &lquo;of obscure origin,&rquo; meaning: To dull, stupefy,
together with another from Cotton's <I>Poems,</I> 1689, p. 96, &lquo;Till ale which crowns
all such pretences, Mull'd them again into their senses.&rquo; It is, however, difficult
to give this sense of dull, stupefy to Cotton's word even ironically. It occurs in a
<I>Burlesque upon the Great Frost</I> and refers to two sides at foot-ball who were literally
frozen stiff, &lquo;With a good handsome space between 'em.&rquo; This points rather to
the sense <I>softened.</I> The <I>N. E. D.,</I> in discussing the origin of <I>mull</I> (to mull ale,
etc.), says: &lquo;Another unsupported conjecture is that the original sense may have
been &ldquo;to soften,&rdquo; &ldquo;render mild&rdquo; (compare Dutch <I>mul,</I> soft), of which Mull [to dull,
stupefy] might be another application.&rquo; The Cotton passage seems to favour that
conjecture.

<C>[3. <B>His remedies are tame, the present peace</B>]</C>
<P>&lquo;i'the&rquo; for &lquo;the,&rquo; the third editor has struck out an appearance of sense from what
before had no shadow of it; but still it is no more than <I>appearance</I> till we can deter-
mine with some sort of certainty what the poet intended by &lquo;his remedies are
tame,&rquo; for the words have more aspects than one. Without ent'ring upon what
may be made of them, it is best to come at once to what the editor thinks their
true meaning. This, as he apprehends, is pointed out by the words that precede
them, &lquo;neither need we fear him&rquo;; his return, and the revenge that would follow
it, were what they had to fear; it is these, therefore, and the instruments that might
bring them about, which the Tribune calls Coriolanus's &lquo;remedies,&rquo; adding that
they were &lquo;tame&rquo; now, that is, still, and unlikely to have any effect.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>,
in reference to Johnson's interpretation, says, &lquo;I rather suppose the meaning of
Sicinius to be this: &ldquo;His remedies are tame,&rdquo; i. e., <I>ineffectual</I> in times of peace like
these. When the people were in commotion, his friends might have strove to
remedy his disgrace by tampering with them; but now, neither wanting to employ
his bravery nor remembering his former actions, they are unfit subjects for the
factions to work upon.&rquo; As regards Mason's suggestion, <I>lame,</I> Steevens adds, &lquo;but
the epithets &ldquo;tame&rdquo; and &ldquo;wild&rdquo; were, I believe, designedly opposed to each
other.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: Omission is not, perhaps, the only defect in the line; the word
&lquo;remedies&rquo; is very equivocal.&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC>: [Instead of Theobald's insertion]
I think it more in keeping with the purport of the passage, and far better for its
rhythm, to strike out &lquo;we&rquo; in l. 5, where it not only breaks down an already well-
laden verse, but substitutes a feeble and unnatural thought for one forcible and
natural. It was in the &lquo;peace and quietness of the people&rquo; that the Tribunes had
their supposed triumph over the Patricians, who had hoped to see &lquo;dissentious
numbers pestering the streets,&rquo; but whom this peace and quietness forced to blush
that the world went well. This is entirely lost if the Tribunes are made to say
that they make Coriolanus's friends blush. The rhythm of ll. 2 and 3 is also much
more Shakespearian with a full pause after &lquo;tame.&rquo; This play is very carelessly
printed in the Folio; and I believe that &lquo;we&rquo; crept in merely by the erroneous
supposition of a printer that a new sentence began at &lquo;Heere,&rquo; and that a nomina-
tive was consequently required for &lquo;make.&rquo; [Reference to the <I>Text. Notes,</I> l. 5,
will show that this reading is substantially&mdash;though White does not say so&mdash;
Hanmer's. White's only change being a shifting of the comma. See also note
by Hudson, l. 5.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>: Let him do his worst; he is harmless so long
as the people, lately so turbulent, are orderly and contented, and give his friends
no pretext for recalling him.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC> [adopting Theobald's reading]:
The sense is, The means which Coriolanus may take to redress his wrongs are no
longer an object of fear while the people are peaceable and quiet.&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC>
(p. 306): What is easier than to construe this line thus, His remedies are tame,
the present [is] peace and quietness of the people, which [that is, who] were before
in wild hurry. On the one hand, the substantive verb is dropped in the second
sentence, because &lquo;are&rquo; has been expressed in the first; on the other hand, &lquo;the
present&rquo; is used as a noun substantive, of which there is no lack of examples. Thus
<I>Tempest,</I> I, i, 57, the substantive verb is left to be understood, albeit it had not
been previously expressed, as &lquo;The king and prince at prayers&rquo;; and in the same
play, I, i, 24, we have, &lquo;to work the peace of <I>the present.</I>&rquo; Yet in this passage
Theobald must needs interpolate &lquo;i&rquo; before &lquo;the present,&rquo; and all break after him
like a flock of sheep.

<P>5. <B>Heere do we make</B>] <SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): Here I am induced by clear reasons,
both of logic and of metre, to adopt the reading of Hanmer. Some change is
evidently required in order to make any sense at all of the passage, and Theobald's
change [in l. 3] saves neither the metre nor the logic. In this present line &lquo;we&rquo;
is palpably redundant in verse and paralogical in sense; the speaker's drift being
not that <I>we,</I> the Tribunes, but that the peace and quietness of the people, make
the Patricians ashamed of having predicted popular commotions as the conse-
quences of the hero's banishment. [Hudson has, however, adopted White's punc-
tuation of Hanmer's reading.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>8. <B>pestring</B>] <SC>W. S. Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.,</I> ii, 351): <I>To pester</I> a place or person, for <I>to
crowd, to throng</I> them. [The present line quoted.] In the following passages we
may see how the change of meaning originated: <I>Hamlet,</I> I, ii, 22, &lquo;He hath not
fail'd to pester us with messages.&rquo; <I>1 Henry IV:</I> I, iii, 50, &lquo;To be so pestered with
a popinjay.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The French &lquo;<I>Empestrer</I>&rquo; is explained by Cotgrave,
&lquo;To pester, intricate, intangle, trouble, incomber.&rquo;
<P>13. <B>'Tis he . . . of late</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 498) quotes this as an example of an ap-
parent Alexandrine, suggesting that the &lquo;O&rquo; might coalesce with the following
vowel.

<P>41. <B>affecting one sole Throne</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): The Tribunes back each

<P>41, 42. <B>without . . . so</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 506) quotes: &lquo;Without assistance. <I>Men.</I>
I think not so,&rquo; as an example of a Shakespearian line of four accents; as will be
seen, this is, however, Theobald's versification, not Shakespeare's.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>41. <B>without assist&atilde;ce</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is without <I>assessors;</I> without any other

text is slightly corrupted, and the versification neglected. Read:

<S>Sic.</S> And affecting one sole throne,<LB>

<S>Men.</S> Nay, I think not so.&rquo;<LB>

<P>[As will be seen, Hanmer's text reads <I>assistants,</I> but inasmuch as Theobald did not
adopt this conjecture in either edition, or mention it in his notes, Hanmer doubt-
less made the change independently.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC> also opines that: &lquo;It is not

<I>occurrence.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>43, 44. <B>We should . . . found it so</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Perhaps the author wrote, We
should <I>have</I> by this, or <I>have</I> found it so. Without one or other of these insertions
the construction is imperfect.&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 415): In this anomalous passage &lquo;should&rquo;
is treated as though it were &lquo;should have,&rquo; owing to the introduction of the con-
ditional sentence with &lquo;had.&rquo; So <I>Richard III:</I> III, v, 56, &lquo;We would have had
you heard.&rquo;
<P>43. <B>our Lamention</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 219): <I>Your, our, their,</I> &amp;c., are often used in
their old signification, as genitives, where we should use &lquo;of <I>you,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. [Compare
I, ix, 45, &lquo;At your only choice.&rquo;]
<P>49, 50. <B>a Slaue . . . Reports</B>] For other examples of this omission of the rela-

<P>90-92. <B>Good Martius . . . vnlikely</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 514): Interruptions are some-

<P>90. <B>Good Martius</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emendations,</I> etc., p. 361): &lquo;<I>God</I> Marcius&rquo;
is the emendation [of the MS. Corrector], which adds vastly to the force of the
passage, and is most accordant with the character of the speaker; &lquo;good Marcius&rquo;
is comparatively tame and unmeaning. Cominius soon afterwards, talking of
Coriolanus, says, &lquo;He is their <I>god,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. Brutus could hardly intend to call Marcius
&lquo;good&rquo; when adverting to his reported return; but he applies the word <I>god</I> to
him in derision, as if Coriolanus were in a manner worshipped by a certain class
of his admirers.&mdash;<SC>Ibid.</SC> (<I>Shakespeare,</I> ed. ii.): Precisely in the same spirit Ulysses,
in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> I, iii, 169, speaks of &lquo;god Achilles,&rquo; but it is not there tamely
printed &lquo;<I>good</I> Achilles.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.): In my former edition I too hastily adopted
the reading of Mr Collier's MS. Corrector, &lquo;<I>God</I> Marcius,&rquo; and I have now to regret
that I should have been partly the cause of Mr Grant White's adopting that errone-
ous reading. [White remarked that he accepted it &lquo;with some hesitation.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. i.): We adopt the change from Mr Collier's second folio
partly because the magnificent sneer expressed by it is in Shakespeare's best manner.
Of course &lquo;<I>god</I> Marcius&rquo; is spoken ironically. [In his ed. ii. Hudson silently adopts
the Folio reading. Under Dyce's castigation the sneer had, perhaps, lost some of
its magnificence.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>[ed. Hughs, p. 162]. <I>Butterfly</I> (as I am informed) is pronounced butterflee (<I>u</I>
as <I>oo</I> in <I>took</I>) in Lancashire; and so also, I doubt not, in Yorkshire, as <I>fly</I> in that
county is pronounced <I>flee.</I> I know not if the difference of spelling which the folio
exhibits in the two words of <I>Coriolanus, Butter-flies</I> and <I>Flyes,</I> indicates anything.
[<SC>Herford</SC> (<I>Eversley ed.</I>) in a note signed simply L. makes the same suggestion as
Walker in regard to the pronunciation of &lquo;butterfly,&rquo; citing in illustration the
above passage from <I>The Muses' Elysium.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC>: Compare
the picture of Coriolanus's child in I, iii, 63, 64.&mdash;<SC>Ulrici</SC> (<I>Zus&auml;tze und Berichti-
gungen zu Coriolanus,</I> p. 179): I have adopted in the text Mason's [Capell's]
emendation <I>sheep,</I> since I am convinced that &lquo;flies&rquo; is a misprint, induced by the
word &lquo;butterflies&rquo; directly above it. Cominius wishes to say: The Volscians fol-
low Coriolanus with the very same confidence in the war against us as do boys
wage war on butterflies, or butchers on sheep. To this undoubted meaning of
the passage &lquo;flies&rquo; is so inconsistent that it can without doubt be nothing other
than a misprint.
<P>123. <B>voyce of occupation</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Occupation&rquo; is here used for <I>mechanics,</I>
men occupied in daily business. So again in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> I, ii, &lquo;An I had been a man
of any occupation,&rquo; &amp;c. So Horace uses <I>artes</I> for <I>artifices,</I> &lquo;Urit enim fulgore suo,
qui pr&aelig;gravat artes Infra se positas,&rquo; [<I>Epist.,</I> II, i, l. 13].&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: The word
&lquo;crafts&rquo; is used in the like manner where Menenius says, l. 147, &lquo;&mdash;you have made
fair hands, You and your crafts.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Verplanck</SC>: A phrase of contempt in the
mouth of a military aristocrat.
<P>124. <B>breath of Garlicke-eaters</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: To smell of garlick was once such a
brand of vulgarity that garlic was a food forbidden to an ancient order of Spanish
knights mentioned by Guevara.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: So in <I>Meas. for Meas.,</I> &lquo;&mdash;he would
mouth with a beggar, though she smelled brown bread and garlic,&rquo; [III, ii, 195].&mdash;
<SC>Steevens</SC>: From the following passage in Dekker's <I>If it be not good Play, the Devil
is in it,</I> 1612, it should appear that garlic was once much used in England, and
afterwards as much out of fashion: &lquo;Fortune favours nobody but Garlicke nor
Garlicke neither now: yet she has strong reason to love it: for tho Garlicke made
her smell abhominably in the nostrills of the gallants, yet she had smelt and stuncke
worse but for garlicke,&rquo; [<I>Works,</I> ed. Pearson, iii, 324].&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): <SC>Steevens</SC>
was not aware that the old dramatist referred to a jig which had been brought out

<P>126. <B>As Hercules . . . Mellow Fruite</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Letter to</I> Warburton, Feb.

<P>130. <B>Regions</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): &lquo;All the <I>legions</I>&rquo; in the corr. fo. 1632; but we
adhere to the old and received text, no change being necessary.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. i.):
The MS. correction is very plausible, for it is doubtful if the old text is to be ex-
plained by what Aufidius says, &lquo;All places yield to him ere he sits down,&rquo; IV, vii,
30; here Cominius, eager to mortify the Tribunes, may be exaggerating the suc-
cesses of Coriolanus; and elsewhere the folio has <I>legions</I> misprinted &lquo;regions.&rquo;
[Dyce refers to <I>1 Henry VI:</I> V, iii, 11, where Warburton conjectures we should
read <I>legions.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Ibid.</SC> (ed. ii.): I have felt strongly inclined to adopt the MS.
correction, but Mr W. N. Lettsom remarks that &lquo;the Romans had no army on
foot, and consequently no <I>legions.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC>: Considering the context,
&lquo;<I>smilingly</I> revolt,&rquo; &lquo;<I>valiant</I> ignorance,&rquo; and &lquo;constant <I>fools,</I>&rquo; and that the Folio has
twice elsewhere the misprint &lquo;regions&rquo; for <I>legions,</I> I have little hesitation in accept-
ing the reading of Mr Collier's folio of 1632.

<P>141-143. <B>they charg'd him . . . And therein shew'd</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Their <I>charge</I>

like enemies.</I> I read <I>shew,</I> not <I>shewed, like enemies.</I>&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC> (<I>Var. 1778</I>): The
old copy has &lquo;charg'd&rquo; and &lquo;shew'd.&rquo; If one is changed, so ought the other. I
read, &lquo;They<I>'d charge</I> him&mdash;and therein <I>shew.</I>&rquo; [As Malone did not repeat this in
his own edition it may be considered as withdrawn.]&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I>
etc., p. 257): There can be no doubt but this passage, as it stands, is very inac-
curate, and that Malone's amendment will correct every error, and render it
grammatical; but it appears to me that the inaccuracy is that of the author him-
self, and, of course, should not be amended, as one of a similar nature occurs in
Act II, sc. ii, ll. 17-19.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;They charg'd, and therein show'd&rquo; has here
the force of &lquo;They would charge, and therein show.&rquo; [See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 361.]&mdash;
<SC>Lettsom</SC> (ap. <SC>Dyce</SC> ii.): Plutarch says that when Coriolanus was besieging Lavinium
with the Volsces, the Roman people were desirous to annul the decree of his ban-
ishment, but the Senate then maintained it. Possibly Shakespeare may here
allude to that circumstance, though it is not mentioned in the play.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden
Sh.</I>): That is, they would be attacking him in the same way as those that had
deserved his hate, and so doing would be confused with them (<I>lit.</I> would seem like
enemies). The sense of charge presents some difficulty; probably it is a shade of
the sense <I>command, enjoin upon,</I> as in <I>All's Well,</I> IV, ii, 56, &lquo;Now will I charge
you in the band of truth. . . . Remain there but an hour,&rquo; etc.; <I>A Lover's Complaint,</I>
220, &lquo;Nature hath charged me that I hoard them not.&rquo;

<P>146. <B>You haue made faire hands</B>] <SC>Whitelaw</SC>: Ironically, &lquo;You have not soiled
your hands at all.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): You have done a fine piece of work,
you have done your work well. So in <I>Henry VIII.</I> the Chamberlain says to the
Porters, &lquo;Ye have made a fine hand, fellows; There's a trim rabble let in,&rquo; [V,
iv, 74]. Not, as Whitelaw takes it, ironically.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC>: So in <I>Fortune by Land and
Sea</I> (Pearson's <I>Heywood,</I> vi, 423), &lquo;We have made a fair hand on't, have we not?&rquo;
The ominous sense here illustrated is related to one of those recorded as still
existent provincially. See <I>Eng. Dialect Dict.,</I> &lquo;<I>Make a hand,</I> to spoil, waste,
destroy.&rquo;
<P>147. <B>You and your Crafts</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes and Emendations,</I> etc., p. 361):
On the authority of the Old Corrector we ought unquestionably to read <I>handycrafts</I>
for &lquo;crafts.&rquo; This change completes the defective line, and shows that Menenius
uses the introductory expression, &lquo;You have made fair hands,&rquo; in order that he
may follow it up by the contemptuous mention of <I>handycrafts.</I>&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC>: No; the
old text is quite right. To &lquo;make fair hands&rquo; (or &lquo;a fine hand&rquo;) is a common enough
expression (so <I>Henry VIII:</I> V, iv, 74); and the change of &lquo;crafts&rquo; to <I>handycrafts</I>
is unnecessary for the sense, because <I>manual</I> labor is sufficiently implied in the
former word. As to &lquo;the metre&rquo;&mdash;the Corrector's alteration deranges it entirely,
&lquo;You and your crafts! <I>you've</I> crafted fair!&rquo; make up a perfect line with &lquo;<I>You've</I>
brought,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Browne</SC> (p. 18) and <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 486) propose, <I>metri gratia,</I> that
&lquo;crafts&rquo; be here pronounced as a dissyllable <I>cra-afts,</I> since &lquo;an emphatic monosyl-
lable is often made to take the place of an entire foot.&rquo;
<P>147. <B>crafted</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Menenius is a great word-maker. We are
already indebted to him for &lquo;empiricutic,&rquo; &lquo;fidiused,&rquo; &lquo;conspectuities.&rquo;
<P>149, 150. <B>A Trembling vpon Rome . . . of helpe</B>] <SC>Whitelaw</SC>: A panic, the
like of which&mdash;so desperate as this is&mdash;never was. Or we might read, referring
&lquo;so incapable of help&rquo; to &lquo;Rome, such as 'twas never&rquo;; such as = such that, a
usage not ungrammatical when Shakespeare wrote.

<P>182-184. <B>Y'are . . . to the Capitoll</B>] <SC>Bayfield</SC> (p. 189): Editors divide thus:
<BQ>
&lquo;Ye're goodly things, you voices.&mdash;You have made<LB>

<P>But we shall get nearer to the original form of the passage if we read and divide
thus:
<BQ>
&lquo;<S>Com.</S> You are &verbar; goodly &verbar; thing, you &verbar; voices.<LB>
<S>Men.</S> You have &verbar; made good &verbar; work,<LB>
You and your &verbar; cry. Shall &verbar; <I>we</I> to the &verbar; Capitol?&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>A quadrisyllabic (&lquo;voices. You have&rquo;) divided between two speakers is extremely
common, and when we restore &lquo;we&rquo; and give it the stress required by the context,
we do not credit the poet with a line of which he would have been ashamed.
<P>184. <B>cry</B>] See III, iii, 146.
<P>184. <B>Shal's</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 215): &lquo;Shall,&rquo; originally meaning necessity or obligation,
and therefore not denoting an action on the part of the subject, was used in the
South of England as an impersonal verb. So Chaucer, &lquo;us oughte,&rquo; and we also
find &lquo;as <I>us</I> wol,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> &lquo;as it is pleasing to us.&rquo; Hence in Shakespeare: &lquo;Say, where
shall's lay him?&rquo; <I>Cymbeline,</I> IV, ii, 233; &lquo;Shall's have a play of this?&rquo; <I>Ibid.,</I> V,
v, 228; &lquo;Shall's attend you there?&rquo; <I>Wint. Tale,</I> I, ii, 178; [also the present line].

<P>10-14. <B>He beares himself . . . be amended</B>] <SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 616): It is said
that for his revenge Coriolanus condescends to fawn upon Aufidius and the Volscians.
This is not very plausible. His speech of greeting certainly shows no servile
propitiation, and, according to Tullus, it is conspicuously absent in his subse-
quent behaviour. [The present lines quoted.] And elsewhere Tullus complains
that his guest has &lquo;waged him with his countenance,&rquo; [V, vi, 45]. The only ground
for saying that he paid court to the Volces is alleged in Tullus' speech that just
precedes this accusation of haughtiness to himself, [V, vi, 27-30]. But the speaker
is an enemy, and an enemy who has to account for the disagreeable circumstance
that his own adherents have gone over to his rival, and who, moreover, at the
time is looking for a plea that &lquo;admits of good construction.&rquo; There is nothing
that we see or hear of Coriolanus elsewhere that supports the charge.
<P>10. <B>more proudlier</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: We have already had in this play &lquo;more worthier,&rquo;
[III, i, 146], as in <I>Timon,</I> IV, i, 36, we have &lquo;more kinder&rquo;; yet the modern edi-
tors read here &lquo;more <I>proudly.</I>&rquo; [See <I>Text. Notes;</I> and for other examples, <SC>Abbott</SC>,
&sect; 11.]
<P>13. <B>Changeling</B>] <SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Here, in sense, <I>shifter, inconstant, turn-coat,</I>
as in <I>1 Henry IV:</I> V, i, 76, &lquo;Of fickle changelings and poor discontents,&rquo; etc. The
expression is found in various places in North's <I>Plutarch,</I> e. g., <I>Alcibiades</I> (ed. 1612,
p. 210): &lquo;But he that had inwardly seene his naturall doings, and goodwill indeed
lye naked before him, would certainly have vsed this common saying, This woman
is no changeling&rquo;; and <I>Agesilaus,</I> p. 620: &lquo;For he was no changeling, but the selfe
same man in state and condition that he was before he took his iourny.&rquo; See also
Gabriel Harvey, <I>Trimming of Thomas Nash</I> (ed. Grosart, iii, 16), &lquo;For indeed
I saw you to be no changeling.&rquo;

<P>19-28. <B>I vnderstand thee well . . . our account</B>] <SC>Craig</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): What did
Aufidius mean by this? After a very careful study of the Life of Coriolanus, in
North, I am inclined to think that this is the explanation: The passage in Shake-
speare's mind seems to have been that wherein it appears, that when the ambas-
sadors came from Rome the first time to treat of peace, Coriolanus demanded that
the Romans should &lquo;restore unto the Volsces, all their landes and citties they
had taken from them in former warres; and, moreover, that they should geve them
the like honour and freedome of Rome, as they had before geven to the Latines.&rquo;
He gave them thirty days for answer and &lquo;departed his armie out of the territories
of the Romaines,&rquo; and the relation goes on: &lquo;This was the first matter wherewith
the Volsces (that most envied Martius glorie and authoritie) dyd charge Martius
with. Among those Tullus was chief; who though he had receyved no private in-
jurie or displeasure of Martius, yet the common faulte and imperfection of man's
nature wroght in him, and it grieved him to see his own reputation blemished,&rquo;
etc. A little later it continues: &lquo;From hence they derived all their first accusations
and secret murmurings against Martius. For private captaines . . . gave it out
that the removing of the campe was a manifest treason,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>MacCallum</SC>
(p. 619): This is, no doubt, suggested by the incident of the thirty days' truce,
of which Plutarch makes so much and which Shakespeare totally suppresses. But
the vague reference becomes all the more pregnant when we are to understand
that Coriolanus has, at unawares and against his purpose, granted some little
concessions to the victims of his wrath. That Aufidius' statement has some founda-
tion is made probable by the words of the Antium Lord, who is no enemy to
Marcius, but reproaches Tullus with his murder and reverently bewails his death:
<BQ>
&lquo;What faults he made before the last, I think,<LB>
Might have found easy fines,&rquo; V, vi, 79.<LB>
</BQ>
<P>Faults, then, from the Volscian point of view, he has committed in the opinion
of a sympathetic and impartial onlooker, which means that as a Roman he has
shown forbearance.

gested; but the betrayal of the Antiates by Coriolanus causes Aufidius to drop
the personal element, and merge it in the more serious charge of treason.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>30. <B>All places yeelds to him,</B> etc.] <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Notes on Coriol.</I>): I have al-
ways thought this, in itself so beautiful speech, the least explicable from the
mood and full intention of the speaker of any in the whole works of Shakespeare,
</CC>
<PB N=474>
<HE>474 <I>THE TRAGEDIE OF</I> [<SC>act iv, sc.</SC> vii.</HE>
<FHL>
<CC>
<C>[30. <B>All places yeelds to him ere he sits downe</B>]</C>
<P>I cherish the hope that I am mistaken, and that, becoming wiser, I shall discover
some profound excellence in that in which I now appear to detect an imperfection.&mdash;
<SC>Verplanck</SC>, in answer to the foregoing remark, says: &lquo;I cannot perceive the diffi-
culty; the speech corresponds with the mixed character of the speaker, too gen-
erous not to see and admire his rival's merit, yet not sufficiently magnanimous
to be free from the malignant desire of revenging himself upon his rival for that
very superiority.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 657): Here there are puzzling expressions in
detail, but they have, on the whole, been satisfactorily explained, and it is not to
them that Coleridge refers. (Of these, the most perplexing to me is the distinction
Shakespeare makes between &lquo;the nobility,&rquo; on the one hand, and &lquo;the senators and
patricians&rquo; on the other. What was in his mind? I fail to find an explanation
even on trying to render his thought in terms of contemporary arrangements in
England. &lquo;Peers,&rquo; &lquo;parliament men,&rquo; and &lquo;gentry&rquo; would not do.) It strikes one
indeed as a series of disconnected jottings that have as little to do with each other
as with the situation and attitude of Aufidius. First he gives reasons for expecting
the capture of Rome; then he enumerates defects in the character of Coriolanus
that have led to his banishment with a supplementary acknowledgement of his
merits; next he makes general reflections on the relation of virtue to the construc-
tion put upon it, and on the danger that lies in conspicuous power; thereafter he
points out that things are brought to naught by themselves or their likes; and
finally, he predicts that when Rome is taken he will get the better of his rival.
Is there here a mere congeries of thoughts as one chance suggestion leads to an-
other with which it happens to be casually associated, or does one continuous thread
of meaning run through the whole? I would venture to maintain the latter opinion
with more confidence than I do if Coleridge had not been so emphatic. In the
first place, we have to remember what goes before. The report of the Lieutenant
confirms the jealousy of Aufidius, who is further embittered by the thought that
he is losing credit, but reflects that he can bring weighty charges against Coriolanus.
Thereupon the Lieutenant meaningly rejoins: &lquo;Think you he'll carry Rome?&rquo;
It is a contingency to be reckoned with, for clearly, if Rome falls, any previous
mistakes or complaisances alleged against the conqueror will find ready pardon.
So Aufidius discusses the matter in the light of these two main considerations:
(1) that he must get rid of his rival, and (2) that his rival may do the state a
crowning service. He admits that Coriolanus, what with his own efficiency, what
with the friendliness of one class in Rome and the helplessness of the remainder,
is likely to achieve the grand exploit. How then will Aufidius' chances stand?
Formerly Marcius deserved as well of his own country when he had overthrown
Corioli, yet that did not secure him. What qualities in himself discounted his
services to Rome, and may again discount his services to Antium? Pride of pros-
perity, disregard of his opportunities, his unaccommodating peremptory beha-
viour&mdash;all of these faults which, in point of fact, afterward, contributed to his
death&mdash;brought about his banishment, though truly he had merit enough to make
men overlook such trifles. This shows how worth depends on the way it is taken,
and how ability, even when of the sterling kind that wins its own approval, may
find the throne of its public recognition to be, more properly, its certain grave.
Thus likes counteract likes; the greater the popularity, the greater the reaction;
the greater the superiority, the more certainly it will balk itself. So, and this is
the conclusion of the whole matter, even when Marcius has won Rome by a greater

sentence as this: &lquo;For they did ground this second insurrection against the Nobility
and Patricians,&rquo; &amp;c. Shakespeare may have thought that they were in some
way distinct.
<P>32. <B>loue him too</B>] <SC>Capell</SC>: &lquo;Too&rquo; has not its ordinary signification of <I>likewise,</I>
but is to be understood as if it came before &lquo;love him&rquo;; both &lquo;senators and patricians
love him,&rquo; for they, and they only, were the Roman nobility.
<P>36. <B>the Aspray</B>] <SC>Pope</SC>: The <I>Osprey,</I> a kind of eagle, <I>ossifraga.</I>&mdash;<SC>Theobald</SC>:
Though one's search might have been very vain to find any such word as &lquo;Aspray,&rquo;
yet I easily imagined something must be couch'd, under the corruption, in its
nature destructive to fish, and that made a prey of them, and this suspicion led
me to the discovery. The Osprey is a species of the eagle of a strong make that
haunts the sea and lakes for its food, and altogether preys on fish. It is called the
Aquila Marina, as also <I>Avis ossifraga;</I> thence contracted first, perhaps, into
<I>Osphrey,</I> and then, with regard to the ease of pronunciation, <I>Osprey.</I> Pliny gives
us this description of its acute sight and eagerness after its prey: &lquo;Hali&aelig;etus,
clarissima oculorum acie, librans ex alto sese, viso in mari pisce, pr&aelig;ceps in mare

<C>[50, 51. <B>he ha's a Merit . . . in the vtt'rance</B>]</C>
<P>no other purpose than to destroy it by boasting it.&mdash;<SC>Boswell</SC>: I rather under-
stand it, &lquo;But such is his merit as ought to choke the utterance of his faults.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Verplanck</SC>: I cannot understand these words [as Johnson explains them], which
seem, on the contrary, to say, Some one of his faults made him feared, but such
is his merit that it ought to choke and stifle the proclaiming his fault, whatever
it was.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: With Johnson's explanation &lquo;but&rquo; is not in accord; perhaps it
would, therefore, be better to read <I>that,</I> and thus connect the latter part with
the foregoing &lquo;banish'd.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Bulloch</SC> suggests that these words be transposed to
follow &lquo;what it hath done,&rquo; l. 55.&mdash;<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): We
think the obscure effect here is partly attributable to the repeated use of the word
&lquo;but&rquo; in the speech, and partly to the mode in which &lquo;it&rquo; occurs in this clause of
the sentence. In the clauses &lquo;but he could not,&rquo; &lquo;but commanding peace,&rquo; and
&lquo;but one of these&rquo; the word &lquo;but&rquo; is used as a particle of objection; whereas in the
last clause, &lquo;but he has a merit,&rquo; &lquo;but&rquo; seems to be used in the sense of &lquo;however&rquo;
or &lquo;nevertheless.&rquo; After having enumerated the faults of character in Coriolanus
Aufidius ends his sentence by the admission, &lquo;Nevertheless, he has a merit,&rquo; &amp;c.
It is this last clause of admission which presents the chief difficulty; and we have
to bear well in mind Shakespeare's peculiarities of style when trying to discover
its precise meaning. Remembering these peculiarities&mdash;his very condensed ex-
pression and elliptical construction, together with his mode of using &lquo;it,&rquo; either to
a just-named antecedent or to an implied particular&mdash;this clause may bear three
interpretations: 1<SUP>st</SUP>, &lquo;However he has one merit, that of checking panegyric on
it&rquo; (his own merit). 2<SUP>nd</SUP>, &lquo;Nevertheless, he has merit sufficient to stifle the decree
of his banishment (implied in the previous words &lquo;so banish'd&rquo; and &lquo;rash in the
repeal,&rquo; &lquo;utterance&rquo; in this case being taken to mean &lquo;carrying out to the utter-
most&rquo;). 3<SUP>d</SUP>, &lquo;Nevertheless, he has a merit to quench what I have been uttering
as to his faults&rquo; (implied in &lquo;one of these, as he hath spices of them all,&rquo; &amp;c.).
There is still a fourth interpretation that the clause will bear, which, considering
the drift of the argument as carried out to the end of the speech, seems to be
probably meant: &lquo;However, he has a merit, a merit which destroys its own power
by striving to assert that power.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>: He did noble service as a soldier,
and, though as a statesman, promoted for his service in the wars, he fell into
disgrace, yet, confronted with the transcendent merit of the man (which only waits
its opportunity, war, not peace), the very name of his fault must stick in the throats
of his accusers.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Henry Irving Sh.</I>): &lquo;It&rquo; may mean <I>detraction,</I> or some
such idea supplied from &lquo;hated.&rquo; If &lquo;it&rquo; refers to &lquo;banishment,&rquo; the sense must be
&lquo;which <I>ought to have</I> choked it in the utterance.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: Johnson's explanation
seems to me to be the meaning, except that to &lquo;utterance&rquo; I would give the less
restricted and older meaning of <I>publishing, displaying,</I> not necessarily in an offensive
way. The gist of the passage is that every good gift conferred upon him is counter-
balanced by some weakness; he has raised himself to a high position by his valour,
but his pride has marred his good fortune; he has, by his force of character, made
himself master of great opportunities, but his defect of judgment has caused him
to misuse those opportunities; he has the faculty of impressing men with his
authority, but he cannot recognize the occasions on which that faculty should
not be exercised; in every case some &lquo;vicious mole of nature&rquo; counteracts the
qualities which would otherwise make his character so perfect. For a very similar
train of thought compare <I>Hamlet,</I> I, iv, 23-38.

<P>53-55. <B>And power . . . what it hath done</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This is a common
thought, but miserably ill expressed. The sense is, the virtue which delights to
commend itself, will find the surest <I>tomb</I> in that <I>chair</I> wherein it holds forth its
own commendations: &lquo;unto itself most commendable,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> which hath a very high
opinion of itself.&mdash;<SC>Monck Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc., p. 259): The obvious objection
to Johnson's and Warburton's explanations arises from the peculiar temper of
Coriolanus, which renders them totally inapplicable to him in the sense which
they give them; for he was so far from boasting of his exploits himself that he
could not bear to hear them extolled by others; and we find that when his arch-
enemy, Aufidius, sums up the defects of his character, that of boasting is not
upon the list. The passage, indeed, is so very obscure that I cannot but think
there is an error in it, and that we ought to read, &lquo;But he has a merit to choak
<I>him</I> in the utterance&rquo; instead of &lquo;to choak it.&rquo; What Aufidius means to say is:
&lquo;That his merit was so transcendent that the recital of it excited the envy and the
apprehensions of the people; and that, therefore, the power with which it was
accompanied had nothing that tended more surely to its destruction than the
chair from which it was applauded.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 97): The words
&lquo;So our virtue&rquo; and the line after them are a general reflection upon the power
of opinion over the &lquo;virtues&rquo; and endowments of all men, arising from the liberties
which he himself had just taken with those of Coriolanus: 'tis opinion, says he,
&lquo;the interpretation of the time, that gives them their hue, and determines the
degree of their goodness; and that opinion will sink them, pronounce sentence
against them, if they are too loud in their own praise and niggards in commenda-
tion of others. Such is the connection between the parts of this speech, and such
the tendency of the three difficult lines that precede the four riming ones. [Capell
quotes with approval Warburton's paraphrase.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: If our author
meant to place Coriolanus in this <I>chair,</I> he must have forgot his character, for,
as Mr Mason has justly observed, he has already been described as one who was
so far from being a boaster that he could not endure to hear &lquo;his nothings mon-
ster'd.&rquo; But I rather believe &lquo;in the utterance&rquo; alludes not to Coriolanus himself,
but to the <I>high encomiums pronounced on him by his friends;</I> and then the lines of
Horace may serve as a comment on the passage before us:

&lquo;Urit enim fulgore suo, qui pr&aelig;gravat artes<LB>

<C>[53-55. <B>And power . . . what it hath done</B>]</C>
<P>Sep., 1853, p. 323): This passage has given a good deal of trouble to the com-
mentators. Aufidius is describing Coriolanus as a man who, with all his merits,
had failed through some unaccountable perversity of judgment in attaining the
position which his genius entitled him to occupy. Our virtues, says Aufidius,
consist in our ability to interpret and turn to good account the signs of the times.
And power, which delights to praise itself, is sure to have a downfall so soon as
it blazons forth its pretensions from the <I>rostrum.</I> The MS. Corrector proposes,
&lquo;&mdash;as a <I>cheer.</I>&rquo; The original text is obscurely enough expressed, but the new read-
ing seems to be utter nonsense. What <I>can</I> Mr Singer mean by his reading, &lquo;Hath
not a tomb so evident as a <I>hair</I>&rquo;<I>?</I>&mdash;<SC>Ingleby</SC> (<I>Sh. Controversy,</I> p. 148): One of
the earliest attempts to prove the modern origin of the manuscript notes of the
Perkins Folio by means of a test-word was made by Mr A. E. Brae, of Leeds.
His test-word was communicated to the editor of <I>Notes and Queries</I> and myself
in 1853, and I made it public in my <I>Shakespeare Fabrications.</I> [Brae's test-word
was the correction <I>cheer;</I> Ingleby also refers to White's change of &lquo;evident&rquo; to
<I>eloquent</I> in the present line.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] But Mr Richard Garnett (<I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> Oct. 15,
1859) proposes to read <I>tongue</I> for &lquo;tomb,&rquo; wondering, with the reviewer of <I>The
Athen&aelig;um,</I> for August 20<SUP>th</SUP>, 1859, how a tomb can extol. Surely it is the <I>chair</I>
which is given to extol what the man of power and virtue has done! I should not
wonder if some future Perkins should adopt all three suggestions and read, &lquo;Hath
not a <I>tongue</I> so <I>eloquent</I> as a <I>cheer!</I>&rquo; I apprehend no intelligent person who reads
the passage as corrected by Perkins will doubt for an instant that <I>a cheer</I> is there
intended to be understood in the sense <I>a shout of applause. . . .</I> It struck Mr
Brae that the word <I>cheer</I> was necessarily employed in a modern sense, and im-
mediately undertook a close examination of the chronology of the word <I>cheer</I> and
<I>cheers,</I> the result of which with some of the details of the investigation he com-
municated to me. That result was that <I>a cheer,</I> in the sense of <I>a shout of applause,</I>
was not in use till the present century, and that, consequently, it is a test-word
which proves the manuscript notes of the Perkins Folio to be of recent origin.
Nothing that has since been written upon the subject has in the slightest degree
invalidated the soundness of this criticism. In the first place, I must call attention
to the distinction between the use of <I>three cheers</I> and <I>a cheer,</I> in the sense of an
audible expression of applause. Supposing that it could be shown that the phrase
&lquo;three&rquo; cheers was employed to express shouts of applause before 1750, <I>and which
I challenge the world of letters to prove,</I> it might still happen that <I>a cheer</I> was not so
employed until 1800 or thereabouts, <I>which I challenge the world of letters to dis-

I find that <I>three cheers</I> is a conventional phrase employed by sailors to express a

I believe that any such a term was used by sailors till it became a land expression
for a shout of applause, and that it did not do till the present century. [The fore-

<P>His interpretation of the present passage differs materially from that in his earlier
work; he says: &lquo;Aufidius is impressing upon his hearers [<I>sic</I>] the consequences of

power, arrogant of commendation, has not so sure, so manifest a grave as the

&ldquo;a chair to extol,&rdquo; &amp;c., to a tomb. The allusion is to the curule chair, which is very
properly made a symbol of power in the state, as in the time of Coriolanus the
right of sitting in it belonged to Consuls, Pr&aelig;tors, &AElig;diles, Flamens, and, of
course, to Dictators. Shakespeare had read in North's <I>Plutarch,</I> &ldquo;There the Con-

meaning the same as cheers, is a loud demonstration of applause, whereas the
strain of the passage requires a feeble one to constitute the requisite antithesis

word never used by Shakespeare, and <I>cheer</I> is never used by him in the modern
sense of shout of approbation. The reading which I have to propose is as follows,

modern associations the word <I>trump,</I> which is here the same in signification as

presenting itself may be that of the trump of the card-table, with its figurative and
slang applications, rather than the trump of fame. In Shakespeare's pages the
term is used solely as the equivalent of trumpet. My proposed reading, after
the first shock has been overcome, will probably be allowed to convert the line into
good sense with that antithetical point and that spice of sarcasm which are

<C>[53-55. <B>And power . . . what it hath done</B>]</C>
<P>finds its surest means of destruction in the pulpit from which it proclaims its own

Sh.</I>): I do not think that &lquo;chair&rquo; means either the chair of the panegyrist or the

saying &lquo;no tomb at all,&rquo; &lquo;not a wooden chair, much less a sumptuous seated statue.&rquo;
Then &lquo;unto itself&rquo; I take as &lquo;in itself,&rquo; an odd construction, but formed from &lquo;to
give commendation unto virtues.&rquo; The whole passage is a general moral drawn
from Coriolanus's fate in Rome, suggested by the thought of his merit just referred
to in l. 50. I paraphrase: &lquo;Coriolanus was meritorious, but merit is as our con-
temporaries choose to think it. A man may have power and deserve commenda-

monument left to speak his praise.&rquo; The kind of sentiment is that so often put in
the mouth of a Greek chorus.&mdash;<SC>W. W. Skeat</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I> 3<SUP>d</SUP> May, 1890):
The whole sense of this passage comes out at once by simply calling to mind that

it so; see &lquo;Chair&rquo; in the <I>N. E. D.,</I> sect. 5. Cotgrave has: &lquo;<I>Chaire,</I> f. a Chair; also

from its doublet, <I>chaise.</I> And this is the solution of the whole matter. The idea
might have been picked up in any church, for, indeed, the pulpit is commonly
more &lquo;evident,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> conspicuous, than any of the fine tombs in the choir. The
general sense is just this: &lquo;Power, however commendable it may seem to itself,
can find no tomb so conspicuous, no tomb so obvious, as when it chooses for itself
a pulpit whence to proclaim its own praises.&rquo; This agrees very nearly with the
explanation in the note to the Clarendon Press edition [W. A. Wright]; but it seems
to be more emphatic and picturesque to explain the word as &lquo;pulpit&rquo; than merely as
&lquo;orator's chair.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Herford</SC> (<I>Eversley Sh.</I>): Our reputation for virtue is in the hands

however great, is conditioned by public opinion, and that self-laudation, above all
in the highly-placed, is suicidal. [Verity cites Malone's objection to the accusa-

<C>[53-55. <B>And power . . . what it hath done</B>]</C>
<P>a common Shakespearian use.&mdash;<SC>Stanley Wood</SC>: The general sense of this seems
to me to be as follows, A man's greatness depends not so much upon his character
or his acts, as upon people's judgment of them. Coriolanus's power in Rome,
intrinsically great and worthy of all praise (unto itself=in itself), has been re-
duced to nothing because the praises which were showered upon him by the
Senate and the nobles were offensive to the people and the Tribunes, whose inter-
pretation of his merits has prevailed. This explanation assumes that Aufidius
knew what course events had taken in Rome, a reasonable assumption consider-
ing his recent association with Coriolanus.&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>):
Only let it be that the virtue or ability in us is equal to understanding the right
moment, let it but co-ordinate itself with the occasion, <I>lie in th' interpretation of
the time,</I> and then the power that is most alone in being merely to itself commend-
able hath no <I>Tombe</I> and epitaph, not a monument, as it were, so ready with praise
of past achievements as it has a <I>Chaire,</I> or throne for them which shall be a new
seat of life and honor. Aufidius is moralizing as to Martius with himself in mind.
He is applying the virtue that in Martius turned banishment into a new sort of
triumph for him, to his own present crisis, due to Martius, when he must await
the ripe moment to turn the present obscuration, practically the <I>Tombe,</I> of his
ability into a new exposition, or throne, of it. As Martius had the strength to
strangle, as it were, in its utterance the sentence against himself, and make it
recoil on those who pronounced it, so he would do. Only let his virtue come out
in the interpreting of the time or right occasion, and his power, most commendable
now unto itself alone, will have not dead and gone honors so obviously as a new
seat of homage. This passage has generally been accounted extremely obscure
and difficult. . . . To us it seems not corrupt, but introspective. It is character-
istic of Shakespeare's most darkly brooding impersonations. The creature of his
dramatic scheme in this case is suffering from a self-caused depreciation of him-
self. It stings him to mental processes born of competition with a nature his own
different nature emulates, and understands while plotting to surmount.&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>:
The meaning is, that power, which is naturally most pleasing to itself, is never
so obviously near its grave as when (speech succeeding to action) the time comes
to pronounce a laudation of its achievements. &lquo;Chair&rquo; means a chair of state
from which official pronouncements are made. Most editors that I have seen go
wrong on this passage. They have a picture of self-satisfied &lquo;power&rquo; openly
extolling itself, and are naturally puzzled to see how this can apply to Coriolanus,
who notoriously hated brag. But &lquo;unto itself most commendable&rquo; does not mean
that power is self-satisfied; it means that power always seems more satisfactory
to the person who possesses it than to those who do not. And it is nowhere said
that power extols &lquo;itself.&rquo; The passage must be taken in connexion with what
goes before, or the sense is lost. Aufidius has just said that no matter what your
merits and achievements may be, everything depends on how your contemporaries
take them. He goes on to add that there is nothing more risky for a man who has
done great things than when the time comes to have them proclaimed. People
may take such praise either way. If they take it one way, he's a hero, and the
saviour of the state; if they take it the other, he's a traitor and a tyrant. The
application to Coriolanus is plain.&mdash;<SC>S. P. Sherman</SC> (<I>Tudor Sh.</I>): The meaning
is that we cannot be judges of our own virtues; they must be stamped with the
approval of the society in which we live before they can become current. Shake-

<C>[53-55. <B>And power . . . what it hath done</B>]</C>
<P>speare seems much interested in what we may call the social sanctions of virtue
in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> In the mood of Aufidius Troilus asks, &lquo;What is aught, but as
'tis valu'd&rquo; (II, ii, 52). Hector replies (II, ii, 53-56):
<BQ>
&lquo;But value dwells not in particular will;<LB>
It holds his estimate and dignity<LB>
As well wherein 'tis precious of itself<LB>
As in the prizer.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>Later in the play (III, iii, 95ff.) Ulysses and Achilles discuss the same point.
[Further]: A person who possesses power, though it merit commendation, cannot
more speedily terminate its effectiveness than by praising what he has accom-
plished by it.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: It is doubtful whether this means &lquo;our virtues depend
(for their efficacy) upon the way in which they are regarded by those among
whom we live&rquo; or &lquo;our virtues depend (for their efficacy) upon the manner in which
we interpret, and adapt ourselves to, surrounding circumstances.&rquo; The latter
view agrees better with the explanation I have given of ll. 50, 51 [<I>q. v.</I>], but it is
doubtful whether &lquo;the interpretation&rquo; can mean &lquo;the interpretation we put.&rquo;
If the reading of ll. 51-55 is genuine, the meaning probably is, &lquo;and power (<I>i. e.,</I>
a man in high position), however much it may consider itself deserving of praise,
has no such certain grave of its reputation as a chair from which it pronounces its
own eulogy.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): I am inclined to interpret this passage in close
connection with <I>the beginning of the speech,</I> and to regard it as a general reflection
referring quite as much, or more, to the Tribunes as to Coriolanus, to whom it is
always confined. Aufidius has declared that the people will recall Coriolanus as
eagerly as they expelled him, and after a digression as to the causes of his over-
throw and a tribute to his merit, he proceeds to this effect. Thus the light in
which our virtues are regarded depends upon the time (the fluctuation of popular
opinion which then denounced Coriolanus and will now acclaim him), and power,
however self-justified, finds a grave in the very seat of authority whence it extols
its actions. What Aufidius describes had, in fact, happened in the last scene, when
the grave of their power opened before the Tribunes at the very height of their
self-congratulations, and &lquo;the interpretation of the time&rquo; begins to change rapidly
under the face of circumstances. So, too, the proverbs that follow refer to the
former reverse and that in progress; perhaps also to the final reverse of all, but
Aufidius does not take up that subject till he has ended his reflections and pre-
pared to go. Then, still thinking first of Coriolanus's triumph, he says, &lquo;When,
Caius, Rome is thine,&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Tucker Brooke</SC> (<I>Yale Shakespeare</I>): Power, though
(when considered absolutely) most worthily attained, is never so near its grave as
when the successful man, seated in the chair of authority, seeks to justify the
means by which he has risen. [I am somewhat loath to add any words of mine
to this long note. I wish, however, to call attention to the <I>Text. Notes,</I> wherein
it will be noticed how negligible has been the influence of any of the proposed
alterations of the original, on subsequent texts. Singer's alteration, <I>hair,</I> had but

afeard the life of Helen, lady, Was foully snatched.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>):
Certain editors have altered &lquo;fouler&rquo;; but why should Shakespeare not have said
that wrong comes to pass through wrong, and often the better through the worse?&mdash;

<P>rection as &lquo;seeming, on the whole, preferable to the others; though <I>founder</I> strikes

falls by stirring up inevitably another power to oppose it. So Coriolanus has
fallen once, at the height of his achievement, by the opposition of the people; so
he will fall again, at the height of his new achievement, by the opposition of
Aufidius.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: Rights give way to other and better rights; power, how-

that any change in the Folio is either necessary or desirable. As the Cowden
Clarkes so ably demonstrate, this elliptical form of expression is eminently char-
acteristic of Shakespeare, particularly in the later plays; besides, the sentiment
is also characteristic of Aufidius. In I, x. he had declared that nothing should
restrain him in the satisfying of his hatred for Marcius. The rights of host to
guest, the prayers of priests which ordinarily restrain fury, shall be by him dis-
regarded. For Aufidius to make such a general statement that rights falter or
founder by other rights is both inconsistent to the situation and weakening to his
character.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>entry of the group was made from the end of the outer-stage (either right or left of
the rear-stage compartment). This entrance stands all through the play for most of
the Roman localities, as the &lquo;Cyprus grove&rquo; side, opposite, stood, all through, for
the open country and the out-of-Rome localities. When Menenius goes on his
errand (l. 73) perhaps he made his exit through the &lquo;Cyprus grove.&rquo; The dia-
logue, after he leaves, gives space of time enough for the audience to suppose him
on his way, and when the Roman group goes off (l. 86) as it had entered, then, at
the point marked now as Scene II, Menenius appeared again from the &lquo;Cyprus
grove&rquo; side, and, approaching the rear-stage or tent of Coriolanus, held his parley
with the two men on guard who barred his progress (see Folio stage-direction II, i.).
<P>5. <B>Which was</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): That is, &lquo;You hear what he hath said, who was
formerly general to Coriolanus.&rquo; The old annotator of the Folio, 1632, did not under-
stand the passage when he altered it, &lquo;<I>To one</I> sometime his general&rquo;; &lquo;he&rquo; refers
to Cominius, not to Coriolanus.
<P>6. <B>In a most deere particular</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, with the strongest
private friendship. Cominius loved him not only as his general for his soldierly
qualities, but with the most affectionate personal regard. The use of the word
&lquo;particular&rquo; is suggested by the word &lquo;general&rquo; in the line before; and the two are
frequently contrasted. Compare IV, vii, 16.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): The <I>N. E. D.</I>
gives an excellent instance of &lquo;particular&rquo; under &lquo;personal relation, . . . personal
interest, regard or favour,&rquo; from Weever, <I>Ancient Funeral Monuments,</I> 1631, p.
797, &lquo;Out of his particular to their Towne, hee procured of Queene Elizabeth a
Charter of Incorporation.&rquo;
<P>8. <B>knee</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, go on your knees. The later folios have
corrupted it to &lquo;kneel.&rquo; In a slightly different sense the word occurs in <I>Lear,</I> II,
iv, 217, &lquo;I could as well be brought To knee his throne.&rquo; Similarly Shakespeare
uses the verbs &lquo;to lip,&rquo; &lquo;to mouth,&rquo; &lquo;to tongue,&rquo; &lquo;to nose,&rquo; &lquo;to foot,&rquo; &lquo;to arm&rquo; =
to take into the arms.

coy, a squeamish or scornfull dame.&rquo; [The <I>N. E. D.</I> quotes the present line as the

In the old copies it is printed &lquo;wrack'd,&rquo; the old orthography of the time for

who would have scorned the very idea of Rome's &lquo;memory&rquo; being &lquo;wreck'd,&rquo; even

&lquo;The court of affection, held by that racking steward, remembrance&rquo;; we still
speak of &lquo;rack-rents.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC>: &lquo;Wracked&rquo; is the word which is set down in the
Folios, and, inasmuch as our word &lquo;<I>wrecked,</I>&rquo; wherever it occurs, is almost invari-
ably spelt in the original copies with an &lquo;<I>a</I>&rquo; and not with an &lquo;<I>e,</I>&rquo; the presumption
is that &lquo;wrecked&rquo; is the word which is here authorized by the Folios. The meaning
would be that the tribunes had (to borrow words from <I>Macbeth</I>) &lquo;laboured in their
country's wreck.&rquo; The preposition &lquo;for,&rquo; coming after &lquo;wreck,&rquo; would be abnormal,
but not necessarily un-Shakespearian. It might be illustrated by such expressions
as the following: &lquo;Revenge the heavens for old Andronicus,&rquo; <I>Titus And.,</I> IV, i,
129; &lquo;How unluckily it happened, that I should purchase the day before for a little
part, and undo a great deal of honour!&rquo; <I>Timon,</I> III, ii, 52; &lquo;Spare for no faggots,&rquo;
<I>1 Henry VI:</I> V, iv, 56. [Perring mentions with scant respect the two emenda-
tions &lquo;<I>Recked</I> for&rquo; and &lquo;<I>Racked</I> for,&rquo; giving as a third &lquo;<I>wreaked</I> for,&rquo; which may be
shrewdly suspected to be his own contribution, as he takes pains to elucidate this
new reading thus: &lquo;They had wreaked their vengeance on Coriolanus by expatriat-
ing him, under colour that it was for the public good; but what had they effected?
They had cheapened coals! and cheap enough they would be when the city was,
as it were, the colliery to supply the fuel for its own conflagration; the allusion, of
course, is to Coriolanus having refused to be called by any title, &ldquo;Till he had forged
himself a name o'the fire Of burning Rome.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): That
is, striven, strained. Menenius ridicules the net result of their strenuous efforts on
behalf of the common weal, viz., a fall in the price of coals. The metaphor is
&lquo;to strain, wrest,&rquo; as by means of a rack or instrument.&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First
Folio Sh.</I>): That is, wrought vengeance for themselves on Coriolanus's name, as
her representative, with ruinous results, to make charcoal cheap when Rome is
burned. Menenius makes words suit his meaning in their suggestive sense. Here
in &lquo;wrack'd&rquo; he seems to have combined the sense of wrought ruin, and wreaked
vengeance in a way according with the usage of &lquo;wrecked&rquo; and &lquo;wreake&rquo; (see IV,
vi, 90). And the words used by Plutarch at this stage of the story are again in
point here, &lquo;In this while, all went still to wrack at Rome.&rquo; As before explained
by editors, merely in the sense of &lquo;laboured&rquo; or &lquo;wrought&rquo; the entire meaning con-
veyed by the passage seems not to be covered.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: No instance has been
cited of the verb [to rack] in the neuter sense [strained for], or of its being coupled
with <I>for.</I> I have therefore followed Dyce in accepting Williams's conjecture
<I>wrccked fair.</I>

<P>25. <B>a bare petition</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: &lquo;Bare,&rquo; for <I>mean, beggarly.</I>&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I
believe rather, a petition unsupported, unaided by names that might give it influ-
ence.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;A bare petition,&rquo; I believe, means only a <I>mere petition.</I> Corio-
lanus weighs the consequence of verbal supplication against that of actual punish-
ment.&mdash;<SC>Monck Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc., p. 260): I have no doubt but we should
read &lquo;a <I>base</I> petition,&rquo; meaning that it was unworthy the dignity of a state to peti-
tion a man whom they had banished. [Sir William Blackstone (<I>Shakespeare
Society Papers,</I> 1844, p. 99) makes the same suggestion, but without further com-
ment.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: In <I>1 Henry IV:</I> [I, iii, 108], and in <I>Timon,</I> [IV, iii, 229],
the word &lquo;bare&rquo; is used in the sense of <I>thin,</I> easily seen through, having only a
slight superficial covering. Yet, I confess, this interpretation will hardly apply
here. In the former of the passages alluded to the editor of the First Folio sub-
stituted <I>base</I> for <I>bare</I> improperly. In the passage before us perhaps <I>base</I> was the
author's word.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: Coriolanus, in the report of Cominius, elucidates that
however royal an unexpected pardon may be, it amounts to no more than a bald
request, a naked petition of a state, extended to one whom the state had punished.
&lquo;Bare&rquo; expresses the disregard such a request deserves.&mdash;<SC>W. W. Williams</SC> (<I>The
Parthenon,</I> 3 May, 1862, p. 19): I hope I may be excused for suspecting that Corio-
lanus had replied scornfully to Cominius that &lquo;It was a <I>rare</I> petition of a state.&rquo;
&lquo;Rare&rquo; and &lquo;strange&rquo; were used by Shakespeare interchangeably in the sense of
<I>extraordinary</I>&mdash;as indeed they still are; and, in the first scene of this drama,
Coriolanus had displayed similar temper and in similar terms when describing
the exultation of the mob at having &lquo;a petition granted them a <I>strange</I> one.&rquo; In
the present passage he appears to have remarked sarcastically that it was a rare
(<I>i. e.,</I> strange or extraordinary) proceeding that a banished man should be petitioned
for mercy by the very men who had banished him.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I>
p. 371): I do not well understand &lquo;bare&rquo; here. Mason's reading is not quite
satisfactory.&mdash;<SC>Bulloch</SC> (p. 188): In I, ix. the speech of Cominius, beginning at
l. 66, gives the history of the hero being named Coriolanus. His after banish-
ment and what followed explain the passage and emendation, &lquo;It was a <I>rebaptizing</I>
of <I>estate</I> To one whom they had punish'd.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): That is,
a bare-faced petition. Rome had not pardoned Coriolanus; yet Rome had the
face to ask pardon from him.&mdash;<SC>Orson</SC>: That is, a petition made by one who
comes bare-headed, cap in hand. Compare Dekker's <I>Gull's Hornbook,</I> ch. i,
&lquo;Antiquity puts off his cap, and makes a bare oration in praise of the virtues of
it.&rquo;&mdash;[The explanation given by Steevens is, to me at least, quite sufficient. For
this figurative use of &lquo;bare&rquo; compare &lquo;uttering bare truth,&rquo; <I>Sonnet lxix,</I> l. 4;
&lquo;they live by your bare words,&rquo; <I>Two Gentlemen,</I> II, iv, 46.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>50-53. <B>Well, and . . . Say't be so</B>] <SC>Badham</SC> (<I>Criticism Applied to Sh.,</I> p. 16):
There are several reasons for doubting the soundness of this passage. The half-
line by itself would excite no suspicion, for there is a natural pause after the words
&lquo;what then?&rquo; [This half-line, &lquo;Unheard; what then?&rquo; is due to Pope, see <I>Text.
Notes.</I>] When, however, we find the next line beginning with &lquo;but,&rquo; a conjunction
which has nothing to do with the preceding clause, we cannot help suspecting that
there is an hiatus to be supplied with some such words as these, &lquo;<I>not as a joyful
herald, But</I> as a discontented friend,&rquo; &amp;c. If this be thought too bold, &lquo;But&rquo;
must be at once discarded; and we are the more inclined to adopt this alternative
because it will also enable us to change the expression of &lquo;discontented friend,&rquo; which
is somewhat unusual in the sense of a friend who has had his request denied, and
to get rid of the Alexandrine in the following line. We propose, therefore, to read:
<BQ>
&lquo;As a <I>discountenanc'd</I> friend grief-shot with his<LB>
Unkindness.<LB>
<S>Sic.</S> Say't be so; yet your good will,&rquo; &amp;c.<LB>
</BQ>

arrangement of these lines. In that interval he has evidently repaired his omission
of consulting either an original folio, or Vernor and Hood's reprint of 1807, since
he transcribes the lines as there given, and so makes no mention of the half-line
due to Pope. He likewise discards his emendation for &lquo;discontented.&rquo; Of the
passage as a whole he says: &lquo;&ldquo;Say't be so&rdquo; ought to be given to Sicinius; as for

<P>The verse of six syllables [l. 51] may be thought by some to be purposely defective;
but, in the first place, there is no pause in the sense after the word &ldquo;as,&rdquo; and

vi, 40, &lquo;I hope it remains not unkindly with your lordship that I returned you an
empty messenger.&rquo;

<P>60. <B>He was not taken well</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, the time for the interview
with him was not chosen wisely. Compare <I>Mid. N. Dream,</I> III, ii, 16, &lquo;Where
I did him at this advantage take.&rquo; So <I>Hamlet,</I> III, iii, 80, &lquo;He took my father
grossly, full of bread.&rquo;
<P>61. <B>The Veines vnfill'd, our blood is cold</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: Lord Bacon somewhere
in his <I>Essays</I> makes this very remark concerning the <I>Seasons of Sollicitation.</I>
[A diligent reading of all of Bacon's <I>Essays</I> has been unproductive in identifying
this vague reference by Theobald. The Essay <I>Of Negotiating</I> gives various meth-
ods of approaching the person solicited, but there is not any reference to a pro-
pitious season. Spedding's exhaustive Index to the Works of Bacon does not
contain any reference to seasonable solicitation. Menenius is evidently familiar
with the offices of the veins; see his reference to them and the function of the Belly
in his apologue, I, i, 136-142.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>64. <B>these Conueyances</B>] <SC>W. S. Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.,</I> p. 243) has collected a large
number of examples wherein &lquo;the plurals of Substantives ending in <I>s,</I> in certain
instances; in <I>se, ss, ce,</I> and sometimes <I>ge;</I> . . . are found without the usual addi-
tion of <I>s</I> or <I>es</I>&mdash;in pronunciation at least, although in many instances the plural
affix is added in printing, where the metre shows that it is not to be pronounced.&rquo;
Walker, on p. 259, quotes the present line as an example. See also <SC>Abbott</SC>,
&sect; 471; compare III, i, 46 <I>supra.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>66. <B>our Priest-like Fasts</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: I am afraid that when Shakespeare intro-
duced this comparison the religious abstinence of modern, not ancient, Rome was
in his thoughts.&mdash;C. (ap. <I>Steevens,</I> 1793): Priests are forbid, by the discipline of
the church of Rome, to break their fast before the celebration of mass, which must
take place after sun-rise and before mid-day. [This note, without further identi-
fication than the single letter C. as here given, is repeated in the subsequent
<I>Variorum</I> editions. As the information imparted is not of great intrinsic value,
let us be content, and allow the modest commentator to retain his anonymity.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>[&lquo;<I>Engoal'd</I>&rquo; is a word of Heath's own coinage, and therefore its interpretation is
quite as fanciful as its origin. The substantive <I>goal</I> if made into a verb could by
no possibility be interpreted as <I>surrounded, imprisoned.</I> The only meaning of the
word is the terminus or end of a race or contest. It is just possible that Heath's
word has been misprinted and that it should be <I>engaol'd,</I> since he interprets his
suggestion as <I>imprisoned.</I> Note also, that in l. 78 &lquo;Gaoler&rquo; was misprinted <I>goaler</I>
by Pope, and passed several successive editors without correction.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC>:
That is, sit enthron'd in pomp and in the terror of majesty; the expression is
doubly figurative, for we are only to understand by it that his approach was as
difficult as a king's, and his presence as awful.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: So, in the old trans-
lation of Plutarch, &lquo;&mdash;he was set in his chaire of state, with a marvellous and
unspeakable majestie.&rquo; Shakespeare has a somewhat similar idea in <I>Henry VIII:</I>
I, i, 19, &lquo;All clinquant, all in gold, like heathen gods.&rquo; The idea expressed by
Cominius occurs also in the <I>Iliad,</I> bk viii, l. 442, in the translation of which
passage Mr Pope was perhaps indebted to Shakespeare, &lquo;Th&rquo; eternal Thunderer
<I>sat</I> throned <I>in gold.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 372): For &lquo;in gold&rquo; we might read
<I>a god,</I> &lquo;He sits amongst men, like a descended god,&rquo; <I>Cymbeline,</I> I, vi, 169. But
it may be his chair of state that is meant.

expressly tells us that he had yielded to new conditions. I conjecture the poet

<P>Here is, I think, a chasm. The speaker's purpose seems to be this: &lquo;To yield to
his conditions is ruin, and better cannot be obtained, so that all hope is vain.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Farmer</SC>: I suppose Coriolanus means that he had sworn to give way to the
<I>conditions</I> into which the ingratitude of his country had forced him.&mdash;<SC>Monck
Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc.): This passage as it stands is evidently wrong, for it is
absolutely unintelligible, and the question is how to amend it; none of the amend-
ments hitherto suggested appear satisfactory; that which I have to propose is a
very slight deviation from the text&mdash;the reading &lquo;<I>in his</I> conditions&rquo; instead of
&lquo;to his conditions.&rquo; To &lquo;yield,&rquo; in this place, means to <I>relax,</I> and is used in the
same sense in scene iii. by Coriolanus in speaking of Menenius:
<BQ>
&lquo;&mdash;to grace him only<LB REND=RIGHT>

<P>What Cominius means to say is &lquo;That Coriolanus sent in writing after him the
conditions on which he would agree to make a peace, and bound himself by an
oath not to depart from them. The additional negative which Hanmer and
Warburton wish to introduce is not only unnecessary, but would destroy the sense;
for the thing which Coriolanus had sworn <I>not</I> to do was to <I>yield in his conditions.</I>&mdash;
<SC>Henley</SC>: &lquo;What he would do,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> the conditions on which he offered to return,
he sent in writing after Cominius, intending that he should carry them to Menenius.
&lquo;What he would not,&rquo; <I>i. e.,</I> his resolution of <I>neither</I> dismissing his soldiers nor
<I>capitulating</I> with <I>Rome's mechanics</I> in case the terms he prescribed should be refused,
he bound himself by an oath to maintain. If these conditions were admitted the
oath, of course, being grounded on that proviso, must <I>yield to them</I> and be cancelled.
That this is the proper sense of the passage is obvious from what follows in V, iii:

and &lquo;what he would not&rquo;; and in justification of the harshness of his demands he
adds that he is &lquo;bound with an oath to yield to his conditions,&rquo; that is, to make his
sole law the &lquo;conditions&rquo; in which he had become placed&mdash;his duty to the Volcians;
to yield himself up entirely to the guidance of those &lquo;conditions.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC>:
The meaning appears to be that Coriolanus bound himself by an oath that Rome
should yield to his conditions. Various changes of the text have been proposed,
but none seems absolutely necessary.&mdash;<SC>Verplanck</SC>: Coriolanus sends his ulti-
matum (to use the language of diplomacy) in writing, stating both what he would
and what he would not consent to, and binding all with an oath that these are
the conditions to which Rome must yield. This line [82] is elliptically expressed,
but the sense is sufficiently explicit. But the editors have not been satisfied, and
propose various emendations, of which &lquo;to yield to no conditions&rquo; is far the most
probable.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: It has been thought that there is here an omission of either
a half or a whole line. Such an ellipsis and anacoluthon is, however, quite in
Shakespeare's style. The sense is: He sent after me in writing what he would do,
what he would not do (<I>i. e.,</I> what he would grant to us and what not); he bound
me with an oath to submit to his conditions. &lquo;Bound,&rquo; which the editors take for
a participle, is rather of the same order as &lquo;sent,&rquo; and out of &lquo;after me&rquo; <I>me</I> is to be
supplied. We may construe this, without ellipsis: he sent in writing after me
what he would do (and) what he would not; and bound me with an oath to yield
to his conditions. Cominius is thus made ambassador to the Romans.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>:
The sense of this passage we conjecture to have been destroyed by the misprint
