<C>[82. <B>Bound with an Oath to yeeld to his conditions</B>]</C>
<P>stated more fully in North's <I>Plutarch;</I> and that here &lquo;what he would do&rquo; refers to
what Coriolanus would grant as expressed in the articles &lquo;sent in writing after&rquo;
Cominius; while &lquo;what he would not&rquo; refers to the proposals made by the Romans,
which Coriolanus would not grant unless under certain conditions that he bound
himself by oath to make them yield to. In the text the concise phraseology scarcely
makes evident that there are two sets of articles, one drawn up by Coriolanus
and sent in writing, the other submitted by the Romans to him, which he vows to
grant only upon his own conditions; but that so it is clearly intended we think
is shown by the account of the incident in Plutarch as well as by the expression &lquo;it
was a bare petition of a state&rquo; in the present scene, indicating a proposal made on
their part.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. i.): A passage hard to be understood at best, and still more
obscure as commonly pointed, thus: &lquo;What he would do, he sent in writing after
me; what he would not, bound with an oath, to yield to his conditions&rquo;; which is
severing &lquo;what he would do&rquo; from &lquo;bound with an oath,&rquo; and &lquo;what he would not&rquo;
from &lquo;he sent in writing after me.&rquo; As now given the sense may be rendered
thus: &lquo;He sent in writing after me both what he would do, and what he would
not; binding the whole with an oath that we should yield to his conditions.&rquo;&mdash;

<P>Rev. <SC>John Hunter</SC>: His conditions were expressed in the writing previously
referred to, and &lquo;what he would not&rquo; he &lquo;bound with an oath&rquo; to be determined
by those conditions. The meaning simply is that he wrote conditions, and swore
to allow nothing but what was expressed therein. The phrase &lquo;to his conditions&rquo;
has been suspected by the commentators, but no alteration is wanted. Shakespeare
judiciously avoids specifying the conditions stated in Plutarch.&mdash;<SC>Whitelaw</SC>:
Sent after me, in writing, what he would, what he would not, consent to do; con-
firming this with an oath which only our acceptance of his terms can cancel. With
the construction &lquo;an oath to yield&rquo; compare &lquo;a merit, to choke it,&rquo; &lquo;a chair to
extol.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): There is ample foundation for suspecting that
there is some corruption between the words &lquo;What he would do&rquo; and &lquo;his condi-
tions,&rquo; and the most probable explanation is that something has been omitted
(which is corroborated by the incomplete line &lquo;So that all hope is vain&rquo;), [due, how-
ever, to Johnson, not Shakespeare.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>], wherein the conditions of Coriolanus
would be demonstrated as unacceptable. If all is, however, in proper order this
line can only be well interpreted thus: that he was bound by an oath to submit
to his conditions, that is, the conditions which he made in the name of the Volscians,
to make them as his own, according as they were decided on in war-council.&mdash;
<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: Unless this line is corrupt, or something has fallen out of the text,

Coriolanus specified in his written despatch what concessions he was willing to
make, adding, as a proviso, that in everything else Cominius should bind himself
by oath to submit to <I>his</I> (Coriolanus') conditions. In the last clause the subject
is changed from Coriolanus to Cominius. The grammar may lack completeness,
but it should be remembered that here we have a brief and hurried summary of
a short and curt interview&mdash;a sort of running conversational comment; say there
is a little looseness, there is no obscurity; the Romans who heard would not be
slow to apprehend what was meant; their fears had already anticipated the sinister
tidings. Brevity here is surely a merit.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Henry Irving Sh.</I>): The
desired meaning is that Coriolanus was bound by an oath to the Volscians to
impose certain conditions, or to make the Romans yield to his conditions; but it
must be confessed that the text does not say this. Or the meaning may be that
the <I>message</I> was affirmed by an oath, viz., that his conditions must be yielded to.
Various punctuations have been proposed, and numerous emendations, none of
them satisfactory. [Beeching, a few years later in the <I>Falcon Sh.,</I> says: &lquo;His
declaration was confirmed with an oath to yield <I>only</I> to his conditions, to retire
from Rome only if his conditions were complied with.&rquo; He compares for this
V, iii, 15-17, &lquo;I have . . . once more offered The first conditions which they did
refuse And cannot now accept.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): I have
put a comma for the colon after &lquo;me,&rquo; and explain: &lquo;He sent me an offer of con-
cessions, strictly limited, and dependent on an oath to observe the conditions laid
down.&rquo; Coriolanus has already begun to waver. He repeats to Menenius in V,
ii, 91 the offer made to Cominius.&mdash;<SC>Cholmeley</SC>: The text is corrupt, but can be
made tolerable by transposing the two parts of l. 81; &lquo;his conditions&rquo; are the terms
of his service with the Volscians, and the words &lquo;Bound with an oath,&rquo; etc., give
the cause of his behaviour; he had sworn not to discuss the situation.&mdash;<SC>Herford</SC>
(<I>Eversley Sh.</I>): The transaction is obscurely described. Apparently it is thus: Corio-
lanus indicates what he will concede, and binds himself by oath to concede nothing
more.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): The passage is undoubtedly corrupt. The diffi-
culty is this: Two later passages (V, ii, 50-52; V, iii, 89-91) show that &lquo;bound with
an oath&rquo; refers to Coriolanus and qualifies &lquo;what he would not&rquo; (do). Coriolanus
would not do certain things (V, iii, 92, 93) because he had sworn not to. But
&lquo;to yield to his conditions&rquo; ought to refer to the Romans; that is the natural inter-
pretation, and it is substantiated by the parallel passage in Plutarch. Coriolanus
told the Roman Ambassadors that &lquo;they had no other means to end this war, if
they did not grant these honest and just conditions of peace,&rquo; which he had just
laid before them. Through some omission in l. 82 the words in l. 81 which refer

twice in North's <I>Plutarch</I> in a later paragraph referring to the same &lquo;articles&rquo; and
&lquo;<I>conditions</I>&rquo; of peace. Of the passage as it stands the best paraphrase seems [to
be that by Beeching in <I>Falcon Sh.</I>]. But to speak of a man &lquo;yielding&rquo; to his own
terms is obviously forced. It simplifies the text to substitute a comma for the
semicolon after &lquo;me&rquo; in l. 81.&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>) does not refer to
the interpretation by Delius, and thus evidently arrived at the same conclusion
independently that if <I>he</I> be understood before &lquo;Bound&rquo; and <I>me</I> after &lquo;Bound&rquo;
the sense is clear. Of Henley's paraphrase Miss Porter remarks: &lquo;To prove that
&ldquo;this is the proper sense of the passage&rdquo; Henley cites the words of Coriolanus
to his mother lat&egrave;r as to &ldquo;the things he has forsworne to grant.&rdquo; But the text
reads &ldquo;the thing,&rdquo; not &ldquo;the things,&rdquo; as Henley quotes it, nor does it there appear
that the two things designated as by treaty forsworn are so exactly specified. He
seems rather to be thinking of what he has forsworn to the Volscians, to show the
Romans no favor. Nor does he speak to his mother of any formal treaty. Instead
of binding himself with an oath to yield anything to the Romans, he has bound
the Romans to yield him beforehand, as the very ground of any agreement, their
acceptance of what he would not do, making what he would do entirely conditional.
That is, he bases any concessions upon their sworn agreement to his conditions.
He will not treat with them, will not agree under such or such conditions to lay
down arms, until they have sworn beforehand to yield these preliminaries. <I>What
he would not</I> do, being <I>Bound with</I> or safeguarded by <I>an Oath</I> from them <I>to yeeld
to his conditions.</I> This accords with what Plutarch states to be his answer to the
ambassadors of Rome.&rquo; [See <I>Appendix</I>: <I>Source of Plot, ad loc.</I>] Later Plutarch
shows again that these preliminary conditions were exactly the bone of contention,
balking any treaty to follow, for &lquo;another ambassade&rquo; proposed &lquo;the remove of
the Volsces . . . that afterward they might with better leisure fall to such agree-
ments together, as should be thought most meete and necessary . . . all the
[Volsces] would reasonably aske should be graunted unto by the Romaines, who
would willingly yield to reason, conditionally, that they did lay downe armes.&rquo;
This was precisely what Marcius would not do until they had bound themselves
as already stipulated, delivering up the articles agreed upon which he had first
delivered them. Or otherwise, that he would not assure their safe-conduct
&lquo;againe to his campe with such vaine and frivolous messages.&rquo; These much dis-
puted lines of Shakespeare's are obviously based on these facts.&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: What
he would not do he bound with an oath that we must yield to his conditions.
Cominius had come as an ambassador from Rome to plead for terms. Coriolanus
refused to treat with him. The conditions he offered (&lquo;what he would do&rquo;) were
final; to discuss them was useless; they should be sent after in writing. Cominius's
proposals (&lquo;what he would not&rquo;) he refused, and clinched his refusal with an oath
that we must yield to his conditions. It was to be his conditions or nothing.&mdash;
<SC>Deighton</SC>: If genuine, this passage may mean he would send in writing after I
had been dismissed a statement of what he would do, and what he would not do,
he being bound by an oath to fulfil the terms on which he had made alliance with
the Volscians. &lquo;Bound&rquo; seems to be an instance of the participle with the pronoun
implied.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): This passage readily suggests a meaning most

<P>only hope is in you, or in him. The same mode of expression occurs in this sen-

considered as difficult surprises me. Many passages in these plays have been
suspected to be corrupt merely because the language was peculiar to Shakespeare,
or the phraseology of that age, and not of the present; and this is surely one of
them. Had he written, his noble mother and his wife are our <I>only hope,</I> his
meaning could not have been doubted; and is not this precisely what Cominius
says? So that we have now no other hope, nothing to rely upon <I>but</I> his mother
and his wife, who, as I am told, mean, &amp;c. &lquo;Unless&rquo; is here used for <I>except.</I>&mdash;

<P>[Of the proposals by Leo, Joicey, and Verity to remedy these lines, that by Joicey&mdash;
as it is the simplest&mdash;is to be preferred. Spence's objection is trifling; in fact,
that the phrase &lquo;I mean to&rquo; is an Americanism at all is quite open to question.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): This is a colloquial, unbookish expression
natural to a speaker, and a slight transposition will make this clear enough.
Cominius declares that unless his Noble Mother solicit him, and his wife, who (as
I hear) means to, all hope is vain.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: This is probably elliptical for,
unless we may consider the intended intercession of his mother and his wife in the
light of hope.&mdash;<SC>Perring</SC> (p. 312): Where, it has been asked, is the verb that should
follow &lquo;unless&rquo;? To which I reply, where is it in <I>Richard II:</I> V, iii, 32, &lquo;My
tongue cleave to my roof within my mouth, Unless a pardon ere I rise or speak&rquo;?
Where is it in <I>All's Well,</I> IV, i, 5, &lquo;We must not seem to understand him, unless
some one among us whom we must produce for an interpreter&rquo;? Where is it in
<I>Othello,</I> I, i, 23, 24, &lquo;Nor the division of the battle knows More than a spinster,
unless the bookish theorie&rquo;? It may be an open question with some whether in
the above passages &lquo;unless&rquo; should be parsed as a conjunction or should be held
to partake rather of the nature of a preposition; but none can fail to be struck with
the remarkableness of the coincidence that in all the passages the same particle is
found without a finite verb actually following it. For my own part I hold that
in the passage before us it is most certainly a conjunction, and that in all probabil-
ity the verb that belongs to it, and that should be mentally supplied after it, is
the verb that occurs in the <I>relative clause which follows</I>&mdash;yes, the same verb, but
not used in exactly the same sense; for, whereas in the relative clause &lquo;solicit&rquo; means
&lquo;to earnestly entreat,&rquo; in the principal clause, where we say &lquo;that&rquo; is understood, it
can only mean &lquo;to prevail by entreaty,&rquo; one verb (as is not uncommon) serving
for two clauses, which in its strict acceptation suits only one of them. There is
surely no maze here to hinder us from treading out the way readily.

<P>2. <B>1. Wat. Stay: whence are you.</B>] <SC>Delius</SC> (<I>Die Prosa in Sh's Dramen; Jahrbuch,</I>
v, p. 269): The two Sentinels for the most part repulse Menenius in blank verse; when
they first begin to lose patience through his importunity they become provoked
and speak in prose, which in the mouth of one of them is not lacking in a certain
strength and fineness of speech. The entrance of Coriolanus calls forth from Mene-
nius a moving heartfelt tone, which, moreover, by its light humour calls to mind his
original nature, and therefore rightly takes on the form of eloquent prose. To this
supplication of his former friend Coriolanus replies, aloof and cold, in blank verse.
<P>13. <B>it is Lots to Blankes</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: A &lquo;lot&rquo; here is a <I>prize.</I>&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC>: What he
would here say is, 'Tis odds but my name has been heard by you; now &lquo;lots&rquo;
can have no other sense than fortunate lots, prizes; and certainly the odds never
lay on their side in a lottery, but there is a waggery in supposing the contrary, and
therefore it is done by Menenius.&mdash;S[<SC>tephen</SC>] W[<SC>eston</SC>]: <I>Lot</I> in French signifies
<I>prize.</I> Le gros lot: The capital prize.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I believe Dr Johnson here mis-
takes. Menenius, I imagine, only means to say that it is more than an equal
chance that his name has touched their ears. &lquo;Lots&rquo; were the term in our author's
time for the total number of tickets in a <I>lottery,</I> which took its name from thence.
So in the <I>Continuation of Stowe's Chronicle,</I> 1615, p. 1002: &lquo;Out of which lottery,
for want of filling, by the number of lots, there were then taken out and thrown
away three score thousand blanks, without abating of any one prize.&rquo; The lots
were, of course, more numerous than the blanks. If &lquo;lot&rquo; signified <I>prize,</I> as Dr
Johnson supposed, there being in every lottery many more blanks than prizes,
Menenius must be supposed to say that the chance of his name having reached
their ears was very small, which certainly is not his meaning.&mdash;<SC>Ritson</SC> (<I>Cursory
Criticism,</I> p. 80): A <I>lot</I> here, Dr Johnson says, is a <I>prize.</I> It certainly is so;
though our sagacious Hibernian [Malone] believes him mistaken. Menenius, he
imagines, only means to say that it is more than an equal chance that his name
had touch'd their ears, which is precisely the effect of Dr Johnson's explanation.

meaning of the word the following extract from the tract <I>The Great Frost of January,
1608</I> may be quoted: &lquo;<I>Countryman:</I> I remember that, as I take it, in the eleventh

right. So much still lies in my memory. <I>Countryman:</I> Marry, that lottery was
only for money, and every lot was ten shillings&rquo; (ed. Arber, p. 94). Again, in the

blanks. . . . There are 7,600 prizes and 42,000 blanks&rquo; (Ibid., p. 95). This is
in reference to a lottery which was held, among other shows and festivals, on the
occasion of the Thames being frozen over in that year. There is, perhaps, here
another slight hint of internal evidence that this play was written in either 1608
or 1609. The great popularity of this lottery would make the phrase used by
Menenius readily understood by his auditors.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>21. <B>I haue euer verified</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Shakespeare's mighty talent in painting
the manners is especially remarkable in this place. Menenius here and Polonius
in <I>Hamlet</I> have much of the same natural character. The difference is only acci-
dental. The one was a senator in a free state, and the other a courtier and minister
to a king; which two circumstances afforded matter for that inimitable ridicule
thrown over the character of Polonius. For the rest, there is an equal complaisance
for those they follow; the same disposition to be a <I>creature,</I> the same love of prate,
the same affectation of wisdom, and forwardness to be in business. But we must
never believe Shakespeare could make either of them say, &lquo;I have verified my
friends with all the size of verity&rquo;; nay, what is more extraordinary, <I>verified them
beyond verity.</I> Without doubt he wrote, &lquo;For I have ever <I>narrified</I> my friends,&rquo;
<I>i. e.,</I> made their encomium. This too agrees with the foregoing metaphors of
<I>book, read,</I> and constitutes a uniformity amongst them. From whence the <I>Oxford
Editor</I> [Hanmer] took occasion to read <I>magnified,</I> which makes the absurdity
much worse than he found it; for to <I>magnify</I> signifies to <I>exceed</I> the truth; so that
this critic makes him say he <I>magnified</I> his friend <I>within</I> the size of verity, that is,
he exceeded truth even while he kept within it.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: If the commentator
had given any example of the word <I>narrify</I> the correction would have been not
only received but applauded. Now, since the new word stands without authority,
we must try what sense the old one will afford. To verify is to establish by testi-
mony. One may say with propriety he brought false witnesses to <I>verify</I> his title.
Shakespeare considered the word with his usual laxity, as importing rather <I>testi-
mony</I> than <I>truth,</I> and only meant to say, I bore <I>witness</I> to my friends with all the
size that verity would suffer. I must remark that to <I>magnify</I> signifies to <I>exalt</I> or
<I>enlarge,</I> but not necessarily to enlarge beyond the truth.&mdash;<SC>Edwards</SC> (p. 98):
&lquo;Verified&rquo; here is certainly wrong, as Mr Warburton in a long note has shown. To
mend it he gives us a word which, if it is not his own, I doubt he can find no better
authority for than the Dictionary of N. Bailey, Philolog., who has taken care to
preserve all the cant words he could pick up. However, he gives the honor of it
to Shakespeare, and says, &lquo;without doubt he wrote &ldquo;I have ever <I>narrified</I> my
friends,&rdquo; <I>i. e.,</I> made their encomium.&rquo; I suppose Menenius read his encomiums out
of a book, or at least learned them there, and then <I>narrified</I> by rote. But though
Mr Warburton makes no doubt of Shakespeare's writing <I>narrified,</I> I must own I
do; and if it were lawful for one, who is not a critic by profession, to make a con-
jecture after him, which yet I would not venture to thrust into the text without
authority, I should imagine that possibly Shakespeare might have written, &lquo;I
have ever <I>varnished</I> my friends . . . with all the size that verity Would without
lapsing suffer.&rquo; That is, I have laid on as much praise as would stick. It is an
allusion either to painting or white-washing; and the word <I>varnish</I> (or <I>vernish,</I>
as it is sometimes spelt) agrees with the following metaphor of <I>size,</I> at least as well
as <I>narrify</I> does with <I>book</I> before. The only misfortune is that the uniformity is

<P>broken; but that is of the less consequence, because otherwise it would be knocked
to pieces by the &lquo;bowls&rquo; which come in the very next line. Whether this be right
or no, I doubt <I>narrifying</I> with <I>size</I> will pass on nobody but a professed critic.&mdash;
<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 428): If I had not learned from the <I>Canons of Criticism</I> that the word
<I>narrified</I> is to be found in Bailey's Dictionary I should scarce have believed it author-
ized by any one writer in the English language. If it be not a cant word, as most
probably it is, it conveys so ridiculous an idea that it can find no place in any
other than burlesque writing. But <I>varnishing</I> with <I>size</I> [as Edwards suggests],
and with all the size that verity would suffer, seems little less exceptionable than
<I>narrifying.</I> I think Sir Thomas Hanmer's correction, <I>magnified,</I> bids fair for being
the true reading. The word <I>verity</I> at the end of the next line might strike the
eye of the transcriber or printer, and hang upon his imagination sufficiently to
occasion the blunder. But Mr Warburton objects, that &lquo;to <I>magnify</I> signifies to
exceed the truth&rquo;; and so makes an impotent effort to pass this expression on the
reader for a bull. His very prayers might have taught him better. To <I>magnify</I>
signifies to extol the greatness of anything in some respect or other, whether the
praise exceed the truth, or keep within the strict bounds of it. The word <I>size</I>
doth not here signify the composition otherwise called paste, as the author of the
<I>Canons of Criticism</I> seems to misapprehend it, but dimension. [Heath, by thus
treating with mock seriousness the <I>jeu d'esprit</I> of Edwards in regard to &lquo;varnish,&rquo;
&lquo;size,&rquo; and &lquo;white-wash,&rquo; places Warburton's emendation in the same ridiculous class.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 99): This unlucky word&mdash;&lquo;verified&rquo;&mdash;has been tum-
bled and tossed about strangely and has chang'd its quarters for <I>narrify'd, magnify'd,
varnish'd,</I> &amp;c.; but, after all its peregrinations, here it is again, and here it should
be. For, in the name of goodness, where is the impropriety of saying, When I
have undertaken to give my friend <I>his due</I> praise, I have sometimes given him
<I>more than his due?</I> Yet this is the amount of what is said by Menenius, but he says
it in his manner. &lquo;Size&rquo; is proportion, dimension.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Dr Johnson's
explanation of the old word <I>verify</I> renders all change unnecessary. To <I>verify</I>
may, however, signify to <I>display.</I> Thus in an ancient metrical pedigree in the
possession of the late Duchess of Northumberland, and quoted by Dr Percy in
<I>The Reliques of Ancient English Poetry,</I> vol. i, p. 279, 3<SUP>d</SUP> edit., &lquo;In hys scheld
did schyne a mone veryfying her light.&rquo; [The <I>N. E. D.</I> does not include <I>to display</I>
under the various senses in which &lquo;verify&rquo; is used. In the line quoted by Steevens
the word may, perhaps, be interpreted as therein given under 2. d., &lquo;To demonstrate
or prove (oneself) to be of a certain character,&rquo; with this example, &lquo;Fortune . . .
Turned her selfe, as shee away would flie, . . . As what she was, her selfe to verifie.&rquo;
1596. Drayton: <I>Leg., Dk. Normandie,</I> cxxxiv. Under 1. c. &lquo;To support or back
up by testimony,&rquo; the present line is quoted as the only example.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>:
The meaning (to give a somewhat more expanded comment) is: &lquo;I have ever spoken
the truth of my friends, and in speaking of them have gone as far as I could go
consistently with truth. I have not only told the truth, but the whole truth, and
with the most favourable colouring that I could give to their actions without trans-
gressing the bounds of truth.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> regards as indisputable the reading of
his MS. Corrector, <I>magnified,</I> but fails to call attention to the fact that this is the
reading of Hanmer's text.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> p. 225) is equally at fault in
commenting upon this reading, and says in conclusion: &lquo;If any change is neces-
sary, which seems doubtful, <I>notified</I> could hardly be distinguished, when written

<P>45. <B>the Virginall Palms</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: By &lquo;virginal palms&rquo; may be indeed
understood the holding up the hands in supplication. Therefore I have altered
nothing. But as this sense is cold and gives us even a ridiculous idea; and as the
<I>passions</I> of the several intercessors seem intended to be represented, I suspect
Shakespeare might write <I>pasmes</I> or <I>pames,</I> that is, swooning fits, from the French
<I>pasmer</I> or <I>p&acirc;mer.</I> I have frequently used the liberty to give sense to an unmeaning
passage by the introduction of a French word of the same sound, which I suppose
to be of Shakespeare's own coining. And I am certainly justified in so doing by
the great number of such sort of words to be found in the common text.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>:
It is not denied that many French words were mingled in the time of Elizabeth
with our language, which have since been ejected, and that many which are known
then to have been in use may be properly recalled when they will help the sense.
But when a word is to be admitted, the first question should be, by whom was it
ever received? in what book can it be shewn? If it cannot be proved to have been
in use, the reasons which can justify its reception must be stronger than any critic
will have to bring.&mdash;<SC>Edwards</SC> (p. 99): Mr Warburton must sure have a very hard
heart if the idea of virgins holding up their hands in supplication for their lives and
honor can seem to him either <I>cold</I> or <I>ridiculous,</I> and nothing will satisfy him but

<P>making them swoon that he may have an opportunity of bringing in a French
word.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 429): The author of the <I>Canons of Criticism</I> hath very justly
exposed Mr Warburton's most ridiculous emendation, . . . though the word
[<I>pasms</I> or <I>p&acirc;mes</I>] as a noun is as unknown to the French as it is to the English
language, and probably to every language that is human. I do indeed admit
that &lquo;a great number of French words are incorporated in our language, and used
by Shakespeare in common with other writers&rquo;; but that there are a great number
of such words to be met with in his writings which are of his own coining, and
peculiar to himself, is a circumstance which, I must confess, hath escaped my
observation. But granting the fact to be true; is that a sufficient justification for
over-loading him with such words by wholesale for mere fanciful conjecture
only, in defiance of the authority of all his editions, and that too when their text
expresses his meaning in English full as well, and frequently much better, and with
more force and elegance? To detect the weakness and insufficiency of Mr War-
burton's defence we need but apply the reasoning on which it is founded to a
similar instance. Whoever hath but dipped into Shakespeare must have observed
a certain obscurity, which may be considered as one of the characteristic peculiar-
ities of his style, arising in great measure from the grandeur, the strength, and the
exactness of his conceptions, which he could not equal by the force of his expression,
though his powers even of this kind were never excelled by any other writer. It
is the business of a critic to illustrate these obscurities, but he would be justly
laughed at and exploded if he should set about multiplying their number under
the pretext that he was strictly adhering to Shakespeare's manner.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>:
The adjective &lquo;virginal&rquo; is used in <I>Woman is a Weathercock,</I> 1612, &lquo;Lav'd in a bath
of contrite virginal tears,&rquo; [III, ii, Hazlett-Dods., p. 53]. Again in Spenser,
<I>Faerie Queene,</I> &lquo;She to them made with mildnesse virginall,&rquo; Bk ii, cant. ix, [v. 20,
l. 4].&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: So in <I>2 Henry VI:</I> &lquo;&mdash;tears virginal Shalt be to me even as the
dew to fire,&rquo; [V, ii, 52].&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> p. 226): It is possible that for
&lquo;virginal palms&rquo; we should read &lquo;virginal <I>qualms</I>&rquo;<I>;</I> the words would be easily mis-
taken for each other in old manuscript. &lquo;Virginal <I>palms</I>&rquo; may, however, mean
the palms or hands of the maidens joined in supplication.&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC> (<I>Sh's
Scholar,</I> p. 366): Indeed, Mr Singer! may it? Is it possible? Can such an obvious
and simple construction of a plain but beautiful passage be dreamt of in your
philosophy? I must ask pardon for noticing such attempts on Shakespeare's text,
and for noticing them as I do; for, in truth, I should as soon expect an intelligent
reader, not to say a competent editor of Shakespeare, &lquo;to expostulate . . . Why
day is day, night, night, and time is time,&rquo; as thus to raise a question on what it
would seem impossible to misunderstand.

<P>58, 59. <B>halfe pinte of blood. Backe . . . hauing</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: As these
words are read and pointed, the sentence &lquo;that's the utmost of your having&rquo;
signifies, you are like to get no further. Whereas the author evidently intended
it to refer to &lquo;the half pint of blood&rquo; he speaks of, and to mean that that was all
he had in his veins. The thought is humorous, and to disembarrass it from the
corrupt expression we should read and point thus, &lquo;Lest I let forth your half pint
of blood; that's the utmost of your having. Back, back.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I believe
the meaning never was mistaken, and therefore do not change the reading.&mdash;
<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 432): Mr Warburton has taken upon him to alter the text in order, as
he says, to preserve the humour. But the common reading gives exactly the same
sense, is fully as intelligible, and by interposing the word &lquo;back&rquo; in the middle of
the sentence gives more humour and spirit to the expression. Let the reader
judge. &lquo;Back, I say, go; lest I let forth your half pint of blood&mdash;back&mdash;that's
the utmost of your having.&mdash;Back.&rquo;

<P>73. <B>looke thee</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 212): Verbs followed by <I>thee</I> instead of <I>thou</I> have
been called reflexive. But though &lquo;haste thee&rquo; and some other phrases with
verbs of motion, may be thus explained, and verbs were thus often used in Early
English, it is probable that &lquo;look <I>thee,</I>&rquo; &lquo;hark <I>thee</I>&rquo; are to be explained by euphonic
reasons. <I>Thee</I> thus used follows imperatives which, being themselves emphatic,
require an unemphatic pronoun. The Elizabethans reduced <I>thou</I> to <I>thee.</I> We
have gone further, and rejected it altogether.
<P>76. <B>your Gates</B>] <SC>Ritson</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> p. 142): &lquo;Your&rquo; cannot be right. If the
speaker mean to call the gates Coriolanus's, which would seem very absurd, he ought
to say <I>thy.</I> It must be either <I>our</I> or <I>their.</I>&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC> (reading with F<SUB>4</SUB>): Menenius
cannot call the gates &lquo;your,&rquo; since Coriolanus afterwards says &lquo;your,&rquo; l. 90. Per-
haps we ought to read <I>yond.</I>&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> retains the folio reading, taking it as an
example of the ethical dative, which is, I think, hardly defensible; his second
reason is the better: &lquo;Perhaps Menenius wishes to bring more nearly home to
Coriolanus that it is his own (Coriolanus's) native city from which he comes.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Case</SC> gives substantially this same reason for retaining the reading &lquo;your gates.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.,</I> ii, ch. xlvi.) gives many examples of the confusion between
<I>your</I> and <I>our</I> not only in the pages of the Folio, but in works by other writers and
printers.

<P><B>Scene III.</B>] <SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): This is perhaps the finest scene in
the play. It is also one of the most important. Two mighty kindred spirits clash
together, and in the clash Coriolanus' second failure is determined. The powerful
individuality of Volumnia, kept in the background hitherto and only suggested,
now dominates the action, and, by contact with her, Coriolanus too rises to a
pitch of higher dignity than he has yet reached.&mdash;<SC>Stopford Brooke</SC> (p. 241):
We find Coriolanus worshipped as a leader, not as a man, by the Volscian soldiery;
apparently on the peak of fortune. But he is really more lost, more alone than
ever. No one loves him. He can have no communion with his comrades. It is
almost pitiable to hear his appeals to Aufidius, who hates him, to tell him what
to do. Then, in his solitude, his affections, the best part of him, which his pride
had smothered, awake again. Though he repulses Menenius, who comes to im-
plore grace for Rome, we feel that he loves him. He longs to see his mother, his
wife, and son, but his position is such that he dare not satisfy his longing. It is
a piteous case, for if we add to his vast loneliness this intense and silent emotion
of natural affection, whose indulgence is forbidden, he becomes (as Shakespeare's
sympathy with sorrow meant him to become) an object of noble pity to the audi-
ence&mdash;and, perhaps, to the gods.

<P>19. <B>Fresh Embasses</B>] Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Shakespeare skips one
embassy described in Plutarch, an embassy of the Roman Priests and Soothsayers.
Plutarch says nothing either of Menenius or Cominius by name as ambassadors.
Shakespeare chose to invent their personal missions on the strength of Plutarch's
statement that &lquo;The ambassadours that were sent were Martius' familiar friends
and acquaintances, who looked at the least for a courteous welcome of him as their
familiar friend and kinsman.&rquo;
<P>21. <B>what shout is this</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (vol. I, pt i, p. 99): The Oxford editor [Hanmer] has
not shown his judgment in changing &lquo;shout&rquo; in this place into <I>sight.</I> Should a pro-
cession, like that which comes presently, make its entry without any announcement?
or could the Volcians, though enemies, see the mother and wife of their general,
together with a large train of ladies, approach the door of his tent without notice
or some mark of respect to them? and what properer in camps than a &lquo;shout&rquo;?

<P>explanation is offered in the play of how the ladies were more successful than

<P>28. <B>But out affection,</B> etc.] <SC>A. C. Bradley</SC> (<I>Coriolanus,</I> p. 13): To me this
scene is one in which the tragic feelings of fear and pity have little place. Such
anxiety as I feel is not for the fate of the hero or of any one else; it is, to use re-
ligious language, for the safety of his soul. And when he yields, though I know,
as he divines, that his life is lost, the emotion I feel is not pity; he is above pity
and above life. And the anxiety itself is but slight; it bears no resemblance to the
hopes and fears that agitate us as we approach the end in <I>Othello</I> or <I>King Lear.</I>
The whole scene affects me, to exaggerate a little, more as a majestic picture of
stationary figures than as the fateful climax of an action speeding to its close.
And the structure of the drama seems to confirm this view. Almost throughout
the first three acts&mdash;that is, up to the banishment&mdash;we have incessant motion,
excited and resounding speech, a violent oscillation of fortunes. But after this
the dramatic tension is suddenly relaxed, and though it increases again, it is never
allowed to approach its previous height. If Shakespeare had wished to do so in
this scene he had only to make us wait in dread of some interposition from
Aufidius, at which the hero's passion might have burst into a fury fatal even to
the influence of Volumnia. But our minds are crossed by no shadow of such
dread. From the moment when he catches sight of the advancing figures, and the
voice of nature&mdash;what he himself calls &lquo;great nature&rquo;&mdash;begins to speak in his heart
long before it speaks aloud to his ear, we know the end. And all this is in har-
mony with that characteristic of the drama which we noticed at first&mdash;we feel but
faintly, if at all, the presence of any mysterious or fateful agency. We are wit-
nessing only the conquest of passion by simple human feelings, and <I>Coriolanus</I> is
as much a drama of reconciliation as a tragedy. That is no defect in it, but it is
a reason why it cannot leave the same impression as the supreme tragedies, and
should be judged by its own standard.

while at this point to recollect to what it was that Coriolanus proposed to sacrifice
all natural ties, because there might be conditions under which such a course would
be justifiable.

<P>31. <B>those Doues eyes</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: So in the <I>Canticles,</I> v. 12, &lquo;&mdash;his eyes are
as the eyes of doves.&rquo; [Also <I>Ibid.,</I> i, 15, and iiii, i.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] Again, in the <I>Interpreta-

<P>32, 33. <B>I melt, and am not Of stronger earth</B>] <SC>Stopford Brooke</SC> (p. 242):
This is Coriolanus at his best, thrilled by those natural affections which last longest,
and which in their natural working are the best medicine for the selfish heart.
Coriolanus fights against them; his promise to Aufidius, his vow of revenge beat
back his yielding and forgiveness. But when his mother finally turns from mere
arguing the question to her ancient way with him, and claims his reverence for his
motherhood; and then, when he is still silent, breaks into scorn of him, and bids
him, repudiating him, seek his family among the Volscians&mdash;why then Coriolanus
can bear no more. His lonely pride is shattered by the dominance of what is tender,
good, and natural in him. For the first time in his life he is truly unselfish. He
gives up his most passionate desire&mdash;revenge. He puts away pride and anger,
the tyrannic qualities of his nature; and he does this knowing, at least suspecting,
that this means his death&mdash;and it does mean it. The man is redeemed. The
repentence is not too late for honour, not too late for moral greatness; for thus
conquered, he is at last great, having won by renouncing all that he once thought
were the sources of his fame, immortal fame. But he is not freed from the results
of his long wrong-doing. Repentence is too late to save his life, and that he knows
he is doomed makes his act the nobler. Thus Shakespeare veils the perishing man
with tenderness, pity, and admiration. We forgive what we hated in him in the
past. His wife and mother, knowing he is lost, yet went home with peace in their
heart, and Rome remembered only his fame as a warrior. Over his dead body
the patricians and the tribunes came to respect each other more. The dead
Coriolanus was greater than the living.

shew, by the lofty Olympus?&rquo; [<I>Poems,</I> ed. Grosart, ii, p. 21, l. 75].&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden
Sh.</I>): See also Massinger, <I>Virgin Martyr,</I> I, i, &lquo;An humble modesty that would not
match A molehill with Olympus,&rquo; [ed. Gifford, p. 20]; <I>The Roman Actor,</I> III, i, 1-4:
&lquo;if you but compare What I have suffered with your injuries (Though great ones, I
confess) they will appear Like molehills to Olympus.&rquo;

<P>52. <B>You Gods, I pray</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Restored,</I> p. 181): I dare say an old
corruption has possess'd this passage for two reasons. In the first place, whoever
consults this speech will find that he is talking to his wife, and not praying to
the Gods at all. <I>Secondly,</I> if he were employ'd in his devotions, no apology would
be wanting for leaving his mother unsaluted. The Poet's intention was certainly
this: Coriolanus, having been lavish in his tendernesses and Raptures to his wife,
bethinks himself on the sudden, that his fondness to her had made him guilty of
ill manners in the neglect of his mother. Restore, as it certainly ought to be,
&lquo;You Gods! <SC>I prate</SC>, And the most noble mother of the world Leave unsaluted.&rquo;&mdash;
Mr <SC>Dennis</SC> (than whom, in my opinion, no man in England better understands
Shakespeare) in his alteration of this play [<I>The Invader of His Country</I>], whether
he made the same correction I now do, certainly understood the passage exactly
with me. An undeniable proof of this is an appeal to the change in expression which
he has put upon it: &lquo;But Oh! ye Gods, while fondly thus I <I>talk,</I> see, the most
noble mother of the world Stands unsaluted.&rquo; I question not, but his reason for
varying the expression was because <I>prate</I> is a term ill-sounding in itself, and
mean in its acceptation. Our language was not so refin'd, tho' more masculine,
in Shakespeare's days; and therefore (notwithstanding the cacophony) when he
is most serious he frequently makes use of the word. In this very play we again
meet with it, &lquo;yet here he lets me prate Like one i' th' stocks,&rquo; [l. 170 below.

<P>Theobald gvies five other passages wherein the words <I>prate</I> and <I>prattling</I> occur;
but the word <I>prate</I> is used more often than that by Shakespeare. Bartlett gives
fifteen examples. This play alone furnishes three others besides that quoted by
Theobald. See I, i, 45; III, iii, 106; and IV, v, 47. For <I>prattling</I> see II, i, 221.
This note, omitting all reference to Dennis, Theobald adopted in his own edition.
The <I>Text. Notes</I> show with what unanimity it has been accepted.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;Miss
<SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Shakespeare changes the order of his salutations
from that given by Plutarch and makes him show his love for his wife first and
irresistibly; but he causes him to make amends for this by excusing himself for
keeping his mother unsaluted while thus he prays Virgilia to forgive him, begs
her not to urge him to forgive the Romans, and then, pleading for a kiss, prays
the goddess of marriage to bear witness to its purity. All this justifies the word
&lquo;pray&rquo; in the text, which Pope has changed to <I>prate.</I> Surely Coriolanus does not
call this true emotion &lquo;prating.&rquo; Although he must be meant to ask pardon of
his mother for leaving her unsaluted during all this, he cannot be meant to excuse
himself by a word uncomplimentary to his wife. Shakespeare has very delicately
done the right thing, and the fact of his altering Plutarch shows it to be peculiarly
his touch. Pope has spoiled it. [I know not why Miss Porter assigns this reading
to Pope. The Cambridge <I>Text. Notes</I> plainly show by the parenthesis containing
Theobald's name, following the reading of Pope's ed. ii, that <I>prate</I> is Theobald's
suggestion adopted by Pope.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>63. <B>Corrected Sonne</B>] <SC>Whitelaw</SC>: That is, rebuked by the sight. [<SC>Delius</SC> takes

<P>64. <B>hungry beach</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: The beach hungry, or eager, for shipwrecks.
Such, I think, is the meaning. So in <I>Twelfth Night,</I> &lquo;mine is all as hungry as the
sea,&rquo; [II, iv, 103]. I once idly conjectured that our author wrote, the <I>angry</I>
beach.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The &lquo;hungry beach&rquo; is the <I>sterile, unprolific</I> beach. Every
writer on husbandry speaks of <I>hungry</I> soil and <I>hungry</I> gravel; and what is more
barren than the sands on the sea shore? If it be necessary to seek for a more
recondite meaning, the shore on which vessels are stranded is as hungry for ship-
wrecks, as the waves that cast them on the shore. <I>Litus avarum</I> [<I>&AElig;neid,</I> iii, 45].
Shakespeare, on this occasion, meant to represent the beach as a mean, and not
as a magnificent object.&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC>: I must avow that I see no fitness (espe-
cially none of the Shakespearian kind) in the epithet as explained [by Steevens].
The context, &lquo;your <I>corrected</I> son&rquo; and &lquo;the <I>mutinous</I> winds,&rquo; seems to me to give
almost sufficient support to [Malone's &lquo;idle conjecture&rquo;] to warrant its reception
into the text. Were I to print a Shakespeare for myself I should print &lquo;<I>angry</I>
beach&rquo;&mdash;the beach angered by the lashing of the waves.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>, ed. i, accepts
Steevens's note and explanation, even going so far as to copy Steevens's misprint
<I>littus,</I> but in his ed. ii. he adopts Malone's idle conjecture, with the following note:
&lquo;As an epithet of <I>beach,</I> taken by itself, <I>hungry</I> may well pass, but that sense has
no coherence with the context here.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, <I>sterile, unproductive;</I>
not, greedy for shipwrecks.&mdash;<SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.,</I> s. v. 6.): Lacking elements which
are needful or desirable, and therefore capable of absorbing these to a great extent;
&lquo;more disposed to draw from other substances than to impart them&rquo; (Johnson);
especially of land, etc. Not rich or fertile, poor. 1577. B. Googe, <I>Heresbach's
Husbandry,</I> I. (1586), 24: &lquo;The land . . . which is nought and yeeldes not his
fruite, is called leane, barren, hungry.&rquo;

<P>69. <B>I hope to frame thee</B>] Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Here possibly

is generally and not particularly appropriate. It suits what has been said by
Coriolanus (ll. 26, 27), but gives us no new word. And since Coriolanus has just
shown a son's acknowledgment to the full of even a mother's desire, it seems
now particularly appropriate to suppose that Volumnia's acceptance of this now
would be marked by more than a reassertion of the fact that she is his mother.
Does she not exclaim joyfully and triumphantly accepting his filial homage,
&lquo;Thou art my Warrior&rquo;?&mdash;and then, because of that recognition, does she not ex-
press more than the same thing again in another form&mdash;this further, &lquo;I hope to
frame thee&rquo;? That is, mould thee to the end for which I came.

<P>Some Roman lady of the name of Valeria was one of the great examples of chastity
held out by writers of the Middle Ages. So in <I>The Dialoges of Creatures Moralysed,</I>
bl. l., no date, &lquo;The secounde was called Valeria: and when inquysicion was made of
her for what Cawse she toke notte the secounde husbonde, she sayde,&rquo; &amp;c. Hence
perhaps Shakespeare's extravagant praise of her namesake's chastity.&mdash;<SC>Dowden</SC>
(<I>Sh.: His Mind and Art,</I> p. 331, foot-note): Observe the extraordinary vital beauty
and illuminating quality of Shakespeare's metaphors and similes. A common-place
poet would have written &lquo;as chaste as snow&rquo;; but Shakespeare's imagination dis-
covers degrees of chastity in ice and snow, and chooses the chastest of all frozen
things. On this subject see an excellent study by Rev. H. N. Hudson, <I>Shakespeare:
His Life, Art, and Characters,</I> vol. i, pp. 217-237.
<P>73. <B>curdied</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: [This] was the phraseology of Shakespeare's time. So

now write <I>mudded,</I> to express <I>begrimed, polluted with mud.</I> Again in <I>Cymbeline,</I>
&lquo;That drug-damn'd Italy hath outcraftied him,&rquo; [III, iv, 15].&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I be-
lieve both &lquo;curdied,&rquo; <I>muddied,</I> &amp;c., are mere false spellings of <I>curded, mudded,</I> &amp;c.
<I>Mudded</I> is spelt as at present in <I>The Tempest,</I> First Fol., p. 13, col. 2, three lines
from the bottom; and so is &lquo;crafted&rquo; in this play, First Fol., p. 24, col. 2, [see
IV, vi, 147.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>].&mdash;<SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.,</I> s. v. <I>Curdy,</I> vb. Obs. rare): To make curd-

<I>curdied</I> is a misprint for <I>curdled</I>).]

<P>82. <B>Sea-marke standing euery flaw</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, every <I>gust,</I> every
storm.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: So in our author's <I>Sonnet</I> cxi, &lquo;O no! it is an ever fixed mark
That looks on tempests, and is never shaken.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. H. Smyth</SC> (s. v. <I>Sea-Mark</I>):
A point or object distinguishable at sea, as promontories, steeples, rivers, trees,
&amp;c., forming important beacons, and noted on charts. By keeping two in a line,
channels can be entered with safety, and thus the errors of steerage, effect of
tide, &amp;c., obviated. These erections are a branch of the royal prerogative, and
by Statute 8, Elizabeth, Cap. 13, the corporation of the Trinity House are empowered
to set up any beacons or sea-marks wherever they shall think them necessary; and
if any person shall destroy them, he shall forfeit &pound;100, or, in case of inability to
pay, he shall be, <I>ipso facto,</I> outlawed.&mdash;<SC>Whall</SC> (p. 73) compares <I>Othello,</I> V, ii, 268,
&lquo;And very sea mark of my utmost sail.&rquo;
<P>84. <B>Your knee, Sirrah</B>] <SC>Cambridge Edd.</SC> ii. (<I>Note XIII.</I>): Dr Nicholson writes
to us: &lquo;The stage action here to which Coriolanus replies is this: the boy refuses
to kneel, but interposes between the kneeling ladies and Coriolanus. See his
after speech, &ldquo;A shall not tread on me,&rdquo; &amp;c. This, if not introduced as a stage-
direction, ought to be explained in a note.&rquo; To us Coriolanus seems rather to com-
mend the boy for doing as he was bid. To refuse to kneel would suit ill with his
&lquo;aspect of nitercession.&rquo; Besides, he kneels, without being specially told to do
so, afterwards (l. 186).

ton</SC> (reading with Rowe): Yet we will continue to make supplication, so that if
we fail to obtain what we ask, the blame may rest upon you for your stubbornness,
not on us for our want of persistency. The reading of the Folio may perhaps be
explained, &lquo;fail in the matter of our request.&rquo;

<P>104-135. <B>Should we be silent,</B> etc.] <SC>Farmer</SC>, in his second edition of his <I>Essay on
the Learning of Shakespeare,</I> p. 13, transcribes these thirty-two lines, together with
the corresponding passage from North's <I>Plutarch,</I> in order to confute a remark made
by Pope in his Preface: &lquo;The speeches copied from Plutarch in <I>Coriolanus</I> may be
as well made an instance of the learning of Shakespeare as those copied from
Cicero, in <I>Catiline,</I> of Ben Jonson's.&rquo; Farmer's intent is to demonstrate that
Shakespeare's knowledge was gained solely by the translation and not by recourse
to the original. Pope has, however, not made any such claim; he clearly says,
preceding the above-quoted sentence, &lquo;There is certainly a vast difference between
<I>Learning</I> and <I>Languages.</I> How far he was ignorant of the latter I cannot determine;
but 'tis plain he had much reading at least, if they will not call it Learning. Nor is
it any great matter, if a man has knowledge, whether he has it from one language
or from another.&rquo; Farmer, in thus quoting but the concluding part of Pope's re-
mark, gives to the reader a quite erroneous impression of Pope's contention. He
certainly did not mean that these parallel passages proved that Shakespeare read
them in the original Greek. The passage in North's <I>Plutarch,</I> which Shakespeare
here follows with but a few verbal changes, in order to make it into verse, will
be found in the <I>Appendix: Source of the Plot, ad loc.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>104, 105. <B>our Raiment And state of Bodies</B>] For other examples of transposi-
tions in noun-clauses containing two nouns connected by &lquo;of&rquo; see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 423.
<P>105. <B>bewray</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, discover, reveal. The word, which
Shakespeare has taken from North's <I>Plutarch,</I> is derived from the Anglo-Saxon
<I>wr&eacute;gan,</I> or <I>wreian,</I> Gothic <I>wrohjan,</I> to accuse, and although used almost inter-
changeably with <I>betray,</I> differs from it in not necessarily involving the idea of
treachery. See <I>King Lear,</I> II, i, 109, &lquo;He did bewray his practice&rquo;; that is, dis-
closed his plot or design.
<P>106. <B>Exile</B>] Here accented on the last syllable; see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 490.
<P>107. <B>How more vnfortunate</B>] See <I>Appendix: Date of Composition,</I> note by
<SC>Halliwell</SC>, p. 600.

<P>131. <B>Rather ... to both parts</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>: The extra syllable is very rarely a
monosyllable, still more rarely an emphatic monosyllable. The reason is obvious.
Since in English we have no enclitics, the least emphatic monosyllables will gen-
erally be prepositions and conjunctions. These carry the attention <I>forward</I> instead
of <I>backward,</I> and are, therefore, inconsistent with a <I>pause,</I> and besides, to some
extent, emphatic. Here &lquo;parts&rquo; is emphatic and &lquo;both&rquo; is strongly emphasized.

<P>to his mother.&rquo; And all his other domestic relations are denied to him. This is
too much for Coriolanus. His strongest tie he can allow to be severed; he might
even contemplate his mother dead; still he would be her son. But disowned&mdash;
denied to be her offspring&mdash;that cuts deeper than her death. He yields, Rome is
saved, but he declares to his mother he will probably have to die for his act. To
which declaration she gives no answer; country is, with her, above son; its salvation
being accomplished, she and the rest of her relatives return to receive its gratitude.
Family has thus mediated the conflict of the State.
<P>136. <B>I, and mine</B>] With Pope's rearrangement of the lines here these words are
used to supply the two final feet missing in l. 135. Even thus Capell's fine ear
detected a missing syllable, and he added &lquo;on.&rquo; Steevens, while adopting this last
reading, remarks that the word &lquo;was supplied by some former editor to complete
the measure.&rquo; For reasons best known to himself Steevens customarily either
ignores Capell or adopts his metrical changes without acknowledgment. To this
Boswell, the editor of the Variorum of 1821, rejoins that this last is perhaps un-
necessary &lquo;if &ldquo;world,&rdquo; according to Tyrwhitt's canon, is used as a dissyllable.&rquo;
Finally <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 482) quotes this arrangement of ll. 135, 136 as an example
wherein a monosyllabic exclamation (&lquo;Ay&rquo;) is frequently used as a complete foot.
In all such discussions is it not well to follow the golden rule, &lquo;verify your refer-
ences,&rquo; before imputing to Shakespeare a fault in prosody?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.):
What reader, if he has common sense, can doubt that Shakespeare, having written
just before &lquo;<I>on</I> thy mother's womb,&rquo; wrote here &lquo;Ay, and on mine&rquo;?

whole of Shakespeare's plays. Alas! like Marcellus, he is but shown and then

shadow of his father rather than an independent living being. We pass over here
the boy in <I>Henry V.</I> and the fool in <I>King Lear,</I> both of whom, though seemingly very

<P>Coriolanus &lquo;affected to imitate&rquo; are terror and mercy, both attributes of their
gods; to express this he is said to thunder as they do, but so to temper his terrors
that mankind is as little hurt by them as they commonly are by thunder, which
mostly spends its fury on oaks.&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): Volumnia means, &lquo;Speak to me!
Confess that thou hast injured thine honour (in being the enemy of thy country)
only for the purpose to be as merciful as the gods.&rquo; [&lquo;Affected&rquo; in the sense
<I>injured</I> is not admissible here, since it clearly means <I>to aim at,</I> as Schmidt (<I>Lex.,</I>
s. v. vb. 3) classifies it, and as this word is used in three other passages in this
play: II, ii, 22; III, iii, 1; IV, vi, 41.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: &lquo;Strains of honour,&rquo;
that is, the emotions or impulses of honour. &lquo;Strain,&rquo; which is etymologically
connected with the Anglo-Saxon <I>str&yacute;nan,</I> to beget, is used for a stock or race, as in
<I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> V, i, 59, &lquo;O, if thou wert the noblest of thy strain.&rquo; Hence it takes the
secondary sense of &lquo;natural disposition,&rquo; as in <I>Lear,</I> V, iii, 40, &lquo;Sir, you have
shown to-day your valiant strain,&rquo; that is, the valiant disposition of your race
which you have inherited. Finally, it denotes feeling, or impulse generally. See
<I>2 Henry IV:</I> IV, v, 171, &lquo;But if it did infect my blood with joy, Or swell my

<P>167. <B>Daughter, speake you</B>] <SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): With
what exquisitely artistic touches Shakespeare finishes his character-portraits!
Here in two half lines he paints Virgilia's habitual silence, and Volumnia's as
habitual torrent of words. She bids her daughter-in-law plead, yet waits not for
her to speak. (See IV, ii, 67 and note.) And then how consistently has he de-
picted Volumnia's mode of appeal to her son throughout, in III, ii. and here; begin-
ning with remonstrance and ending with reproach; her fiery nature so like his
own and so thoroughly accounting for his inherited disposition.
<P>168. <B>Speake thou Boy</B>] <SC>J. C. Collins</SC> (p. 77) calls attention to this as a touch

<I>Iphigenia in Aulis</I> (ll. 1241-5), where the little Orestes is employed by Iphigenia
for the same reason and for the same purpose.&rquo; Inasmuch as there was not any
translation in English of Euripides until long after Shakespeare's time&mdash;except
the <I>Jocasta,</I> by Gascoigne and Kinwellmarsh, in 1566&mdash;the <I>Iphigenia</I> is a very
doubtful source of his inspiration. There is a similarity in situation between this
whole scene and that in Act I, sc. ii. of the <I>Jocasta,</I> as in the foregoing translation
(ed. Cunliffe, pp. 274-277), but nothing can be argued from that, as Shakespeare is
here following Plutarch, and it may be that Euripides was the inspiration for
Plutarch's fictitious account of Volumnia's intercession.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>194. <B>Holds her by the hand silent</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes and Emendations,</I> etc.,
p. 363): The following descriptive addition [to this stage-direction] is made in
manuscript, <I>long, and self-struggling.</I> After this protracted strife, which shook the

What have you done?&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): It is impossible to believe

<P>195, 196. <B>Corio. O Mother, Mother! What haue you done?</B>] <SC>Horn</SC> (iv, 25):
I have no desire to bestow upon this much-admired scene the ordinarily expressed
praises, but for all that extol it highly, since it does not in any way tend towards
a soft and gentle quietude, which here would be quite out of place. As soon as
this mother, by her own person, has shown to him his mother Rome, and he feels
himself vanquished, what words has our poet given him? Is the bow of peace
again set forth in the heavens? and dare the hero recognise himself as the saviour
of his country? Nay! his dreadful mistake is but brought more clearly to him,
he feels it, and would willingly retract it and make good, but complete atonement
is impossible, since a revolt from one's country is not to be expiated by such easy
means, and he is henceforth for all time at variance with his native land and with
himself.&mdash;<SC>R&ouml;tscher</SC> (p. 25): The tragic power of this scene lies in this, that
Coriolanus, with the consciousness that this victory of filial duty will bear for him
deadly fruit, yet bows before the might of filial duty. Therein is its wizardry, its
most hidden skill revealed. The actor has here the task of presenting to us the
hero overwhelmed by the power of filial love and his pride and obstinacy melting
during the exhortation of Volumnia.

<P>201. <B>Most dangerously you haue with him preuail'd</B>] <SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 621):
This collapse of Coriolanus' purpose means nothing more than the victory of his
strongest impulse. There is no acknowledgment of offence, there is no renovation
of character, there is not even submission to the highest force within his experi-
ence. Our admiration of his surrender is not unmixed. It is a moving spectacle
to see a man, despite all the solicitations of wrath and revenge, of interest and
fear, obedient to what is, on the whole, so salutary an influence as domestic affec-
tion. But loyalty to this will not of itself avail to safeguard anyone from criminal
entanglements, or to equip him for beneficial public action, or to change the cur-
rent of his life. It may mean the triumph of a natural tendency that happens to
be good over other natural tendencies that happen to be bad, but it does not mean
acceptance of duty as duty, or anxiety to satisfy the claims that different duties
impose. Hence Coriolanus, to the very end, leaves unredeemed his inherited
obligations to Rome, while he leaves unfulfilled his voluntary pledges to his allies.
Even in Plutarch's narrative Shakespeare's insight is not required to detect this
underlying thought, but in the <I>Comparison,</I> which there is proof that Shakespeare
had studied, it is set forth so clearly that he who runs may read. That Shakespeare,
with his patriotism and equity, perceived the double flaw in Coriolanus' act of
grace can hardly be doubted. He was the last man to put the household above
the national gods, or to glorify breach of contract if only it were sanctioned
by domestic tenderness. In point of fact, he does not acquit his hero on either
count.

Norfolk sprightfully and bold.&rquo; And <I>Othello,</I> III, iv, 79, &lquo;Why do you speak
so startingly and rash?&rquo;

<P>205. <B>would you haue heard</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Heard&rquo; is here used as a dissyllable.
The modern editors read, <I>say,</I> would you have heard.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: As my ears
are wholly unreconciled to the dissyllabifications <I>e-arl, he-ard,</I> &amp;c., I continue to
read with the modern editors. <I>Say,</I> in other passages of our author, is prefatory
to a question. So in <I>Macbeth,</I> &lquo;Say, if thou hadst rather hear it from our mouths,&rquo;
&amp;c., [IV, i, 62].&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 483) by emphasizing strongly the monosyllable &lquo;you&rquo;
following &lquo;Were,&rquo; makes it practically a dissyllable, and thus pieces out the metrical
deficiency. Such &lquo;dissyllabifications&rquo; are to my ears more disagreeable than
Malone's suggested <I>he-ard.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>207. <B>I was</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.,</I> ii, 203): <I>Thou wert</I> (sometimes written in the old
poets <I>Th'wert</I>), <I>you were, I was,</I> &amp;c., occur frequently, both in Shakespeare and
contemporary dramatists, in places where it is clear they must have been pro-
nounced as one syllable, in whatever manner the construction was affected. Here
I believe we ought so to pronounce &lquo;I was.&rquo;
<P>213. <B>Stand to me</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: That is, stand by me, support me. See
III, i, 250.

<P>216. <B>a former Fortune</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I will take advantage of this concession to
restore myself to my former credit and power.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: Since &lquo;former&rquo; in the
older tongue was used not only as simply referring to time but also to class and
position, it is, therefore, more likely here used in the sense of an advanced fortune,
a fortune that stands more in the very first rank. Thus it appears in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I>
V, i, 80, &lquo;our former ensign.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emendations,</I> ed. ii, p. 368):
We do not insist upon the change, but we are told, in this speech of Aufidius, to
substitute &lquo;a <I>firmer</I> fortune&rquo; for &lquo;a former fortune.&rquo; We think the emendation
extremely admissible.&mdash;<SC>Tycho Mommsen</SC> (<I>Der Perkins Folio,</I> p. 224): How un-
natural is the indefinite article with &lquo;former&rquo; instead of, possibly, &lquo;<I>my</I> former&rquo;;
how striking and clear <I>firmer,</I> since Aufidius already sees in spirit the fortune of
Coriolanus declining, from whose downfall he will construct for himself a more
stable fortune, firmer than his own was before, and rehabilitate himself from that
of Coriolanus. The words &lquo;former&rquo; and <I>firmer</I> are so nearly alike that the error was
an easy one.&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC>: &lquo;Former,&rquo; the Folio reading, is clearly a trifling mis-
print, as Aufidius does not say &lquo;<I>my</I> former fortune&rquo;; which, even if such were the
text, would be a less appropriate reading [than Collier's MS. correction].&mdash;<SC>H.
Wellesley</SC> (p. 29): &lquo;Former&rquo; with the indefinite article reads harshly. The ante-
cedents of Aufidius make it more consistent with his part to read, &lquo;a firmer for-
tune.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): That is, such fortune as I possessed formerly.
So in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> &lquo;You have seen and proved a fairer former fortune Than that
which is to approach,&rquo; [I, ii, 33, 34. Johnson's explanation of the phrase &lquo;former
fortune&rquo; has been adopted by most modern editors. To the parallel passage from
<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> given by Schmidt, Case adds: &lquo;but please your thoughts In feeding
them with those my former fortunes,&rquo; <I>Ibid.,</I> IV, xv, 52-54. That the phrase
thus occurs in two other passages besides the present shows, I think, that it was
one that commended itself to Shakespeare; this would be sufficient to cause a
rejection of the reading of Collier's MS. Corrector, <I>firmer.</I> The interpretation by
Delius and his comparison of the phrase &lquo;our former ensign&rquo; are not to the point.
<I>Former,</I> in this latter passage, is the regular use of the word, signifying that which
is in the forward part, as in &lquo;the former part of the head.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

ladies, and this colloquy, seen but not heard by the audience, he closes with the

<P>217. <B>we will drinke together</B>] <SC>Farmer</SC>: Perhaps we should read <I>think.</I>&mdash;
<SC>Steevens</SC>: Our author, in <I>2 Henry IV,</I> having introduced <I>drinking</I> as a mark of
confederation, &lquo;Let's drink together friendly and embrace,&rquo; [IV, ii, 64], the text
may be allowed to stand, though at the expense of female delicacy, which, in the
present instance, has not been sufficiently consulted.&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC>: Though I
cannot accept Farmer's proposition to read &lquo;<I>think</I> together,&rquo; and have no better
word to propose, I cannot but believe that &lquo;drink,&rquo; addressed to Volumnia and
Virgilia, is a corruption.&mdash;<SC>Herwegh</SC> (ap. <SC>Ulrici</SC>: <I>Sh.,</I> p. 171): This invitation to
drink extended to Volumnia and Virgilia has given offence to certain English
commentators. It is quite true that North's <I>Plutarch</I> says nothing on this point.
If drinking is not Roman, yet, on the other hand, it is characteristically English,
and, therefore, Shakespeare has here assuredly written &lquo;drink,&rquo; just as in I, ix, 110
he has made the exhausted Coriolanus cry out, &lquo;Have we no wine here?&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): Every doubt as to the correctness of the reading &lquo;drink
together&rquo; may be dismissed. Such was the sign of peace and friendship, just as in
<I>2 Henry IV.</I> [quoted above by Steevens] and also in other passages. [Notably
in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.,</I> on the conclusion of the quarrel between Brutus and Cassius. Brutus
there says, &lquo;Give me a bowl of wine. In this I bury all unkindness, Cassius,&rquo;
IV, iii, 158, 159.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> in his ed. i. accepts the Folio reading without com-
ment, apparently unconscious of the slur thus cast upon the fair fame of Volum-
nia and Virgilia, but White, in his note, with its excusatory hint as to a corruption
in the text here, doubtless opened the eyes of Hudson to this grievous fault, so
in his ed. ii, in order to preserve the &lquo;female delicacy,&rquo; he made the slight change
in the text, &lquo;We will but drink together&rquo;; and we have at once the picture of
Coriolanus and Aufidius retiring to the back of the tent for a surreptitious drink
while the ladies patiently await them. The words &lquo;Come enter with us,&rquo; l. 221,
militate somewhat against this.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

you deserve,&rquo; which is absurdly given to Coriolanus, belongs to Aufidius. For
it cannot be supposed that the other, amidst all the disorder of violent and con-

ment to the ladies. Let us further observe from this speech, where he says, &lquo;all
the swords In Italy, and her confed'rate arms,&rquo; and from that a little before,
&lquo;Let the Volscians Plough Rome, and harrow Italy,&rquo; that the poet's head was
running on the later grandeur of Rome, when, as at this time, her dominion ex-
tended only a few miles round the city.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: The speech suits Aufidius
justly enough if it had been written for him; but it may, without impropriety, be

<P><B>Scene IV.</B>] Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): Scene iv. is in Rome again, and the
audience may understand it to be so, not only from the reappearance of Menenius
on the fore-stage, but from his words as to &lquo;yon'd Coin a'th Capitol.&rquo; Whatever
part of the wall at the back of the stage or column buttressing the side served to
be pointed at thus, it was enough, apparently, imaginatively to reset the scene,
while at the same time making more graphic the speech of Menenius.&mdash;<SC>Verity</SC>
(<I>Student's Sh.</I>): Here again we have the &lquo;irony&rquo; of misplaced assurance. And the
scene illustrates the pleasant vanity of Menenius, who thinks that where <I>he</I> failed
Coriolanus's wife and mother must fail too.
<P>2. <B>Mene. See you yon'd Coin,</B> etc.] <SC>Delius</SC> (<I>Die Prosa in Sh's Dramen,</I> Jahrbuch,
v, p. 270): This conversation, where even in such an extremity Menenius is true
to his peculiar character, is held in the familiar form of prose, which is here espe-
cially incisive. With the entrance of the Messenger, who brings terrible news,
the blank-verse is resumed and then continues to the close of the play.

<P>17-24. <B>The tartnesse of his face,</B> etc.] <SC>E. Scherer</SC> (p. 48): The only thing
which can be brought against Shakespeare is at times a too sharp change&mdash;one,
so to speak, affected on the stage&mdash;in the sentiments of his characters. Aufidius,
for example, passes too quickly from hatred to sorrow when he sees Coriolanus
fall, and in <I>Richard III.</I> Anne accepts with too great ease the ring of the man on
whom she has just spit in contempt; while Elizabeth is too quick in giving her
daughter to the man who has massacred her sons. This is certainly turning the
corner too sharply, and there is a want of truth in it. I think that something
of the same kind may be said of Shakespeare's style. The language which he
puts into the mouths of his characters is not always appropriate&mdash;is sometimes
far from being appropriate&mdash;to the circumstances, even to the characters them-
selves. The poet delights too much in the expression for itself and its own sake.
He dwells on it, he lingers over it, he plays with equivalents and synonyms.
Menenius thus complains of the change which has occurred in Coriolanus, [ll.

<P>21. <B>He sits in his State</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: In a foregoing passage he was said to <I>sit
in gold.</I> The phrase &lquo;as a thing made for Alexander&rquo; means &lquo;as one made to
resemble Alexander.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;His state&rquo; means his chair of state as described
by Plutarch, &lquo;he was set in his chaire of state, with a marvellous and unspeakable
majestie.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): In my opinion these are not Shakespeare's words.
Perhaps he has written, . . . <I>as a king, great as . . .,</I> or something similar; but
the words which stand in the text seem to me almost nonsense, because I cannot
agree with Malone, who understands &lquo;state&rquo; as &lquo;a chair of state,&rquo; and consequently
must refer &lquo;thing&rquo; to &lquo;state,&rquo; so that in this case the sense would be, &lquo;He sits in
his state as in a thing . . .&rquo; [The construction here would doubtless be puzzling
to a foreigner, but scarcely any English reader could fail in understanding that
&lquo;as a thing&rquo; refers to Coriolanus and <I>not</I> to &lquo;his state.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>22. <B>as a thing made for Alexander</B>] See note by Johnson, preceding line.
<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Mr Hart supplied the following from Holland's Plinie, 1634
ed., Bk xxxiv, ch. 8, pt ii, p. 499: &lquo;But above all, he (Lysippus) got the greatest
name for making in brasse a chariot drawne with four steeds. . . . The personage
of King Alexander the Great hee likewise expressed in brasse, and many images
he made of him, beginning at the very childhood of the said Prince: and verily
the Emperor Nero was so greatly enamoured of one state image of Alexander,
that he commanded it to be gilded all over.&rquo;
<P>25. <B>Yes, mercy, if you report him truly</B>] At first sight it would seem that what
Sicinius means is, that the attribute, mercy, which belongs to a god is lacking in
Coriolanus, but from the reply of Menenius it is evident that he takes it as the
reverse, that is, If one should speak the truth about Coriolanus he is merciful.
&lquo;You report&rquo; is, I think, here general, like the French &lquo;Si on voulait dire,&rquo; but
Menenius takes it in the particular perhaps with a strong emphasis on &lquo;<I>I</I> paint
him,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Birch</SC> (p. 499) says in regard to this passage: &lquo;Thus Shakespeare
paints the characters of Coriolanus and the gods; and, whilst he thus represents
them distinctly, points out the attribute of mercy wanting in them and existing
in the man. Was not the mockery of religion partly the purpose of this play, its
judgments and punishments, and its want of pity and benevolence? Pardon to
the Romans is granted by the man, but none is provided for Coriolanus, who falls
a sacrifice to his forgiveness of injuries, the triumph of love over hate.&rquo; In the
foregoing pages I have purposely omitted many of Birch's comments on passages
in this play, which, as they bear witness to their author's utter lack of any dramatic
perception, are calculated to make the judicious grieve. Wordsworth, in his
<I>Shakespeare's Knowledge and Use of the Bible,</I> p. 114, says, in reference to this
passage: &lquo;I am inclined to think that in <I>Coriolanus</I> it is <I>purposely</I> left a doubtful
point whether mercy was an attribute of the Deity or no.&rquo; But is not Shakespeare
here referring to the gods of the Romans?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

article is here emphatic, as in V, ii, 110, 111. Compare <I>King John,</I> II, i, 396,
&lquo;Smacks it not something of the policy?&rquo;

<P>50. <B>an Arch . . . the blowne Tide</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: So in our Author's <I>Lucrece,</I>
&lquo;As through an arch the violent roaring tide Out-runs the eye that doth behold his
haste,&rquo; [ll. 1667, 1668]. &lquo;Blown&rquo; in the text is <I>swell'd.</I> So in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> &lquo;here
on her breast There is a vent of blood, and something blown,&rquo; [V, ii, 352]. The
effect of a high, or spring tide, as it is called, is so much greater than that which
the wind commonly produces that I am not convinced by the following note
that my interpretation is erroneous. Water that is subject to tides, even when
it is not accelerated by a spring tide, appears swoln, and to move with more than
ordinary rapidity when passing through the narrow strait of an arch.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>:
The &lquo;blown tide&rquo; is the tide blown, and consequently accelerated by the wind.
So in another of our author's plays, &lquo;My boat sails swiftly both with wind and
tide.&rquo; [Steevens was trusting too much to his memory, which has here played
him false&mdash;he not only did not remember the name of the play, but has grossly
misquoted a line from <I>Othello,</I> &lquo;My boat sails freely both wind and stream,&rquo; II, iii, 65.
The adjectives <I>swiftly</I> and <I>freely</I> are quite different in signification.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;
<SC>Whitelaw</SC> agrees with Steevens that &lquo;blown&rquo; means here the tide driven before
the wind; but <SC>Schmidt</SC> both in his <I>Lexicon</I> and his edition of this play adopts
Malone's interpretation <I>swoln</I> or <I>swell'd,</I> &lquo;since the wind would not have such an
effect upon water retarded by the arch of a bridge; besides, if it be not taken in
this sense, it must be readily admitted that the expression of augmented water is
here otherwise not suitable.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. S. Walker</SC> (<I>Criticisms,</I> iii, 213): Not, I imagine,
<I>driven by wind,</I> but <I>swollen,</I> as in Beaumont and Fletcher, <I>Queen of Corinth,</I> III,
i, &lquo;&mdash;my blown billows must not Strive 'gainst the shore, that should confine me.&rquo;
So &lquo;blown ambition,&rquo; <I>King Lear,</I> IV, iv, [27]; &lquo;our blown sails,&rquo; <I>Pericles,</I> V, i, [256].&mdash;
<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>: The swoln tide. Compare <I>Lear,</I> IV, iv, 27, &lquo;No blown ambition
doth our arms incite.&rquo; Shakespeare had frequently seen the tide rushing through
the narrow arches of old London Bridge, the shooting of which by the boats was
a difficult and often dangerous operation.
