<P>52. <B>Hoboyes</B>] <SC>Naylor</SC> (p. 175): This is an important musical term and occurs
about fourteen times in eight plays. It always implies a certain special impor-
tance in the music, and is generally connected with a Royal banquet, masque, or
procession. In six cases at least the direction has some special qualification&mdash;
<I>e. g.,</I> Hautboys playing <I>loud</I> music; <I>A lofty strain or two</I> to the hautboys; Trumpets
and hautboys sounded, and drums beaten all together. In <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> IV, iii,
12, Hautboys supply the supposed ominous &lquo;music in the air.&rquo; In the last of the
above examples, from <I>Coriolanus,</I> we have the extreme limit of power of this time
provided for&mdash;viz., trumpets <I>and</I> hautboys <I>and</I> drums, <I>all together.</I> It is interest-
ing to notice the wording of Menenius's description of this stage music. &lquo;The
trumpets, sackbuts, psalteries, and fifes, Tabors and cymbals.&rquo; The &lquo;sackbut&rquo;
was merely our modern slide trombone, while the rest of these instruments were
in common use in the 16<SUP>th</SUP> century, except the Psaltery, which Kircher (b. 1601)
says is the same as the Nebel of the Bible. The picture he gives is remarkably
like the dulcimers which may be seen and heard outside public houses to this very
day, <I>i. e.,</I> a small hollow chest with the strings stretched across it. An instru-
ment of this kind could be played with the fingers, like a harp, or with a plectrum
like a zither, or with two little knob-sticks, like the dulcimer. Marsennus (b. 1588)
also identifies the Psaltery with the dulcimer.
<P>53, 54. <B>The Trumpets . . . Psalteries . . . and Symboles</B>] <SC>W. A. Wright</SC>:
Shakespeare probably had in his mind the list of musical instruments mentioned in
<I>Daniel,</I> iii, 7. The word &lquo;psaltery&rquo; comes to us from the translation of the Bible,
where the Hebrew is also rendered &lquo;lute.&rquo; The Greek <I>psalterion</I> was a stringed
instrument played with both hands. &lquo;Every stringed instrument which was
played upon with the fingers of both hands, instead of by one hand and a plectrum
held in the other, came under the denomination of a psaltery&rquo; (Chappell, <I>History
of Music,</I> p. 307). In the Wicliffite Versions the word appears in the form psautrie,
sautree or sawtree, and sautrie or sawtrye; and in Chaucer's <I>Canterbury Tales,</I>
3213, we find that &lquo;hende Nicholas&rquo; had
<BQ>
&lquo;a gay sawtrye,<LB REND=RIGHT>
On which he made a-nightes melodye.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>

<P>and his companions go out to meet the ladies as they proceed through the city
homewards; but their meeting is not brought before the eyes of the audience, nor
was it necessary that it should be.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): It can hardly be doubted
that with this scene v. there is no change of scene in the usual sense of that term
with Shakespeare, and Delius is quite right in continuing this with scene iv.;
but for the sake of the line-numbering as in modern editions we have not desired
to depart from the usual division.&mdash;<SC>Herwegh</SC> (ap. <SC>Ulrici</SC>: <I>Coriolan.,</I> p. 172):
In nearly all editions of <I>Coriolanus</I> there is here marked a division of scenes with
change of locality. To us it seems much simpler that Menenius and Sicinius
on the point of departure should be overwhelmed by the triumphal entry of the
ladies, which should be set forth in the most brilliant manner possible in order to
contrast with the funeral train of the son at the close of the next scene.
<P>6, 7. <B>Vnshoot . . . Repeale him</B>] <SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 515): In Shakespeare's
account the action of Rome becomes much more dignified [than in Plutarch].
In none of the negotiations, in no chance word of citizen, tribune, or senator
is there any hint of the sentence on Coriolanus being revoked. Only when peace
is concluded does his recall follow quite naturally, as an act of gratitude, in the
burst of jubilant relief. This, too, is one of the indications of Shakespeare's feeling
for Roman greatness that we should bear in mind when elsewhere he seems to
show less sense even than Plutarch of her civic virtue.

<P><B>Scene VI.</B>] <SC>Singer</SC> (ed. ii.): The place of this scene has been hitherto marked at
Antium, but from what Aufidius says at l. 110 it must have been at Corioli.&mdash;<SC>Leo</SC>
(<I>Coriolanus</I>): Aufidius' words, &lquo;thy stolne name Coriolanus in Corioles,&rquo; may be read
in two different ways: &lquo;thy in Corioli stol'n name,&rquo; and then Antium may be right
[as the locale of this scene]; but if we read, &lquo;Dost thou think I'll grace thee in
Corioli,&rquo; then Antium must give way for Corioli, though Plutarch calls Antium
the native town of Aufidius, and the Conspirator says, &lquo;your native town,&rquo; l. 59.&mdash;
<SC>C. &amp;. M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): We believe&mdash;judging from other points
in the scene&mdash;that ll. 109, 110 do not mean, &lquo;Dost thou think I'll grace thee in
Corioli with that robbery, thy stolen name of Coriolanus?&rquo;&mdash;we believe that they
mean, &lquo;Dost thou think that <I>I'</I>ll grace thee with that robbery, thy name of
Coriolanus stolen in Corioli?&rquo; If the emphasis be thrown on &lquo;<I>I,</I>&rquo; we think the
author's intention in the sentence will be clear. The points in the scene which
make us believe that Shakespeare intended it to be laid in Antium are these:
In the first place Antium was the <I>capital</I> of the Volscian territory, Corioli only
one of the towns on its borders; therefore it was likely that the capital was the
place to which Coriolanus and Aufidius would return to render an account of their
expedition to Rome; and, accordingly, the latter begins by sending to &lquo;tell the
lords of the city,&rquo; &amp;c. When they enter they bid him &lquo;welcome <I>home</I>&rquo;<I>;</I> and we
know that Aufidius' residence was at Antium. The First Conspirator says, &lquo;<I>Your
native town</I> you enter'd like a post, and had no welcome <I>home.</I>&rquo; Coriolanus tells
the lords of the city, &lquo;We have made peace, with no less honour to the <I>Antiates</I> than
shame to the Romans&rquo;; and these very lords of the city are also here styled &lquo;heads
of the state,&rquo; which shows that they were chief rulers, rulers of the Volsces gen-
erally, and not merely city authorities belonging to any one of the Volscian towns.
Finally&mdash;and which we think conclusive, because North's <I>Plutarch</I> was evidently
the authority that Shakespeare followed throughout most closely&mdash;Plutarch
distinctly states that Marcius and Aufidius returned to <SC>Antium</SC> when they came
back from Rome.&mdash;<SC>Herwegh</SC> (ap. <SC>Ulrici</SC>: <I>Coriolan.</I>) brings forward substantially
the same reasons for accepting Antium as the locale of this scene, but says, &lquo;At
the same time we do not wish to lay any special stress on the remark of the Con-
spirator to Aufidius in regard to his entrance into his native town, since possibly
may be urged against this the remark of Volumnia, &ldquo;His wife is in Corioli.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Rolfe</SC>: We should infer from l. 138 that this scene is not in Corioli. Surely

<P>Coriolanus would not have said this, but rather &lquo;in this city here,&rquo; or to that effect;
but we believe that none of the commentators have referred to this as a reason
for not following Singer in placing this scene in Corioli. According to Plutarch
Antium should be the place.&mdash;<SC>Beeching</SC> (<I>Falcon Sh.</I>): There can be no doubt
that the scene is laid in Antium. For (1) it was from Antium that Coriolanus
received his commission, and he returns to report upon it; and (2) in l. 97 he speaks
as though the Antiates alone were involved in the war. Further, in l. 59, the scene
is called Aufidius's native town, and this was Antium. It is an additional argu-
ment that Plutarch makes him perish at Antium.&mdash;<SC>Gordon</SC>: Editors are divided
whether to place this scene in Antium or Corioli. The solution seems to me to
be this: Shakespeare meant the scene to be Antium, and wrote with Antium
in his mind until he came to Aufidius's speech, ll. 109, 110. There he was carried
away by the magnificent opportunity of placing &lquo;Coriolanus in Corioli,&rquo; and for
the rest of the scene thought rather of Corioli than of Antium.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>):
That the army should come back to a small town like Corioli seems most im-
probable, and ll. 96-98 must have been spoken in Antium, not in Corioli. There,
not the Antiates but the Volscians would have been named. Mr Gordon's solution
seems very reasonable.&mdash;<SC>Tucker Brooke</SC> (<I>Yale Sh.</I>: The text of this scene is
inconsistent in locating it first at Antium, the Volscian capital, and later at
Corioli. Professor Gordon's explanation is highly satisfactory.

<P>27, 28. <B>He watered . . . so my Friends</B>] <SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Here we are told
figuratively that Coriolanus fostered with refreshing flattery the new growths of
intimacy and ascendency arising in his favor from union with the Volscians in a
common cause. The use of &lquo;watered&rquo; is illustrated by a passage supplied by Mr
Charles Crawford from a letter from Sir Francis Bacon to Sir George Villiers,
August 12, 1616: &lquo;After that the King shall have watered your new dignities, with
the bounty of the lands which he intends you,&rquo; etc. Some, including Craig, are
confident that Aufidius wilfully misrepresents Coriolanus here, knowing well that
&lquo;He would not flatter Neptune for his trident, Or Jove for's power to thunder.&rquo;
At any rate even courtesy would seem flattery in the jealous eyes of Aufidius.

<P>41. <B>holpe to reape</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Restored,</I> p. 182), evidently misled by the
fact that the Second, Third, and Fourth Folios here read &lquo;hope&rquo; or &lquo;hop'd,&rquo; and
unfortunately not consulting the First Folio, offers as an original emendation the
present reading, &lquo;holpe.&rquo; His note on this is to the effect, that <I>hop'd</I> could not
be the reading intended by Shakespeare, which is undoubtedly true. Theobald
in his edition adopts the Folio reading without comment, doubtless having dis-
covered his error on collating the Folios. <SC>Heath</SC> (<I>Revisal,</I> p. 433) is even more
astray than was Theobald; he goes out of his way to find fault with Warburton
for his failure to credit the reading &lquo;holpe&rquo; to Theobald, and enters upon a defense
of the reading <I>hop'd,</I> &lquo;being persuaded that it is right and genuine.&rquo; As his note is,
however, merely an interpretation of a reading which has not been accepted by
any editors other than Rowe, and Pope in his ed. i, it is needless to repeat it
here.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>42. <B>Which he did end all his</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emendations,</I> p. 364): Shake-
speare is here only using a metaphor which he has often employed before, and
it is obvious from the context that for &lquo;end&rquo; we ought to read <I>ear</I> [the MS. cor-
rection], which means in its derivation, as well as in its use, to plough; therefore
when Aufidius says that he had &lquo;Holp to reap the fame Which he did <I>ear</I> all his,&rquo;
he means that Coriolanus had ploughed the ground, intending to reap a crop of
fame, which Aufidius had assisted him to harvest. The use of the word &lquo;reap&rquo;
proves what was in the mind of the poet. It is needless to enumerate the places
where Shakespeare employs the verb, to <I>ear,</I> in the sense of to plough.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC>
(ed. ii.), after quoting with approbation the foregoing MS. correction, adds: &lquo;We
are not satisfied that Shakespeare's word was not <I>in</I> instead of &lquo;end&rquo;; to <I>in</I> a
harvest is to get it in; and in <I>All's Well,</I> I, iii, 47, our poet uses both &lquo;ear&rquo; and <I>in</I>
technically, &ldquo;He that ears my land, spares my team, and gives me leave to in
the crop.&rdquo; So we might amend the passage before us thus, &ldquo;&mdash;holp to reap
the fame Which he did <I>in</I> all his&rdquo;; that is to say, &ldquo;I helped to reap the crop,
which he harvested as entirely his own.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;W. N. L. (<I>Notes &amp; Queries,</I> April 16,
1853): To <I>ear</I> is to <I>plough.</I> Aufidius complains that he had a share in the harvest,
while coriolanus took all the ploughing to himself. We have only, however, to
transpose <I>reap</I> and <I>ear,</I> and this nonsense is at once converted into excellent sense.
The old corrector blindly copied the blunder of a corrupt but not sophisticated
manuscript. This has occurred elsewhere in this collection. [The initials W. N. L.
are but a transparent disguise through which we may detect Collier's redoubtable
opponent, W. N. Lettsom. <SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vindicated,</I> p. 227) repeats substantially
the foregoing communication, duly crediting it to &lquo;a correspondent in N. &amp; Q.,&rquo;
and in his ed. ii. remarks that the reversal is also to be found on the margin of his

<P>annotated 2<SUP>nd</SUP> Folio.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Tycho Mommsen</SC> (<I>Der Perkins Folio,</I> p. 181):
Although the common reading, &lquo;end,&rquo; gives an intelligible meaning, yet it would
have been much finer to have had here some word which continued the metaphor.
Certainly <I>ear</I> does this, but on further examination the doubt arises whether <I>ear</I>
and <I>reap,</I> the former in the sense <I>to plough,</I> should not be reversed, that thus in
the original manuscript there may have been an interlineation and an erasure.
In his ed. ii. of <I>Notes &amp; Emend.</I> Collier proposes <I>inne.</I> This emendation of the
MS. corrector would then be one of the most dubious. Could <I>to ear</I> be made to
signify, as does the German <I>&auml;rndten,</I> the gathering in of the grain, then the emenda-
tion would be excellent; the reading of <I>gleaning</I> can hardly be accepted, but that of
<I>ploughing</I> is impossible. It may be urged against this meaning and reversal
(which I notice Singer also proposes) that <I>to ear</I> has for its object <I>the ground,</I> and
not <I>the corn,</I> as has <I>reap.</I>&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: Is not &lquo;end&rquo; an erratum for <I>bind?</I> So in
<I>As You Like It,</I> III, ii, 113, &lquo;They that reap must sheaf and bind.&rquo; Again, in
Beaumont &amp; Fletcher's <I>Bonduca,</I> IV, iii, &lquo;&mdash;when Rome like reapers, Sweat blood
and spirit for a glorious harvest, And bound it up, and brought it off,&rquo; [ed. Dyce,
p. 71]. And in the ancient Harvest Song, &lquo;Hooky, hooky, we have shorn And
bound what we did reap.&rquo;&mdash;W. W. [<SC>Williams</SC>] (<I>Parthenon,</I> August 16, 1862): When,
in the <I>Literary Gazette</I> of March 15, I submitted what I thought to be a new reading
of a passage in <I>Coriolanus,</I> Act V, scene vi, I was not aware that Mr Staunton had
proposed the same alteration in a note in his edition, and had confirmed it by pas-
sages from other writers. The correction occurred to me long prior to the publica-
tion of Mr Staunton's Shakespeare; but any credit that may attach to it is fairly
due to Mr Staunton as having been the first to print it. I am but too happy to
find my conjecture so satisfactorily confirmed. [It is gratifying to record such
generosity as this in those past days characterized by bitter controversy and jeal-
ousy as to priority among emendators, and we can but sigh, <I>Utinam sic omnes,</I>
etc.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Arrowsmith</SC> (<I>Editor of Notes &amp; queries, and Mr Singer,</I> p. 8): Since
when has this word [&lquo;end&rquo;] been a stumbling-block to the commentators? The
answer to the inquiry would supply a shrewd conjecturer with the means of fixing
the date of the old commentator's era. If Mr Singer's interpretation of the old
commentator's <I>ear</I> be true, if by <I>ear</I> is here meant <I>plough,</I> then is his corruption of
the text . . . open to an objection which ousts it from its usurped place in the
text altogether, either as a substitute for <I>reap</I> or for <I>end,</I> and remands it to the
shop from whence it issued. <I>Fame</I> in the passage represents the <I>crop,</I> and what-
ever be the custom in Cockneydom, we country folk do not <I>plough</I> the <I>crop,</I> but
the <I>land</I> for the crop. If this, then, be a sample of the old or any other commenta-
tor's critical acumen&mdash;if this be the process by which Shakespeare's nonsense is
to be distorted into &lquo;resplendent sense&rquo;&mdash;it is a quality and an art that working-
day men would hardly covet. Should, however, the old commentator's <I>ear</I> sig-
nify something else than <I>plough,</I> then all that is got through his corruption of the
text is <I>ignotum per ignotius,</I> and the sense, if sense there be, is very obscurely
resplendent; nor would it prove a Herculean labour to match him at his own game.
Thus, &lquo;holp to reap the fame which he did <I>inn</I> all his.&rquo; The metaphor is preserved,
the term pertinent and familiar, and the resemblance in the letters of <I>inn</I> and
<I>end</I> as close as in those of <I>end</I> and <I>ear.</I> [Arrowsmith was quite unaware that he
had been forestalled in this emendation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] To them, on the other hand, that
regard the old commentator as an authority, that imagine his readings are derived

<P>but it was after a Storme.&rquo; Cotgrave has &lquo;Engranger, To inne corne, &amp;c.; to put,

When the true word is once corrupted to &lquo;end,&rquo; of course a meaning is fitted to it,
and it is interpreted of ending or finishing the harvest. In this sense it is still
in use in Surrey, Sussex, Hallamshire, and probably elsewhere. The insertion
of &lquo;d&rquo; after a liquid is frequent in common pronunciation. Hence &lquo;vile&rquo; becomes
&lquo;vild,&rquo; and we know that Johnson gave as a proof of Mrs Pritchard's vulgarity
that she called a gown &lquo;a gownd.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Rolfe</SC>: That is, made all his own at last.
The use of &lquo;end&rquo; would not be singular, even if it had not been shown that it is a
provincial term for getting in a harvest, still used in Surrey, Sussex, and elsewhere.&mdash;
<SC>Deighton</SC>: That is, which he garnered up for himself.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): The
metaphor in <I>reap</I> is believed to be carried on in <I>end,</I> taken as a dialectal term for
getting in or stacking a crop. The <I>Eng. Dial. Dict.</I> cites Milton, <I>L'Allegro,</I> 109,
&lquo;His shadowy flail hath threshed the corn That ten day-labourers could not end.&rquo;

Aufidius helped to reap the crop, but in the end Coriolanus made it all his own.
The <I>Glossary</I> of the <I>Globe Ed.</I> says that <I>end</I> is &lquo;a corruption of <I>in</I>&rquo; (quite a com-
mon verb = &lquo;to get in the harvest&rquo;); I do not know what evidence there is to sup-
port this view.

certaine souldiours, and presently departed to Calice.&rquo; [Under 9. To pay wages to.
Bradley gives many more examples; in some of the earlier quotations the word
is spelt as here, <I>wadge.</I> The use of the word &lquo;Mercenary&rquo; here in connection with
&lquo;wadg'd&rquo; is evidently Bradley's justification for giving it this special, almost
technical, meaning.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC> quotes Johnson's interpretation, and re-

<P>Miss <SC>C. Porter</SC> (<I>First Folio Sh.</I>): An obscure word still more obscured by the
change of Rowe to &lquo;waged&rquo; [see <I>Text. Notes</I>], but which seems from the context to
mean something more pictorial in shake and thrust out of the face during vehement
and authoritative speech than the unsatisfactory <I>waged</I> of the modernising editors.
Their only explanation is &lquo;patronized,&rquo; of which they give no example. It clearly
is not the case that it here means, hire or pay wages to. [I regret that I must
here take exception to Miss Porter. In the first place, if the Folio reading is more
obscured by the modern spelling the editor of the Third Folio, not Rowe, is respon-
sible. Secondly, no modern editor, as far as I know, has interpreted &lquo;wadg'd&rquo; or
<I>wag'd</I> as <I>patronized.</I> Wright explains the whole line, &lquo;rewarded me with his pat-
ronage,&rquo; but this last word refers to &lquo;countenance,&rquo; for which use he gives two good
examples. Thus also Hunter. Thirdly, why, from the context, does the word here
clearly mean other than <I>hire,</I> or <I>pay wages?</I> At the time of Miss Porter's writing
the <I>N. E. D.</I> had not extended as far as this word, but the <I>Century Dictionary</I> records
it (s.v.&dagger;6); in fact, under its definition &lquo;to hire for wages&rquo; this very passage is quoted
in illustration.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): He gave me his patronage as wages, as if
I had been on hire. The idea that is added by Johnson in &lquo;thought me sufficiently
rewarded with good looks,&rquo; and adopted by others, has no justification in the text.
The sting is not that Coriolanus thought his favour a fair reward, but that he
should have assumed the right of patronage at all. [Case quotes the same passage
from North's <I>Plutarch</I> as that in Hunter's note <I>ante.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>84. <B>no excuse</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 462) quotes this line as an example wherein, for the
sake of rendering the metre exact, these words are to be pronounced as though
but two syllables&mdash;<I>noxcuse.</I> It is, I think, gravely to be questioned whether this
trifling gain in metrical exactness be worth the slurring of two such important
words in this accusation. Who among the auditors would detect that the line,
if uttered slowly and gravely, was prosodically defective?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>88. <B>Haile Lords,</B> etc.] <SC>A. C. Bradley</SC> (<I>Coriolanus,</I> p. 14): Since we know that
Coriolanus's nature, though the good in it has conquered, remains unchanged, and
since his rival's plan is concerted before our eyes, we await with little suspense,
almost indeed with tranquillity, the certain end. As it approaches it is felt to
be the more inevitable because the steps which lead to it are made to repeat as
exactly as possible the steps which led to his exile. His task, as then, is to excuse
himself, a task the most repugnant to his pride. Aufidius, like the Tribunes
then, knows how to render its fulfilment impossible. He hears a word of insult,
the same that he heard then&mdash;&lquo;traitor.&rquo; It is followed by a sneer at the most
sacred tears he ever shed, and a lying description of their effect on the bystanders;
and his pride and his loathing of falsehood and meanness explode, as before, in
furious speech. . . . As he turns on Aufidius the conspirators rush upon him,
and in a moment, before the vision of his glory has faded from his brain, he lies
dead. The instantaneous cessation of enormous energy (which is like nothing
else in Shakespeare) strikes us with awe, but not with pity.
<P>95. <B>a full third part</B>] For other examples of this transposition of an adverbial
expression see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 420. Compare I, i, 37.

<P>124. <B>Aufid. No more</B>] <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>: This should rather be given to the <I>first
Lord.</I> It was not the business of Aufidius to put a stop to the altercation.&mdash;
<SC>Monck Mason</SC> (<I>Comments,</I> etc., p. 48): It appears to me that by these words
Aufidius does not mean to put a stop to the altercation, but to tell Coriolanus
that he was <I>no more</I> than a &lquo;boy of tears.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.): That is, No more than
a boy of tears. But perhaps Tyrwhitt is right in supposing that these words
belonged to the <I>First Lord,</I> and in understanding them to mean <I>Have done.</I>&mdash;
<SC>C. &amp; M. Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Shakespeare</I>): Perhaps these words are meant to express,

no more than a boy of tears.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): This may mean either, enough,

also wishes at the same time to give a signal to the conspirators; or, no more than

<P>137, 138. <B>That like an Eagle . . . in Corioles</B>] <SC>M. Sherlock</SC> (p. 16): A more
just, a more noble, a more apposite comparision cannot be conceived. A lion
among heifers, a wolf among sheep; this has been said a thousand times. An
eagle among doves presents a new image. But it is more than an eagle among
doves; it is an eagle among doves in a dove-house, where the disturbance and the
terror are far greater. This image is here a characteristic stroke, it is a sentiment,
and a sentiment which can only suit that particular moment. It is to the <I>valiant,</I>
the <I>susceptible,</I> the <I>proud</I> Coriolanus that Tullus gives an affront which touches
him in the most delicate point&mdash;his military glory. Coriolanus makes a comparison
without knowing it; nor does the reader, who also takes fire, perceive it any more
than he. He only sees one line of character, which completely discovers to him
the whole Coriolanus, and a sublime sentiment, which transports his soul. . . .
The brilliant, the flowery, the light Voltaire has introduced a fashion, as it were,
of reading without attention. This magician has infused into our minds a most
pernicious idleness, and a beauty which is not superficial passes unobserved. One
of the first lords of the city speaks to Coriolanus. Coriolanus, transported with
rage, does not hear him; this is <I>one</I> beauty; he makes a violent apostrophe to the
soldiers; this is <I>another</I> beauty; and with the same fierceness, the same fury he
makes, at the same instant, another apostrophe to Tullus; and these <I>three</I> beauties,
founded in nature and in the particular character of Coriolanus, will never be
perceived by those who are accustomed to read superficially.&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.,</I> ii,
167) places these lines among his examples of apparent rhymes in Shakespeare,
remarking that it is only when the modern reading <I>Corioli</I> is used that there is any
suggestion of rhyme. See <I>Text. Notes.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>138. <B>Flatter'd</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): This is Shakespeare's own word (com-
pare the German <I>flattern</I>), not the modern word <I>fluttered,</I> the correction of later
editors.&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>, commenting on the foregoing, says: There is also the
Dutch <I>fladderen,</I> and the Swedish <I>fladra.</I> But in the absence of better evidence
for the existence of the form &lquo;flatter'd&rquo; than the spelling of the first and second
folios I have preferred the more usual form which is found as early as Spenser, and
has the support of the analogous form &lquo;floteren,&rquo; which occurs in the fourteenth
century.
<P>138. <B>in Corioles</B>] See note by <SC>Rolfe</SC> on locality of this scene, <I>ante.</I>

<P>157. <B>kils Martius</B>] <SC>MacCallum</SC> (p. 626): It is not as a martyr to retrieved patri-
otism that Coriolanus perishes, but as the victim of his own passion. In truth,
the victory he won over himself under the influence of his mother, though real,
is very incomplete. His piety to the hearth saves him from the superlative infamy
of destroying his country, which is something, and even a good deal; but it is not
everything; and beyond that it has no result, public or personal. On the contrary,
Coriolanus' isolated and but partly justified act of clemency receives its comment
from the motives that induced it, the troth-breach that accompanied it, and the
rage in which he passed away. If, like his son with the butterfly, he did grasp
honour at the close, it was disfigured by his rude handling. But at least he never
belies his own great, though mixed, nature, and it is fitting that his death, needless
but heroic, should have its cause in his nature and be such as his nature would
select. Indeed, it is both his nemesis and his guerdon. For he would not be a

<P>Roman, he could not be a Volsce; what part could he have played in the years to
come? Perhaps Shakespeare read in Philemon Holland's rendering the alter-
native account that Livy gives of the final scene: &lquo;I find in Fabius, a most ancient
writer, that he [Coriolanus] lived untill he was an old man: who repeateth this
of him: that oftentimes in his latter daies he used to utter this speech: <I>A heavie
case and most wretched, for an aged man to live banisht.</I>&rquo; At all events some such
feeling as his regrets in this variant tradition suggest makes us prefer the version
that Plutarch followed and that Shakespeare adapted. Coriolanus deserves to
be spared the woes that the future has in store. As it is, he falls in the fullness of
his power, inspired by great memories to greater audacity, and, no doubt, elated
at the thought of challenging and outbraving death, when death is sure to win.&mdash;
<SC>Stanley Wood</SC>: Poetic justice requires that Coriolanus should die in order to
make atonement for the wrongs he has committed in his life. His death has been
more than once foreshadowed, by himself and by Aufidius. Our remaining interest
is in the circumstances and in the manner of his death, and this we shall find to
be such that when his mother hears of it she shall still hear nothing of him but
what was like him formerly. His physical bravery remains with him to the last,
and as he dies at the hands of the Volscian conspirators it seems to fall as a shroud
around him.

<P>169. <B>did owe you</B>] <SC>Verity</SC> (<I>Student's Sh.</I>): Literally &lquo;possessed <I>for</I> you,&rquo; hence
&lquo;made you liable to.&rquo; [<SC>Gordon</SC> also so interprets &lquo;owe&rquo; here.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>:
That is, which while this man lived was owing to you, would sooner or later have
fallen upon you.&mdash;<SC>Case</SC> (<I>Arden Sh.</I>): Deighton puts this clearly. But for the
irresistible attraction which obsolete meanings exert upon commentators it would
be difficult to see why several make &lquo;owe&rquo; = <I>possess</I> here, with the further awk-
wardness of making &lquo;owe you&rquo; = <I>possess for you.</I> The modern meaning is, in
fact, rather the most frequent in Shakespeare, and occurs in this play, III, i, 292,
&lquo;One time will owe another.&rquo; [Deighton is unquestionably right.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>176, 177. <B>Herald Did follow to his Vrne</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: This allusion is to a
custom unknown, I believe, to the ancients, but observed in the public funerals
of English princes, at the conclusion of which a herald proclaims the style of the
deceased.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Coriolanus</I>): So in <I>Henry V:</I> I, ii, 228, &lquo;Or lay these bones
in an unworthy urn, Tombless, with no remembrance over them.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. A. Wright</SC>:
Compare also <I>Hamlet,</I> I, iv, 49, where &lquo;inurn'd&rquo; is the reading of the folios, while
the quartos have &lquo;interr'd.&rquo;
<P>178-180. <B>His owne impatience . . . the Best of it</B>] <SC>Stopford Brooke</SC> (p.
243): These lines might serve as Coriolanus's epitaph. Yet, Aufidius is not
ignoble. He can see more clearly than either patrician or plebeian what is of a
fine nature in Coriolanus. He has not been subjected as much as they to the
worry of his pride and rage. Even when he most envies Coriolanus he can make
a judgment of his character and career&mdash;as he does to the Lieutenant at the
end of Act IV.&mdash;which is at once tolerant and wise, and which in itself is a most
noble piece of poetry. It is given almost against his will, for he is as determined
as the Tribunes were to put an end to Coriolanus: &lquo;When, Caius, Rome is thine,
Thou'rt poor'st of all; then shortly thou art mine.&rquo; He has now done this work;
he has sated his hatred and envy, and thinks it politic to seem sorry for his fate.
It is not true sorrow; envy has no grief; it is only to seem noble that he says, &lquo;My
rage is gone, And I am struck with sorrow.&rquo;

<P>181. <B>My Rage is gone,</B> etc.] <SC>A. C. Bradley</SC> (<I>Coriolanus,</I> p. 16): Such an emotion
as mere disgust is out of place in a tragic close, but I confess I feel nothing but
disgust as Aufidius speaks the last words, except some indignation with the poet
who allowed him to speak them, and an unregenerate desire to see the head and
body of the speaker lying on opposite sides of the stage.&mdash;[T. A. Buckley, editor
of the Oxford translation of the <I>Ajax</I> of Sophocles (p. 284), calls attention to the
similarity between this speech of Aufidius and that of Ulysses over the dead body
of Ajax: &lquo;I wish to help bury this dead body here, to share the labor, and omit
nothing of all that is man's duty to care for in honor of the noblest of mankind,&rquo;
ll. 1377-80.]&mdash;<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.</I>): The closing speech is well put
in the mouth of Aufidius, who throughout the play has been divided between envy
and admiration of his rival.
<P>183. <B>three a'th'cheefest Souldiers, Ile be one</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: Not one of the
three, but one to assist them; he would make the fourth man. So in the con-
clusion of <I>Hamlet,</I> &lquo;Let four Captains Bear Hamlet like a soldier to the stage,&rquo;
[V, ii, 406].
<P>185. <B>Traile your steele Pikes</B>] <SC>J. W. Fortescue</SC> (<I>Sh's England,</I> vol. i, p. 116:
<I>The Army</I>): A special occasion for trailing a pike was a military funeral, a duty
which the train-bands enjoyed immensely. The classical instance of a military
funeral at St Paul's is that of Sir Philip Sidney in 1586. Shakespeare must have
witnessed more than one; and hence at the close of <I>Coriolanus</I> we find Aufidius
saying over the corpse of the hero, &lquo;Trail your steel pikes.&rquo; [In Lant's plates of
Sir Philip Sidney's Funeral, which are reproduced accompanying this description,
the pikes are shown reversed.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>188. <B>a Noble Memory</B>] That is, a noble memorial. See also IV, v, 73.
<P>189. <B>Exeunt</B>] <SC>Figgis</SC> (p. 276): As the tragedies proceed in their course a change
can be noticed coming over them, and it is <I>Macbeth</I> that makes the border-line
of distinction. In <I>Hamlet, Othello,</I> and <I>King Lear</I> the conclusions are about as
</CC>
<PB N=583>
<HE><SC>act v, sc.</SC> vi.] <I>CORIOLANUS</I> 583</HE>
<P>perplexing as they well may be. Everything ends in disorder and disaster; scarce
anything is resolved on this earth, all things, even subsidiary perplexities, being
dismissed to a further court for settlement. But in the tragedies that succeed,
<I>Antony &amp; Cleopatra</I> and <I>Coriolanus,</I> the ends are far more peaceful, owing to
the fact that they fall to more of a conclusion. They are in no way so perplexed.
In <I>Antony &amp; Cleopatra</I> the judgment beyond is plainly hinted at, and so in a
measure achieved. In <I>Coriolanus</I> the end is not one of perplexity, but one of rest:
Tullus Aufidius' words, together with something in Coriolanus that altogether
loses our patience, make the end seem something complete in itself.
<P>189, 190. <B>A dead March Sounded</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Emendations,</I> p. 365):
We have before said that the stage-directions are little added to or altered in this
play, but, at the very close, some words are subjoined which require notice; the
old printed stage-direction is: <I>Exeunt bearing the body of Martius. A dead march
sounded;</I> to which the following words are appended in manuscript&mdash;<I>whiles they
leave the stage, marching round;</I> the dead march was, therefore, continued to be
played until the whole procession had passed round the stage, in order doubtless
to render the ceremonial more distinct and impressive. This, we believe, is a
traditional practice which has ever since been continued.

<C>THE TEXT</C>
<P><SC>Knight</SC> (<I>Introd.,</I> p. 147): <I>The Tragedy of Coriolanus</I> was first printed in the
Folio collection of 1623. It is entered in the <I>Stationers' Registers</I> of that year
by the publishers of the folio as one of the copies &lquo;not formerly entered to other
men.&rquo; In this Folio edition it stands the first of the tragedies in the order of
paging; but this arrangement, as in every other case, was, in all likelihood, an
arbitrary one. The text is divided into acts and scenes, according to the modern
editions; and the stage directions are very full and precise. [After the first caption,
<I>Actus Primus, Sc&oelig;na Prima,</I> there are no scene divisions throughout the play.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>] With the exception of a few obvious typographical errors, such as invari-
ably occur even under the eye of an author when a book is printed from manu-
script, the text is wonderfully accurate.
<P><SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i.): <I>The Tragedy of Coriolanus</I> is, on the whole, well printed
for the time in the Folio of 1623; but in Act II, sc. iii. either the transcriber of
the manuscript or the compositor must have omitted a line, which Pope supplied
from conjecture (with the aid of North's <I>Plutarch</I>), and which has ever since been
received into the text, because it is absolutely necessary to the intelligibility of
the passage. [See II, iii, 259.] <SC>Ibid.</SC> (ed. ii.): It is printed in the folio with a
number of evident blunders, as pointed out in our notes.
<P><SC>R. G. White</SC>: <I>Coriolanus</I> is the worst printed play in the whole First Folio.
Every page of it is spotted with corruption. In several passages Mr Collier's
Folio of 1632 gives unwonted aid to conjecture in the restoration of the text; but
even with this help some of the confusion must be abandoned as hopeless.
<P><SC>Cambridge Edd.</SC>: The text [of <I>Coriolanus</I>] abounds with errors, due, probably,
to the carelessness or the illegibility of the transcript from which it was printed.&mdash;
<SC>E. K. Chambers</SC> (<I>Warwick Sh.: Introd.</I>): I am inclined to think that this verdict is
the true one [rather than Knight's]. Certainly an editor has to admit an unusual
number of emendations and to rearrange an unusual number of lines in this play.
<P><SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. i.): <I>The Tragedy of Coriolanus</I> stands the second in the division
of tragedies, as originally published: the acts are regularly marked, but not the
scenes; the stage-directions are remarkably full and complete; while the text,
though very well printed in the main, has perhaps a larger number of difficult
and seemingly corrupt readings than any other in the volume. Some of these
readings have hitherto baffled and nonplussed all the resources of editorial ingenuity
and learning. Several of them, however, have, we think, at length been greatly
relieved, if not entirely removed, by the help of the manuscript corrections lately
<PB N=588>
<HE>588 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>discovered by Mr Collier in a copy of the Second Folio, which presents a greater
number of valuable new readings in this play than in any other where we have
thus far consulted it.
<P><SC>G. S. Gordon</SC> (<I>Introd.,</I> p. xviii.): The text of <I>Coriolanus</I> has a bad name. It is
one of those texts which editors call corrupt. Their efforts to restore it, to recover
out of the damage done by copyists and compositors the very words which Shake-
speare wrote, have left a hundred marks on every page of the play. Their foot-
notes bristle with improvements, and altogether there is such a twisting of lines,
such changing of forms, such tossing of commas, such triumphing and groaning as
obscurities yield or win the day, that an ordinary reader begins to wonder if the
wars of the Volces have not strayed into the margin among the notes. It is to be
feared that, like some other great events, this textual battle was hatched from a
very small egg. The editors, one encouraging another, have exaggerated both their
difficulties and their exploits. Much less has been done to improve the text than
their foot-notes give out, and much less was needed than has been done. They
found the play abrupt and irregular, full of fierce rapidities of speech and cultural
dissonance of metre. They have left it, after two centuries of tidying, not yet quite
neat, but neater and tidier certainly than it ever left its author's hands. They have
been indeed &lquo;too good for it.&rquo; They scotched it and notched it. They have put a
hook into the &lquo;horn and noise of the monster&rquo; and sent him into the world tame.
Now this may be to improve the play, but it is not to correct it. Editors have
assumed too readily that they were correcting errors when they were only making
a difficult play more readable. The play is rough; but it was not meant to be
smooth. It is difficult; but it was not meant to be easy. And it is certainly not
corrupt. A corrupt text should contain corrupt passages. But there are only
three such passages in the play&mdash;I, iii, 46; I, ix, 59, 60; II, iii, 259&mdash;and the last
of these is a slip.
<P><SC>S. Lee</SC> (<I>Jefferson Press Sh.: Introd.,</I> p. 9): The Folio text of <I>Coriolanus</I> is excep-
tionally corrupt. The &lquo;copy&rquo; was obviously ill-written, although, from the fulness
of the stage-directions, it may be inferred that it was a transcript which belonged
to the theatrical manager. Despite the efforts of textual critics, several passages
remain barely intelligible.

<SHL>
<C>COLLIER'S <I>TRILOGY</I></C>
<P>[J. P. Collier printed for distribution among his private friends in 1874 a
treatise in three parts entitled &lquo;Trilogy&rquo;; it was cast in the form of Conversation
between himself and two other fictitious characters on the subject of the MS.
Emendations in his Folio of 1632 and the treatment accorded these corrections
by recent editors. In his Preface he says: &lquo;If the asperity of the notes and criti-
cisms of my adversaries have here and there tinged my style, or led me astray
from the narrow line of mere vindication, I am heartily sorry for it.&rquo; This refers
to the sharp attacks made on him by Dyce and Singer. The many MS. corrections
in <I>Coriolanus</I> form the subject of one of the Conversations, and for that reason
alone I have thought it of interest to include this ensuing extract in the discussion
on the text of this Tragedy.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P><S>Alton.</S> It is now more than a quarter of a century since you bought from
Rodd, the bookseller, the corrected copy of the Folio Shakespeare dated 1632;
and about twenty years since you published your volume of &lquo;Notes and Emenda-
tions&rquo; derived from it. Have you since had any reason to doubt their genuineness,
or to alter your opinion of their value?
<P><S>Collier.</S> None to doubt their genuineness, but some for altering my opinion
as to the value of a few of the manuscript emendations. In my joy at my dis-
covery I was here and there disposed to give some of the proposed changes an
importance and a value which I now think does not really belong to them.
<PB N=590>
<HE>590 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P><S>Newman.</S> I am not at all surprised at that: it was natural, and to be expected;
but, surely, as to the great majority of them, and especially of those affecting the
sense of remarkable passages in the text, you have not altered the opinion in some
cases so emphatically expressed in your volume of &lquo;Notes and Emendations&rquo;
published in 1853.
<P><S>Collier.</S> Certainly not. I am more than ever confirmed in my judgment as
to the value of a good many of them, if only by the use which subsequent editors of
Shakespeare have made of them.
<P><S>Newman.</S> True; not a small number of the emendations have found their
way into the text of, I think, all impressions of Shakespeare since the year 1853.
<P><S>Alton.</S> But some of them have been most violently resisted; and all sorts of
injurious epithets applied to them, and even to yourself personally.
<P><S>Newman.</S> But the changes have been adopted nevertheless, so that they can
never again be excluded; they are now admitted to be the true language of the poet.
<P><S>Collier.</S> Seeing how my volume of &lquo;Notes and Emendations&rquo; has been treated,
some editors and would-be editors inveighing furiously, and without common
decency, against them, and yet after all most grudgingly admitting them, I have
sometimes thought that my better course would have been, first to print the
changes as mere suggestions on my part, and then afterwards to produce my old
corrected copy of the Folio 1632 in the justification.
<P><S>Newman.</S> Or better still: if you had condescended to play the rogue, you
might have produced, as your own, all the indisputable improvements of Shake-
speare's text&mdash;improvements that now are sanctioned by the approbation of
everybody, readers or rival editors; and having thus been acknowledged as the
most gifted speculative annotator that ever existed, you might have destroyed
your corrected copy of the Folio 1632, and left your enemies to wonder how it had
happened that you alone had guessed at what, beyond all cavil, was the true
language of our great dramatist in some of his most notorious and admired
passages.
<P><S>Alton.</S> Such, for instance, as which?
<P><S>Newman.</S> Well, I hardly know where to choose; but take the grand speech in
&lquo;Coriolanus&rquo; (Act III, sc. i.), where the hero is furiously blaming the patricians
for yielding to the claims of the plebeians by giving them the contents of the
public granaries:
<BQ>
&lquo;Well, what then?<LB REND=RIGHT>
How shall this bisson multitude digest<LB>
The Senate's courtesy?&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The words &lquo;bosom multiplied&rquo; instead of bisson multitude (as the text must now
forever stand) have puzzled every editor of Shakespeare from the time of Rowe
to our own day; even Theobald was obliged to reprint &lquo;bosom multiplied&rquo; without
an attempted change; later endeavours, such as that of Malone, to explain &lquo;bosom
multiplied&rquo; as bosom multitudinous, have utterly failed; but the old Corrector of
the Folio 1632 puts the passage right at once, and shows that bosom was a mis-
print for &lquo;bisson&rquo; (the old word for blind), and multiplied a misprint for &lquo;multi-
tude.&rquo; The passage can never again be printed in any other words than those
substituted in his margin by the old Corrector of the Folio 1632.
<P><S>Alton.</S> They certainly cannot be disputed; and you will see that Dyce (VI,
255, edit. 1864), without hesitation, calls it &lquo;an excellent emendation.&rquo; Singer,
too, says it is &lquo;happy,&rquo; and there can be no doubt about it.
<PB N=591>
<HE><I>COLLIER'S TRILOGY</I> 591</HE>
<P><S>Collier.</S> Singer so often inserts in his text important changes of the kind with-
out acknowledgment that his avowed consent to accept &lquo;bisson multitude&rquo; is
perhaps the more remarkable. However, we can hardly consider him in the rank
of an independent editor. It is quite certain that &lquo;bosom multiplied&rquo; will never
again make its appearance in any impression of Shakespeare to the end of time.
<P><S>Newman.</S> I only produce it as a short and decisive proof of, I may say, the
inestimable value of some of the changes in the corrected Folio 1632, in answer
to Alton's demand for an instance.
<P><S>Alton.</S> I admit the answer; and, were it wanted, we might confirm it by another
authority, if we may so call it. Of course you know what is entitled &lquo;the Globe
Edition of the Works of Shakespeare,&rquo; of which it is generally said that twenty or
even thirty thousand copies have been sold; and we need not wonder at it, con-
sidering its beauty and extraordinary cheapness: there we see &lquo;bisson multitude&rquo;
given as if it had always been Shakespeare's text, and &lquo;bosom multiplied&rquo; never
heard of, though it had been invariably printed &lquo;bosom multiplied&rquo; during the
course of two hundred and fifty years.
<P><S>Newman.</S> I have not till now seen, though I have heard of, the &lquo;Globe Shake-
peare.&rquo; Do they not give any information that the old reading was bosom mul-
tiplied, and the new reading &lquo;bisson multitude&rquo;?
<P><S>Alton.</S> Nothing of the sort; and it is the more surprising because they state
in the preface that they mark by an &lquo;obelus&rquo; (&dagger;) such corrections as they intro-
duce in the text of the poet as it has been usually handed down to us. They some-
times keep their word in this particular, but by no means always; and only two
lines above that in which &lquo;bisson multitude&rquo; occurs they very properly alter
native to &lquo;motive,&rquo; yet give no hint of the change. This looks unfair, though I
dare say it was not meant so; but recollecting the enormous sale of &lquo;the Globe
Edition,&rquo; it was the more important that this and other emendations should be
clearly distinguished; we could not expect them to state that &lquo;bisson multitude&rquo;
was derived from &lquo;Mr Collier's corrected Folio 1632,&rquo; but they ought to have in-
formed the reader by the obelus that it was a new reading.
<P>(Part iii, p. 11) <S>Newman.</S> There are many trifling points adverted to by various
editors that might be passed over entirely or, at all events, dismissed summarily.
Dyce has no fewer than 257 notes upon this drama, occupying nearly forty closely
printed pages, at least two-thirds of which might have been advantageously
omitted; and why are we to waste time upon them?
<P><S>Collier.</S> And many of them are beyond the pale of our inquiry; we ought to
limit ourselves to those notes only which illustrate the manner in, and the extent
to, which he, in particular, has been indebted to the old Corrector of my Folio 1632.
<P><S>Newman.</S> There are scores of places in his notes on &lquo;Coriolanus&rquo; where Dyce
has been compelled to mention and quote that surprising and, to many, unwelcome
volume.
<P><S>Alton.</S> And of not a few of those we need say nothing, but, on the other hand,
there are nearly twenty places in which he has most unwillingly been driven to
admit his obligations to the old Corrector, having actually derived his text from
him, and from him only. In all those instances, and on that authority merely, he
has made his edition different from any that preceded it, excepting always your own.
<P><S>Newman.</S> How often does he not say &lquo;I here give the text of Mr Collier's
MS. Corrector&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;So Mr Collier's MS. Corrector&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;I adopt the reading of Mr
Collier's MS. Corrector&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;This is the excellent emendation of Mr Collier's MS.
Corrector,&rquo; etc.
<PB N=592>
<HE>592 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P><S>Collier.</S> Besides the numerous places where he couples the old Corrector with
Hanmer, Mason, Ritson, Capell, and others, always taking care to put the Cor-
rector last, as if in truth they had all preceded him and he was merely a follower.
This is a course unworthy of Dyce, who had previously admitted, incautiously
perhaps, that the MS. Corrector had &lquo;lived long before&rquo; Pope, Theobald, Capell,
or any of the modern commentators.
<P><S>Alton.</S> Dismissing that really trifling matter, let us look at the first emenda-
tion, of any importance, that he derived from your corrected folio.
<P><S>Collier.</S> Just turn to Act I, sc. iii, and to the words &lquo;at Grecian swords con-
temning.&rquo; So I printed it conjecturally in my first edition of 1844, but Dyce, in
his first edition of 1857, at once refused &lquo;contemning&rquo; and printed contending from
the Second Folio, quoting in his support a writer in &lquo;Blackwood's Magazine.&rquo; But
what did he do in his second edition of 1864? He saw that I persevered in favour
of &lquo;contemning,&rquo; and that it was the emendation of the old Corrector of my Folio
1632, and on that authority alone, in his own teeth and in spite of Blackwood, he
adopted &lquo;contemning,&rquo; adding, fairly enough, the real source of the emendation.
<P><S>Newman.</S> A remarkable instance of his absolute reliance upon that book which
has been the source of so many other improvements.
<P><S>Alton.</S> But you had preferred &lquo;contemning&rquo; ten years before you discovered
it in your contemned and despised corrected folio, 1632. Now it must be the
text as long as Shakespeare is admired and reprinted; even the Globe Shakespeare
adopts the word, tho' as usual, and consistently with its plan perhaps, it gives no
notice of the improvement, or of the cause of it.

<P><S>Newman.</S> Then this brings us to Act II, sc. i, where in the speech of Menenius

<P><S>Collier.</S> For this correction I would willingly rely upon the common sense of

<P>in favouring the thirst complaint.&rquo; Only substitute first for &lquo;thirst&rquo; and what

Tarlton's &lquo;Tragical Discourses,&rquo; 1567, Fo. 135, he speaks of &lquo;glutting the lascivious

<P><S>Alton.</S> Surely we may dispense with other proofs not merely because those

other people. As to &lquo;the thirst complaint&rquo; there cannot be a doubt.
<P><S>Alton.</S> So I say of &lquo;empyric phisique,&rquo; often spelt so of old, while the com-

<P><S>Newman.</S> Next we come to &lquo;the napless vesture of humility,&rquo; printed in the

<P><S>Alton.</S> Which may, however, properly introduce us to the &lquo;woolvish tongue,&rquo; as

There can be no doubt, however, that tongue must be read togue or toge, <I>i. e.,</I>

<P><S>Collier.</S> Johnson tells us that it means hirsute, and Steevens says a great deal

<P><S>Collier.</S> That, I take it, is quite certain. And now we may go on, without

<P><S>Newman.</S> Yes, something more must be done; for &lquo;impotence&rquo; must be sub-

<SHL>
<C>DATE OF COMPOSITION</C>
<P><SC>Malone</SC> in his first edition of <I>The Chronological Order of Shakespeare's Plays,</I>
which was given in the prefatory matter in vol. i. of the <I>Variorum</I> of 1778, assigns
<I>Coriolanus</I> to the year 1609, and thus it appears also in his own edition of 1790.
Malone gives for this arbitrary date no reasons other than, that as the other
plays derived from Plutarch are assignable to the years between 1607 and 1609,
<I>Coriolanus</I> naturally follows <I>Julius C&aelig;sar</I> and <I>Antony &amp; Cleopatra.</I> In his final
revision of the list which appears in the <I>Variorum</I> of 1821 Malone advances the
date one year and assigns <I>Coriolanus</I> to 1610. Abandoning his former reasons
<PB N=596>
<HE>596 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>for accepting 1609 as the date of composition he says: &lquo;Cominius, in his panegyric
which he pronounces on Coriolanus, says:
<BQ>
&ldquo;He <I>lurch'd</I> all swords <I>of the garland.</I>&rdquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>In Ben Jonson's <I>Silent Woman,</I> Act V, Sc. last, we find (as Mr Steevens has ob-
served) the same phraseology: &ldquo;You have <I>lurch'd</I> your friends of the better half
<I>of the garland.</I>&rdquo; I formerly thought this a sneer at Shakespeare; but have lately
met with nearly the same phrase in a pamphlet by Thomas Nashe, and suppose it
to have been a common phrase of the time.<SUP>*</SUP> [See note by Malone, II, ii, 113.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>] This play is ascertained to have been written after the publication of
Camden's <I>Remaines,</I> in 1605, by a speech of Menenius in the first Act, in which
he endeavors to convince the seditious populace of their unreasonableness by
the well-known apologue of the members of the body rebelling against the belly.
This tale Shakespeare certainly found in the <I>Life of Coriolanus</I> as translated by
North, and in general he has followed it as there given; but the same tale is also
told of Adrian the Fourth by Camden in his <I>Remaines,</I> p. 199, under the head of
<I>Wise Speeches,</I> with more particularity; and one or two of the expressions, as well
as the enumeration of the functions by each of the members of the body, appear
to have been taken from that book.
<P>In Camden the tale runs thus: &ldquo;All the members of the body conspired against
the stomach, as against the swallowing gulfe of all their labours; for whereas the
eies beheld, the eares heard, the handes laboured, the feete travelled, the tongue
spake, and all partes performed their functions; onely the stomache lay ydle and
consumed all. Hereuppon they joyntly agreed al to forbeare their lazie and
publike enemy. One day passed over, the second followed very tedious, but the
third day was so grievious to them all, that they called a common counsel. The
eyes waxed dimme, the feete could not support the body; the armes waxed lazie,
the tongue faltered, and could not lay open the matter. Therefore they all with
one accord desired the advice of the heart. There Reason layd open before
them,&rdquo; &amp;c.
<P>The heart is called by one of the citizens, &ldquo;the counsellor-heart&rdquo;; and in making
the counsellor-heart the seat of the brain or understanding, where Reason sits
enthroned, Shakespeare has certainly followed Camden.
<P>The late date which I have assigned to <I>Coriolanus</I> derives likewise some sup-
port from Volumnia's exhortation to her son, whom she advises to address the
Roman people&mdash;
<BQ>
&ldquo;&mdash;now humble as the ripest mulberry.<LB REND=RIGHT>
Which cannot bear the handling.&rdquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>In a preceding page I have observed that mulberries were not much known in
England before the year 1609. Some few mulberry-trees, however, had been
brought from France and planted before that period, and Shakespeare, we find,
had seen some of the fruit in a state of maturity before he wrote <I>Coriolanus.</I>&rquo;
<FHL>
<NOTE>* <SC>W. A. Wright</SC> (<I>Clarendon Preface; Sh.,</I> p. ix.): But in Nashe there is only
the word &lquo;lurch,&rquo; which is of frequent occurrence, and the combination of this
with &lquo;the garland&rquo; by Ben Jonson seems to me to indicate that he had Shakespeare's
phrase in mind, whether he intended to sneer at it or not, and I am therefore
inclined to attach to the coincidence more weight than Malone felt himself justified
in doing.</NOTE>

<HE><I>DATE OF COMPOSITION&mdash;HURDIS&mdash;CHALMERS</I> 597</HE>
<P><SC>Hurdis</SC> (p. 38): I cannot agree with Mr Malone in ranking <I>Timon of Athens,
Antony and Cleopatra,</I> and <I>Coriolanus</I> among the later productions of our author.
Of <I>Antony and Cleopatra</I> I have already declared it to be my opinion that it was
a very early performance, and I make no doubt but that <I>Coriolanus</I> was written
soon after it. For though Dr Johnson has with great truth observed that the
latter is a very amusing play, and embellished with great diversity of character,
yet is it accompanied with a multitude of metrical faults almost equal in number
to those of <I>Antony and Cleopatra.</I> The lines are always those of a young poet
who is scarce a master of numbers, and are often made up in a manner which to
a musical ear is ridiculous and disgusting. It was probably written a short time
before <I>Timon of Athens,</I> since both these pieces abound in faults of the same com-
plexion. There is in both an unskilful and sometimes a laughable confusion of
British with Roman and Athenian customs, many anachronisms, many broken
and ill managed lines, and a dissolute mixture of verse and prose. Add to this
that the proper names in <I>Coriolanus</I> are often introduced in a manner truly awk-
ward and bungling. It is nevertheless a performance of considerable merit.
It has passages of true sublimity and poetical excellence; and here and there
surprises us with a few of those delicate touches of nature by which the author
renders himself so irresistible in his appeal to the heart. <I>Timon of Athens</I> takes
place of it only as being a piece more correct in its metre and abounding more in
observations drawn from nature.
<P><SC>G. Chalmers</SC> (<I>Supplemental Apology,</I> p. 434): This Tragedy, which is said by
Johnson to be one of the most amusing of our author's performances, was neither
entered in the Stationers' Registers nor printed till the publication of the First
Folio, in 1623. The writing of <I>Coriolanus</I> has been assigned, though with a hesi-
tating tone, to the year 1610. Mr Malone seems to have proved, with some
acuteness, indeed, that the speech of Menenius, in the first act, whereby he endeav-
ored to convince the seditious populace of the unreasonableness of their clamours,
on the account of the scarcity, by the apologue of the several members of the body
rebelling against the belly, was copied from Camden's <I>Remains</I> rather than from
North's <I>Plutarch.</I> Yet, this proof goes only the length of showing, that as Camden's
work was published in 1605, Shakspeare must have written his <I>Coriolanus</I> sub-
sequent to that publication; we are still left to enquire, even admitting this proof
in its full extent, for the particular year.
<P><I>Coriolanus</I> opens with the entry of a company of mutinous citizens, who are
&lquo;all resolved rather to die than to famish.&rquo; Caius Marcius, being deemed by
them the chief enemy of the people, is, by a general verdict, sentenced, tumultu-
ously, to death; the first citizen crying out: &lquo;Let us kill&rquo; him; and we'll have corn
enough, at our &lquo;own price.&rquo; Menenius, when he came to speak to the citizens,
remarks:
<BQ>
&lquo;&mdash;For your wants;<LB>
Your suffering in this dearth, you may as well<LB>
Strike at the Heaven with your staves, as lift them<LB>
Against the Roman state:<LB>
&mdash;For the dearth,<LB>
The Gods, not the patricians, make it.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The dearth is afterwards acknowledged, in the senate-house, to be great. Now,
the fact is, that the years 1608 and 1609 were times of great dearth; though the
<PB N=598>
<HE>598 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>first was a year of greater dearth than the last.<SUP>*</SUP> King James, on account of the
high prices of provisions, issued a proclamation against monopolists in 1608.<SUP>&dagger;</SUP>
It is said, in Raleigh's <I>Remains,</I> that two millions sterling were sent out during
those two dear years for the importation of corn. The tragedy turns upon the
existing dearth. And, therefore, the play was probably written in 1609, while the
pressure was yet felt.
<P>Mr Malone tries, indeed, to support his own epoch of the year 1610 by saying
that mulberry trees were not much known in England before the year 1609; Mr
Steevens has some doubt, with regard to this position, about the mulberries. But
the books upon horticulture, which were published during the reign of Elizabeth,
had made the mulberry tree sufficiently familiar to our poets of every kind. Among
several elegies on Sir Philip Sydney there is a pretty poem, by Mathew Roydon,
which was published in <I>The Ph&oelig;nix Nest,</I> in 1503, and which speaks of&mdash;
<BQ>
&lquo;Alcides speckled poplar tree,<LB>
The palme that monarchs do obtain,<LB>
With love juice stain'd the Mulberie,<LB>
The fruit that dews the poet's braine,<LB>
And Phillis philbert there away,<LB>
Compar'd with myrtle and the bay.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The fact, however, is that King James, in order to encourage the breeding of
silk worms, sent circular letters all over England, in 1609, to incite the inhabitants
to plant the mulberry tree. These letters, probably, induced Shakspeare, while he
was writing his <I>Coriolanus,</I> to draw a comparison, from what was already known
to graffers, and to poets:
<BQ>
&lquo;Now humble, as the ripest mulberry.<LB>
That will not hold the handling.&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P><SC>Coleridge</SC> in his attempts at classification of the Plays limits these merely to
periods without assigning any definite dates. In his earliest list, 1802, the Roman
Plays are given under one head following <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> and preceding <I>King John</I>
in the Fifth, or last, Epoch. In his later Classification, 1819, <I>Coriolanus</I> is again
assigned to the Last Epoch, &lquo;when the energies of intellect in the cycle of genius
were, though in a rich and more potentiated form, becoming predominant over
passion and creative self-manifestation.&rquo; In the Plays of this period Coleridge
places <I>Coriolanus</I> third in order, preceded by <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> and <I>Timon,</I> and
followed by <I>Jul. C&aelig;s., Ant. &amp; Cleo.,</I> and <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> He concludes with this
remark: &lquo;Merciful, wonder-making Heaven! What a man was this Shakespere!
Myriad-minded, indeed, he was!&rquo;
<P><SC>Drake</SC> places <I>Coriolanus</I> No. 31 in his list of thirty-five plays following <I>Ant. &amp;
Cleo.</I> and preceding <I>Winter's Tale,</I> with the date 1609.
<P><SC>Knight</SC>: We state, unhesitatingly, that there is no internal evidence what-
ever for the dates of any of the three Roman plays. We believe that they belong
to the same cycle; but we would place that later in Shakspere's life than is ordinarily
done. Malone places them together, properly enough; but in assuming that they
<FHL>
<NOTE>* Combrune's Chron. Prices, p. 38. There was an insurrection, in Northamp-
tonshire, on account of inclosures, in May, 1607.</NOTE>
<NOTE>&dagger; Ib., 39.</NOTE>
<PB N=599>
<HE><I>DATE OF COMPOSITION&mdash;COLLIER&mdash;WHITE</I> 599</HE>
<P>were written in 1607, 1608, and 1609 his theory makes Shakspere almost absolutely
unemployed for the last seven years of his life. We hold that his last years were
devoted to these plays. The proof which Chalmers offers that <I>Coriolanus</I> was
written in 1609 is one of the many ingenious absurdities with which he has sur-
rounded the question of the chronological order of Shakspere's plays. The citizens,
he says, are resolved rather to die than to famish&mdash;they require corn cheap; there
is a dearth. He adds, very gravely, &lquo;Now the fact is, that the years 1608 and 1609
were times of great dearth. . . . And therefore the play was probably written in
1609 while the pressure was yet felt.&rquo; We say, now the fact is, the original story
turns upon the dearth. In North's <I>Plutarch</I> we have the causes assigned &lquo;which
made the extreme dearth&rquo;; and Plutarch also tells us there was great scarcity of
corn within the city. If Shakspere found the dearth in the original story, what
could the dearth of 1608 possibly have to do with the mode in which he drama-
tized it?
<P><SC>Collier</SC>: Malone supposed that <I>Coriolanus</I> was written in 1610; but we are
destitute of all evidence on the point beyond what may be derived from the style
of composition; this would certainly induce us to fix it somewhat late in the career
of our great dramatist.
<P><SC>Delius</SC>: The several passages in this play which are difficult of explanation
are not so much so on account of misprints, although these are not lacking, as on
account of the involved and elliptical style, which is characteristic of Shakespeare's
last period. And to this period, which begins about the year 1608, <I>Coriolanus</I>
undoubtedly belongs; and while no definite year is furnished us by any notice
of a representation of the tragedy during Shakespeare's lifetime, the composition
itself allows us to allot only an approximate date.
<P><SC>Lloyd</SC> (ap. <SC>Singer</SC> ii, p. 478): Malone points out that the Apologue of Shake-
speare's Menenius bears as evident traces of obligations to <I>Camden's Remains
concerning Great Britain,</I> &amp;c., as to North's <I>Plutarch.</I> If this be so, it fixes the
date of the play at least after 1605, which is in every way probable&mdash;more so, I
think, than that the coincidences are due to Camden's memory of the play.
<P>It is with regret that I pass from the question of the date of the play with so
unsatisfying result, but as matters stand there is no help for it. Not alone the
excellence of the play in itself renders it desirable to fix it to a year, but from the
subject matter of it there would be great interest and instruction in knowing pre-
cisely the current page of contemporary history that was open before the dramatist
when he embodied in living action this illustration of the virtues and the vices that
are shared and contrasted in the factions of the many and the few.
<P><SC>Gervinus</SC> (p. 746): We have no certain external means of settling the date of
<I>Coriolanus,</I> but the style, and a few expressions and passages which recall con-
temporary plays, allow of a few conjectures, and these almost all combine to place
the piece about the year 1610.
<P><SC>R. G. White</SC>: This play first appeared in the folio of 1623; and as no mention
of it at an earlier date is known, and it is without allusions to contemporary
matters, the period of its production cannot be determined with any approach of
accuracy. Its style, however, clearly shows that it is the fruit of Shakespeare's
later years. It was probably written after 1610.

<HE>600 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P><SC>Hudson</SC>: As to the date of the writing of <I>Coriolanus</I> we have no external evi-
dence whatsoever. The internal evidence of metre, diction, and temper refers it
to the Poet's latest period of composition. In all the qualities of style and versi-
fication it clearly falls into the same class with <I>The Tempest, The Winter's Tale,</I>
and <I>King Henry VIII.</I> in being as nearly like them as the difference of the subject-
matter would readily admit. Malone, accordingly, assigns the year 1610 as the
probable date of the writing. We should be strongly inclined to place it some
three or four years later, partly from the ease and texture of the workmanship
itself, and partly from the tradition that Shakespeare continued to write for the
stage after his retirement to Stratford. The most, however, that we can affirm
with any great degree of confidence is that <I>Coriolanus</I> was written somewhere
between 1610 and the time of the Poet's death, which, as every reader ought to
know, took place in April, 1616.
<P><SC>Furnivall</SC> and <SC>Halliwell-Phillipps</SC> (<I>New Sh. Trans.,</I> 1874, p. 367): Mr

Phillipps&mdash;had long promist me a Letter on the date of the Roman Plays. But

<P>Neither Mr Halliwell nor I have any desire to special-plead the point, or to
strain the evidence beyond the presumption for the late date of <I>Coriolanus</I> that
it justifies.
<P>Professor <SC>J. R. Ingram's</SC> table of the numbers of the light and weak endings
in the Plays (<I>New Sh. Soc. Trans.,</I> p. 450) yields the following results:
<P>1. During the first three-fourths (or thereabouts) of Shakspere's poetic life
he used the light endings very sparingly, and the weak endings scarcely at all.
<P>2. The last fourth (or thereabouts) is obviously and unmistakably distinguished
from the earlier stages by the very great increases of the number of light endings,
and, still more, by the first appearance in any appreciable number, and afterwards
the steady growth, of the weak endings.
<P>3. Hence, in any discrimination of periods which is founded on metrical con-
sideration, this last may be called the &lquo;weak-ending Period.&rquo;
<P>In this tabular list <I>Coriolanus</I> stands No. 27, with these percentages: Light
endings, 2.34; Weak endings, 1.71; percentage of both, 4.05; following <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I>
and preceding <I>Pericles</I> (Sh's part); <I>Tempest; Cymbeline,</I> and <I>Winter's Tale.</I>
<P><SC>Fleay</SC> (<I>Sh. Manual,</I> p. 52): <I>Coriolanus</I> is usually dated 1609-10; I prefer 1609.
Menenius' fable (Act I, sc. i.) is taken from Camden's <I>Remaines</I> (1605), and not
from North's <I>Plutarch.</I> The play must have been written before 1612 for this
reason; Mr Halliwell has found that in every edition of North's <I>Plutarch</I> up to
1603 &lquo;unfortunately&rquo; is printed for &lquo;unfortunate&rquo; in the passage corresponding to
Act V, sc. i, l. 98. This is an evident misprint, as it spoils the meaning. Shake-
speare corrected it, and wrote &lquo;unfortunate,&rquo; which was adopted in the 1612 edition
of North's <I>Plutarch.</I> As to Shakespeare's own copy being the one in the Greenock
library dated 1612, if it was so, he must have used another. He did not write
<I>Julius C&aelig;sar</I> after that date. [This is, substantially, Fleay's opinion as given in
his <I>Introduction to Sh. Study,</I> published the following year, but in his <I>Sh's Life,
Art, and Work</I> issued four years later the date for this play is given as 1608, with no
reasons or grounds for this change.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P><SC>Brandes</SC> (ii, p. 231) takes exception to the use of a word being applied by

<HE><I>DATE OF COMPOSITION&mdash;DOWDEN&mdash;WRIGHT</I> 603</HE>
<P>We have, therefore, no occasion to abandon 1608 on that ground, and we have
certainly no need to do so for the sake of a fanciful approximation of the position
of Coriolanus to that of James at the dissolution of Parliament in 1614.
<P>Thus much, at any rate, can be declared with absolute certainty, that the anti-
democractic spirit and passion of the play sprang from no momentary political
situation, but from Shakespeare's heart of hearts. We have watched its growth
with the passing of years. A detestation of the mob, a positive hatred of the mass
as mass, can be traced in the faltering efforts of his early youth. We may see its
workings in what is undoubtedly Shakespeare's own description of Jack Cade's
rebellion in the Second Part of <I>Henry VI.,</I> and we divine it again in the conspicuous
absence of all allusion to Magna Charta displayed in <I>King John.</I>&rquo;
<P><SC>Dowden</SC> (<I>Sh. Primer,</I> p. 140): <I>Coriolanus</I> was written about 1608, as appears
from the metrical characteristics. The light-ending test puts it next after <I>Antony
and Cleopatra,</I> and it is probable that such is its actual place in the chronological
order.
<P><SC>Stokes</SC> (p. 149): We must allow for considerable change and growth of mind
before Shakespeare would choose such a story as this, and treat it in the way he
has treated it; that an interval should be allowed between, say, the emotional
phases of Antony and the peculiar mental attitude of Coriolanus; and so with
regard to minor characters, for instance, between the feeble and pompous gar-
rulity of Polonius and the sarcastic wit and shrewd good sense of Menenius. Again,
the fact that there is no entry of it on the <I>Stationers' Register,</I> coupled with the
circumstance that after 1609 no entry (with the single exception of <I>Othello</I> in 1621)
of any of Shakespeare's plays occurs, favours a date later than 1609; while I can-
not but think, comparing the position of <I>The Tempest</I> (also late) in the arrange-
ment of the comedies in the First Folio, with that of <I>Coriolanus</I> at the beginning of
the tragedies, that this arrangement was due to the fact that each of these plays
had been produced late in Shakespeare's writing days. These facts, and the pecu-
liar diction alluded to above, lead me to date the drama at least as late as 1610.
<P><SC>W. A. Wright</SC> (<I>Clarendon Sh.,</I> p. v.): In the Register of the Stationers' Com-
pany for Nov. 8, 1623, <I>Coriolanus</I> is enumerated as one of sixteen plays of which
copies had not been formerly entered to other men. Of the date of its composi-
tion nothing is known. It is conjectured that it may have been written from about
1608 to 1610, and although the evidence is not sufficiently strong for any positive
conclusion, it appears that these limits represent with sufficient accuracy the time
to which the play belongs, corresponding roughly to the close of the third period
in Shakespeare's career of authorship. Malone, in his essay on the &lquo;Chronological
Order of Shakespeare's Plays,&rquo; assigned <I>Coriolanus</I> to the year 1610, but in his
notes to the play itself he puts it to 1609. He seems to have been guided to the
latter date by a theory that mulberries were not much known in England before
1609, and that therefore the comparison in III, ii, 98, 99, to
<BQ>
&lquo;The ripest mulberry<LB>
That will not hold the handling,&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>could not have been written previously to that date. But Shakespeare was familiar
with mulberries at least fifteen years before, as is evident by the mention of them
in <I>Venus and Adonis,</I> 1103, and <I>Midsummer Night's Dream,</I> III, i, 170; and a refer-
